units.la: SEPTENNIVM nunc est, inclyte & generosissime Comes, Domine clementissime, nobilissimi amplissimiq; Ordines, cum huc venit Franciscus Petitaeus Bethuniensis, historiam meditans confoederatarum regionum in hac Germania inferiore, & materiam conquirens, meq; tum precibus suis, tum aliorum intercessione perpulit, ut summatim de statu rerum provinciae huius aliquid conjicerem in chartā, quod cederet in usum historiae ipsius. Sed erat id, quod tum effluxit mihi festinanti, & alijs curis occupato, rude & imperfectu, ac magi [?] sylva quadam congesta tumultuarie, quàm opus digestum formatumque. Deinde quum acciperem, plerosq; opinari, Petitum propositi sui naufragium factu-rum, intereaq; diligentius expensare in eâ sententiam adducerer, non parum è dignitate provinciæ hujus futurum, & ad historiæ nostratus universæ cognitionem non exiguam lucem allaturum, si huj uscemodi σύν-ταγμα in publico extaret, resumpsi sylvulam illam in manus, adjeciq; multa, mutavi, interpolavi, redegi omnia in ordinem, deniq; id effeci, ut formam aliquam operis habe-rent, & cum commodum esset, emitti [?] in publicum possent. Forma dictionis usus sum quàm maximè vulgari & simplice, & ad statum rerum præsentium significandum accommodato atque inflexo, ut res ab omnibus latini sermonis cognitione vel leviter imbutis facilius ac planius intelligi queant: confultoq; omni cultu abstinui, præsertim in materia, quæ per se haud facile cultus capax est. Nam præter enumerationem locorum, ac situs designationem, consuetudinum, legum, juris, potestatum publicarum expositionem, pactorum, fœderum, decretorum, latarum sententiarum recitationem, & similia fere habet nihil. Opus molestum mihi, sed, ut spero, publice futurum non in-utile, nec ingratum ijs, qui hanc civitatem & agrum, ut patriam suam, amant, quive inter exteros peregrina hæc cognoscere non fastidiunt. Fuit vero hoc, cum secunda ope-ram in hanc rem conferre, anno M.D.XCIX. exeunte. Quam ob causam, cum eo anno commemoratio quoque nostra & status pro-vincia expositio desinit. Consilium autem fuit, cum hoc agerem, ut cum decade quarta conjunctam lucubratiunculam hanc fine-rem in publicum prodire. Sed ea cum cuderetur tandem (tardius quippe id factum quàm initio constitueram, cuius causas in præfatione exposui) & tunc festinatio eorum, quorum sumptu excudebatur, propter nundinas Francof. ingruentes non pateretur id fieri, quod constitueram, hactenus hac apud me delituit. Nunc cum stimularer ab amicis, qui συνταγμα viderat, & videretur id per se libelli modum exple-re posse, omnibus denuò cum publicis literis diligentissimè collatis, excudendum seorsim typographo dedi. Quibus vero rectius, pro more recepto, quam Clementia tua, inclyte Comes, & A.A.V.V. amplissimi & nobilissimi Ordines, dedicare idipsum, & inscribere possem, non reperi. Nam vestra haec provincia est, vestraeque cura commissa, quam descripsi, cujusque status ab aliquot saeculis repetitum, atque ordine explicatum posui ob oculos, & quantum in me fuit, a posteritatum oblivione vindicavi. Rogo etiam atque etiam, ut contra momorum morsus in vestrum patrocinium recipere prodeuntem hunc libellum, & consilium hoc meum, quod dixi, clementer benigneque interpretari non dedignemini. Valete. Groninga die XVI Januarii anno MDCV, quem ut faustum & felicem nobis & provinciae totiusque reipub. Christianae esse velit Christus omnipotens, toto eum pectore precor.
units.tr: It is now seven years, illustrious and most noble Count, most gracious Lord, most noble and most distinguished Orders, since Franciscus Petitus of Béthune came here, meditating a history of the united provinces in this Lower Germany and seeking material. He persuaded me, both by his entreaties and through the intercession of others, to set down on paper something in summary about the condition of affairs in this province, which might be of use for his history. But what then flowed from me in my haste, and with my attention occupied by other cares, was rough and unfinished, and was heaped together like a wood thrown up in confusion rather than a work digested and shaped. Then, when I learned that many thought Petitus would be wrecked in his purpose, and when, weighing the matter more carefully, I was brought to the view that it would be no small honour to this province, and would shed no little light on our knowledge of the whole of our history, if a work of this kind stood in public, I took that little wood up again in my hands. I added much, changed, polished, and brought everything into order; at last I achieved that it had some form of a work, and could be sent out to the public when it was convenient. I used a style of expression as plain and simple as possible, adapted and bent to signify the present state of affairs, so that the matter might be understood more easily and clearly by all who have even a slight acquaintance with the Latin language. I deliberately abstained from all ornament, especially in a subject which of itself hardly admits of ornament. For apart from the listing of places and the description of their situation, it has almost nothing but the explanation of customs, laws, rights and public powers, the recital of agreements, treaties, decrees and sentences passed. It is a troublesome task for me, but, as I hope, it will prove useful to the public, and not unwelcome to those who love this city and its country as their homeland, or who among foreigners do not disdain to learn these things about a strange land. Now, I put my second effort into this matter at the end of the year 1599. For this reason, since our commemoration and the exposition of the province's condition end in that year. My intention, moreover, when I was doing this, was to bring this little work out in public together with the fourth decade. But when that was finally printed (it was indeed done more slowly than I had first planned, the causes of which I have set out in the preface), and the haste of those at whose expense it was being printed, because of the approaching Frankfurt fair, would not allow what I had intended to be done, it has hitherto remained hidden with me. Now, since I was urged by friends, who had seen the συνταγμα and who thought it could by itself fill the form of a little book, I have given it to the printer to be printed separately, after having again collated everything most carefully with the public records. But I have not found to whom I could more fittingly, according to accepted custom, than to your Clemency, illustrious Count, and to your A.A.V.V., most distinguished and most noble Orders, dedicate and inscribe it. For this province is yours, and it is committed to your care; I have described it, and I have set before your eyes its condition, traced back over some centuries and explained in order, and, so far as lay in me, I have rescued it from the forgetfulness of posterity. I ask again and again that you deign to take this little book, now coming forth, under your patronage against the bites of the carping critics, and that you graciously and kindly interpret this my purpose, as I have said. Farewell. Groningen, 16 January 1605, which may Christ almighty wish to be fortunate and happy for us, for the province, and for the whole Christian commonwealth; this I pray with my whole heart.

units.la: Clem. A.A. atq; vestris dediti s.
units.tr: Your Clemency's devoted servant, most humbly.
UBBO EMMIUS.

units.la: TRIA sunt, de quibus monitum te, lector,cupio ad hunc libellum pertinen-tia. Primum, quòd fœdera, quæ cum Drentinis vicinis suis diversa diversis temporibus civitas iniit, ad hæc certamina pactaque quædam cum Frisiis Orientalibus, conventa quoque cum Comitibus Benthemiis ac similia, brevitatis studio in hoc compendio consulto præterierim.
units.tr: There are three things, reader, which I wish to bring to your notice concerning this little book. First, that I have deliberately passed over, for the sake of brevity in this compendium, the treaties which the city made at various times with its neighbours the Drenthers, and the agreements and similar arrangements concluded with the East Frisians and with the Counts of Bentheim, as well as those struggles.

units.la: Alterum, quòd id, quod pagina 148. in sententia secundâ Hagæ pronunciatâ anno M.D.XCIX. de quinta omnium censuum ex formula anni M.D.LXXVII. conferenda, non multò post interpretatione ordinum generalium sit expositum commodiùs.
units.tr: Second, that what is set out on page 148, in the second sentence pronounced at The Hague in the year 1599, concerning the fifth of all the levies to be compared with the formula of the year 1577, has been explained more conveniently not long afterwards by the interpretation of the General States.

units.la: Tertium, quòd pagina 135 error sit commissus in tempore,quo captus fuit Bartholdus Entenius: quem cùm ista scriberem, arbitratus sum, profectis jam & absentibus domo legatis partis utriusq;, turbas dedisse,& in potestatem Groningensium venisse: sed post, cùm hoc excusum jam esset, certius cognovi, ante legatorum abitum illa accidisse.
units.tr: Third, that an error was made on page 135 concerning the time when Bartholdus Entenius was captured. When I was writing this, I supposed that the disturbances had been caused, and that he had come into the power of the Groningers, after the envoys of both parties had already left and were absent from home; but afterwards, when this had already been printed, I learned more certainly that those events happened before the envoys departed.

units.la: Animus enim ad fœdera, pacta, conventiones, decreta, sententias intentus, quæ huius libelli propria sunt, in circumstantia illa temporis, velut in παρέργῳ[?] erravit.
units.tr: For my mind, intent on the treaties, agreements, conventions, decrees and sentences, which are the proper concern of this little book, went astray in that circumstance of time, as it were in a digression.

units.la: Nunc absoluta hac opella in officina typographica, cui me quoque vacare succisivis horis emaculandis mendis oportuit, ad edenda, quæ in historia
units.tr: Now, with this little work finished in the printing house, where I too had to give my spare hours to correcting the errors, I turn again to write what remains, for the things to be published in the history,

units.la: post ea, quæ jam emisi, parata habeo & scriben- da, quæ restant, rursum me verto ; unde hac o- pellà abduƈtus fui. Sibilos & clamores ca- lumniatorum, quibus lacessor, non curo, nec pereos ab optimo proposito abduci me, aut in cursu turbari sino. Per me licebit hominibus hujusmodi, ex cohorte Medij Thessali, ingenio ac genio suo obsequi, & hoc scriptionis genere atque hac arte se pascere, stylumque & facun- diam suam exercere. Licebit quoque, quos tondere se jactant, ut tondeant, quamdiu se, ad quos id pertinet, tonderi patientur. Non enim hoc ad me, Me optima sustentat optimæ vo- luntatis, qui patriæ gratis in hoc studij genere servio, conscientia. Ea cum approbatione bo- norum ingenio, doctrina, judicio præstantium sat magna mihi merces. Vale, & quod hic do, boni consule. Erraris ignosce.
units.tr: after those I have already put out, which I have ready and to be written; from which this little work drew me away. I do not care for the hisses and shouts of the slanderers by whom I am assailed, nor do I allow myself to be diverted from my excellent purpose or disturbed in my course. As far as I am concerned, such men from the cohort of Medius Thessalus may indulge their own nature and inclination, and feed themselves on this kind of writing and this art, and exercise their pen and their eloquence. They may also, as they boast, shear those whom they claim to shear, so long as those to whom it pertains allow themselves to be shorn. For this does not affect me, who am sustained by the consciousness of my excellent good will, since I serve my country without reward in this kind of study. With the approval of good men, of those who excel in talent, learning and judgement, this is a sufficiently great reward for me. Farewell, and take in good part what I give here. Forgive me if I have erred.

units.la: Reliqua lectorper se observabit, & boni consulet.
units.tr: The reader will observe the rest for himself, and take it in good part.
AMULETUM.

units.la: EN syntagma datum, indubio magis inclyta vero Gruningea dein quo foret historia:Ars nulla hic mythici, κολακείαve Macrobiani,Cum sua sint rebus fila sacrata suis.Nil clandestina quod libertate petulce:Nil vage quod rodas hic Holerin[?]Lepus:Lactucas labris aliunde requirire vellis;Mente tamen memori quo fugiatis ea.
units.tr: Here is the book given, more famous than doubt, and truly of Gruningen, whatever history it may be. No art is here of the mythic kind, nor Macrobian flattery, since its sacred threads belong to their own matters. Nothing is to be found here that is petulantly clandestine; nothing that a vagrant hare might gnaw in Holerin. You do not wish to seek lettuces for your lips from elsewhere; yet with a mindful memory, take note of where you should flee from them.

units.la: In laudem historiæ solidumq; autoris honorem,In fremitum at vobis, en epigrammation:Mordeat vt Momus, vt liveat Invidus, amplo estVBBO fide Livio plus mihi, parq; stylo.
units.tr: In praise of history and the solid honour of the author, but for your grumbling, behold an epigram: let Momus bite, let the envious man burst with spite; I am, in faithfulness, more than Livy, and equal in style.
By the study of R. Wicheringius.

units.la: DE AGRO FRISIÆ INTER AMASVM ET LAVICAM FLVMINA.
units.tr: On the Land of Friesland between the Rivers Ems and Lauwers

units.la: Vrbs GRONINGA proximis aliquot saeculis amplissima, splendidissima, & validissima in Frisijs fuit: eademq; situ pene medio regionis ab occidente in orientem porrecta, ideoq; omnib. fere rebus ejus magnis bello ac pace implicita; denique reip. forma prae cateris insignis, atq; optime habens. Quapropter opera pretium visum, seorsim quaedam de ea differere, & explicare accuratius, eaq; explicatione lucem affundere multis partibus historia no-stratis. Et primum quidem de agro dicam bre-viter, in quo urbs sita est, deq; fluminib. agrum percurrentibus: tum de ipsa urbe, de jure VLTRAIECTINO, de pactis & foederibus ejus, de conatu & armis SAXONVM, DE EDSAR-DI, GELDRI, BVRGVNDORVM imperio, summatim agam; post de αὐτονο-[?] μία[?] & præclaro jure civitatis addam nonnulla: postremo ordinem magistratuum & caterarum curationum in urbe & extra urbem totamq; formam regiminis civilis exponam. Ager sic habet, quemadmodum & in historiæ libro primo exposui. Post LAVICÆ æstuarium, & alveum ejus pene emortuum, Ostergoa ac totius Frisia occidentalis terminum, ad quem Vifuleta vicus celebris, & cœnobium Gerriconiu sunt, ager hic noster, de quo agimus, venientibus ab occasu sequitur, longeq; litoris tractu non minus quinis milliaribus secundum latus boreum, ac vadosa æstuaria in ortum porrigitur. Inde in meridiem se referens Amasi fluminis ostio, ac sinu Dullarto, quem a fluctuum rabie sic nominant, ortivo latere clauditur, sed sinuosis admodum, ac variè flexis litoribus. Nam primum a septentrionibus ubi sensim per aliquot passuum millia descendit ad portum fere Delffilanum[?], inde rursum in ortum convertitur, Amasio oram radente: mox ad Dullarti initium, in terras se insinuantis, vel linguam aut cuneum efformans, cujus in extremitate Reidæ vicus quondam percelebris, nunc castellum modo militare est, inter meridiem & occasum aliquovsq;, deinde quasi, incitantibus se in terram fluctibus, ulterius etiam in occidentem longo spacio litus retrahit, iterum brevi flexu in ortum redit, atq; eodem pene, quo in occidentem erat, spacio, in quo Widwoldi[?]cum fanum quatuor turribus conspicuum sese offert, rursus procurrit: postremo alijs etiam minoribus ribus finibus receptis ad terminum austrinum, contendit, ubi cœnobium est Hilligerlaum, His-panica clade nuper nobilitatum, & Bellingwoldy.
units.tr: The city Groningen was in the last few centuries the largest, most splendid and most powerful city in Friesland. Since it lay almost in the middle of the region, stretching from west to east, nearly all its great affairs, in war and in peace, were bound up with it, and its form of government was outstanding above the rest and in excellent condition. For this reason I thought it worth while to discuss certain things about it separately and to explain them more carefully, and by this explanation to throw light on many parts of our history. First I will briefly speak of the land in which the city lies and of the rivers that run through the land; then of the city itself, of the law of Utrecht, of its pacts and treaties, of its attempts and arms against the Saxons, of Edzard, Guelders and Burgundy rule. I will treat these briefly; afterwards concerning autonomy [αὐτονομία] and the distinguished law of citizenship I will add some things. Finally I will set out the order of the magistrates and of the other offices in the city and outside it, and the whole form of civil government. The land is as I set out in the first book of the history. Beyond the estuary of the Lauwers and its almost dead channel, which marks the boundary of Ostergo and of all western Friesland, where the famous village of Vifuleta and the monastery of Gerriconium lie, this land of ours, which we are discussing, follows for those coming from the west. Along its northern side it stretches eastward for a coastline of no less than five miles, with shallow estuaries. Turning from there to the south, it is closed on the east by the mouth of the Ems and by the bay called the Dollard, which they so name from the fury of the waves; but its shores are very winding and variously bent. For first, from the north, where it gently descends over some miles to the harbour of Delfzijl, it turns again eastward, skirting the Ems shore. Then at the beginning of the Dollard, where it pushes into the land, forming a tongue or wedge, at whose tip lay the village of Reide, once very famous and now merely a military fort, it runs for some distance between south and west. Then, as if the waves were driving it into the land, it draws the shore back a long way further west, returns eastward with a short bend, and over about the same distance as it went west, where the church of Widwold with its four conspicuous towers comes into view, it juts out again. Finally, taking in some other smaller boundaries, it stretches to the southern boundary, where lies the monastery of Heiligerlee, lately made famous by the Spanish defeat, and Bellingwolde.

units.la: Ab eo termino per palustria & arenosa ad Ostergoa limitem longo tractu recurrit, Wester-woldios primum, dein Drentiam ad meridiem habens: idq; latus meridionale omnium ejus late-rum est maximum, XXVI millib. pass. non breVius. Ager totus dimidio fere, quam Translavi-canus, minor: argilloso ut plurimū, & hubere[?] ad pascua pariter ac frumenta solo: palustris tamen & nemorosus, quā Dullarto adjacet, quāq; Ostergois ad meridiem cohæret, sabulosus hic illic quā Drentiæ conjungitur. Hanc ego re-gionem à Lavica in Amasum ac Dullartum, minoris Frisiæ nomine affectum interdum avorum & proavorum nostrorum memoria reperio. usus[?] dudum invaluit, ab urbe Groninga sive quod in solo ejus hæc sit ad austrinum limitem, quamvis id in dubium trahant nonnulli, ut post ostendam, sive quod fœderibus antiquitus connexa, seu utramq; ob causam simul, Groninganam vocitare.
units.tr: From that boundary it runs back in a long stretch through marshy and sandy ground to the boundary of Ostergo, having Westerwolds first and then Drenthe to the south. This southern side is the longest of all its sides, not less than twenty-six miles. The whole land is nearly half the size of the land beyond the Lauwers. It is for the most part clayey, with soil suited to pasture as well as to grain; yet where it borders the Dollard it is marshy and wooded, and where it joins Drenthe it is sandy here and there. I find that this region, from the Lauwers to the Ems and the Dollard, was sometimes called by the name of Lesser Friesland within the memory of our grandfathers and great-grandfathers. But the custom has long since prevailed of calling it Groningen land, either because the city of Groningen lies on its southern boundary within its soil, though some dispute this, as I will show later, or because it was joined by treaties from ancient times, or for both reasons together.

units.la: Divisa quondam in plures provincias, seu populos quosdam minores, legibus & imperio inter se distinctos, quos tamen commune sædus & respublica quædam major plerumq; in unum rursus colligebat. Et sunt ejus divisionis etiam nunc in usu notissima vestigia, paulo post exponenda. Eandem hanc regionem vel agrum duo amnes præcipui olim percurrerunt, & percurrunt quoq; hodie, quanquam nominibus [?]am aliis aliys noti,nec eodem ubiq; retento meatu. Alter HVNESVS quondam dictus in Drentia exoriens, collectis primum aquis palustribus tenuis, deinde lacum Laraum magnum profundumq; ingressus ac permensus, ejusq; copia auctus, iusti iam flumi-nis instar latus atq; altus, Gronenbergiam arcem olim haud incelebrem allapsus, imo pene circum-lapsus, relicta ad iv circiter stadia Groninga, quæ ei ad occidentem & meridiem erat, in circuum deferebatur: mox milliari uno magno infra Gro-ningam flexo cursu recta occasum versus se inci-tabat per Hunesgonios, qui ex eo nomen habue-runt, donec in æstuarium Lavica, ut nunc quoq; facit, exiret, & communi cum eo ostio se exonera-ret inter insulas in Oceanum. Nunc oppida-norum studio oppositis aggeribus, obstructo quâ urbem prætervehebatur, vetere alueo, relicto ad dextram Gronenbergio solo, ad urbem multos ante annos derivatus magno urbis commodo, auctusq; illic amnis AHA[?] aquis e Drentia si-militer venientibus, perq; longum spatium infra urbem eiusdem Aha alueo vectus Underwe-rumum usq;, atq; ibi veteri alueo redditus, agge-ribus ab urbe ad exitum utrimq; compressus, toto hoc infra urbem spacio ab arundinum copia voce Germanica Fleitdiep vulgo jam nuncupatur, ve-teri nomine illo Hunesi prorsus obliterato, & ac-colis etiam omnib. ignoto, ac pene inaudito. Quæ vero pars eius est supra urbem, per Drentiam & præfecturam suburbanam means, hodie à na-vium certa specie, quarum in ea usus est frequens comcomportandis ad urbem cesspitibus, id est, glebis palustrib. in usum ignis, vocatur dat Schuten-Diep/ habetq; utrinq; agros humiles & uliginosos, per quos decurrit; & praeterquam, qua aggeribus constricta est, eosdem saepe inundat. At alter amnis e duob. quos dixi hunc agrum olim secuisse, nomen FIVELÆ habuit iam prorsus etiam ignotum, & e Duerswoldiis finitimis praefectura veteri, aut ex ipsa vetere praefectura se proferens primum, locumq;, ubi nunc coenobium Werumanu est, antiquitus, deinde mutato cursu modico a coenobio intervallo humilia camporum perluens, longo ac tortuoso meatu illam agri partem permensus fuit, quae Amaso propinquat, cuiq; nomen ex se tribuit. Fivelingia vel Fivelgonia: (utraq; n. forma hodie quoq; vulgo dicitur) ac demum apud Sondios (id vico tum nomen) se effudit. Verum is exitus eius ante annos plus minus cccc obiecto aggere transfuerso oppilatus, & alveus ipse magna partem una cum nomine paulatim extinctus est. Collegit ille ex omni fere Fivelgonia aquas eas, & exoneravit, quas iam rivus Dammonensis, hoc nomine hodie notus, eodem ex agro collectas (nam per eundem hunc agrum defluit, & multis locis eundem quoq; alveum servat) per canales Delffilanos in Amasum egerit. Et hunc quoq; oppidani quam plurimos ante annos depressa per aliquot passuum millia perampla fossa ab eo loco, qui ab aggeris flexu nomen fert, ad moenia usq; sua derivarunt, meabilem actuariis navibus maiusculis, quanta sciliscilicet per canales Delffilanos traduci possunt. Quin etiam studio Casparis Roblefij guberna-toris regij non ita multos ante annos claustra ad vrbem huiusmodi constituta sunt, vt quoties oppidani velint, omnes hos duos Fivelam & Hune-sum ad vrbem dudum deductos confundere, ac rursum per eadem claustra disiungere queant. Ac Fivela quidem, qui nunc Dammonensis rivus est, (Dammonam quippe duob. milliaribus Germanicis magnis ad ortum solstitialem ab vrbe Groninga perluit) non jam liber, vt Hunesum, in Amasum effunditur, sed exitum ejus quatuor ingentes canales coercent, tres ad castellum Delf-silanum continuis lateribus, quartus prope Farm-sumum vicum loco proximo, paucis modo passibus Delffila disiunctio. His porro amnib. qui hanc Frisiae partem perluerunt olim, addiderit quis tertium haud minorem prioribus, cui EA. nomen. Is in Monasteriensium finibus ortus, & a meridie in septentrionem se incitans, omnem q; agrum Westerwoldicum primum, deinde planiciem illam camporum per quam Dullartus sinus ingens jam se fundit, & lato & profundo alueo permensus, haud procul exitu in occasum, & rursus in borea flexo cursu inter duas Reidas, vicos olim haud incelebres, per septem canales in aggere defossos in Amasum se exoneravit, & agrum hunc quem jam describimus, ab eo qui Frisiae Orientalis nomine nunc censetur, & Comitatus titulum fert, secrevit. Nunc post Bellenwoldios, qui in ora austrina si-nusunt, Dullartinis flustib.[?] tectus, quanq; alueum sub fluftibus fervet, nusquam tamen apparet, ut & cætera omnia, ville, vici, fana, quæ in eo spa- cio fuerunt. In hos autem, qui supersunt, amnes, ut & in æstuaria vicina, rivi complures scaphis & lintrib. meabiles se effundunt: quorum alij orti ex se, aquis viam sibimet facientibus, alij humana industria excavati, hic illic regionem secant, & vicos plerosq; celebriores alluunt, duplici regionis bono. Nam & humiles atq; vdos agros aquis levant, & commeandi vectandiq; facultatem incolis commodissimam præstant. Sed qui Hunefum augent, aut in æstuaria aut Dullartum effunduntur, claustris in exitu coercentur: cæteri libero lapsu Fivela fe miscent. Duo etiam ad urbem ipsam Groningam longis brachijs se porrigunt, Honæus in occidente, Botteranus a borea. Populorum minorum hanc regionem habitantium nomina, situs, ratio ita habent. Ad occidentem & meridiem Hunefi fluminis Langowoldii Oftergois finitimi, complexi vicos finis insignes XIII: FREDOWOLDII in eadem plaga Sylvestrib. ac Drentia propinqui, vicis X comprehensi, tenui in solo utriq; : HVMMERTZII in latere æstuarij Lavicani ad effluxum fluminis jam dicti, eluvionib. ad tres tantum vicos redacti, sed agri felicis, ubi rivus ex Drentia descendens, & Transhunefanam omnem regionem pererras canali novo ad castellum militare copressus in idem [?] æstuarium exit, & alluvio nunc reddit, & diluvia quondam & tempestatum vis abstulerunt: MEDACHII ad eiusdem fluminis ripa introrsum magis timentes in vicos IX in solo perubere ac lato sparsi, ex quibus quinq, abbati Adoardo vicino suo parent. Hos vero & Oftopagicos olim vocatos, & Hunesgonijs sequentibus accensos deprehendo. Ad orientem & septentrionem amnis Hunesi deinde reliqui HVNESGONII secundum litus regionis boreum longo tractu extensi, atq; hinc interiora versus, Hummereriys & Medachiys pariter adversa in ripa secundum amnis lapsum oppositi, donec in proxima urbis Groningana, & in rivum Dammonensem meridiano latere incurrant, latis simul pro modo priorum, & omni ex parte tum natura, tum hominum opere bene cultis finib. quippe quib. non minus LV vici cum singulis fanis contineantur: Distincti in praefecturas minores quinq; quarum ea, quae ad ostium fluminis, vadumq; Lavicafita est, Mamensis dicitur [?]; altera Ubbingana secundum superiorem fluminis partem Groninga in eorum vicina; tertia, quam mediam vocant, priorib. confinis, in fluminis ripa, qua in occasum se vertere incipit, ad litus boreum pertinens; quarta ab aggere interiore cognominata, in aquilonem ab urbe vergens, rivoq; Dammonensi in caeciam ventum ab urbe defluenti contigua; postrema cunctis prioribus major per quina passuum millia juxta litus idem exterius porrecta, pariq; fere spacio intus patescens: FIVELGONII Hunesgonios ad ortum sequentes in Amasi ora, similiter in duas divisi partes, quarum prior XXXI vicos complexa insignes nulli superiorem felicitate cedit, tum ob terra bonitate, tum ob commoda fluminis vicini: altera altera vicis rarior, quos ix tantum habet, palustri fere, & passim humili ac vliginoso solo, in australem priorem sequens, ad interiora vergens, per quam ab ortu venientibus iter Groningam est: eam Duerswoldiam proprio nomine appellitant. Atq; hactenus quidem populi hujus regionis, quos jam quidam inepte velut proprio & peculiari horum nomine, ac vocabulo absolute VMLANDOS nuncupant, & nuncupari debere contendunt, cum certius nihil notiusve sit ex etymi ratione, & exemplis in literarum monumentis, quam vocabulum id appellativum aut commune esse, & in genere τῶν πρὸς τι referendum ad urbem aut locum aliquem celebrem, circum quem ager populive siti sunt; atq; hos ipsos populos sic dictos, quod positu suo Groningam fere circum veniant. Unde ista in antiquiorib. literis, adeoq; nuperis etiam ante inventum hoc litis ergo σοφὸν φάρμακον, Die Omblanden bp Groningen / bin Groningen / ban Groningen: quemadmodum alibi, die Omblanden / bin offte bp Franeker / Wolstwerdt / Leiwerden & similia: Item Groningen mit ere bimlanden / vt Dcko thom Wlaoech / Sibet tho Susttringen mit ehre bimblanden.
units.tr: Once divided into several provinces, or certain smaller peoples, distinguished from one another by their own laws and government, which nevertheless a common covenant and some greater commonwealth usually gathered back into one. Traces of this division, which I shall explain shortly, are still very well known in use even now. Two principal rivers once flowed through this same region or territory, and they still flow through it today, though they are known by other names and do not keep the same course everywhere. The first, once called the Hunesus, rises in Drenthe. At first it is a thin stream, gathering waters from the marshes; then it enters and passes through the great and deep Lake Laram, and, swollen by its waters, it becomes a river of real size, broad and deep. It once flowed past the castle of Gronenberg, which was once no small fame, or rather it nearly flowed around it, and left Groningen about four stadia off, on its west and south side, and was carried around the city in a curve. Soon after, after a great bend of about one mile below Groningen, it hastened in a straight line towards the west through the Hunesgoi, who took their name from it, until it went out into the estuary of the Lavica, as it still does now, and discharged itself into the Ocean through the islands by a common mouth with it. Now, through the zeal of the townspeople, the old channel was blocked by dams placed across the place where it used to run past the city, and the old bed was left on the right of Gronenberg; many years ago it was diverted to the city, to the great advantage of the city, and the river, increased there by waters likewise coming from Drenthe, was carried a long way below the city along the bed of the same Aha, as far as Onderwerum; and there, returned to its old bed, and hemmed in on both sides by dykes from the city to its mouth, it is now commonly called, throughout this whole stretch below the city, by the German word for the abundance of reeds, Fleitdiep, the old name Hunesus being utterly forgotten, and unknown and almost unheard of by all the inhabitants too. The part of it above the city, through Drenthe and the suburban district, is now called the Schuten-Diep, from a certain kind of boat, of which there is frequent use in it for carrying peat-turves to the city, that is, marsh clods for use as fuel; and it has low and boggy fields on each side through which it runs, and apart from where it is confined by dykes, it often floods these same fields. But the other river of the two I mentioned, which once cut through this territory, had the name Fivela, now also quite unknown, and it rises first from the neighbouring Duerswold, from the old district, or from the old district itself, and in ancient times it had its source at the place where the convent of Werum now is; then, after a slight change of course, about a short distance from the convent, it watered low stretches of the fields, and passed through that part of the country which is near Ameland, by a long and winding course, and it gave its own name to it. It is called Fivelingia or Fivelgonia (both forms are still commonly used today), and at last it discharged itself at Sondia (which was then the name of a village). But that outlet of it, about four hundred years ago more or less, was blocked by a transverse dam thrown across, and the channel itself, for the greater part, together with its name, was gradually extinguished. It gathered and discharged those waters from almost all of Fivelgonia which the Dammonian stream, known today by this name, now carries off into the Ameland, after gathering them from the same district (for it flows down through this same district, and in many places keeps the same bed too), through the Delfzijl canals. Many of the townspeople also, many years ago, diverted it by a very broad ditch dug through several miles, from the place that takes its name from the bend of the dyke, right up to the walls of their city, navigable by small cargo boats, as large as can be taken through the Delfzijl canals. Indeed, through the zeal of Caspar Roblefius, the royal governor, not many years ago barriers were set up at the city of such a kind that, whenever the townspeople wish, they can join both of these, Fivela and Hunesus, long since led to the city, and again separate them through the same barriers. And the Fivela, which is now the Dammonian stream (for it flows past Damme, about two great German miles to the east-northeast from the city of Groningen), is no longer free, like the Hunesus, to pour into the Ameland; but its outlet is confined by four great canals, three alongside the castle of Delfzijl with continuous banks, and the fourth near the village of Farmsum, close by, only a few paces separated from Delfzijl. Moreover, to these rivers which once watered this part of Friesland someone might add a third, no less than the former, called Ea. It rises in the territory of the Münsterites, and, hurrying from south to north, having first traversed the whole Westerwolde district, and then that broad plain through which the great Dullart bay now pours itself, with a wide and deep bed, not far from its outlet it turned westward, and then again with a northward bend, between two Reids, villages once of no small fame, it discharged itself into the Ameland through seven canals dug into the dyke, and it separated this territory which we are now describing from the one which is now reckoned under the name of East Friesland and bears the title of County. Now, after the Bellenwold villages, which lie on the southern shore, it is covered by the Dullart waves, and although its bed continues beneath the waves, it nowhere appears, just like all the other things, towns, villages, and temples, which were in that space. Into those rivers, however, which remain, as also into the neighbouring estuaries, several streams pour themselves, navigable by skiffs and small boats: of these, some arose of themselves, the waters making a way for themselves, others were dug out by human industry, and here and there they cut through the region and wash most of the more famous villages, to a double benefit of the region. For they both raise up the low and wet fields with water, and provide the inhabitants with the most convenient facility for travelling and carrying goods. But those which swell the Hunesus, or flow into the estuaries or into Dullart, are confined at their outlet by barriers; the rest flow freely and mingle with the Fivela. Two also stretch their long arms right up to the city of Groningen itself: the Honaeus on the west, the Botteran from the north. The names, situation and organisation of the smaller peoples inhabiting this region are as follows. To the west and south of the river Hunesus, bordering on the Langewold and the Oostergo, the Langewold district comprises thirteen notable villages; the Fredewold district, on the same side, near the Sylvestrians and Drenthe, comprises ten villages, both on thin soil; the Hummerts, on the side of the Lavican estuary at the outflow of the aforesaid river, have been reduced to only three villages by floods, but of fertile land, where a stream descending from Drenthe and wandering through the whole Trans-Hunesan region, having been confined by a new canal at the military castle, flows out into the same estuary; this land is now restored by alluvial deposit, while floods and the force of storms once carried it away. The Medachi, scattered on the bank of the same river further inland, in nine villages on a very fertile and wide soil, of which five obey the abbot Adoard, their neighbour. But I find that these were also formerly called the Oftopagi, and, following the Hunesgonians, were reckoned among them. To the east and north, beyond the river Hunesus, the remaining Hunesgonians, extended along the northern shore of the region in a long stretch, and from there towards the interior, opposed to the Hummerts and Medachi alike on the bank along the course of the river, until they run into the neighbouring Groningen, and into the Dammonian stream on the southern side, equally broad according to the measure of the former, and with boundaries well cultivated on every side, both by nature and by human labour; indeed, they contain no fewer than fifty-five villages, each with its own temple. Divided into five smaller districts: of these, the one at the mouth of the river and the ford of the Lavica is called the Mamensis; the second, the Ubbingana, along the upper part of the river towards Groningen, in their neighbourhood; the third, which they call the middle one, bordering the former, on the bank of the river where it begins to turn westward, extending to the northern shore; the fourth, named from the inner dyke, facing north from the city and adjoining the Dammonian stream which flows from the city into the blind wind; the last, larger than all the former, stretching five miles along the same outer shore and spreading almost as far inland: the Fivelgonians, who follow the Hunesgonians to the east on the shore of Ameland, are likewise divided into two parts, of which the first, comprising thirty-one notable villages, yields to none of the above in prosperity, both on account of the goodness of the soil and the advantages of the neighbouring river; the second, with fewer villages, which has only nine, on a soil almost marshy, and everywhere low and boggy, following the former to the south, and lying towards the interior, along which the road from the east to Groningen runs: this they call by its proper name Duerswold. And so far indeed the peoples of this region, whom some now foolishly call by the proper and peculiar name of these people, and insist they should be called absolutely the Omlanden, although nothing is more certain or better known, from the reasoning of the etymology and from examples in the monuments of literature, than that this word is an appellative or common one, and must be referred in the category of relatives to a city or some famous place around which the fields or peoples lie; and these very peoples are so called because by their position they nearly surround Groningen. Hence those expressions in older writings, and even in more recent ones before this quarrel-remedy, the wise cure was discovered: Die Omblanden bp Groningen / bin Groningen / ban Groningen: just as elsewhere, die Omblanden / bin offte bp Franeker / Wolstwerdt / Leiwerden and similar: Item Groningen mit ere bimlanden / vt Dcko thom Wlaoech / Sibet tho Susttringen mit ehre bimblanden.

units.la: Sed quo abeo? ad rem revertor. Omnes hi populi, quos ja recensui, in tres partes, ceu membra regionis, hodie divisi sunt, & dudum divisi fuere: quarum prima, qua trans Hunesum ad occidentem & meridiem est, usq; in Lavicam & Ostergoos, ac occidentalis vulgo nuncupatur: altera Hunesgomes eis Hunesum, tertia Fivelgonios compleElitur.[?] Hi in conventibus generalib. coeunt plerunq; & conjunctim de reb. deliberant, & suffragia ferunt, sæpe etiam, si dissensio sit, singulæ seorsim, disiunctæ cellis, & quo duæ inclinant, eo tertiam quoq; accedere ex more aut lege cogunt.
units.tr: But where am I going? I return to the subject. All these peoples that I have now enumerated are today divided into three parts, like the limbs of a region, and have long been divided: of which the first, the part that lies beyond the Hunesus to the west and south, extends as far as the Lavica and the Ostergoi, and is commonly called the western; the second is the Hunesgomes, the people beside the Hunesus; the third is the Fivelgonians. These meet in general assemblies, mostly, and deliberate together on common affairs and cast their votes; often too, if there is disagreement, each part meets separately, in separate chambers, and by custom or law they compel the third also to join whichever side the other two lean towards.

units.la: Ad juridicos vero confessus superiores, ad quos à tribunalibus inferioribus in singulis territoriis provocatio est, separatim Transhunesani & Cishunesani certis anni temporib. in urbem Groningam conveniunt, ut nunc mos habet, & diu habuit: quamquam aliquando aliter quoq; habuerit. De qua re rursum dicetur nobis amplius, in sequentibus.
units.tr: For the higher judicial assemblies, to which appeal lies from the lower tribunals in each district, the Transhunesians and the Cishunesians meet separately at fixed times of the year in the city of Groningen, as the custom now is and has long been; although at times it has been otherwise. We shall speak of this matter again, more fully, in what follows.

units.la: Five-lingys PRÆFECTVRA VETVS sequitur, ab Amasio flumine initium sumens, & ad Dullartum sinum toto ejus occiduo ac sinuoso latere, ut hodie res habet, strata, vimq; ab eo quondam & jacturam passa maximam, agris & vicis fluctu obrutis, ut e magno horum numero vix XVII hodie, ac pleriq; semilaceri mutilaq; supersint: cujus pars borea Amasio vicina soli pinguis ac argillosi, reliqua fere exilioris, minusq; lati, partim palustris ingenii partim arenesi, nemoribus frequens; qua meridionalis maxime, Reideria quondam accensa, Tiamma rivulo e paludib. defluente à proximis direpta, nomine hoc ne nunc quidem istic obliteratò, capite ejus Winscota. Tota vero hac ab Amasio ad australinum limitem civitati Groninga ab annis prope cc bonis conditionibus paret. Ejus australino limiti ad Dullarti finem VVESTERVVOLDII connectuntur, & ipsi Reideriorum quondam pars, hinc porro in latere ortivo Dullarti ejusdem secundum Amasum longo tractu duob. magnis milliaribus, & dimidio haud breviore pertinentium: hi vicis censentur quinq;, agrumq; colunt, nisi quantum Dullarto sinui proximum est, haud felicem, ac paludosa fere natura: in quos imperium, aut imperij umbram habuit multis saeculis Addingia familia nobilis, Wedda arcis vetusta eodem in agro domina, WefterWoldico cognomine posteris quam gentili notior: nunc ad Arembergios omnia translata. Postremo TERRITORIVM SVBVRBANVM est totius regionis fines ad austrum longo tractu contra Drentiam tuens, vicos ambitu suo continens XII cum fanis rusticis VI, & coenobia duo, ambiguo inter Drentiam & eam, quam jam exponimus, Frisiam jure, quib. se debere hinc atq; inde decerptis quibusdam partib. coagmentatisq; videtur: lingua tamen, legibus, institutis per multa nunc saecula illam magis quam hanc referens, & Ultrajectinum praesulem olim summum dominum agnoscens. Antiquissimi ejus rectores Gronenbergij feruntur: ab hiis ad Selverdios, a Selverdijs vicissim ad Ultrajectinos, Geldros, Burgundos ordine pervenit; Burgundi postremo senatui populoq; Groningano, nihil imminuto veteri vicanorum jure ac libertate, attribuerunt. Atq; hujus in solo, ubi arenis gleba pinguior jungitur, editiore in dorso inter campos humilia linguae instar seperrigete, sede habet GRONINGA nostra, de qua nunc scribimus potissimum, universæ regionis nunc descriptæ, vt & totius Drentiæ commune velut horreum.
units.tr: There follows the ancient prefecture of the Fiveling-lands, beginning at the river Amasius and extending to the Dullart bay along its whole western and winding side, as things now stand, paved; and once it suffered very great loss and damage from the water, its fields and villages overwhelmed by the flood, so that of its large number scarcely seventeen survive today, and most of them half-ruined and mutilated. Its northern part, next to the Amasius, is of rich and clayey soil; the rest is for the most part of poorer soil and less broad, partly of marshy nature and partly sandy, and full of groves; its southern part, once called Reiderland, was ravaged by the Tiamma, a little stream flowing down from the marshes nearby—a name not even now forgotten there—its chief town being Winschoten. This whole district, from the Amasius to its southern boundary, has been subject to the city of Groningen on good terms for nearly 200 years. To its southern boundary, at the end of the Dullart, are joined the Westerwolde, and the part that was once of the Reiderlanders itself, which extends from there along the eastern side of the Dullart, along the Amasius, over a long stretch of two great miles and not less than half a mile. These are reckoned as five villages and cultivate their land, which, except where it lies nearest the Dullart bay, is not fortunate, and is for the most part of marshy nature. Over these the noble family of the Addingas held power, or the shadow of power, for many centuries; Wedda, an ancient castle in the same district, gave its lady, better known to posterity by the surname Westerwoldic than by her family name. Now all has been transferred to the Aremberg family. Lastly, the suburban territory is the whole region's border to the south, stretching along a long line against Drenthe, containing within its circuit twelve villages with six rural churches and two monasteries; lying between Drenthe and that Frisian district which we are now describing, it seems to owe its allegiance to both, having been put together from certain parts plucked from either side; yet in language, laws and institutions it has for many centuries now resembled the former more than the latter, and it once acknowledged the bishop of Utrecht as its supreme lord. Its most ancient rulers are said to have been the Gronenbergs; from these it passed in order to the Selverds, from the Selverds in turn to the Utrechters, the Gelderlanders and the Burgundians; finally the Burgundians assigned it to the senate and people of Groningen, without any diminution of the old rights and liberty of the villagers. And on the soil of this district, where richer clay joins with sand, on a higher ridge between the low fields, lying like a tongue, our Groningen has its seat, of which we now write principally, as the common granary of the whole region now described and of all Drenthe.

units.la: Regio universa ab exitu Lavicæ per ambages varias, quà æstuarium se curvat, quà Hunesius egredитur, quà vadum à septentrionib. alluit, quà Ámasus, quà Dullartus se sinuant, in ora aggerib. perpetuis, opere difficillimo, sepitur & defenditur contra aquarum influxum: idemq;, vt dixi jam ante, secundum Hunesi lapsum fit non ab urbe solum, sed & supra urbem, usq; ad ejusdem ostium. In ea post Groningam nobilissima & maxima DAMMONA est, non vilis oppidi instar, si ambitum, & frequentiam habitatorum, si ædificiorum numerum, magnitudinem, formam, si viarum habitum speciem, sed honore mœnium, & jure imperii civilis magistratuum carens, amœna, in circulum fere se colligens, fosaq; ut plurimum cingens, teplo illustri cum turre late spectabili insignis; fanum quoq; monasticum peramplum, sed extra ambitum, lateri tamen occiduo pene contiguum habens familiam Augustinianam, nunc ab omni cultu desertum, ac vix se sustinens: sita ad Fivelam amnem duab. infra Groningam milliaribus caeciam versus, eodemq; amne navigabili media divisa, pontibus intus conexa quinq;: unde ad exitum amnis, ubi Delffilæus portus & castellum, milliare dimidium: vallo, fossa, portis quondam munita ab Edsardo ante annos centum, & triennio post à Georgio Saxone civitatis quoq; jure atq; ordine magistratuum tuum donata, sed his ab eodem post annos XI, illis à Geldro anno sequente rursus exuta nuda-tá: à Tautenburgio demum Burgundica militia duce anno M. D. XXXV excidio damnata, & vix precibus suorum incolumis conservata. Ipsa caput quondam Fivelgonia : à cujus ordinib. jura ejus qualiacunq; ac statuta vetera, per manus accepta, & in more posita, qua privilegia sua Dammonenses vocant, solenni in conventu, anno post natalem Christi M. D. XXVII re-tenta probataq;, & mox paucos post dies ab omnib. quoq; Frisiis in comitijs universa gentis ad Upstallesbomum confirmata esse, in historia exposui. In statutis his haec reperio, Dammonam, ut nunc habet, ita tunc habuisse judices suos ex indigenis lectos: his finito muneris sui tempore (triennè id esse solet) cum primario loci sacerdote jus fuisse, die xxi Februarij successores sibi designare: hoc; cognoscendi judicandiq; potestatem habuisse de negocijs & querelis omnibus omnium hospitum ac peregrinorum Dammonam venientium sine contradictione: similiter de contractib. quibusvis coram ipsis judicib. initis, de promissionibus itidem apud eos factis, decisa æstimationis parte quarta; præterea de damnis pecudum vi Dammonensi à Dammonensi illatis: at de membrorum mutilatione, & de vulnerib. judicium eorum non fuisse, nisi facinus patratum esset ipsis præsentibus, aut incendij tempore: Et tamen in eo quoq; casu consulis, id est, judicis superioris, quem Redgerum dicere mos est, multam ex lege fuisse, non secus ac si ipse judicasset: dicasset : eosdem judices illos ter quotânis judicia exercuisse per dies quinos: ter item pondera & mensuras examinasse; panis quoq; venalis, cerevisiæ, vini, viarum, puteorum & similium rationem & curam habuisse, quod ædilium annonæ præfectorum solet munus esse : litem introductam ad horum tribunal, si lis hujusce tribunalis esset, non licuisse litigantibus, judicib. his despectis, alio traducere: si quis contra fecisset seu actor sive reus, eum sex solidos judicibus, totidem ædituis solvere multam oportuisse : curæ judicibus ijsdem fuisse, ne facinorosi sedem Damnonæ habe-rent : si quis Dammonensium Consulatus,id est,imperij ac jurisdictionis superioris jus habeat,idq; in alium non Dammonensem conferret, xxx marcas mulctâpopulo Dammonensi solvisse: eandem pœnam ei fuisse, qui aream suam in oppido venderet extero; quam si is solvere ob inopiam non posset, aream publico cessisse; & hæc si pretium mulctæ non æquaret, propinquos proximos defectui supplendo x marcas adjecisse: uni eidemq; judici simul & ædituo esse non licuisse: Dammonensem cultello vulnerantem vicinum suum sex solidos dependisse judicibus his, & totidem ædituis. His addita de advenis sedem Dammonæ componere, domos emere aut conducere volentibus, deq; nuptys ac rebus nuptialibus non mepta certe. Qua omnia si quis volet considerare attentius, facile intelligeret, amplius tum Dammonensibus jus, & potestatem judicibus eorum ampliorem in jure dicundo fuisse, quam nunc est, & à multis annis fuit. Nam praetorium imperium, & jurisdictionem pene omnem soli Ripperdai & Houverdai, aut qui his successere, dudum nunc tenent, &, quem volunt, Consulem, id est, Redgerum oppidanis dant. Iudices illorum vix umbram rei, cuius nomen ferunt, retinent; nec vocare quenquam, nec prehendere, nec coercere, aut in vincula dare, non causas, non crimina cognoscere, nec de his, nec de illis sententias ferre possunt. De Dammona plus satis.
units.tr: The whole region, from the outflow of the Lavica, through its various windings—where the estuary bends, where the Hunesus flows out, where the shore is washed by the northern shallows, where the Amasius and the Dullart curve—is enclosed and defended against the inflow of the waters by continuous dikes, a work of the greatest difficulty; and this, as I said before, runs along the course of the Hunesus not only from the city but also above the city, as far as its mouth. In this district, after Groningen, the most noble and largest is Dam. It is no mean town in size and in the number, size, shape and appearance of its buildings, and in the layout of its streets, if one judges by its circuit and the number of its inhabitants; but it lacks the honour of walls and the right of civic government and magistrates. It is pleasant, gathering itself almost into a circle and mostly surrounded by a moat, distinguished by a famous church with a tower widely visible. It also has a very large monastic church, outside the circuit but almost adjoining the western side, belonging to the Augustinian order, now deserted by all worship and barely standing. It lies on the river Fivel, two miles below Groningen towards the blind (the north-east), and is divided in the middle by this navigable river, joined within by five bridges; from there to the mouth of the river, where the harbour and fort of Delfzijl lie, is half a mile. Once fortified with a rampart, a ditch and gates, it was granted by Edzard a hundred years ago, and three years later by George of Saxony, both the rights of a city and the order of magistrates; but after eleven years these were taken away again by the same man, and in the following year were stripped away once more by Gelderland; finally, in the year 1535, it was condemned to destruction by Tautenburg, leader of the Burgundian soldiery, and was preserved unharmed only by the prayers of its own people. It was once the capital of the Fivelgonians; from whose orders its rights, whatever they were, and its ancient statutes, received by hand and kept in custom—which the Dammers call their privileges—were, in a solemn assembly in the year of Christ's birth 1527, retained and approved, and a few days afterwards were confirmed by all the Frisians also in a general assembly of the whole nation at Upstallsboom, as I have set out in my history. In these statutes I find that Dam then had, as it now has, its own judges chosen from among the natives; when their term of office ended (usually three years), the right belonged to them together with the chief priest of the place to name their successors on 21 February; that they had the power of hearing and judging, without dispute, all the complaints and affairs of all guests and strangers coming to Dam; likewise concerning contracts of any kind entered into before these very judges, and promises likewise made before them, with a fourth part of the value being settled; besides, concerning damage to livestock done by violence from a Dammer to a Dammer; but judgment on the mutilation of limbs and on wounds was not theirs, unless the deed had been done in their presence or at the time of a fire. Yet even in that case the consul, that is the higher judge whom they customarily call the Redger, received the fine by law, just as if he himself had judged. The same judges, it is said, held courts three times a year for five days each; likewise they examined weights and measures three times; they also had the care and oversight of bread for sale, of beer, wine, roads, wells and the like, which is usually the duty of the aediles and prefects of the grain supply. A suit brought before this tribunal, if it belonged to this tribunal, the litigants were not allowed to transfer to another court, scorning these judges; if anyone, plaintiff or defendant, acted otherwise, he was bound to pay a fine of six shillings to the judges and as many to the sextons. These judges were also charged with ensuring that criminals did not make their home at Dam. If any Dammer held the consulship of Dam, that is the right of higher office and jurisdiction, and conferred it on someone who was not a Dammer, he was to pay thirty marks as a fine to the people of Dam. The same penalty applied to anyone who sold his plot in the town to an outsider; and if he could not pay it because of poverty, the plot passed to the public; and if this did not equal the value of the fine, his nearest relatives were to make up the shortfall, adding ten marks. It was not permitted for one and the same man to be judge and sexton at once. A Dammer who wounded his neighbour with a knife was to pay six shillings to these judges and as many to the sextons. Added to these were provisions about strangers who wished to settle at Dam, to buy or rent houses, and about marriages and matters pertaining to marriage, which are certainly not to be despised. If anyone considers all these things more carefully, he will easily understand that the Dammers then had greater rights, and their judges greater power in administering justice, than now, and than for many years now. For the praetorian authority and almost all jurisdiction have long since been held by the Ripperdas and Houverdas, or by those who succeeded them, and they give the Redger, that is the consul, to the townsfolk as they please. Their judges retain barely the shadow of the thing whose name they bear; they cannot summon anyone, arrest, restrain, or put in chains, nor hear causes or crimes, nor pronounce sentences on either. Enough about Dam.

units.la: Reliqua per omnem agrum vici tenent, & in his fanis insignes plus minus CLX; quorum non pauci ea magnitudine & cultu, ut oppidula videri queant. Cujusmodi sunt Visleta ad Lavicam, & Northorma in Longowoldis: Winsumum ad Hunesi flexum una[?] infra Groningam milliari, Bedumum, Utbusa, Middelsthemum, Warsumum in Hunesgonis: Lopperfhemum, Berumum, Farmsumum, & quae nominata jam est Farmsumo proxima, unaq; cum eo in ora Amasi[?] posita ad Fivela exitum, Delssyla[?], amplis nunc munitionibus & firmis, velut urbs, cincta, portu quoq; celebris, in Fivelingis: Winscota, & quondam floreus, nunc fluctibus Dullarti attrita, penèq; hausta, Midwolda, cum fano quatuor turribus late conspicuo, in praefectura veteri: ut de Reiderwolda, ijdem in partibus funditus delata, quâ medium fere Dullartus fluctus nunc agitat, sileam, omnibus prioribus quondam ampliore ac ditiore. Egregia ad hæc ædificys ac opulentia monachorum & sacrarum virginum cœnobia in agro fuere numero xxv: ante catera verò Ado-ardia in Medachys, quinq; vicus imperans, famosissq; opibus inclita, superbo imprimis fano, ad modum & dimensionem ædis Claravallensis magnificentissimè structo, visenda, ædificys variys ac multis frequens, munitionibus & portis, vt oppidum, clausa, familia Bernardina: tum vetus Dammona vicinum Benedictinarum virginum, & alterum eodem nomine ac ejusdem ordinis in Marnensibus: Rottumum, Warsumum, Thesingaum, Seluverdia, Grisomonachum, Witta-werumum, Ofterwerumum, Wytwerdia, Hilli-gerlea, SchiltWolda; Effena etiam in præfectura suburbana. Præterea prapositura, sacerdotij genus opimum & honoratum, à Monasteriensi præsule εὐταξίας [?] ac quietis causa introductum in hæc loca, quatuor, Farmsumana, Loppershemia, Ufquerdia, Leensia: quinta in Hommercys jamdudum extrita. (collegium quoq; canonicorum, aut vt tum vulgo loquendi mos habebat, ecclesia collegiata apud Bedumanos cum fano ibidem illustri, supra fanorum rusticorum modum; cum primus sacerdos non temere alius, qui aut genere aut doctrinæ titulo conspicuus solet dari, magno honore atq; autoritate in populo. Deniq; pastura Baffloa in Hunesgoniys, itemq; Middelstbemia, vacatio munere pro Mona-steriensi. steriensi[?] olim decorata. Nec ad hac, quod mi- veris, regum aut principum liberalitas quicquam contulit, sed rustica plebis studia, paucorumq; nobilium ista sane, quam pro re ac agri modo, majora congessere. Quibus omnibus si quis ad-dat[?] nobilitatis domicilia toto agro sparsa, cultu & mole magnifica, inveniet, nihil ad ejus pul-chritudinem ac fortunam pene posse adjici. Stella vero militaria in agri ora, Soltcampaum ad Hunesi ostium, Delfsilaevm sæpe jam dictum, pra cæteris ingens, Reidanum in Amasi & Dullarti angulo communi, Bellingwoldium ad Dullarti recessum intimum, Buertangaum in palustribus inter Westerwoldios & Monasterienses medijs, integra adhuc omnia, & prasidijs insessa ad servandos regionis aditus contra hostes; catera complura iam exarmata. Jurisdictio per omnem agrum (excepta præfectura vetere, quae ad civitatem, & Westerwoldijs, quae ad Addingios, & ab his ad Arembergios certis legibus devoluta fuit, & territorio suburbano, cujus etiam peculiaris ratio) cum pradijs antiquitus liberis ac immunib. connexa est, ut qui pradia illa ut sua tenet, jurisdictionem cum imperio quoq; teneat. Juris dicundi autem causa agri totius partes illæ jam expositæ in territoria quaedam minora sunt subdivisa. Et horum alia vicos singulos, alia binos, alia ternos quaternosve complectuntur; quaedam etiam singulos vicos disjungunt. Est q; in unoquoq; territorio certus tribunalis locus. Ad quaedam[?] in territoriis singulis prædia hujusmodi complura sunt, accidit fere, ut per vices & successiones annuas prædiorum domini jurisdictionem cum imperio habeant, idq; secundum modum aut numerum prædiorum, quæ possident. Nam qui prædium hujusmodi unum tantum tenet, unius tantum anni jurisdictionem in eodem territorio habet, qui duo duobus, qui plura pluribus: & si quis omnia, perpetuam quoq; juris dicundi potestatem eo in tribunali obtinet: idemq; valet in iis, qui jus illud prædys cohærens à prædiorum dominis prædia ipsa retinentibus, quamquam id veteri instituto plane contrarium sit, pecunia, pactione, dono, cessione, deniq; quoqno modo sibi acquisiverunt. Qua ratione Dammonense tribunal, quod olim multorum fuit; nunc ad solos Ripperdæos & Houver-dæos, aut eos, qui his successere, Farmsumanum vero, vicorumq; aliquot vicinorum ad unos etiam ac solos Ripperdæos devolutum videmus.
units.tr: The rest of the villages hold the territory throughout the whole district, and in these there are more or less 160 notable churches; not a few of them are so large and well kept that they might seem to be small towns. Of this kind are Visleta on the Lauwers, and Northorma in Longowold; Winsum on a bend of the Hunze, one mile below Groningen; Bedum, Utbusa, Middelsthem, and Warsum in Hunsingo; Loppersum, Beerum, Farmsum, and the one named just now next to Farmsum, lying together with it on the shore of the Ems at the mouth of the Fivel, Delfzijl, now a city girt by strong and ample fortifications, also famous for its harbour, in Fivelingo; Winschoten; and Midwolda, once flourishing, now battered and nearly swallowed by the waves of the Dollard, with a church whose four towers are conspicuous from afar, in the old prefecture; and as for Reiderwolde, which the same waves have utterly carried off in those parts, where the Dollard's flood now churns about the middle of it, I will be silent, though it was once larger and richer than all the earlier ones. Besides these, there were once in the district twenty-five monasteries and convents of monks and consecrated virgins, of outstanding buildings and wealth. Above all, Adorp in Medenblik, a village commanding five others, famed for its wealth, with a church especially splendid, built in the manner and dimensions of the church of Clairvaux, worth seeing, crowded with various buildings, and, like a town, enclosed with fortifications and gates, of the Bernardine order; then old Dammona, near the Benedictine nuns, and another of the same name and order in Marne; Rottum, Warsum, Thesinga, Selwerd, Grijsmonnik, Wittewierum, Oosterwierum, Wierhuizen, Hillegerlaa, and Schildwolde; and also Eenum in the suburban prefecture. Besides, there were prepositures, a rich and honoured kind of priesthood, introduced into these places by the Bishop of Münster for the sake of good order and quiet: four, at Farmsum, Loppersum, Uithuizen, and Leens; a fifth at Hummerzijl, long since worn away. There was also a college of canons, or, as the custom of speech then went, a collegiate church, at Bedum, with a famous church there, beyond the measure of the rustic churches, since its first priest, not lightly given to another, usually one distinguished either by birth or by a reputation for learning, held great honour and authority among the people. Finally, the pastorate of Baflo in Hunsingo, and likewise Middelstum, once adorned by a vacancy in the office, for the Münster bishop.

units.la: Nec desunt hujus generis exempla quoq; alia, sed & pauca, & fere recentiora.
units.tr: Examples of this kind are not lacking elsewhere, but they are few and mostly more recent.

units.la: Porro prædiorum domini aut ipsi jus dicunt, aut aliis hominibus idoneis id delegant, prout cuiq; commodum aut gratum est. Est enim hoc arbitrij ipsorum.
units.tr: Moreover, the lords of the estates either pronounce judgment themselves or delegate it to other suitable men, as each finds it convenient or pleasing. For this is at their own discretion.

units.la: Jus dicens sive jure suo, sive delegato patria lingua Redgerus, nonnunquam etiam in locis ad occidentem Grietmannus more Tranflavicano vocatur: quæ voces judicem significant.
units.tr: The one who pronounces judgment, whether by his own right or by delegated right, is called in the native tongue Redjer, and sometimes in places toward the west Grietman, after the Trans-Lauwers manner; these words mean judge.

units.la: Is unum aliquem, ut nunc lege cautum est (nam plures fuere ante, si territorium vico uno majus esset) è territorio virum honestum dari sibi ab iis, qui territorio comprehenduntur, curat, cui Wedmanno nomen est, qui non solum assidet jus dicenti, sed iudicij quoq; minister est, & quaedam momenti minoris sine iudice per se expedit.
units.tr: He takes care, as the law now provides (for there were several before, when a district was larger than one village), to have given to him by those who are included in the district one honest man from the district, who is called Wedman; he not only sits beside the one pronouncing judgment but is also an officer of the court, and dispatches by himself certain matters of minor weight without the judge.

units.la: Qui in iuris dicundi munere est, merum & mixtum imperium habet, mandandi, prehendendi, multandi, coercendi, capite puniendi potestate praeditus est: multas & cetera iudicij commoda percipit ipse, aut cum Wedmanno pro rato communicat. Ab his tribunalibus omnib. appellatio est ad conventus iuridicos, aut cameram Hovetmanorum Groningensium, de quib. post nobis erit dicendi locus. Olim autem non Hovetmani solum, sed etiam consules senatusq; Groninganus plerisq; in causis appellati sunt, interponendi edicta ac mandata tum suo tum ordinum agrariorum nomine potestatem habuerunt, taufasq;[?] ipsas una cum ceteris in conventib. iuridicis recognovere & definivere, ut ex iis, quae infra de iure civitatis dicentur fiet manifestum.
units.tr: The one who holds the office of pronouncing judgment has merum and mixtum imperium, and is endowed with the power of commanding, arresting, fining, restraining, and punishing by death; he himself takes the fines and other profits of the court, or shares them with the Wedman in proportion. Appeal from all these courts lies to the judicial assemblies, or to the chamber of the Hoofdelingen of Groningen, of which we shall have occasion to speak later. Formerly, however, not only the Hoofdelingen but also the consuls and senate of Groningen were appealed to in most cases; they had the power to issue edicts and mandates both in their own name and in that of the agrarian orders, and they themselves recognised and settled the customs together with the others in the judicial assemblies, as will become clear from what is said below concerning the right of the city.

units.la: Sed & aliud quondam tribunal in agro fuit, & adhuc est, ad crimina graviora, quae capitalia putantur, controversiasq; de iurisdictionib. cognoscedas & iudicandas pertinet, & vocat communiter Oberrecht: quod vicos complures eiusdem vicinia colligit, e quibus iis, qui eo iure praediti sunt, (id similiter ut prius praediis certis cohaeret) vertente anno coeunt certo loco, ubi antiquitus tribunal hoc locatum fuit, & in leges ac incorruptam iustitiae administrationem iuramento obstringunt sese, ad quos vices illa annua rediere: ydemq; quoties res poscit, vocati conveniunt eodem, causasq; cognoscunt & sententias ferunt: tum domum in diversa recedunt. Et sunt tribunalia hujusmodi cis Hunes-gonios & Fivelingios complura, sed alibi eo, quo dixi, vocabulo, alibi die Langkrechte Teuto-nice nuncupata, nomine non re diversa. Atqui jus hoc, quod dixi prædiis connexum, in hac ratione nonnunquam vico quoq; integro uni aut alteri, id est, toti plebi vicanæ, non prædiis in vico singulis, alicubi & uni familiæ nobili pro toto vico coharet: eiq; vico aut familiæ nobili potestas hæc est perpetua. Qui potestatem hanc tenet jure loci eius, ubi sedes judicij est, is stato die cæteros omnes illuc coeuntes sacramenti religione obligat, eosdem, cum opus est, convocat, id quod ijs placet, pro sententia pronunciat. Et accidit non raro, ut qui in hoc judicatu est, reliquam quoq; jurisdictionem eodem tempore teneat.
units.tr: But there was once, and still is, another court in the district, belonging to graver crimes, which are thought capital, and to the hearing and judging of disputes over jurisdictions, and it is commonly called the Oberrecht; for it gathers together several villages of the same neighbourhood, and from among those who hold that right (which, like the estates before, is attached to certain holdings), each year in turn they meet at a fixed place where this court was anciently located, and bind themselves by oath to the laws and to the incorrupt administration of justice; and to whom that yearly turn has come round. Whenever the matter requires, those summoned gather there, hear the cases and pronounce sentences; then they go home to their separate places. There are several courts of this kind on this side of the Hunsingo and Fivelingo, but in some places they are called by the term I mentioned, in others by the German name Landrecht [Langkrechte], which differs in name but not in substance. Yet this right, which I have described as attached to estates, in this arrangement is sometimes attached, in some places, to a whole village for one or another, that is, to the entire village community, not to the holdings within the village, and in some places to a single noble family on behalf of the whole village; and this power is perpetual for that village or noble family. The one who holds this power, by right of the place where the seat of judgment is, binds all the others gathering there to the religion of an oath on the appointed day, summons them again when there is need, and pronounces as sentence what pleases them. And it not infrequently happens that whoever holds this judicial office holds the rest of the jurisdiction at the same time.

units.la: Præter hæc curationes quoq; sunt in hac regione bina, honestissima conditionis, nec minus ne-cessaria reip. quam utiles: Quarum altera ad aquarum clausturas, & quæ cum his copulata sunt, altera ad aggeres pertinet: illa deducendis è regione aquis pluviis & palustribus, aut rupto aggere infusis, hæc excludendis marinis aut fluviatilibus est instituta, utraq; cum potestate, & quadam imperij specie, imprimis prior. In ea qui sunt, non solum clausturis ipsis, quorum maximus usus, maxima impendia, præsunt, sed aquarum quoq; ductus, ac derivationes, & pontes amnibus & rivis impositos curant. Diuisi in classes aut col-legia plura fecundum regiones & claustra diversa: & classes singula in gradus diftinfta. In his in-seriores die Schlrichters[?] / superiores die Schepp-pers / summi die vppersie[?] Scheppers vocitantur. Et inferiores quidem singulis in classibus, quas Schlbesten[?] appellant, complures numero sunt, pro multitudine pagorum, qui qualibet classe comprehenduntur. Quilibet enim vicus ex fui medio edit unum duosve per eos, qui hoc ius habent, viros idoneos ac muneris capaces: qui omnes iurati in leges ad hanc rem pertinentes vicissim[?] ex sese edunt duos aut plures superiores velut προεστῶτας, praeditos potestate maiore, & fere ex nobilitate, aut ut ante hac tempora res habuit, ex ordine antistitum cænobijs praefeftorum. Atq; his, in claffib. tribus, qua totidem claustra Delfenfia curant, additus olim abbas Werumanus, velut praeses aut redlor fummus, penes quem suprema autoritas: in classe Winfumana, qua duplex quoq; est, praefeftus villa, quam in Hunef-gonius Adoardiy habebant: in Adoardiana cellarius, uti vocant, Adoardius. Reliqua classes hoc praeside carent. Et in uniuersum, ut per-plexa admodum atq; impedita aquaductuum ratio in hac regione est, dum sibi quifq; vicinia sua consulit ac studet, ita varia, inter fe difcre-pantia, intricata plurima sunt in toto hoc instituto, aliudq; alijs in claffib. ac locis valet. Qui in Delfucis classibus sunt, trienne munus habent, qui in Winfumana, & Adoardiana, bienne: alibi aliter. aliter. Potestas omnibus mandandi, vocandi, cognoscendi multandi secundum leges. Conve-niunt quotannis ter in classib. iuris deliberandi[?] & statuendi causa statuto tempore & loco. Et ut pleraq; alia communia habent, sic hos quoq; conventus classes Delficae propter claustrorum suorum coniunctionem: habent & Winsumanae duae, curantes claustra totidem. In his conventibus si res requirere videatur, decernitur tributum: id colligitur per inferiores: collectum traditur superioribus: ab his apud praesidem summum, vbi praeses huiusmodi est, depositur: is ex decreto com-muni impendit, quo poscit usus. In controversiis mos fuit in classibus Delficis, (puto etiam in Winsumana vtraq; & Adoardiana) si quis laesum se sententia aut mandato inferiorum arbitra-retur, appellare superiores, post hos ad cognitionem vocare etiam ceteros eiusdem ordinis in classib. isdem cum summo praeside, ab istis quod decre-tum esset, id ratum habere, nec tendere longius: Post ex conventione sic institutum inter Del-fenses, Winsumanos, Adoardios, vt ab unis ad proximos, a proximis ad tertios esset provocatio: in tertiorum sententia esset litium finis. Atq; hoc nunc quoq; apud eos in usu manet. In ca-teris classib. omnib. quae praefecturae veteris non sunt, Hovetmanorum Groningensium summum iudicium est.
units.tr: Besides these, there are in this region two other offices of the highest standing, no less necessary to the commonwealth than useful: the one concerns the water-sluices and the matters joined with them, the other the dykes. The former is established for draining off rain and marsh water from the district, or water let in when a dyke is breached, the latter for keeping out sea water or river water. Both carry authority and a certain semblance of rule, the former especially. Those who hold this office not only preside over the sluices themselves, whose use is greatest and whose costs are greatest, but also look after the water-courses and drainage channels and the bridges laid over streams and ditches. They are divided into classes or colleges according to districts and the different sluices, and each class is distinguished into grades. Among these the lower officials are called die Schlrichters[?], the higher die Schepp-pers, and the highest die vppersie[?] Scheppers. The lower officials in each class, which they call Schlbesten[?], are numerous, according to the number of villages included in each class. For every village elects from its midst one or two suitable men, capable of the office and holding the right to do so. All of these, sworn to the laws pertaining to this matter, in turn elect from themselves two or more superiors, as it were προεστῶτες [chiefs], endowed with greater authority, and generally drawn from the nobility or, as things stood before these times, from the order of prelates set over monasteries. To these, in the three classes which look after the three Delfzijl sluices, was formerly added the abbot of Wierum, as president or chief rector, in whose hands lay the supreme authority; in the Winsum class, which is also double, a steward of the estate that the Hunesgonius family held of Adoardi; in the Adoardi class, a cellarer, as they call him, Adoardius. The remaining classes have no president. And in general, since the system of water-courses in this region is very intricate and beset with difficulties, while each person looks after and attends to his own neighbourhood, so the arrangements are many, varied, at odds with one another and tangled throughout the whole institution, and one thing holds force in one class or place and another in others. Those in the Delfzijl classes hold office for three years, those in the Winsum and Adoardi classes for two; elsewhere it is otherwise. All have power to order, to summon, to examine and to fine according to the laws. They meet three times a year in their classes, at a fixed time and place, for deliberating on law and making decisions. And as they have many other things in common, so these classes of Delfzijl also hold assemblies because of the joining of their sluices; the two Winsum classes, which look after as many sluices, do likewise. In these assemblies, if the matter seems to require it, a tax is decreed; it is collected through the lower officials, handed over to the superiors, and by them deposited with the chief president, where there is one of that kind; he spends it by common decree as need demands. In disputes it was the custom in the Delfzijl classes (I think also in both Winsum and Adoardi classes) that if anyone thought himself wronged by a sentence or order of the lower officials, he could appeal to the superiors; after these, they summoned to the hearing also the rest of the same rank in the classes, together with the chief president, and whatever decree was made by them they held valid, going no further. Afterwards, by agreement, it was thus instituted among the Delfzijl, Winsum and Adoardi people that appeal should go from one to the nearest, from the nearest to the third, and the judgment of the third should be the end of the lawsuits. And this still holds among them in use now. In the other classes which are not of the old prefecture, the court of the Hovetmen of Groningen is the supreme tribunal.

units.la: Aggerum praefecti, & ipsi secundum regiones ac loca inter se distinguuntur, potestatemq; am-plam habent, parem pene cum priorib. sed decreta omnium, omnium extra eandem præfecturam vetere, hovet-mannis subjecta sunt. In præfectura veteri, ut illi, sic hi quoque senatum urbis summum judicem agnoscunt. Operam dant, ut aggeres fluctuum violentia objecti sarti tecti ferventur[?], disiecti reficiantur, interdum augeantur, proferantur, contrahantur ex usu patria. De quibus dicere plura non libet, ne fiam prolixior.
units.tr: The prefects of the dykes are themselves also distinguished from one another according to districts and places, and they have wide authority, almost equal to that of the former, but the decrees of all of them outside the same old prefecture are subject to the Hovetmen. In the old prefecture, these as well as the others acknowledge the city senate as supreme judge. They take care that the dykes, set against the violence of the waves, are kept whole, repaired when broken, and at times enlarged, extended or narrowed, as the custom of the country requires. I do not wish to say more about these, lest I become too long.

units.la: Denique præpositi, quos dixi, singuli suis in finibus olim descriptis eutaxia Ecclesiastica præ-sidebant ante hæc tempora, & sacris de rebus judicebant, assidentibus sacerdotibus sacerdotum causas cognoscebant, delicta omnia contra matrimonii leges castigabant[?], ædium[?] ac rerum sacrarum curam gerebant, rationes creditorum[?] examinabant, fœneratores comprimebant, pœnas ab ijs poscebant. Præter hos Officialis quoq; & commissarius, ut vocabantur in curatione rerum talium pro episcopo erant: sed in populo libero tantum non poterant, quantum fere alijs in regionib. solent.
