Quæ omnia duraverunt, quandiu regnum pontificium cum imperio Hispanico hic stetit: eo vero finito, hæc quoq; interiere. Quib. quæ succedere classib. congregandis, & habendis synodis, ut verbo divino & primæva ecclesia propiora, sic usu quoq; ipso, si pietas modo in virentib.[?] sit, sine dubio meliora. Sacer-dotes in agro numerati olim supra cc. xx, quantulo[?] in spacio[?] præter tot monachos & monachas, quot capita multis, & quidem peramplis ac opulentis cœnobijs potuere: quorum numerus fide[?] multo major fuit. Populi universus cum reliquis Frisiis à teporib. Caroli Magni ad Saxonum arma per annos fere DCC liber fuit, suiq; juris, domini nescius: summi principis Cæsaris solummodo majestatem comiter agnovit, nec tributis pressus, nec angarys obnoxius, omnisq; adeo servitutis ignarus. Qua si quis cuncta consideret, intelliget sane, haud facile populum alium rus colentem posse reperiri in his orbis regionib. qui libertate ac felicitate hunc antecesserit. Sed ipsa luxurians ac pene nimia libertas saepe magno ei malo fuit, veramq; & genuinam libertatem prope evertit. Nam ambitiosa ingenia factiones peperere, pestem liberis populis proprias, sibiq; potentiam struxerunt. Inde ad tumultus & bella civilia ventum, regioq; graviter afflicta. Ad hæc singula regionis partes separatim sibi consulere, suisq; commodis studere, quid in commune omnibus, & toti regioni expediret, non expendere, nec istuc consilia referre: hinc rursus simultates, odia, iniuriæ: ex injuriis eadem armata vis, & furor intestinus. Nec iudicia sine vitiis ingentibus fuere, gratia, pecunia, odio, inimicitia corrupta: & licentia peccatum frequenter: ea occasione pax turbata. Quibus malis remedium societate Groningensium pluries quaesitum, eaq; ancora fluctuans, & vix se sustinens libertas periculis erepta firmataq;, eo medio judiciorum integritas reparata, & per aliquot sa-cula conservata, ac denique licentia repressa fuit. In legibus suis populus ista habet memoratu digna, Pacta dotalia rite inita, ut mos aut jus regionis poscit, rata sunto, testamenta nisi de bonis acquisitis, acquisitis, non sunto. Res soli ex hereditatibus profecta, aedificia, & quicquid in bonis immobilibus, à defuncto relicta ad proximos sanguine devolvuntur, nisi aliter pactis dotalibus sit eautum.
units.tr: Finally, the prelates I mentioned, each within his own bounds once marked out, formerly presided over ecclesiastical discipline in these times, and judged in sacred matters; with the priests sitting beside them, they examined the causes of the clergy, punished all offences against the laws of marriage, had charge of the church buildings and sacred goods, examined the accounts of creditors, restrained usurers and exacted penalties from them. Besides these, the official and the commissary, as they were called, acted in the management of such affairs in place of the bishop; but among the free people they could not do as much as they usually do in other regions. All these things lasted as long as the papal rule stood here together with the Spanish dominion; when that ended, these also perished. What should succeed them, for gathering the classes and holding synods, is closer both to the divine Word and to the primitive Church, and so, in practice itself, if only piety flourishes, is undoubtedly better. Priests counted in the countryside were once more than 220, in so small a space, besides as many monks and nuns as the many and very large and wealthy monasteries could hold; their number was far greater than is believed. The whole people, together with the other Frisians, remained free and subject to no one from the times of Charlemagne until the wars against the Saxons, for nearly 700 years; they acknowledged only the majesty of the supreme prince, the Emperor, courteously, pressed by no tributes and liable to no forced services, and wholly ignorant of servitude. If anyone considers all this, he will clearly understand that hardly any other people tilling the land can be found in these regions of the world who have surpassed this one in liberty and happiness. But their luxuriant and almost excessive liberty was often a great evil to them, and nearly overturned their true and genuine liberty. For ambitious minds bred factions, a plague peculiar to free peoples, and built up power for themselves. Hence came tumults and civil wars, and the region was grievously afflicted. Besides, each part of the region looked to its own interests separately and studied its own advantage, and did not weigh what was useful in common for all and for the whole region, nor refer such counsels there; hence in turn rivalries, hatreds, injuries; from the injuries came armed force and internal fury. Nor were the courts free from great faults: they were corrupted by favour, money, hatred and enmity; and licence often made sin, and peace was disturbed on that occasion. For these evils a remedy was sought many times through the alliance of the Groningers; and by that anchor the liberty, which was tossing and barely holding itself up, was snatched from dangers and strengthened, by that means the integrity of the courts was restored, kept for several centuries, and finally licence was repressed. In their laws the people have these things worth recording: dowry agreements duly entered into, as the custom or law of the region requires, shall stand; wills shall not be valid except concerning goods acquired. Property of the soil that came from inheritances, buildings, and whatever immovable goods were left by the deceased, pass to the nearest by blood, unless otherwise provided in the dowry agreements.

units.la: ℰMobilia omnia, quae conjuges matrimonium ineuntes possident, & in usum matrimonii conferunt, quaeve stante matrimonio ex hereditatib. accrescunt, omnia item industria conjugum acquisita, etiam sine pactis dotalibus conjugum sunto pari jure, alteroq; defuncto semissis haeredum ejus esto, reliquum superstiti maneto.
units.tr: All movable goods which spouses possess when entering marriage and bring into the use of the marriage, or which accrue from inheritances during the marriage, and likewise all goods acquired by the industry of the spouses, even without dowry agreements, shall belong to the spouses by equal right; when one dies, half shall be his heirs', and the rest shall remain with the survivor.

units.la: Donationes inter vivos robur habento, si bonorum cessio à donatore vivente fiat.
units.tr: Gifts between living persons shall have force, if a cession of goods is made by the donor while living.

units.la: Quae propter nuptias fiunt in pactis dotalibus, ut ratae sint, in pactis dotalia haeredes proximi, imprimis parentes, avi, aviae, fratres, sorores consentiunto.
units.tr: The marriage settlements that are drawn up on account of a wedding, so that they may stand, shall have the agreement of the nearest heirs, above all the parents, grandparents, brothers and sisters, in the marriage contracts.

units.la: ℰMinores annis xxv nuptias inire, & pacta dotalia scribere si volent, sub curatoribus aut tutoribus agentes, eos scribendo adhibento. Cades [?] quae prius pecunia luebantur, nunc ex lege capitis poenam habent. Cateris maleficiis omnibus graves quoque poenae sunt in legibus descriptae.
units.tr: Minors under twenty-five years of age, if they wish to enter into marriage and draw up marriage contracts, shall have them written up by their guardians or tutors acting with them, and with those present as witnesses. Crimes which were formerly punished with money are now punished by the law with capital punishment. For all other offences, severe penalties are also laid down in the laws.

units.la: Hactenus de agro seorsim: sequitur de urbe.
units.tr: So much for the country considered separately; now follows the city.
Concerning the City of Groningen.

units.la: Hujus[?] situs sic habet. Decurrunt ex Drentia per præfecturam suburbanam superiorem duo amnes, quos dixi, Humesius, & Aha, pariter ab Euronoto in circium euntes, non longo inter se spacio disiuncti, nonnunquam VIII, nonnunquam VI, nonnullubi etiam IIII tantum stadys, feruntur q; per humiles & uliginosos hinc inde agros. In quorum amnium medio ab ipsis humilibus agris, qui latiusculè ab amnium ripis se extendunt, dorsum paulatim se erigit editius, ac molliter declive utrimq;, à Drentia campis sublimibus ac spaciosis veniens, velut lingua exilis, sed longa, & sensim se versus finem coartans, omnem fere præfecturam suburbanam percurrēs. In ejus dorsi parte pene ultima, qua amnium alter Aha ipsum dorsum propius accedens quasi stringit, posita Groninga est, arctior olim & in ipsissimo solum dorso aedificata, deinde ampliata paulatim, & devexa ac humiliora utrinque largius complexa, loco perquam felice, curribusq; & navigijs ad importandum pariter commodo, segetibus & pascuis in [illegible, ~2 letters]itu inprimis fortunato.
units.tr: Its situation is as follows. Two streams, the ones I have mentioned, the Humesius and the Aha, flow down from Drenthe through the upper suburban district, both running from the south-east towards the north-west, separated from each other by no great distance: sometimes eight stadia, sometimes six, and in some places only four. They flow through low and marshy fields on either side. Between these two streams, rising gradually from the low fields themselves, which spread out fairly wide from the banks of the streams, a ridge rises somewhat higher. It slopes gently on both sides, coming down from the high and spacious plains of Drenthe, like a slender but long tongue, gradually narrowing towards its end, and running through almost the whole suburban district. In the nearly last part of this ridge, where the Aha, the one of the two streams, comes close to the ridge and as it were grips it, Groningen is situated. Formerly it was narrower and built on the very crest of the ridge; later it was gradually enlarged and embraced more widely the lower-lying ground on either side. It is a place exceedingly favourable, equally convenient for carts and for ships to bring in goods, and especially fortunate in its crops and pastures.

units.la: Dorsum autem illud modicè ad bina circiter stadia ultra urbem boream[?] versus procurrit, ibiq; molliter se deponens in humilem & æquam plani-ciem definit, media fere inter urbem & cœnobiū Selwerdicum via. Et amnis quidem Aha, ut nunc dudum res habuit, & habet, in angulo ur-bis, qui inter meridiem & occidentem prominet, mœnibusque insinuat, per amplos fornices sub val-lo structos, intraque mœnia occiduo in latere ur-bem stringens longo tractu, & ponte arcuati o-peris laterití junctus tandem in angulo altero oc-casum æstivum spectante per similes fornices val-lo subjectos ex urbe rursum exit alveo profundo & capace multarum navium, ibiq; in ipso egressu amni alteri Hunesæ ad urbem derivato, duobusq; a lateribus ortivo & boreo mœnia foris complexo miscetur. Hunesus vero urbi allapsus in ipso orien-tis angulo, atque ibi muro transverso rejectus, ne ab austrino quoque latere mœnia circumveniat, & ea parte etiam Aha urbem ingressuro se jun-gat, ortivo latere vallum radens, suburbium ejus loci insigne, duabus objectum portis ab ipsa urbe secludit, eodemq; modo longius progrediens, ac a septentrione in occidente sen[?] sim se flectens tandem eo, quo dixi, loco sub ipsi[?] mœnib. Aha cofunditur.
units.tr: The ridge, however, runs on moderately for about two stadia beyond the city towards the north, and there, gently sinking, it ends in a low and level plain, lying roughly midway between the city and the monastery of Selwerd. The Aha, as the matter has long stood and still stands, flows past the corner of the city, which projects between the south and the west, and it pushes into the walls through wide arches built under the rampart. Within the walls it skirts the city along its western side for a long stretch, and, joined by an arched bridge of brick, it finally leaves the city again at the other corner, which faces the north-west, through similar arches beneath the rampart. It flows out in a deep channel capable of carrying many ships. There, at the very point of its exit, it mingles with the other stream, the Hunesus, which has been diverted to the city, and which surrounds the walls on the outside on two sides, the east and the north. The Hunesus, having reached the city at the very eastern corner, and there being turned back by a transverse wall so that it does not also encircle the walls on the southern side, and so that it may join the Aha on that side as it enters the city, skirts the rampart on the eastern side. It separates from the city, by two gates, the suburb of that place, which is notable. Continuing further in the same way, and gradually bending from the north towards the west, it finally joins the Aha at the place I have mentioned, just beneath the walls.

units.la: Urbs ampla hodie, & spaciosa, ac publicis privatisq; ædificijs magnifica, tum foris duobus, & munitionibus maximis superba. Ambitus mœnium ejus in exteriore fossa labro passibus bis M. DC. XVIII patet, suburbijs exclusis. Fana in ea sunt in universum XII. ex quibus tria sunt parochialia, uti vocant, quinque mo-nastica, quatuor xenodochiis conjuncta. Parochiale amplissimum cum editissima & firmissimi ac peregregij operis turri, quadam[?] fastigio jam mutila & trunca, [?]Martinianum: Antiquissimum & cum urbe ipsa, aut ante urbem natum, ac, ut quidam putant, superstitioni Ethnicæ quondam dicatum, Walburgicum, in eadem quadrata area, seu cœmiterio spatioso, cum [?]Martiniano, forma pene rotunda, ac plane diversa a formis templorum communium; cui etiam cohæret sublimis fastigij turris: utrumq; hoc in parte urbis inter orientem & boream proximè ad ipsa mœnia, & [?]Martinianum etiam in angulo fori majoris.
units.tr: Today the city is large and spacious, magnificent with public and private buildings, and proud both of its two gates and of its very great fortifications. The circuit of its walls, measured along the outer edge of the ditch, extends to 2,618 paces, the suburbs being excluded. There are twelve churches in it altogether, of which three are parish churches, as they are called, five are monastic, and four are attached to hospitals. The largest parish church, with a very high tower of most solid and excellent workmanship, now maimed and truncated at its spire, is called St Martin's. The oldest, which was born with the city itself or before it, and which, as some think, was once dedicated to Ethnic superstition, is the Walburgis church. It stands in the same square area, or spacious churchyard, as St Martin's, and is almost round in shape, quite different from the forms of ordinary churches; to it too is attached a lofty tower with a spire. Both of these lie in the part of the city between the east and the north, very close to the walls themselves, and St Martin's is also at the corner of the greater market.

units.la: Tertium in parte urbis in occidentem vergente, ab Aha[?] amne cognominatum, quondam Nicolao, nunc [?]Mariæ virgini sacrum, ( Vnser lieben Frouwen thor Atha ) foro alteri accubans, cum visenda etiam turre alte fastigiata; in qua nola complures egregio inter se soni temperamento, concentu harmonico horis singulis belle præcinunt, easdemque in semisses dividunt, cum voluptate civium, & peregrinorum audientium. Et secundum hæc tria templa tota civitas in tres fuit distincta parochias. Nunc Walburgica [?]Martiniana addita est, & ex tribus duæ factæ. Ex monasticis amplissimum Franciscanum cum cœnobio spatioso in urbis fere medio; quod cœnobium jam schola literaria sedes est toti civitati communis: alterum Jacobæum cum cœnobio Monachorum Dominicanorum in boreo urbis latere ad ipsa mœnia, brevissimo intervallo dissitum ab area, in qua Walburgicum & Martinianum: Tertium monachorum, quos fratres nuncupabant, modicum, item cum coenobio in angulo areae eiusdem Walburgicae boreo, ac in latere urbis eodem, moenibus etiam contiguum; id coenobium ante triginta circiter annos in sedem & aulam Knifii primi & postremi episcopi Groning: versum; deinde gubernatoris provinciae domicilium satium[?]: quem usum etiam nunc praestat: quartum monialium sororum S. Clarae cum claustro item peramplo, spacio inter Franciscanos & Jacobaos medio: quintum virginum nobilium non initiatarum angustius, Franciscanis cohaerens ad boream. Ex xenodochicis sanis maximum, & parochici instar, ad S. Spiritum in latere civitatis austrino, cum xenodocheio peraplo, ac ad coenobij iusti modum: secundum Gertrudis in oppidi parte ortiva iuxta moenia similiter, cum Xenodocheio bene dotato: tertium Jacobi modicum in extremo urbis angulo, qui est versus occasum aestivum, prope portam, quae a machina tra-ctoria[?], quam gruem vocant, ex similitudine lon-gi colli, nominatur: quartum Antonianum porta orientali cohaerens, omnium minimum: utrumque horum postremorum itidem cum xenodocheo, sed postremum angustum. Fora, ut dixi, in urbe duo insignia & spatiosa; alterum ex latitudine cognominatu (Dat brede markt) rara magnitudinis, & vix alibi in civitate pari inveniendae; incipiens ab area Martiniana, & c.LXXIX passuum spacio inde in occidente hybernum hybernum procurrens, latitudine paulo minore; intra cuius ambitum curia modica cum œnopolio curia haud paulo majore cum turricula in vertice, contiguis parietibus: a quo trames perbrevis in alterum superiore etiam longius, Piscarium, quod piscium illic mercatus fit, nuncupatum; in cuius fine area ac templum, quod dixi, parochiale tertium ab amne Aha nomen ferens. Id in longitudinem patet, si templi aream comprehenderis paff. cc. XLI, si non comprehenderis paff.
units.tr: The third, in the part of the city sloping towards the west, takes its name from the river Aha. It was formerly dedicated to St Nicholas, now to the Virgin Mary (the church "Unser lieben Frouwen thor Atha"). It lies beside the other market, and has a tower with a tall spire, worth seeing, in which several bells, harmoniously tuned among themselves, ring out beautifully every hour in harmonious concert, and divide the hours into halves, to the delight of the citizens and of the strangers who hear them. According to these three churches, the whole city was divided into three parishes. Now the Walburgis has been added to St Martin's, and from three there have become two. Of the monastic churches, the largest is the Franciscan, with a spacious monastery almost in the middle of the city; this monastery is now the seat of the Latin school, common to the whole city. The second is the Jacobean church with the monastery of the Dominican friars, on the northern side of the city, close to the walls, at a very short distance from the area in which the Walburgis and St Martin's stand. The third is a small one of the friars whom they called Brothers, also with its monastery, at the northern corner of the same Walburgis area, and on the same side of the city, also adjoining the walls. This monastery, about thirty years ago, was turned into the seat and palace of Knifius, the first and last bishop of Groningen; afterwards it became the residence of the governor of the province, and it still serves that purpose. The fourth is the monastery of the nuns of St Clare, with a cloister likewise very large, in the space between the Franciscans and the Jacobeans. The fifth is that of the noble unprofessed virgins, rather narrow, adjoining the Franciscans to the north. Among the hospital churches, the largest, which is like a parish church, is that of the Holy Spirit on the southern side of the city, with a very large hospice, and fashioned after the manner of a proper monastery. The second, that of St Gertrude, in the eastern part of the town, likewise beside the walls, with a well-endowed hospice. The third is the small church of St James, in the farthest corner of the city, which is towards the north-west, near the gate named after the hoisting machine, which they call the crane, from the likeness of its long neck. The fourth, St Anthony's, adjoining the eastern gate, is the smallest of all. Each of these last two has likewise a hospice, but the last is narrow. There are, as I have said, two notable and spacious markets in the city. One, named from its breadth (the Broad Market), is of rare size, and hardly to be found of equal size anywhere else in a city. It begins at the area of St Martin's and runs on from there towards the west for 179 paces, of a width somewhat less. Within its circuit stands a small court together with the cloth-hall, a court by no means smaller, with a little turret on its top, the walls being contiguous. From it a very short street leads to the other, which is further up, called the Fish Market, because the fish market is held there. At its end is the area and the parish church, which I mentioned, the third, bearing its name from the river Aha. It extends in length, if you include the church area, 241 paces; if you do not include it, 243 paces.

units.la: cc. XLIII.Ad hac fora duo, quod mireris, capita non minus XVII platearum, & fere amplissimarum in tota urbe pertinent: e quib. praecipua VI a totidem urbis portis (portae autem sunt in universum VIII) recta linea veniunt, Polana, Orientalis, Dominica, Pontana, Botterana, Ebbinganaq[?]; eadem tota fere urbe longissima, excepta Polana, qua paulo est brevior: omnes suis portis cognomines, praeter Pontanam, qua a ponte Aha impolito ad Amnicam portam, unde procedit, nomen invenit.
units.tr: Besides these two markets, which may surprise you, there run into them no fewer than seventeen streets, and these fairly large, throughout the whole city. Of these the chief six come in a straight line from as many gates of the city (there are eight gates in all): the Polana, the Eastern, the Dominican, the Pontana, the Botterana and the Ebbingana. These are almost the longest in the whole city, except the Polana, which is a little shorter. All of them take their names from their gates, except the Pontana, which takes its name from the unpaved bridge over the Aha, from which it runs to the Amnica gate.

units.la: Catera dua porta pla-teas excipiunt etiam suas, sed per angulum a reliquis derivatas, quarum portarum altera a grue machina (Kraenpoorte) altera ab attollendis lapidibus ut vulgus arbitratur, ut autem veritas habet, a ponticulo lapideo, qui quondam isto in latere civitatis fuit, quem Germani Stenentill dicunt, (Stenentilpoorte[?]) nomen ferunt. Platea in urbe majores ad XXXVI[?], minores VII, praeter angiportus aliquot. Antiquitus, cum minor esset civitatis fortuna, ut omnia solent a parvis principijs oriri, pro mœnibus usa est septo ligneo è trabibus contexta. Deinde ante annos plus minus CCCC. L. muro lateritio firmo, cum fossa in morem reliquarum urbium cincta fuit, angustiore etiam tum, quàm jam est, ambitu. Nunc ab eo fere tempore, quo tormentorum æneorum usus percrebuit, maximè verò à Caroli bellatoris ducis Burgundiæ ævo, cum is arma Frisiæ minaretur, vallo terreo cum fossa patentiore ampliatis terminis est circumdata: cujus valli ambitus est, in summa superficie, passuum MM. CC. LXXXVI, & in eo mola, quæ ventis agitantur, XII; duæque præter has extra mœnia in latere septentr. Hac amplificatione mœnium postrema versus ortum, meridiem, occasum accessio urbi facta; solum latus boreum, ab eâ amne urbem egrediente, portaque vicina cum parte lateris ortivi ad portam usque Polonam, loco motum non est: atque ita Botterana quoque porta, & Ebbingana, & Polana sedem suam retinuere; reliquæ, maximè Dominica, Orientalis, Steentillana, sunt promotæ. Ex portis his Polona pyramidibus excelsis ac magnis moles duabus, Orientalis etiam quatuor sed gracilioribus, Dominica quinque similibus magnifica specie longè lateque conspicua, decorem civitati non exiguum addidere. Nunc duæ posteriores quondam contra Carolum Burgundum extructæ, altera à Casparo Roblesio gubernatore confulto anno M. D. LXXV, altera tormentorum aneorum vi postrema obsidione, qua reducta ad foederis Belgici societatem civitas est, anno M. D. XCIV, pyramidib. privata, totoq; opere lateritio superiore deiecto humiliata sunt, vt iam supra vallum nihil earum appareat. Ad Dominicam vero Hispani ad initia belli huius Belgici validam & amplam excitaverant arcem quinquangularem, singulis in angulis ingenti pro pugnaculo terreo instructam, partem moenium, ipsamq; portam complexam, qua tamen arx antequam perfici posset, a transactione Ganda-vensi publicata, capto a militibus suis Casparo Roblesio gubernatore, per cives rursum eversa est.
units.tr: The other two gates also have streets of their own, but these are branched off at a corner from the rest. One of these gates takes its name from the crane machine (Kraenpoorte), and the other, as the common people think, from the lifting of stones, but as the truth has it, from a little stone bridge which was formerly on that side of the city, which the Germans call the Stenentill (Stenentilpoorte). There are, in the city, about thirty-six greater streets and seven lesser ones, besides several alleys. In antiquity, when the city's fortune was smaller, as all things are wont to arise from small beginnings, it used as its walls a wooden fence made of timbers interlaced. Then, about four hundred and fifty years ago, it was enclosed with a firm brick wall, in the manner of the other cities, with a ditch, its circuit being then still narrower than it is now. Since about the time when the use of bronze cannon became widespread, and especially in the age of Charles the warlike, Duke of Burgundy, when he threatened the arms of Friesland, it was surrounded with an earthen rampart and a wider ditch, and its boundaries were enlarged. The circuit of this rampart, measured along its top surface, is 2,286 paces, and on it there are twelve windmills, which are driven by the winds; and outside the walls, on the northern side, there are two more. By this enlargement of the walls, an addition was made to the city on the last side, towards the east, south and west. Only the northern side, where the river leaves the city, and the gate nearby, together with the part of the eastern side up to the Polish gate, was not moved; and so the Botterana gate, the Ebbingana and the Polana have kept their place. The others, especially the Dominican, the Eastern and the Steentill gates, have been pushed out. Of these gates, the Polana was adorned with two large and lofty pyramids, the Eastern with four, but more slender, and the Dominican with five similar ones, magnificent in appearance and conspicuous far and wide, which added no small grace to the city. Now the two last of these, built formerly against Charles of Burgundy, the one in the year 1575 by order of the governor Caspar Robles, the other in the year 1594 by the force of bronze cannon in the last siege, by which the city was brought back into the fellowship of the Belgic covenant, were deprived of their pyramids, and with the whole upper brick work thrown down, they have been so lowered that nothing of them now appears above the rampart. At the Dominican gate, indeed, the Spaniards, at the beginning of this Belgic war, had raised a strong and large fortress of five corners, equipped at each corner with a huge earthen bastion, which embraced a part of the walls and the gate itself. But before this citadel could be completed, it was thrown down again by the citizens, after the Pacification of Ghent had been published and the governor Caspar Robles had been taken by his own soldiers.

units.la: Omitto propugnacula e terra aggerata magna molis, quorum tria intra fossam vallum ambientem, vallo ipsi connexa, duo ad boream portas tegentia, tertium in australi parte: quartum item, sed extra fossam, nec vallo contiguum, portae Orientali objectum: adhaec alia duo eiusdem generis, vallo coniuncta sed minora: & praeter ea ex lateribus structa VII, quaedam turriculis fastigata, quaedam sine fastigiis: omnia munienda urbi contra vim hostilem instituta.
units.tr: I pass over the bulwarks of heaped earth and great mass: three of them lie within the ditch that surrounds the rampart, joined to the rampart itself, two of them guarding the gates on the north side and a third on the south; a fourth, likewise, but outside the ditch and not contiguous with the rampart, stands opposite the East Gate; besides these there are two more of the same kind, joined to the rampart but smaller; and in addition to these, seven built of brick, some crowned with small towers and some without. All of them were constructed to defend the city against hostile violence.

units.la: Quinetiam durante hoc bello Belgico, suburbium quod ante dixi, & ingens, & aedificiis non infrequent, a navicularys habitatum, a quorum navigiis & amne nomen quoq; traxit (Schutendiep, n. vulgo noncupatur) duabus portis praetextum, Polana ac Steentillana, vallo terreo haud infirmo, & fossa bene profunda est incinctum, vt pene non minus urbe vrbe ipsa tutum sit ab hostili incursu & vi, ac quasi urbi adiectum. Cetera suburbia egregia, praesertim ante portam Dominicam, Botteranam, Amnicam belli injuriis iam periere: quamquam ante ex[?] Amnicam vallum cum fossa, castelli in modum, ductum partem suburbij etiam nunc includat. Id vero suburbium, q; ante portam Dominicam fuit, longissime procurrens cum pago proximo Helpena, qui VIII stadijs non minus ab urbe recessit, continua domorum serie pene se coniunxit. Et praeter suburbia haec toto meridionali & septentrionali latere (ea est civitatis longitudo) in eodem dorso editiore, in quo urbs est sita, amoenis ac sumptuosis hortis, & aedificijs elegantib. totu post pomaria locus longe lateq; obsitus ac conteclus fuit. Taceo insulas virorum nobilium complures in meridionali potissimum plaga. Cuncta nunc per bellum vastata, vix ut hic illic reliquiae tenues appareant. De-niq; situs urbis in universum hujusmodi, ut quae-admodum per amnes, ac rivos, quos dixi, ex Amafo fl. ac Lavica ostio, ipsoq; adeo mari, itemq; ex agro circumiecto, maioribus, minoribusq; navigijs, sic per Drentiam itinera nullo non anni tempore idonea, ex ipsa Drentia & caeteris circumiectis Germaniae partibus rhedis ac currib. percommode res omnes importari in eam, & rursum exportari possint. Tanto quidem ipsa etiam hinc felicior, quod in omni agro in omnem mundi plagam circumfuso sola sine aemulis negotiationes possideat.
units.tr: Moreover, during this Belgian war, the suburb I mentioned before, large and not thinly built up with houses, inhabited by boatmen, from whose boats and the river it also took its name (commonly called Schutendiep), is protected by two gates, the Polana and the Steentillana, and is enclosed by an earthen rampart of no small strength and a fairly deep ditch, so that it is almost as safe from hostile attack and violence as the city itself, and seems joined to the city. The other suburbs, which were splendid, especially the ones before the Sunday Gate, the Botteran and the Amnica Gate, have already perished from the injuries of war, although the rampart with its ditch, built in the manner of a castle before the Amnica Gate, still encloses part of the suburb even now. But that suburb which lay before the Sunday Gate, stretching out very far, almost joined itself by a continuous row of houses to the nearby village of Helpen, which lies no less than eight stadia from the city. And besides these suburbs, along the whole south and north side (that is the length of the city), on the same higher ridge on which the city is situated, the whole place was widely and densely covered with pleasant and costly gardens and elegant buildings, behind the orchards. I pass over the many islands of noblemen, chiefly on the south side. All these things have now been laid waste by the war, so that scarcely a thin remnant appears here and there. Finally, the situation of the city in general is such that, just as goods can be brought in and taken out again very conveniently by the rivers and streams I have described, from the Amasis River and the mouth of the Lavica, and even from the sea itself, and from the surrounding countryside by larger and smaller ships, so the roads through Drenthe are suitable at every season of the year, and from Drenthe itself and the other neighbouring parts of Germany all goods can be very conveniently imported into it and exported again by wagons and carts. Indeed it is all the more fortunate in this respect, because it alone, in the whole countryside spread around on every side of the world, holds its trade without rivals.

units.la: De antiquitatib. ejus primis, & de origine quae vulgo feruntur, incerta sunt, pleraq; etiam indubie fabulosa, ac inepta: qualia sunt, quae nugator Kempius memorat. Nomen à viridib. pratú aut arboretis, quæ sunt circum circa, videri potest deductum; cum quo convenerit Gracum φυλλέιον (si recta hæc lectio) veteribus circiter hæc loca collocatum. Melius forte à Gruno aut Gryno principe vel conditore loci, non illo quidem Troiano, aut Frisonis nepote originis indicia (nugæ enim ista sunt anilis) sed homine Frisio: Quo cum congruere videtur forma vocabuli, quo Frisij & olim & hodie tam occidui quà orientales appellare hàc civitatem solent, GRINSE aut GRENSE eam vocantes. Est autem frequens in tota hac vicinia derivata nomina hujusmodi à proprijs hominum, aut fluminum, aut aliarum rerum, similium nominibus in fine per INGE formare; ut Hun-finge, Fivelinge, Offringe, Ruftringe, Harlinge, Hufinge, Efinge, Wetzinge, Thezinge, Thedinge, Appinge, Cortinge, Femminge, Pauvinge, Baltringe, Schuringe, Mackinge, Mitlinge, Tinaldinge, & in ipsa vrbe Ebbinge, Botteringe, Harderinge, Folkeringe, Gaddinge, Gelkinge, ut patronymica infinita ejusdem definentia in Frisia & Drentia prætereamus.
units.tr: Concerning its earliest antiquities and its origin, which are commonly reported, there is uncertainty, and most of them are indeed plainly fabulous and silly, such as those which the trifler Kempius relates. The name may seem to be derived from the green meadows or the groves that surround it; with this agrees the Greek φυλλέιον (if this reading is correct), placed by the ancients roughly in these places. Perhaps better, it comes from Grunus or Grynus, a prince or founder of the place; not indeed that Trojan, or a grandson of Frisius by origin (for those things are old wives' tales), but a Frisian man. With this the form of the word seems to agree, by which the Frisians, both western and eastern, have been accustomed both formerly and today to call this city, calling it GRINSE or GRENSE. Moreover, it is common throughout this whole neighbourhood to form derived names of this kind from personal names, or river names, or names of other similar things, with the ending INGE; such as Hunfinge, Fivelinge, Offringe, Ruftringe, Harlinge, Hufinge, Efinge, Wetzinge, Thezinge, Thedinge, Appinge, Cortinge, Femminge, Pauvinge, Baltringe, Schuringe, Mackinge, Mitlinge, Tinaldinge, and in the city itself Ebbinge, Botteringe, Harderinge, Folkeringe, Gaddinge, Gelkinge; not to mention the countless patronymics of the same ending in Friesland and Drenthe.

units.la: DE CONIVNCTIONE CIVITATIS GRONINGÆ CVM VLTRAIECTINIS.
units.tr: ON THE UNION OF THE CITY OF GRONINGEN WITH THE UTRECHTERS.

units.la: P[?]Rimam sub hoc nomine mentionem ejus in probatis & fidis literarum monumentis (nam de tabula Romana ætate ac fide cur dubitem, demonstratum à me alibi est) usurpatam invenio in instrumento quodam donationis, quod est in tabulino Ecclesiæ Ultrajectinæ, scripto & signato anno Christi M. XL : quo in instrumento HENRICVS III Imp. cognomento NIGER, filius Conradi II Saliqui, eidem Ecclesiæ tempore Bernoldi præsulis confert jus prædij, quod ipse in villa GRONINGA videbatur possidere. Qua de donatione pauca dicam, ut & antiquitatem & veritatem in hac re illustrem. Cum Normanni vastatores totius tractus maritimi Ultrajectum quoq; occupassent, sacraq; & profana illic diripuissent, cuncta ferro & flamma pessum dedissent, successoresq; Hungeri, qui manus vastatorum vix fugiens evaserat, Daventriæ domicilium ac sedem collocassent, tandem Baldericus è Comitib. Clivia prognatus, quintus post Hungerum episcopus, primum per se vivente adhuc Henrico Aucupe rege, sed parvo profectu, dein benevolentia & liberalitate Ottonis imperatoris, & fratris ejus Brunonis, quos ipse in bonis literis erudierat, adjutus eandem urbem instaurare, ac sedem ibidem figere rursum coepit. Sed exoleverant fere episcopatus jura, quae ex liberalitate priorum principum ei fuerant collata, amissis una cum usu, ac possessione donationum haud paucis literis; vicinaq; nobilitas, ceu fieri solet, pleraq; vacantia invaserat. Itaq; instauratis donationibus ad restituendam episcopatus fortunam fuit opus. Quod incoatum a Conrado Franco imperatore, mox ab Henrico Aucupe promotum, ab Ottone primo factum multo uberrime, novaq; beneficia ab eo prioribus addita. In his & venationum jus in Comitatu Everhardi in pago Drentia fuit; quod cum ex procerum vicinorum ordine nonnulli invito episcopo usurparent, & traherent ad se, ab imperatore soli episcopo, & cui ille permitteret, est tributum, cuius annus fluxeret a nato Christo D. CCCC. XLIV. Idem repetitum ac firmatum ab Henrico II, cui Claudi cognomen, in gratiam Aufridi, anno M. VI. Et ab eodem comitatus ipse Drentiae (sic loquuntur tabulae) ecclesiae eidem in gratiam Adelboldi praesulis donatus in perpetuum: eoq; modo imperium regionis huius in genere, uti ego existimo, juris Ul-traiectini factum. Post mortuo Conrado II imperatore, cuius ipsius quoq; animus Ultraiectina sedes ob episcopum Bernoldum, & studio coningis Gisela impense deditus fuerat, cum filius ejus Henricus III cognomento Niger intestina defuncti parentis in aede Martiniana ibidem condidisset, donationibus novis priores cumulavit; in quarum una est ea, quam dixi, Groninga huius nostrae memoriae celebrata. Sic. n. illic scriptum, Henricum regem ecclesiae Vltrajectinae in honorem Martini structae, in remedium animae patris, & sui memoriam perpetuam, praesule tum Bernoldo, concedere & donare TALE PRAEDIUM, QUALE IN VILLA GRONINGA NUNCUPATA VIDEBATUR TENERE, SITUM IN COMITATU DRENTIÆ, cum areis, aedificiis, mancipiis, agris cultis & incultis, pratis, campis, pascuis, aquis, aquarumve decursibus, piscationibus, viis, inviis, exitib. & reditibus, quaesitis & inquirendis, cum omni ejusdem Comitatus strictione, monetis, teloneis, causis agendis, & discutiendis, cum omnibus appenditiis & pertinentiis, quae ad praesens retineri videntur, aut quicquid imposterum ibi Deo adjuvante acquiri poterit, eo videlicet tenore, ut supradictum praedium perpetuo respondeat servitio & utilitati fratrum ibi Deo servientium inceffabiliter, scilicet ut ex ejusdem praedii utilitate quotannis habeant xxx carradas vini, reliquum vero ex praedio proveniens a praeposito in usum eorundem exponatur fideliter, nec liceat quicquam ejus in usus aliqs conferre, priusquam id quod jam dictum est vinarium tributu fuerit solutum. Quae verba apud posteros aliter atque aliter accepta diversas & diffidentes sententias peperere. Quidam sic accepere, quasi villa aut civitas Groninga (id est, sine dubio anu & ide) in Comitatu Drentiæ dicatur sita, eademq; cum omni jure & annexis donata sit his tabulis ecclesiæ Vltrajectinæ, velut Drentiæ membrum. In quorum numero multi fuere episcopi hujus sedis, & canonici plerique, & eorum ministri, propterea quod suis reb. eam interpretationem commodam esse arbitrabantur: fuere etiam non pauci nostri temporis, qui litis ergo, quam cum civitate habebant, ut se ab ea seiungerent, e finibus Frisiæ hodiernæ eam exterminare voluerunt. Alii contra in alia omnia euntes, & longe quidem rectius judicio meo. Nec enim dici in tabulis regijs, Groningam in Drentia sitam, aut ipsam ecclesiæ Vltrajectinæ donatam, sed prædium, quod Rex videbatur in villa Groninga tenere, & id situm in Comitatu Drentiæ esse, & dono ecclesiæ ei datum, eﬀeq; verba regis donantis in istam sententiam planissima. Id vero prædium præfecturam suburbanam esse volunt, Dat den Woltrecht[?] ut appellavit posteritas, aut certè maximam hujus partem, quam ego jam ante ostendi partim se Drentiæ, partim Frisiæ contiguæ debere: Eam quippe à prima usq; memoria ex oppido Groninga tanquam præfecti sede, quem dare Vltrajectini solent, fuisse administratam: atq; hoc regem voluisse, cum scriberet, prædium illud in Drentiæ quidem Comitatu situm, in villa tamen Groninga se tenere. Atq; hæc interpretatio vel eò mihi videtur verosimilior, imò verior, quod idem Rex eodem anno, adeoq; eodem illo die, quo dedit has, si me antigrapha, quæ vidi, tionis non fallunt (is est dies xii Calend. Junij) binas quoq; tabulas alias signavit, quarum alteris prae-dia etiam alia in eodem Drentia (comitatu po-sita, in alteris rursum alia in Comitatu Radulfi, & quicquid de ijs inter Amafo [?] & Lavesco, id est, inter Amasum & Lavicam locatum, quae omnia Vffonis & fratrum eius, hominum nocentium, justo judicio damnatorum prius fuerint, huic eidem sedi Vltrajectina eodem modo cum areis, aedificijs, mancipijs, agris, pratis, campis, pascuis, aquis, piscationibus, vijs, invijs, exitibus, reditibus, caeterisque prius recitatis dono obtulit. Sic enim sentio, has partes omnes trinis his tabulis ab Henrico donatas coaluisse paulatim in unam praefecturam, quam Gho [?] & Woltrecht nuncupatus, earumq; tribunalis sedem in vrbe esse collocatum. De Comitatu vero in eadem Drentia, qui Gozelonis Lotharingiae ducis (is est, qui in Frisia & Hollandia res gessit, & imperium aliquandiu tenuit) & altero VMBALAHA dicto, qui (comitis Enobardi fuisse perhibentur, & non tam ecclesia, quam episcopo ab eodem rege aliquot annis post donati sunt, ἐπέχω. Et hoc ex his omnibus, & compluribus aliis eorum temporum tabulis disco, tum morem fuisse, ut pagus maius aliquid significaret quam Comitatus, plurefq; (comitatus pago uno, ac praedia plura uno Comitatu comprehenderentur: ita unam eandemq; Drentiam, item Tuentiam, item speciales Frisiae regiones in plures tunc fuisse Comitatus distinctas. Quod in Frisia potissimum habuit diutiuscule, vti est à me alibi demonstratum. Dicebatur Comes vulgò in his oris, qui ab imperatore vel rege iurisdictionem summam in Comitatu aliquo, id est, in dioecesi habebat cum imperio. Sed de sententiarum discrepantia quod dixi, id lectores diiudicanto: ego, quamquam quid sen-tiam, exposuerim, me tamen iudicem controver-sia non interpono. Episcopi certè plerique, qui proximis sæculis secuti sunt, id quod ante etiam notatum à me est, in rem suam, ecclesiaeq; suae verba diplomatis traxere, iusq; in oppidum, prætorium q; in oppido imperium haud minus quàm præfectu-ram suburbanam, quæ eorum sine controversia erat, sibi vendicarunt. Et tenuerunt quidem id diu, sed non sine tumultibus crebris ac difficilibus ex hoc fonte enatis, adeò vt armis arma sæpè con-currerint, sæpè castra in oppido castris opposita, bellumq; intra moenia gestum sit. Populus enim ad libertatem respiciens, aut libidini præfectorum, quos in urbe episcopi habebant, obviam ibat, aut episcoporum imperium indies latius tendens recu-sabat. De quibus omnib. prolixè à me in histo-ria est dictum. Attamen prævaluit episcoporum vis & potentia, quæ magna tum fuit, succinctâ etiam autoritate sacrosanctâ, & religionis opinio-ne, tenuibus verò adhuc oppidi rebus. Quæ res si tanta tunc fuissent, quanta post factâ sunt, non minus hic quam in Ostergoa & Westergoa, in quas diplomata similia ab Henrico IV Cæsare impetrata extitere, eadem ambitio & avaritia episcopalis operam perdidisset. Sic verò observa-tum tum de his porrò inuenio, vestigia rerum in monumentis sequens, clerum Vltraiectinum in initio præfectum territorio suburbano dedisse, quem vellet, & in annos, quot vellet, eumque præfectum in vrbe sedem & tribunal habuisse: huic simul & prætorium munus gerendum in vrbe, & nomen præfecti vrbani imposuisse ipsum episcopum, eumque Scvltbe-sivm[?] summum judicii ministrum, ceu legatum suum constituisse: mox præfecturam vtramque in feudum perpetuum esse versam, feudi rursum post aliquot sæcula in emphyteuseos conditionem, aut emphyteusi similem commutatum: in feudi possessione fuisse per aliquot ætates Gronenbergios, Supperochios, rursum Gronenbergios, Gronenbekios, Selwerdios, familias nobiles, interdum coniunctim, interdum divisim. Post cum ad Coverdios hereditas Selwerdiorum transisset cum Ida hærede vnica atque vltima domus istius, Hermanno Coverdio denupta, emphyteusis induQta est jure an iniuria, nescio. Emphyteuta facti Ioannes & Reinoldus Coverdij cum singulis filijs, & Goverdus Hovius anno Christi M. CCC. LXXI, mortuo paulo ante episcopo Ioanne Vernenburgio: lex his dicta, ut emphyteusis durarent ad tempus vitæ ipsorum. Verum vt suburbanus præfectus limitibus arctis finitum imperium in plebem rusticam habebat, nec causas cognoscebat, aut sententias ferebat, sine collegio judicum, quos plebs ei assessores dabat, plebsque in cæteris libertate fruebatur sua. sic pratoria potestas in urbe collata ab episcopo jurisdictionem senatus, & imperium eiusdem, ut falso quidam credunt, non tollebat. Nam senatus pacta saepe iniit cum vicinis, quo tempore praefecti in urbe erant, quae sine imperio & jurisdictione haudquaquam locum habere poterant, & de foro in urbe agendo, cognoscendisque controversiis foedera habuerunt: denique publica tabula testes sunt, quondam anno a Christi natali M. CC. LXXXIII, cum praefecti Gronenbergii essent, & forte e Selwerdica domo nobili duo criminis publici facti fuissent rei, quaesitum in conventu fuisse, ab Hunesgonys, an civitate Groningana, an denique ab Egberto Gronenbergio, ut territorii suburbani praefectio, propterea quod ubi horum omnium fines concurrebant, arx Selwerdia sedem haberet, viderentur judicandi: & cum ipsis reis permissum esset, ut ex his tribus, quem vellent judicem sibi esse in perpetuum, hos Egbertum cum successoribus eius elegisse. Quibus omnib. locus esse nullo potuisset modo, si judicandi potestatem cum imperio nullam senatus tenuisset. Ad hac, quamquam praefecto, muneriq; eius locum daret apud se, tamen episcopi imperium in se agnoscere, sive ut principi suo aut domino iusiurandum dare, paremque cum ceteris diaecesis civitatibus conditionem ac legem subire civitas haec nostra multo tempore recusavit. Nec exemplis destituebatur aliarum civitatum liberarum, quae & praefectos huiusmodi a vicinis reciperent principibus, & tamen iisdem[?] iureiurando, ut subdita, se non obligarent. Et cum ipsa in Frisia solo, ac Frisici iuris esset, relicta libertate gentis alienigenis dominis se subiicere tergiversabatur. Et quamvis mussarent sæpe episcopi, præsertim si qui ingenijs erant ambitiosis, tamen ad vim descendere ob hanc causam aut si non sunt. Nam creverant iam opes civitatis, & fœderum pactis de tuenda libertate cum vicinis firmabantur.
units.tr: I find the first mention of it under this name, in reliable and trustworthy written records (for why I should doubt the Roman tablet as to its age and authenticity, I have shown elsewhere), in a certain deed of gift, which is in the archive of the Church of Utrecht, written and sealed in the year of Christ 1040. By this deed the Emperor Henry III, surnamed the Black, son of Conrad II the Salian, grants to the same Church, in the time of Bishop Bernold, the right of an estate which he himself was seen to possess in the village of Groningen. I will say a few words about this donation, so as to make clear both its antiquity and its truth in this matter. When the Normans, who had ravaged the whole maritime region, had also seized Utrecht, plundered its sacred and profane buildings, and destroyed everything with sword and fire, and when Hunger's successors, who had barely escaped the hands of the ravagers, had established their home and seat at Deventer, at last Balderic, born of the counts of Cleves, the fifth bishop after Hunger, began, first while King Henry the Fowler was still living, but with little success, and then with the goodwill and generosity of the Emperor Otto and of his brother Bruno, whom he had himself taught in good letters, to restore the city and to fix the seat of the see there again. But the rights of the bishopric, which had been granted to it by the generosity of earlier princes, had nearly fallen into disuse, lost together with the use and possession of the gifts, the written records of not a few of them having perished; and the neighbouring nobility, as is usually the case, had seized most of the vacant lands. Therefore, to restore the bishopric's fortunes, the donations had to be renewed. This was begun by the Emperor Conrad the Franconian, promoted soon after by Henry the Fowler, and carried out very abundantly by Otto I, who added new benefits to the earlier ones. Among these was the right of hunting in the county of Everhard, in the district of Drenthe; and since some of the neighbouring nobles, against the bishop's will, were seizing it and drawing it to themselves, it was granted by the Emperor to the bishop alone, and to whomever he might permit, in the year from the birth of Christ 944. The same was repeated and confirmed by Henry II, surnamed the Saint, in favour of Aufrid, in the year 1006. And by the same [king], the county of Drenthe itself (so the records put it) was given in perpetuity to the Church of Utrecht, in favour of Bishop Adalbold; and in this way, as I think, dominion over this region in general came under the right of Utrecht. After the death of the Emperor Conrad II, whose own mind had also been devoted to the see of Utrecht, both because of Bishop Bernold and through the zealous attachment of his wife Gisela, his son Henry III, surnamed the Black, having buried his deceased father's remains in the church of St. Martin there, increased the earlier gifts with new ones; and among them is the one I mentioned, which is celebrated in our memory as Groningen. For there the writing says this: that King Henry, in honour of the church of Utrecht built to St. Martin, for the remedy of his father's soul and for his own perpetual remembrance, with Bernold then bishop, grants and gives such an estate as he was seen to hold in the village called Groningen, situated in the county of Drenthe, with its yards, buildings, slaves, cultivated and uncultivated fields, meadows, plains, pastures, waters and watercourses, fisheries, roads, and waste lands, its revenues and incomes, both those already obtained and those to be obtained, with the full authority of the same county over the dispensing of justice, coinage, tolls, the conducting and hearing of lawsuits, with all its appendages and dependencies, whatever is now seen to be held or whatever may hereafter, God helping, be acquired there; on this condition, namely, that the aforesaid estate shall perpetually and unfailingly serve the use and benefit of the brothers serving God there, so that from the profit of that estate they may have thirty cartloads of wine every year, and that the remainder of the proceeds of the estate be faithfully spent by the provost on their use, and that nothing of it be applied to any other uses until the wine tribute just mentioned has been paid. These words, understood in different ways by later generations, have produced divergent and conflicting opinions. Some have taken them as if the village or city of Groningen (that is, without doubt, the same place) is said to lie in the county of Drenthe, and to have been given with all its rights and appurtenances by these records to the church of Utrecht, as a member of Drenthe. Among these were many bishops of this see, and most of the canons and their ministers, because they judged that interpretation to be convenient for their affairs; there were also not a few of our own time who, on account of the lawsuit they had with the city, wished to be separated from it and to drive it out of the borders of present-day Friesland. Others, going in the opposite direction, judge far more rightly, in my opinion. For it is not said in the royal records that Groningen lies in Drenthe, or that the city itself was given to the church of Utrecht; but that the estate which the King was seen to hold in the village of Groningen, and that this estate lies in the county of Drenthe, and was given to the church by him; and the words of the donating king are most plainly to this effect. They maintain that this estate was the suburban prefecture, which posterity has called the Woltrecht [?], or at least the greater part of it, which I have already shown above belongs partly to Drenthe and partly to the neighbouring Friesland. For from the earliest memory it had been administered from the town of Groningen, as the seat of the prefect whom the Utrechters are accustomed to appoint; and that the King meant this when he wrote that the estate lay in the county of Drenthe, yet that he held it in the village of Groningen. And this interpretation seems to me all the more likely, indeed more true, because the same King, in the same year and on the very same day on which he gave these records (if the copies I have seen are not deceived; that day is the 20th of May), also sealed two other charters, in one of which other estates in the same Drenthe county are placed, and in the other further estates in the county of Radulf, and whatever lies between the Amasus and the Lavica [?], that is, between the Ems and the Lauwers, all of which had previously belonged to Uffo and his brothers, men guilty of crimes, condemned by just judgment; these he gave in the same way as a gift to this same see of Utrecht, with yards, buildings, slaves, fields, meadows, plains, pastures, waters, fisheries, roads, waste lands, outgoings, revenues, and the other things previously listed. For thus I perceive that all these parts, given by Henry in these three charters, gradually coalesced into one prefecture, which is called Gho and Woltrecht, and that the seat of its court was established in the city. But concerning the county in the same Drenthe which was of Gozelo, duke of Lorraine (he is the one who acted in Friesland and Holland and held power for some time), and the other called Umbalaha, which is said to have belonged to Count Enobard, and was given not so much to the church as to the bishop by the same King some years later, [I say nothing further] (ἐπέχω). And from all these and from many other records of those times I learn that then it was the custom for pagus to signify something greater than comitatus, and several comitatus to be included in one pagus, and several estates in one comitatus; thus the one and the same Drenthe, likewise Twente, and the special regions of Friesland were then divided into several counties. This practice held longest in Friesland, as I have shown elsewhere. In these parts a count was commonly called one who had, from the emperor or king, the highest jurisdiction with power of the sword in some comitatus, that is, in a diocese. But concerning the disagreement of opinions which I have mentioned, let the readers judge; I, although I have set out what I think, do not put myself forward as a judge in the controversy. Certainly most of the bishops who followed in later centuries, as I have also noted before, drew the words of the diploma to their own advantage and to that of their church, and claimed for themselves the right over the town and the rule (praetorium imperium) in the town no less than the suburban prefecture, which was undisputedly theirs. And they indeed held this for a long time, but not without frequent and difficult disturbances arising from this source, so much so that arms often clashed with arms, camps were often set against camps in the town, and war was waged within the walls. For the people, looking to liberty, either opposed the caprice of the prefects whom the bishops kept in the city, or refused the bishops' power, which was growing wider every day. I have treated all these matters at length in my history. Nevertheless the might and power of the bishops prevailed, which was then great, supported also by sacred authority and the reputation of religion, while the affairs of the town were still slender. If those matters had then been as great as they later became, the same ambition and greed of the bishops would not have wasted their effort here any less than in Ostergo and Westergo, where similar diplomas obtained from Emperor Henry IV also came to light. Thus, following the traces of events in the records, I find on further examination that the clergy of Utrecht at the beginning gave the suburban prefecture of the territory to whomever they wished, and for as many years as they wished, and that this prefect had his seat and court in the city; that the office of praetor was at the same time to be exercised in the city, and the bishop himself gave it the name of city prefect, and appointed him as his deputy, the chief minister of justice (Scultetus); soon both prefectures were turned into a perpetual fief, and the fief was again, after some centuries, changed into the condition of emphyteusis, or into something similar to emphyteusis. For some ages the Gronenbergs, the Supperochs, again the Gronenbergs, the Gronenbeks, and the Selwerds, noble families, held the fief, sometimes jointly, sometimes separately. Afterwards, when the inheritance of the Selwerds passed to the Coverds, with Ida, the sole and last heir of that house, married to Hermann Coverd, the emphyteusis was introduced, whether rightly or wrongly I do not know. John and Reinold Coverd, with their individual sons, and Goverd Hovius became emphyteutae in the year of Christ 1371, shortly after the death of Bishop John of Vernenburg; the terms were set that the emphyteuses should last for the lifetime of those men. But since the suburban prefect had authority over the rural common people within narrow limits, and did not hear cases or pass sentences without a college of judges whom the common people gave him as assessors, and since the common people in other matters enjoyed their own liberty, so the praetorian power conferred in the city by the bishop did not, as some falsely believe, remove the jurisdiction and authority of the senate. For the senate often made agreements with its neighbours at the time when the prefects were in the city, which could by no means have had place without authority and jurisdiction; and they had treaties concerning the conduct of the market in the city and the hearing of disputes. Finally, public records bear witness that once, in the year 1283 from the birth of Christ, when the prefects were Gronenberg men, and two men accused of a public crime happened to be from the noble house of Selwerd, it was asked in the assembly by whom they ought to be judged, whether by the Hunesgonys, or by the city of Groningen, or lastly by Egbert Gronenberg as prefect of the suburban territory, because the arx of Selwerd, where the boundaries of all these met, would seem to have its seat; and since it was permitted to the accused themselves to choose from these three whom they wished to be their judge for ever, they chose Egbert with his successors. None of this could have had any place had the senate held no power of judging with authority. Moreover, although it gave the prefect and his office a place among itself, nevertheless this city of ours for a long time refused to acknowledge the authority of the bishop over itself, or to swear an oath to him as to its prince or lord, or to undergo the same condition and law as the other cities of the diocese. Nor was it lacking examples of other free cities, which both received such prefects from neighbouring princes and yet did not bind themselves by the same oath as subjects. And since it was in Friesland, and under Frisian law, while leaving the liberty of its people, it held back from submitting itself to foreign lords. And although bishops often murmured, especially those who were of ambitious temperament, yet they descended to force for this cause, or if not, [they did not]. For the resources of the city had already grown, and by treaties of alliance with its neighbours it was strengthened in defending its liberty.

units.la: Accedebat quod in societatem fœderis Anseatici, cuius tum & magnum robur, & non vilis autoritas & prompta auxilia erant, civitas iamdudum esset cooptata, nec abiectam conditionem in sociarum civitatum ordine teneret. Quæ cum sic haberent, quamquam Florentius episcopus, familia Wevelichovius, vir sapiens & industrius à Wenceslao Cæsare diploma obtinuisset signatum anno M. CCC. LXXXII, ipsis Cal. Maij, quo diplomate copia ei fiebat repetendi ac recuperandi omnia, quæ incuria antecessorum ipsius, aut quovis modo ab episcopatu defluxerant, eoq; fretus haud segniter res suas curaret, tamen Groningam lacessere armis, aut iniquis urgere postulatis veritus fuit. Demum cum cætera desperaret, per collegium suum (nam factum hoc vivente adhuc ipso deprehendo, etsi cum historia scriberem, secus opinarer) alio modo sub beneficij specie obligandam sibi aut ecclesiæ suæ civitatem putavit. Anno enim M. CCC. XCII, qui penultimus vitæ eius fuit, collegium summum, cui proprie donatum fuisse prædium illud ab Henrico rege ostendi, autore hortatoreq; ipso, licet pactis cum Coverdijt haberet, tamen posthabitis his, omne ius suum, quod ex Henrici donatione profluebat, sive id in urbe, sive extra urbem esset, certa lege civitati tradidit. Lex hac fuit, ut civitas ius & iurisdictionem istam a collegio teneret in annos proximos centum, eoque nomine eidem collegio solveret quotannis canonem scutatorum Francicorum veterum LXXXIII cum dimidio, loco & tempore certo, & praeter canonem hunc vigesimo quoque anno honorarium munus septem marcarum argenti puri offeret Vltrajecti: exciperentur census, reditus, decimae & res hereditariae, quaeve canonicorum erant in territorio hoc eodem, ex quibus pactione hac nihil iis decederet: Exactis vero centum annis, ut eadem haec omnia valerent in annos centum alios, si vellet civitas in pactorum fide manens, & ejus rei gratia marcas argenti puri [?] ante Calendas Septemb. collegio eidem Vltrajecti offerret, novaque pactionis literas iisdem verbis scriptas poscceret daretque: & rursum, his quoque annis finitis, repeterentur eodem modo ac lege omnia: idemque extenderetur in perpetuum. Cautum tamen duobus Hovis cum matre ad tempus vitae ipsorum, quorum triens totius huius iuris ex pacto priore fuerat. Ita civitas Groninga sine controversia, ut ipsa rebatur, vndequaque iam libera, ac sui iuris facta, & imperio quoque territorij suburbani auctu, canonis tantilli onus ne sentiens quidem, episcopi modo honorem ac dignitatem, ut patroni, comiter agnoscens. Sed Fridericus BLANCHENHEMIVS in locum Florentij suffectus episcopus scopus, vir ambitiosissimi & inquietissimi ingenij, quanquam per literas solennes fidem civitati dedisset initio regiminis sui, omnia se ei jura ac privilegia conservaturum, pacta cum suis inita rata habiturum, patronum & protectorem ejus ubique; ex aequo & bono futurum, aliaque facturum hujusmodi, rursumque a quadriennio peramice cum ea convenisset, cum metus & periculum ab armis Hollandicis urgerent, tamen paulo post, periculo eo metuque amoto, cum videret recenti bello externo pariter ac sociali sessam[?] civitatem, commodum id ratus cupidini suae callidissimo consilio novis eam armis domi implicuit.
units.tr: In addition, the city had long since been admitted into the Hanseatic League, whose strength at that time was great, whose authority was not slight, and whose help was ready at hand; nor did the city hold a lowly place among the allied cities. Matters being thus, although Bishop Florentius, of the Wevelichove family, a wise and industrious man, had obtained from the Emperor Wenceslaus a charter sealed on the first of May in the year 1382, by which he was given the right to reclaim and recover everything that had fallen away from the bishopric through the negligence of his predecessors or in any other way, and although, relying on this, he looked after his affairs with no little energy, he nevertheless shrank from attacking Groningen with arms or pressing it with unjust demands. At last, despairing of everything else, he thought (for I find this done during his own lifetime, though when I wrote the history I supposed otherwise) that he could bind the city to himself or to his church in another way, under the appearance of a benefit. For in the year 1392, which was the second-last of his life, the chapter, to which that estate had properly been granted by King Henry, was, at the bidding and urging of the bishop himself, although it had an agreement with the Coverdians, nevertheless, setting this aside, handed over to the city, by a fixed law, all its right that flowed from Henry's grant, whether it lay within the city or outside it. The law was this: that the city should hold that right and jurisdiction from the chapter for the next hundred years, and on that account should pay the same chapter each year a rent of 83 and a half old Frankish gold shields, at a fixed place and time; and besides this rent, once every twentieth year it should offer at Utrecht an honorary gift of seven marks of pure silver. Rents, revenues, tithes and inherited property belonging to the canons within this same territory were excepted, so that nothing would be lost to them by this agreement. When the hundred years were over, the same arrangements were to hold for another hundred years, if the city, remaining faithful to the agreements, wished it; and for this purpose it was to offer the chapter at Utrecht marks of pure silver before the Kalends of September, and was to request and receive new letters of agreement written in the same words. And again, when these years too were over, everything was to be renewed in the same way and by the same law, and the arrangement was to be extended in perpetuity. It was, however, provided that for the lifetime of two Hovius brothers together with their mother, one third of the whole of this right should belong to them under the earlier agreement. Thus the city of Groningen, without dispute, as it itself believed, was now free and in control of itself on every side, its territory around the suburbs had been enlarged, and it felt hardly any burden from the small rent, while it courteously acknowledged the bishop only as an honour and dignity, as its patron. But Frederick Blankenheim, appointed bishop in place of Florentius, a man of most ambitious and restless disposition, although at the beginning of his rule he had given the city a solemn written pledge that he would preserve for it all its rights and privileges, would honour the agreements made with its people, and would be its patron and protector everywhere, and would act fairly and justly in other such matters; and although, four years earlier, he had come to a very friendly understanding with it when the danger and fear of Dutch arms pressed upon them, nevertheless shortly afterwards, when that danger and fear had been removed, and when he saw the city, still weary from a recent foreign war as well as from the war with its allies, he judged this a convenient moment for his desire and, with most cunning design, entangled it in new armed conflict at home.

units.la: Primum enim pro exulibus, capitalibus civitatis inimicis, intercessorem se ingessit: mox non impetrata re, quasi supplicibus deesse non posset, simul aliis quoque causis, quas cupido suggerebat, praetextis, bellum movit. Eo moto, quod futurum praevidebat, canonis annui ex pacto Canonicis debiti solutio est impedita.
units.tr: For first he thrust himself forward as an intercessor on behalf of exiles, the city's deadly enemies; then, when he did not obtain his request, as though he could not refuse to help suppliants, and with other pretexts that his desire supplied, he began war. With the war begun, which he had foreseen would follow, the payment of the annual rent owed to the canons under the agreement was blocked.
Thus some pretext for annulling the agreement was found.

units.la: Inter causas alias hanc jactabat praecipue, quod civitas imperium omne, quod quoquo modo ex HENRICI I dono profluxisse videri potuerat, redemisse se pactione nupera censebat, episcopus autem ad urbanam praefecturam pactionem non pertinere contendebat, praefectumque ajebat ab antecessoribus suis dari solutum a se quoque dari oportere. Nec ante destitit armis civitatem premere, omnia circum circa infesta et facere, majora minitari, quam ad dictatas conditiones descendere. descendere eam, compulisset. Conditiones hæ fuere. Exules ad sua, ut tum erant, redi-rent, nec actiones de damno haberent: Canon quinquennio non solutus collegio ob bellum, starim solveretur: civitas episcopo ius praefecturæ suburbanæ cederet: is praefectum pro arbitrio daret, qui sedem & tribunal habe-ret in urbe, id est, ut verbo dicam, pactio prior cum collegio esset irrita. Id pridie Michae-lis anni M. cccc. v. confectum. Triduo post, de urbano jure sic porro transactum. Civitas Groninga e numero civium suorum Scul-THESIVM, id est, praefectum ederet, quem vellet, munus ei abrogaret, successōrem daret, continuaret, quando, quoties, quandiu placeret: editus vero, successore datus apud praefectum suburbanum episcopi ministrum ju-raret[?] juramenti summa hæc esset, jus & justitiam se administraturum omnib. integre atque incorrupte secundum morem fori istius: praefecto suburbano ultra triduum tergiversante, consuli potestas esset hoc juramentum ab eo recipere eadem verborum forma. Pro hoc jure civitas quotannis aureos scutatos Franci-cos xxviii penderet episcopo ipsi Ultrajecti, & vigesimo quoq; anno marcas duas argenti puri cum marcæ triente praefecto Coverdiæ, utrumq; ante exitum Octobris: Et hæc pactio vim haberet in annos c. quibus finitis, si civitas ante exitum ejusdem Octobris offerret episcopo marcas argenti similis xvi, & trientem marcarum duarum, peteretq; ejusdem juris & pacti continuationem, eadem omnia valerent in annos totidem; & ab eorum fine rursum repetitis ijsdem, & pactis purè servatis in annos totidem alios atq; alios; idq; extéderetur in perpetuū, nec liceret episcopis abnuere. Sic episcopi cupidini iniquæ vtcunq; tum satisfactum, belloq; finis impositus. Sed ne hic quidem stetit hominis istius immensa ambitio: quinimò cum successu rerum progrediens longius eo demum rem redegit, vt civitas eadem omnibus vexata incommodis fessaq;, quietis ac pacis causa coacta demum sit, ipsi velut domino fidelitatis juramentum dicere, & eandem conditionem parendi cum cæteris civitatib. majorib. diœceseos Vltrajecto, Daventria, Campis, Suollis subire, ac subditam se, membrumq; diœceseos profiteri, reliquo tamen jure omni incolumi, & salvis, quæ cum vicinis habebat, fœderibus. Factum hoc anno post Christum ex virgine natum M. eccc. xix. Ab hoc autem tempore pax & concordia inconcussa civitati cum episcopis & diœcesanis stetit, relaq; in eodem hoc statu mansit, quem iam exposui, ad Davidem usq; Burgundum. Hic Vltraiectinus rebus potitus anno Christi M. cccc. Lx, cum pecunia egeret, acceptis à civitate nostra mutuo aureis Rhenanis M. DC, restituit illi suburbanæ præfecturæ jus ac imperium ad tempus vitæ suæ, & in sexennium à vita proximum, conditionemq; addidit, ut à civitate solveretur sibi hoc nomine canon annuus aureorum similium centum; nec verò fas esset prius à civitate repetere successores suos præfecturam dictam, quam mutuum omne restituissent. Davidi defuncto anno M. cccc. xcvi. Successit apud Vltraiectinos Fridericus Badensis: qui cum nondum quinquennium rebus præfuisset, armis Saxonicis petita civitas est, belloq; diutur-no æque ac graví vexata: in quá cum auxilium suo episcopo patroni ac principis sui sæpe rogasset, nec solum non invaretur ab eo ita uti par erat ex contractu conditione, sed haud obscure premeretur etiam, tandem necessitate ultima circumventa, & coacta, sequens id quod erat in pacti formula distertis verbis nuncupatum, in fidem principis alius, Edsardi scilicet Frisiæ Transfa-masanæ Comitis, concessit. Atq; hic Vltraiectini iuris in civitatem finis fuit. Ab Edsardo deinde ad Carolum Geldrum, a Geldro ad Burgundos imperium hoc devolutum est. Quod quomodo factum, infra monstrabitur.
units.tr: Among other reasons he was especially boasting of this: he believed the city had, by its recent agreement, bought back all the authority that might have seemed to flow in any way from Henry I's grant, whereas the bishop contended that the agreement did not extend to the urban prefecture, and said that the prefect, who had been given by his predecessors, ought also to be given by him, now paid off. Nor did he cease to press the city with arms, to make everything hostile all around, and to threaten greater things, until he had forced it to come down to the conditions he dictated. These conditions were as follows. The exiles were to return to their homes as they then were, and were to have no actions for damages; the rent, unpaid to the chapter for five years because of the war, was to be paid at once; the city was to cede to the bishop the right of the suburban prefecture; and he was to appoint a prefect who would have his seat and tribunal in the city. In short, the earlier agreement with the chapter was to be void. This was concluded on the day before Michaelmas in the year 1405. Three days later, the urban right was settled in this way: the city of Groningen was to present to the bishop, from among its own citizens, a man named Sculthesius, that is, a prefect, whom he might choose; he might remove him from office, appoint a successor, continue him or not, whenever, however often and for as long as it pleased him. Once presented and appointed, the successor was to swear an oath to the suburban prefect as the bishop's minister; the sum of the oath was that he would administer law and justice to all with integrity and without corruption, according to the custom of that court. If the suburban prefect delayed for more than three days, the consuls were to have the power to receive this oath from him in the same form of words. For this right the city was to pay the bishop himself at Utrecht twenty-eight gold Frankish shields each year, and, once every twentieth year, two marks of pure silver with a third of a mark to the prefect at Coevorden, both before the end of October. This agreement was to have force for a hundred years; when these had ended, if the city, before the end of the same October, offered the bishop sixteen marks of similar silver and a third of two marks, and asked for the continuation of the same right and agreement, all the same things were to hold for as many years again; and at their end, again renewed by the same terms and the agreements kept purely, for as many more years and so on, and this was to be extended in perpetuity, nor might the bishops refuse. Thus the bishop's unjust desire was in some measure satisfied, and an end was put to the war. But even here the immense ambition of that man did not stop; rather, advancing further as his fortunes improved, he at last reduced the matter to this: that the same city, worn out and weary from all the afflictions it had suffered, was finally forced, for the sake of quiet and peace, to swear an oath of fidelity to him as to its lord, and to accept the same condition of obeying along with the other larger cities of the diocese of Utrecht, Deventer, Kampen and Zwolle, and to profess itself a subject and member of the diocese, while keeping all its other rights intact and preserving the alliances it had with its neighbours. This was done in the year 1419 after Christ was born of the Virgin. From this time on, peace and concord stood unshaken between the city and the bishops and the diocesans, and the rest remained in this same state which I have now described, down to David of Burgundy. This prelate of Utrecht, who took power in the year of Christ 1460, being short of money, received from our city a loan of 1,600 Rhenish gold coins and restored to it the right and rule of the suburban prefecture for the term of his life and for six years after his death, adding the condition that the city should pay him a yearly rent of a hundred similar gold coins on this account; and his successors were not to reclaim the said prefecture from the city before they had repaid the whole loan. David died in the year 1496. Frederick of Baden succeeded among the Utrechters. Since he had not yet governed for five years, the city was attacked with Saxon arms and vexed by a long and burdensome war. In this, although it had often asked its bishop, its patron and its prince, for help, not only was it not assisted by him as the terms of the contract required, but was even plainly oppressed; at last, surrounded by extreme necessity and forced, it followed what had been expressly named in the wording of the agreement and placed itself under the protection of another prince, namely Edzard, Count of East Frisia. And so this was the end of the rule of Utrecht over the city. From Edzard the lordship then passed to Charles of Guelders, and from Guelders to the Burgundians. How this came about will be shown below.

units.la: DE IVRE CIVITATIS IN AGRVM VICINVM.
units.tr: On the Right of the City over the Neighbouring Land.

units.la: PRoximum nunc, vt, quæ acta cum vicinis sunt inter Amasum & Lavicam, quæq; cum ijs iura sociata, videamus. Nec vero hic ea repetemus, quæ sunt Historiæ decade prima nobis expositæ: sunt enim minus congrua instituto nostro: sed quæ secunda & sequentib. exposuimus, aut expo-nemus fusè ac sparsim, eadem breviter contra hostes[?], & rem totam velut in synopsi lectori statuemus ob oculos. Finito tandem diuturno & exitiali bello, de quo decimo libro decad. I in historia scripsi, quo in Gronenbergios & Gelekingios divisa civitas, & intestinis armis miserri-mum in modum afflicta, & cum civitate tota regio vicina in partes distracta, sese attriverant, velut calamitate cautiores factæ ab anno M. CC. LII diu deinceps quietæ fuere. Post cum minuti tumultus in agro inter ipsos agrarios ex ambitione hic illic rursus existerent, deinde maiores quoq;, imprimis vero in Fivelingiys renascerentur, civitas tamen in quiete perstitit & quasi spectatrix fabula fuit. Et quoniam vacillabat sæpe jurisdictio[?] in agro ob partium studia, contumaciamq; potentium, quibus pro jure vis ac libido erant, simul etiam commercia actionib. violentis turbabantur, tum firmandorum judiciorum, tum commerciorum tuendorum causa cum his aut illis agri partib. ut occasio ferebat, pactis fœderibusq; eadem se civitas junxit, eoq; modo publica pacis ancora fuit. Atq; hæc pax cum ad annum usq; M. CCC. XXXII stetisset, interea, opib. & negociationū multitudine oppidani creuissent, eo, quem dixi, anno in dissensionem cum sociys suis, ex dissensione in tumultus, ex tumultib. in apertum & magnum bellum inciderunt. Eo bello omnes, qui inter Lavicam fl. & Dullartum fl-uum[?] sunt, exceptis, qui præfecturam veterem tenent, tenent, & cum his bona Drentinorum pars, in civitatem conjurarunt, nec ante destituere, quam acceptis illatisq; gravibus detrimentis anno de- mum sexto post arma sumpta summis viribus in civitatem euntes in eas eam angustias & necessitatem adegere, ut ipsa intercessorum arbitrio sub- mittere sese, & deditionem facere coacta sit. Con- ditiones dicta dua aspera ac dura parentanda hostium odio: prior, ut pars muri oppidani lon- go tractu a porta Ebbingana versus portam Botteranam dejiceretur, locus ligneo septo rursum clauderetur: altera, ut vi in urbe do- mus ex lateritio opere firmæ & sublimes, tur- rium aut arcium instar, ad medium usq; for- nicem, ne novis turbis occasioni essent, humi- liores fierent. Reliqua æquiores : quales hæ, ut vetusta pacta & fœdera inter partes servaren- tur, omnibus jura sua cum jurisdictionibus integra utrimq; manerent, oppidani agrarii in defendenda libertate auxilio essent, in col- lybi & commerciorum ratione fraudem ipsi non facerent; quaterni ex tribus agri partibus præ- tores cum quatuor Drentinis, quatuor consulib.
