Grouinganis, duobus item antistiti- bus Adoardiano & V Verumano, quotannis Groningæ in curia convenirent, & monetam examinarent, remq; numariam ex commodo totius regionis constituerent. Pronunciatum prid. Petri & Pauli Apostolorum anno M. CCC. XXXVIII, sed sigillis trib. tantum signatum Fivelingio, Hunesgonio, Drentino, reliquis, quib. signari debuerat, Groningano, Fredowoldio, Langoweldio, Hummercio, Oftopagico, non adjessis. Unde suspicio mihi ast, conditiones illas duriores recusasse civitatem. Nec tamen eo minus pax coiit. Ab[?] annis deinde non multis arx Selwerdia bono reip. a Groninganis, Hunefgonijs, Fivelgonijs, Langowoldijs pecunia publica empta est, & solo æquata: pecuniaq; in hunc usum a sociis omnibus collata. Periculosa quippe arcis ejus firmitas non solum urbi, sed cæteris quoq; de libertate sua sollicitis videbatur. Et cum pecunia ejus gratia controversia inter urbanos & Langowoldios enata esset, eam anno M. CCC. LXI, die decollationis Joannis Baptistæ compositam invenio.
units.tr: Next, let us see what was done with the neighbours between the Ems and the Lauwers, and what rights were joined with them. Here we will not repeat what has been set out for us in the first decade of the History, since that is less suited to our plan. But what we explained in the second and following decades, or will explain at length and scattered through the work, we will briefly go over again against the enemies, and set the whole matter before the reader's eyes as in a synopsis. At length the long and ruinous war, which I described in the tenth book of the first decade of the History, came to an end. In it the city, divided into the Gronenbergers and the Gelekingers and miserably afflicted by civil arms, together with the whole neighbouring region, which was torn into factions, had worn itself out. Made wiser by this calamity, they remained quiet for a long time from the year 1252 onwards. Afterwards, though small disturbances arose again here and there in the country among the landholders themselves through ambition, and then greater ones too, above all among the Fivelingers, the city nevertheless stayed at peace and was, as it were, a spectator of the play. And since the jurisdiction in the country often wavered because of the partisan zeal and the obstinacy of the powerful, for whom force and desire took the place of law, and trade was at the same time disturbed by violent acts, the city joined itself by pacts and alliances to these or those parts of the country, as occasion offered, both to secure judgments and to protect commerce. In this way the city became the anchor of public peace. This peace held until the year 1332. Meanwhile, the townsfolk had grown in wealth and in the multitude of their dealings. In that year I have mentioned, they fell into dissension with their allies, and from dissension into tumults, and from tumults into an open and great war. In that war all who live between the river Lauwers and the river Dollart, except those who hold the old prefecture, together with the greater part of the Drenthers, conspired against the city. They did not give up until, after heavy losses were inflicted and received, in the sixth year after taking up arms they came with their full strength against the city and drove it into such straits and necessity that it was forced to submit to the will of the mediators and make surrender. The two conditions dictated, harsh and hard, had to be obeyed out of hatred for the enemy. The first was that part of the town wall, over a long stretch from the Ebbing Gate towards the Botter Gate, should be pulled down, and the space closed again with a wooden fence. The second was that within the town the houses built of brick, firm and lofty, like towers or citadels, should be lowered to the height of the middle of the arch, so that they could not give occasion for new disturbances. The remaining terms were milder, and were these: that the old pacts and covenants between the parties should be kept, that all should retain their rights with their jurisdictions unimpaired on both sides, that the townsfolk should help the country people in defending liberty, and that they should not defraud one another in the matter of tolls and trade; that four praetors from each of the three parts of the country, together with four Drenther, four Groningen consuls, and likewise two bishops, Adoardian and Verumian, should meet each year in the court at Groningen, examine the coinage, and establish the money matters for the advantage of the whole region. This was announced the day before the feast of Saints Peter and Paul in the year 1338, but it was sealed with the seals of only three parties, Fivelingo, Hunesgo and Drenthe; the seals of the rest, who ought to have sealed it, namely Groningen, Fredowold, Langewold, Hummerce and Oostpago, were not added. Hence I suspect that the city refused these conditions as too harsh. Nevertheless the peace was still made. A few years later the fortress of Selwerd was bought with public money by the Groningers, the men of Hunesgo, Fivelgo and Langewold, and levelled to the ground for the good of the commonwealth; the money for this purpose was collected from all the allies. For the strength of that fortress seemed dangerous not only to the city but also to the others who were anxious about their liberty. And when a dispute between the townsmen and the men of Langewold had arisen over its money, I find it settled in the year 1361, on the day of the beheading of John the Baptist.

units.la: Eodem vero anno M. CCC. LXI, delecti ex Hunefgonijs, Fivelgonijs, Hummerciis, præfectura vetere, & prater hos etiam Ostergoi, Westergoi, Reiderij, Amasani, Broecmerij Groninga congressi cum consulibus ac senatu huius civitatis, pacis & libertatis Frifica tuenda ergo fancivere, ut rata essent omnia, quæ olim in solennibus comitijs gentis ad Vpstallishomum fuerant decreta, eademq; sanctè colerentur: Et his addidere alia: ut prætores omnes cum singulis assessoribus suis ac antistitib. aut sacerdotibus quotannis Groningæ convenirent ipsis Calendis Iulij, ac de reip. negocijs deliberarent & constituerent, nec nisi confessis aut definitis negocijs inde discederet sub gravissima pœna: ut Selandijs, id est, partib. Frisiæ singulis ratæ essent cosuetudines suæ in electione judicum; ne socij à socijs proscriptos receptarent, neve ijdem novis ac insolitis vectigalibus se mutuo oneraonerarent, ut omnes in defendenda libertate, & repellenda notoria injuria, si necessitas premeret, & prompte & tempestive pro modo virium suppetias sibi mutuo ferrent, nec absi-sterent ante, quam periculum esset depulsum: deniq; si quæ existeret controversia in aliqua Frisiæ regione, ea ex specialib. illius regionis constitutionibus, consuetudinibus, privilegijs bonis honestisq; finiretur. Hoc MODO GRC-NINGA ID ESSE COEPIT, QUOD ANTE UPSTALLISBOMUM FUERAT, locus scilicet concilij aut comitiorum universa nō-stra gentis velut proprium, ac reip. libera METROPOLIS. Certè ab hoc tempore ad UPSTALLESBOMUM in e[?] Americano agro conventus huiusmodi, cujusmodi solent, fuisse non reperio, GRONINGÆ vero sæpe fuisse reperio: ut mirere merito homines, qui ista cum scirent, tamen urbem è Frisiæ regione eliminare litigijs suis conati sunt. Atqui prater hac totius gentis concilia etiam tum invaluerat mos, ut ij qui Amafo & Lavica claudunt, conventus juridicos seorsim agerent Groninga, idq;, vel quotannis, vel quoties commodum videbatur. Nam & loci commoditas allicie[?]bat, & civitas opib. ac magi-stratuum ordine & sapientia valida in societatem judiciorum adscita contumacia potentum terrori, & fluctuanti jurisdictioni firmamento ac subsidio erat. Nec enim tum quoq; æquabilis in jure diceundo ratio in subsellijs prætorum per agrum ubiq; servabatur, & qui opibus valebant in nobilitate, non facile se legum scitis & judicum sententijs suæ cupidini adversis subjiciebant: Unde mala metuebantur, qua affligenda patria, & evertenda libertati poterant esse. Quę cum priori more vix jam reprimi posse videbatur, remedio maiore opus esse sapientes in provincia, ac patria & pacis amantes judicarunt. Itaq; omnes omnino inter Amasum & Lavicam, qui potestatis publicae partem tenebant, quos feorsim per minores populos in oppido coire, & cum oppidanis sententias judicum recognoscere mos erat, simul Groningę adesse jussi sunt, cum anus ageretur a Christo in terris nato M. CCC. LXVIII. Ibi consensu omnium decretum solenniter, ut bis quotannis judices, qui inter flumina jam dicta sedes habebant, in quorum numero expresse Reiderij & VVesterwoldij cum ijs qui sunt in prae-sectura vetere, recesentur, semel die octava post pentecostes, iterum die xv Septembris, aut saepius etiam, si res poscêret, Groningę convenium agerent, in eoq; causas cum magistratu oppidano recognoscerent. Atq; ita legis esse coepit, quod moris liberi esse solet. Sunt q; multa alia praeclara & egregia illic fancita, adrem judiciarium, totumq; jurisdictionis ordinem ac modum, imprimis vero ad judicorum sanctissimam atq; integritatem pertinentia, quae nos in historia decadis II libro IV expressimus: quae talia sunt, ut ne eruditissimae quidem & sapientis-simae civitates eorum merito possit pudere. Ad haec foedera vetera instaurata pacis causa, vis omnis vetita, multa violatorib. gravis ere Gronin-gano indicta. Signatum decretum sigillis Reiderorum, praefectura veteris, Wefterwoldiorum.
units.tr: In the same year, 1361, chosen men from Hunesgo, Fivelgo and Hummerce of the old prefecture, and besides these also the men of Ostergo, Westergo, Reiderland, Ems and Broekmerland, met at Groningen with the consuls and senate of this city, and for the sake of keeping the peace and the liberty of the Frisians they decreed that everything which had once been decided at the solemn assembly of the people at Upstalsboom should remain valid and be sacredly observed. To these they added other provisions: that all the praetors, each with their own assessors and bishops or priests, should meet every year at Groningen on the very Kalends of July, and deliberate and decide on the affairs of the commonwealth, and that no one should depart from there until the business was concluded or settled, under the most severe penalty; that for the Selwerders, that is, for each part of Frisia, their own customs in the election of judges should be kept valid; that the allies should not harbour those proscribed by their allies, nor burden one another with new and unusual tolls; that all should mutually bring aid, promptly and in good time, according to the measure of their strength, in defending liberty and repelling open injustice, if necessity pressed, and should not hold back until the danger had been driven off; and finally, that if any controversy arose in any region of Frisia, it should be settled by the particular constitutions, customs, privileges, and good and honest usages of that region. In this way Groningen began to be what Upstalsboom had been before: the place of the council or assembly of our whole nation, as it were its own, and the free metropolis of the commonwealth. Certainly from this time I do not find that assemblies of this kind, such as are usually held, were ever held at Upstalsboom in the Ems country; but I do find that they were often held at Groningen. So one may rightly wonder at men who, knowing these things, nevertheless tried by their lawsuits to drive the city out of the region of Frisia. And yet, besides these general councils of the whole nation, the custom had by then also taken hold that those who dwell between the Ems and the Lauwers should hold separate judicial assemblies at Groningen, and this either every year or as often as seemed convenient. For both the convenience of the place attracted them, and the city, strong in its wealth, its order of magistrates and its wisdom, admitted into the fellowship of judgments, was a terror to the obstinacy of the powerful and a support and prop to a wavering jurisdiction. For at that time even, an even-handed method of giving judgment was not everywhere observed in the praetors' courts across the countryside, and those who were powerful among the nobility did not readily submit themselves to the decrees of the laws and the sentences of the judges when these were contrary to their desire. Hence evil things were feared, which could be ruinous to the fatherland and could overthrow liberty. When this could hardly be restrained by the former custom, the wise men of the province, lovers of their country and of peace, judged that a greater remedy was needed. So all those between the Ems and the Lauwers who held a share of public power, whom it had been the custom to assemble separately in smaller peoples' districts in their town and to review the judges' sentences with the townsfolk, were together ordered to be present at Groningen, in the year of Our Lord 1368. There it was solemnly decreed by the consent of all that twice a year the judges who held seats between the rivers already named, among whom the men of Reiderland and Westerwolde are expressly counted together with those of the old prefecture, should meet at Groningen, once on the eighth day after Pentecost, and again on the fifteenth of September, or more often still if the matter required, and in that meeting should review the causes together with the town magistracy. And so it began to be law what is usually free by custom. There are also many other excellent and distinguished provisions enacted there concerning the judicial business and the whole order and manner of jurisdiction, and especially those pertaining to the most sacred integrity of judges, which we have set out in the fourth book of the second decade of the History. They are such that even the most learned and wisest cities could rightly be ashamed of them. To these old covenants, renewed for the sake of peace, all violence was forbidden, and a heavy fine was imposed on violators by the Groningers. The decree was sealed with the seals of the Reiders, the old prefecture, and the Westerwoldians.

units.la: Ęx Lavicam, quos Ꝓ Hunefgoniæ, Hummerciæ, Fivelgoniæ, Fredo-Woldiæ, Langowoldiæ, civitatis Groningenæ, die Magni Martyris. Huius fœderis & decreti beneficio pax rursum inconcussa stetit in hac regione toto pene decennio. Tum vero, cum se factiones denuo commovissent, & vis jure potior esse captisset, maxime eis ultraq; Hunefum amnem, coacti sunt ij, qui partem reip. in Hunefgonia gerebant, ni remp. & autoritatem suam pariter perditam vellent, arctius se cum civitate rursum conjungere. Coniunctionis præcipuum caput fuit factionum compressio: quarum causa si civitati ad arma eundum, & in contumaces aut turbulentos ducendum esset, de sumptu omni, & detrimento illi cautum per obsides ex sociis pro arbitrio eiusdem legendos: decretumque, ut, in quos sumpta sint arma, eorum bona interarium referrentur: horum dimidiū civitati, reliquum sociis agrariis cederet: agrarii suis sumptib. ac periculo rem gererent: eorum præfecturę[?] si dissiderent inter se, cognitio ac iudicium civitatis esset: huius sententiam reliqui exequerentur. Adiecta his omnibus conditio, ut tandiu valerent, quamdiu non esset iis solenniter renunciatum, annoq; integro post renunciationem factam. Huic fœderi statim se adscripsere, qui Adoardianis parent, ipsumq; collegium Adoardianum: & post semestre Hummercii quoq; accessere Hunefgoniis confines, conditionibus modo de impendiis expeditionum nonnihil variatis, & accuratius descriptis. Anno deinde M, CCC, LXXXI, cum princeps nobi[?]itatis in Frisia Orientali Occo BROEC-MERIVS, [?]studio augenda potentia sua, in clientelam se ALBERTI BAVARI Hollandiae, Selandiae, Hannoniae Comitis, qui iamdudum Frisijs imminebat, contulisset, Frisij omnes inter Flevum & Lavicam fl. OSTERGOI, VVES-TERGOI, SEVENVVOLDII, qui erant periculis ab Hollandis proximi, metuentes libertatis suae foedus cum civitate Groningana in hoc summo discrimine percusserunt. Nam non Broecmerius solum formidini erat novus Bavari clientis, praepotens opibus, qui scindere in partes gentem, proprijs viribus atterere posse videbatur, sed factiones quoq; in Fivelgonia ac Hunefgonia se subrigentes, in quib. nobilitatis pars eundem Bavarum ac Hollandos spectare ferebatur. His vero periculis nil validius opponi posse omnes existimabant, quam cum civitate hac nostra foedus. Eo foedere promisit civitas, fidam se sociam foederatis, omnibusq; Frisijs liberis futuram, societati huic fortunas & corpora, si posceret res, impensuram, libertatem suam & foederatorum contra vim perogrinorum principum quorumvis, & factiosae nobilitatis pro viribus defensuram, si qua clades sociis accideret in praelio, iis periculo perculsis & receptum quaerentibus portas se suas aperturam, factiosos in Hunefgonia & Fivelgonia huic foederi obnitentes, & concordiam distinentes, ne reip. malo sint, compressuram. Idem foedus anno proximo M. CCC. LXXXII repetitum solenniter, & amplius quoque [?]factum, adscriptis omnibus, qui
units.tr: From Lavicum, which (the districts) of Hunefgonia, Hummercia, Fivelgonia, Fredo-Woldia and Langowoldia, of the city of Groningen, on the day of the Great Martyr. By the benefit of this covenant and decree, peace again stood unshaken in this region for almost the whole of a decade. Then indeed, when the factions had stirred again and force had begun to be stronger than right, those who held a share of the commonwealth in Hunefgonia, chiefly on the far side of the river Hunef, were compelled, unless they wished to lose the commonwealth and their authority together, to join themselves more closely again with the city. The principal point of the union was the suppression of the factions. If the city had to take up arms on their account and lead an expedition against the rebellious or turbulent, provision was to be made for all expense and loss to the city by hostages, to be chosen from among the allies at the city's discretion. And it was decreed that the goods of those against whom arms were taken should be reckoned as spoils of war: half of these to the city, the rest to the rural allies, and the rural allies were to carry on the business at their own expense and risk. If their prefectures disagreed among themselves, the inquiry and judgment would belong to the city, and the others would carry out its sentence. To all these terms was added the condition that they should hold good only so long as they had not been solemnly renounced, and for a full year after such renunciation was made. Those who obey the Adoardians, and the Adoardian college itself, at once enrolled themselves in this covenant; and after six months the Hummercians also, neighbours of Hunefgonia, joined, the conditions being only somewhat varied as to the costs of expeditions and described more precisely. Then in the year 1381, when the leader of the nobility in East Frisia, Occo Broecmerius, by his eagerness to increase his power had placed himself under the patronage of Albert of Bavaria, Count of Holland, Zeeland and Hainault, who had long been threatening the Frisians, all the Frisians between the rivers Flevum and Lavicum, the Ostergoians, the Westergoians and the Sevenwoldians, who were nearest to the Hollanders and fearful of danger, struck a covenant for the safety of their liberty with the city of Groningen in this most serious crisis. For Broecmerius alone was not the cause of dread, the new client of Bavaria, mighty in resources, who seemed able to split the nation into parties and wear it down by his own strength, but also the factions rising up in Fivelgonia and Hunefgonia, in which part of the nobility was reported to look towards that same Bavarian and the Hollanders. Yet all men thought that nothing could be set against these dangers more effectively than this covenant with our city. By that covenant the city promised to be a faithful ally to the confederates and to all free Frisians, to spend its fortunes and bodies for this alliance if the situation demanded, to defend its liberty and that of the confederates with its strength against the force of any foreign princes whatever and of the factious nobility, and, if any defeat befell the allies in battle, to open its gates to them when struck down by the danger and seeking refuge, and to restrain the factious in Hunefgonia and Fivelgonia who opposed this covenant and disturbed concord, so that they might not be to the harm of the commonwealth. The same covenant was solemnly renewed the following year, 1382, and was even further extended, all who [...]

units.la: [illegible, ~6 letters] inter Lavicam & Amasum colunt, cum condi-tione temporis in⸗ septennium, atq; ita e curia urbis præconis voce in magna hominum frequen-tia publicatum⸗. Idemq; anno sequente iteratum similiter. Et cum triennio post rursus se factio-nes in agro vicino moverent violentius, ac turbas cadesq; cierent, autoresq; a civitate & sociis com-pressi, atq; in⸗ ordinem redacti essent, & fœdus hoc demum sanctitum[?] publicatumq;, & pax factio-nis Fivelgoniys & Hunesgoniys, omnibusq; omnino huic fœderi subiectis, severe mandata. Id factum anno M. CCC. LXXXVII. Itamotum, & res nova a Frisia ad tempus tum aversa. Post annos deinde IX Albertus expeditione in Fri-siam suscepta, & pugna ad Scoterfilam commissa, vicit quidem Frisios, sed longius tamen cum⸗ propter cruentam victoriam, tum propter tempe-states, & inclinans in autumnum⸗ anni tempus progredi non⸗ fuit ausus. Sed a biennio reversus majori cum apparatu & exercitu, anno nimi-rum⸗ M. CCC. XCVIII, victoria rursum parta, & Stavera civitatum tunc temporis in⸗ Frisiæ partibus validissima obsessa, & deditio-ne capta, omnem regionem inde usque in Lavi-cam redegit in⸗ potestatem⸗, omniq; a populo jusjurandum⸗ accepit. Sed deditioni qui af-sentiri nolebant⸗, GRONINGAM, & in⸗ a-grum vicinum se contulerunt⸗. Qua fortuna Alberti commoti, qui in⸗ factione erant⸗, Vete-coperorum cis ultraq; Amasum⸗ fl. (hujus enim factionis principem & patronum se AlBertu profitebatur ) fusulerunt animos : Et eum istuc quoq; ab Alberto legati de dedi-tione venissent, filius Occonis Broecmerij jam extinct VVIDSELDVS, & cum ea FOLCMARVS ALLENA Offer-hufanus[?] ad ipsum profecti se & totam illam Orientalem Frisiam, quae Comitatus nomine hodie censetur, ei tradiderunt hac lege, ut eandem in feudum ab ipso mox reciperent, fierentq; ejus beneficiarij. Hoc vero fecere, CVM FACIENDI BIVS IVS OMNINO NVLLVM HABERENT. (um his idem fecere horum exemplo animati e nobilitate quidam in agro hoc Groningano, numero sex, Ailco Onstenius Ferhildemaus, Reinerus Eisingius[?], Tamme Gockingius, Menno Honuerdaus, Omeo Snelgeri, Haijo Wibenus, quorum animi jam dudum factionum & rerum novarum studio prurierant: a quibus totum inter Lavisam & Dullartum ager velut ex aequo & bono divisus, ac Alberto datus, ab Alberto vero ipsis in feudum redditus. Quae omnia literis comprehensa signataq; sunt III Idus Septembris.
units.tr: …who dwell between the Lavica and the Amasus, with the condition that it hold for seven years; and so it was published by the herald's voice from the city hall, in the presence of a great crowd of people. The same was repeated in the following year. And when, three years later, the factions in the neighbouring countryside stirred again more violently, and raised disturbances and slaughter, and the instigators were checked by the city and its allies and brought back into order, then this covenant was at last confirmed and published, and the peace between the Fivelgoniers and the Hunesgoniers, with all who were subject to this covenant, was strictly enjoined. This was done in the year 1387. Thus the matter was quieted, and the new affair was turned away from Friesland for the time being. Then, nine years later, Albert undertook an expedition into Friesland and fought a battle at Scoterfila; he did indeed defeat the Frisians, but because the victory was bloody, and because of the weather, and as the season of the year was leaning towards autumn, he did not dare to advance further. But returning two years later with a larger force and army, in the year 1398 indeed, he won the victory again; and Stavera, then the most powerful of the cities on the Frisian side, was besieged and taken by surrender, and he brought the whole region from there as far as the Lavica under his power, and received an oath of allegiance from the people. But those who were unwilling to assent to the surrender withdrew to Groningen and the neighbouring countryside. Stirred by this turn of fortune, those who were of Albert's faction on either side of the Amasus in Vetekoper country (for Albert declared himself the leader and patron of this faction) took heart; and when envoys from Albert had come there too concerning surrender, the son of Occo Broecmerius, now deceased, Widsel, and with him Folcmar Allena of Offerhus went over to him in person and surrendered to him the whole of that Eastern Friesland which today is reckoned by the name of the County, on this condition, that they would immediately receive it back from him as a fief and become his vassals. They did this, although they had no right at all to do so. Following their example, some men of the nobility in this Groningen countryside, six in number, were likewise emboldened: Ailco Onstenius Ferhildemaus, Reinerus Eisingius, Tamme Gockingius, Menno Honuerdaus, Omeo Snelgeri, and Haijo Wibenus, whose minds had long been itching with a zeal for factions and revolutions; by them the whole territory between the Lavisa and the Dullart was divided, as if on equal and fair terms, and given to Albert, and by Albert given back to them as a fief. All these things were recorded in writing and sealed on the 11th of September.

units.la: Et hi ipsi novi clientes pollicit Alberto sunt, datis ei literis, ad subigendam GRONIN-GAM, si in recusanda deditione & obseqvie ea persistaret, (nam istuc etiam legatos Albertus miserat, & optimis propositis conditionibus, ostentataq; benevolentia summa ad deditionem hortatus cives fuerat, ac si deditio fieret, obsidionem & vim denunciaverat.) summis viribus auxilio se futuros. Qua omnia cum vulgo innotescerent, ut erant iniqua & invisa, merito magnas turbas in agro circum Gro-ningam dedere.
units.tr: And these very new clients promise Albert that, having given him letters, they will help him with all their strength to subdue GRONINGEN, if that city persisted in refusing surrender and obedience. (For Albert had also sent envoys there, and had urged the citizens to surrender, with the best proposals and every show of the utmost goodwill; and he had declared that, if they surrendered, he would threaten siege and force.) All these things becoming known among the common people, since they were unjust and hateful, they rightly stirred up great disturbances in the countryside around Groningen.

units.la: Nam diversae factionis viri nobiles, & quotquot libertatis amantes erant, exagitate exaggeratoq; facinore, & multitudine concitata, nonnullos ex factione adversa, atq; in his unum alterumq;, qui regionem Alberto dederant, per tumultum occiderunt. Sed novis clientibus cum ab Alberto auxilia aliquot cohortium e vicinia subito venissent, qui ante inimicos suos presserant, vicissim presi ab ipsdem in extre-ma necessitate ad urbem Groningam confugerunt. Quibus cum statim porta non aperirentur ob insidiarum metum, instantibus & terga pene cadentibus inimicis, perterrita plebs conclamare coepit, si intra portas admissa defenderetur in hoc suo periculo, se in potestate civitatis imposterum futuram. Sic demum propius discreta re, porta aperta, multitudo trepida in urbem recepta: hostes a moenibus reiecti: conditio tamen illa, sed[?] quod in discrimine confuse ac nulla ratione iactata, sive quod ad paucos solum pertineret, pene pro nulla habita.
units.tr: For the men of the opposing faction, the leading nobles and all who loved liberty, having inflamed and exaggerated the crime and stirred up the crowd, killed some of the opposing faction in the tumult, one or two of them being the men who had handed the region over to Albert. But when some auxiliary cohorts had suddenly arrived from Albert's neighbourhood to assist the new clients, those who had earlier pressed their enemies were in turn pressed by them, and in extreme danger they fled to the city of Groningen. Since the gate was not opened at once for fear of an ambush, while the enemy pressed hard and nearly cut them down from behind, the frightened common people began to shout that if they were admitted through the gates and defended in their danger, they would thereafter be under the power of the city. So at last, the matter having been settled more closely, the gate was opened and the terrified crowd was received into the city, and the enemy was driven back from the walls. That condition, however, having been proposed in confusion and without any reasoned plan in the crisis, or because it concerned only a few people, was almost regarded as nothing.

units.la: Albertus quamq; rogatus a novis clientibus ac tota eorum factione, exercitum ingentem in vicinia habens, & in Groninganos odio ardescens, tamen ut progrederetur se tempore, ac civitate invaderet, persuaderi non potuit. Nam hyems saeviebat, & exercitus morbo infestabatur, & erat ipse ob senium tardior, & civitatis oppugnationem existimabat fore diffidilem. Quapropter praesidio in castris Ostergoê in littore, & aliis locis relicto, cum exercitu in Hollandiam est revorsus. Nec multos post menses omnis etiam Frisia in Flevum usq; durius a principe & ministris eius habita, servireq; nescia, constantiaq; Groningensium animata, percusso cum isdem Groningensibus & cateris Stiringys fœdere, ab eo rursum deficit, omniaq; eius praesidia, excepta Stavera, eorundem quoq; auxilio expugnavit, cum ex Hollandia domesticis tumultibus impedita suppetia venire laborantibus in tempore non possent. Eo facto in omnium ore erat civitas GRONINGA, eius pene unius constantia accepta ferebatur recuperata libertas. Sic quippe omnes habebant, si hanc quoq; urbem sua potestatis hostis fecisset, haud cuiquam eorum, qui iam parebant, satis animi futurum fuisse, ut se contra eum rursus commoverent; cateros vero, qui liberi adhuc erant, facile subiici ex hac belli arce potuisse. Tum, qui se Alberto & patriam tradiderant, nec a proposito volebant discedere, tanquam perduelles a Groninganis & sociis vicinis sunt proscripti. Hi ab Alberto domi occupato deserti ad Fridericum Blanchenhemium Ultrajectinum praesulem, civitati proprias ob causas succensentem, ut ostendi ante, se contulerunt, eumq; in Frisiam attraxere cum exercitu. Qui cum frustra urbem obsedisset aliquandiu, discedensq; Blancowera uno ab urbe milliari praesidium in eam reliquisset, oppidani & socij agrarij confecto exercitu res proscriptorum invasere, arcesq; redegerunt in potestatem. Hæc gesta anno M. cccc, & M. cccc. I. Mansitq; res in eodem hoc statu ad annum usq; M. cccc. V, quo pax inter Groninganos & Episcopum reparata, exules quoq; perduelles in patriam recepti, & rebus suis restituti, civitati honos quam maximus ubiq; habitus. Tranquilla deinde civitati & socijs omnia ad annum M. cccc. xiii, novis turbis insignem.
units.tr: Albert, however, though he was urged by the new clients and their whole faction, and though he had a huge army in the neighbourhood and was burning with hatred of the Groningers, could not be persuaded to advance and attack the city at that time. For the winter was raging, the army was afflicted by sickness, and he himself was slower on account of his old age, and he judged that the siege of the city would be difficult. Therefore, leaving a garrison in the camp at Ostergoo on the coast and in other places, he returned with the army to Holland. Not many months later, all of Friesland as far as the Vlie, treated too harshly by the prince and his ministers, and unaccustomed to slavery, and spurred on by the steadfastness of the Groningers, made a treaty with the same Groningers and the other Stellingwerfers, and again revolted from him. With their help, and since the people of Holland, hindered by domestic disturbances, could not bring timely aid to those labouring, they stormed all his garrisons except Staveren. As a result of this deed the city of Groningen was on everyone's lips, and it was said that freedom had been regained chiefly through the steadfastness of that one city. For everyone thought that if this city too had been made an enemy's stronghold, none of those who were already submitting would have had the courage to rise against him again, and the rest, who were still free, could easily have been subjected from this citadel of war. Then those who had surrendered themselves and their country to Albert, and did not wish to abandon their purpose, were proscribed by the Groningers and their neighbouring allies as traitors. Deserted after Albert had seized control at home, they betook themselves to Frederick Blankenheim, bishop of Utrecht, who was angry with the city for his own reasons, as I showed before, and they drew him into Friesland with an army. After he had besieged the city in vain for some time, and when Blankenheim departed, leaving a garrison one mile from the city, the townsmen and the allied country folk, having assembled an army, attacked the proscribed men's position and recovered the fortresses under their control. These events took place in the years 1400 and 1401. The situation remained in this state until the year 1405, when peace was restored between the Groningers and the Bishop, the exiles and traitors were also received back into their country and restored to their property, and the greatest honour was everywhere shown to the city. Afterwards all was quiet for the city and its allies until the year 1413, which was marked by new disturbances.

units.la: Nam Hisco Em-danus, oppidi eius Rector & præpositus, Scirin-gicarum partium in Amasana regione princeps, a KINONIS Broecmerio Occanis filio Emda anno precedente ejectus, fortunaq; omni exutus Groniugam ad civitatem sociam & amicam confugerat. Ejus in civitatem adventu factiones priscæ, jam per aliquot annos quieta sopitaq; sunt resuscitata. De reducendo enim Hiscone diversis sententiis inter proceres contendebatur. Ea contentio usq; eo exarsit, ut COPPENO IARCMO duce, qui erat Sciringicarum partium princeps, & acerbus odij persecutor, naturaq; turbidus & sævus, aliquos adversæ factionis proceres in curia, in foro, in domibus suis per tumultum sint interempti, reliqui earundem partium magno numero, & in his viri nobiles consulari & senatoria dignitate, ejecti in exilium: exules ad KENONEM trans Amasium sunt profecti, auxilij in inimicos communes spe. Scirin-gicarum civitate potiti, autore eodem Coppeno, demo egressi ex agro etiam amulos[?], adversæ factionis homines, ejecerunt.
units.tr: For Hisco Emdanus, rector and provost of his town and the leader of the Sciringian party in the Amasian region, had been driven out the year before by Keno Broecmerius, son of Occo Emda, and stripped of all his property; he had fled to Groningen, a allied and friendly city. His arrival in the city revived the old factions, which had been quiet and dormant for some years. Opinions among the leading men were divided over whether Hisco should be brought back, and the dispute flared up to such a degree that, under the leadership of Coppeno Iarcmo, who was the leader of the Sciringian party, a man bitter in his hatred of his enemies, turbulent and savage by nature, several leaders of the opposing party were killed by mob violence in the council chamber, in the marketplace and in their own homes; the rest of that party, including men of noble birth with consular and senatorial rank, were driven into exile in large numbers. The exiles went across the Amasius to Keno, hoping for help against their common enemies. Having seized the Sciringian city, on the advice of the same Coppeno they drove out from the countryside also the rivals, men of the opposing faction.

units.la: At hiemi[?] post, cum sueret annus à Christo nato . cccc. xv, KENO Broecmerius assiduus exulum precibus exoratus, & ut suis quoq; rebus contra Hisco-nem & socios eius Scringios consuleret, exercitum clam confecit, captaq; per insidias nocturnas urbe, & eiectis cum Coppeno factiosissimis quibusq; Scringicarum partium, exulibus & Vetcoperis cæteris remp. reddidit. Tum consules creati Reinoldus Hugingius, Conradus Vossius, Arnoldus SteenWicensis, Bruno Clingius : qui omnes in magistratu hoc manserunt, quoad vixere: idemq; observatum in Henrico Bruggio & Ottone Clantio, qui Vossio & SteenWicensi successerunt.
units.tr: But a year later, in the year 1415 after the birth of Christ, Keno Broecmerius, won over by the constant entreaties of the exiles and also wishing to look after his own interests against Hisco and his Sciringian allies, secretly raised an army. Taking the city by a night attack, and driving out Coppeno and the most factious of the Sciringian party, he restored the government to the exiles and the rest of the Vetcopers. Then the consuls were chosen: Reinoldus Hugingius, Conradus Vossius, Arnoldus SteenWicensis, and Bruno Clingius. All of them remained in office as long as they lived, and the same practice was observed with Henricus Bruggius and Otto Clantius, who succeeded Vossius and SteenWicensis.

units.la: Ab hoc vero tempore, quo restituti exules sunt, summa concordia inter se civitas atq; ordines omnes, qui in agro à Lavica usq; in Dullartum sinum sunt, egere, pene ut una esse resp. videretur. Repetitq; tum statim sunt fœdera & pacta vetera: novaq; veteribus subinde addita, honori commodisq; civitatis augendis, & amicitiæ conjunctionisq; mutua magis ac magis firmanda. Qua cuncta ut intelligantur planius, distincte singula, sed æque succincte, ut brevitas operis poscet, per summa rerum capita explicabo.
units.tr: From this time, when the exiles were restored, the city and all the orders that dwelt in the countryside from the Lavica to the bay of the Dullart lived together in the greatest harmony, so that they almost seemed to be one commonwealth. Immediately the old covenants and pacts were renewed, and new ones were from time to time added to the old, to increase the honour and advantages of the city and to strengthen more and more the mutual friendship and union. To make all these matters clearer, I will explain them one by one, but as briefly as the nature of this work demands, by setting out the main heads.

units.la: Depulso, quod ab Hollandia impenderet periculo, deinde & cum Ultraiectinis bello composito, ordines agrarij experimento edocti, quantum momenti temporibus dubijs in civitate esset, ejusq; amicitia ac fides quam firmum esset contra hostes libertatis præsidium, quam magna in ea vis ad confervandam simul sociorum concordiam, & judiciorum integritatem, id consilij habuere, ut eam indies sibi devincirent arctius. Itaq; sensim concessa civitati aliqua, quæ decori & emolumento ei ipsi, cui tribuebantur, nec tamen detrimento iis, qui tribuebant, esse posse videbantur. Cuius generis illud est vel maxime de Hovetmannis, quod memorabo postea, non magis honorificum & egregium urbi, quam ipsis agrariis ob juris & iustitiæ administrationem, & contumaciæ coercitionem salutare: item illud de stapula, uti vocant, rerum ἐγχωρίων[?], deq; negociationib. & mercatus jure: & illud de cerevisiæ solius Groningana in tabernis aut hospitiis publicis usu: Quorum alia maturius, alia tardius initium habuere.
units.tr: After the danger threatening from Holland had been averted, and the war with the Utrechters settled, the agrarian orders, taught by experience how great a weight the city carried in uncertain times, and how firm its friendship and loyalty were as a bulwark of liberty against enemies, and how great its power was in preserving both the concord of the allies and the integrity of their courts, resolved to bind it to themselves ever more closely each day. Thus, little by little, some concessions were granted to the city which seemed able to bring honour and profit to the very party to which they were given, yet without harm to those who granted them. Of this kind is above all the matter of the Hovetmanni, which I shall mention later: no less honourable and distinguished for the town than it was wholesome for the agrarians themselves, for the administration of law and justice and the restraint of the stubborn. Likewise that concerning the staple, as they call it, of local goods, and the right of trade and markets; and that concerning the use of Groningen beer alone in taverns or public inns. Of these, some began earlier, others later.

units.la: HOVET-MANNOS primos, de quibus mihi cognoscere licuit hactenus, vidi in indice notatos sola nomina habente, ad annum Christi M. cccc. x, si memini recte, qui index in chartophylacio est curiæ urbanæ. Proximos ab his observavi memoratos in literis publicis Kenonis Broecmeryi in membrana exaratis anno M. cccc. xvi, qua litera arguunt, eos tum colligendo tributo per agrum præfisse, quemadmodum per urbem consules. Et rursum nominatos inveni in literis Occonis Broecmeryi Kenonis filij anno M. cccc. xvii scriptis & signatis mense Augu-sto, atque ita nominatos, ut tractasse pecuniam publicam totius provinciæ cum consulib. oppidanis sit manifestum. Iterumq; anno M. cccc. XXIV, nomen eorum in publico transfationis instrumento impressum animadverti. Post tempus cum exissent adhuc anni XII, jam continuum eorum indicem, qui in eo munere fuerunt ad Saxonica usq; bella per annos circiter LXIII, quamdiu libera & sine principe respub. hæc mansit, curia adservat. Sed de his infra rursum. Urbem autem hanc emporium fuisse antiquitus vicinis regionibus, præcipue Staverana fortuna ruente, nec solum propinquas sed etiam longinquas negotiationes facilitasse, ac in possessione earum floruisse, maritimaq; non minus quam mediterranea commercia coluisse, extra controversiam est.
units.tr: The earliest Hovetmanni of whom I have so far been able to learn I saw noted in an index that contains only names, dating to the year of Christ 1410, if I remember correctly, which index is kept in the town hall archive of the city council. The next after these I observed mentioned in public documents of Keno Broecmerius, written on parchment in the year 1416, which documents show that they then, by collecting the tax throughout the countryside, presided over it just as the consuls did in the town. And again I found them named in the documents of Occo Broecmerius, son of Keno, written and sealed in the year 1417 in the month of August, and named in such a way that it is clear they handled the public money of the whole province together with the town consuls. And again, in the year 1424, I noticed their name printed in a public instrument of transfer. Afterwards, when twelve more years had passed, the council keeps a continuous list of those who held this office down to the Saxon wars, a period of about sixty-three years, during which the commonwealth remained free and without a prince. But more on these things below. That this city was in ancient times a trading centre for the neighbouring regions, especially when the fortune of Stavoren was failing, and that it facilitated not only nearby but also distant trade, and flourished in its possession of these, and cultivated maritime commerce no less than inland commerce, is beyond dispute.

units.la: Nec illud dubium, jus atq; mercatus solennis aut nundinationum in toto agro vicino, fluminibus Amafo [?] & Lavica clauso, solam hanc si non lege aut pacto, quod tamen verum reor, at saltem more & tacito consensu, qui pro lege est, etiam multo ante Bavari bellum tenuisse.
units.tr: Nor is it doubtful that the right of staple and of the solemn market or fairs in the whole neighbouring countryside, enclosed by the rivers Amasus and Lavica, was held by this city alone, even long before the Bavarian war, if not by law or agreement (which, however, I believe to be true), at least by custom and tacit consent, which stands in place of law.

units.la: De stapula rerum venalium ἐπιχωρίων[?], quando coeperit, quæri potest: potest etiam de cerevisia Groningana usu iam dicto. Priorem ego aut post Bavari arma, aut post recuperatam a Kenone Groningam statim initia habuisse, alterum postea cœpisse existimo, & cur existimem, rationes habeo, quas ex iis, quæ sequuntur, lector etiam non monitus intelliget. Primum post Hollandica & Ultraiectina arma a civitate cum vicinis percussum foedus, quod mihi in literas relatum haberi videri licuit, est, quod paulo ante Kenonis adventum, cum ipsa adhuc a Sciringys teneretur, cum cum Hunefgoniorum parte, qui praefectura media nomine censentur, in Kenonem inyt [?] anno M. cccjc. xv, mense Martio: in quo caput praecipium est, libertatis patriae contra Kenonem & omnes exteros propugnatio, collatis in eam subsidiis mutuis: & praeter hanc, quod quifq; juris teneret, ejus conservatio, denique redituum & locariorum familiae Onfteniae, quoad ea exul erit, in aerarium affcriptio.
units.tr: It may be asked when the staple of local goods for sale began, and the same question may be asked about the use of Groningen beer already mentioned. I think the former began either after the Bavarian arms or immediately after Groningen was recovered from Keno, and the latter began later; and I have reasons for thinking so, which the reader will understand even without my pointing them out, from what follows. The first covenant concluded by the city with its neighbours after the Holland and Utrecht wars, which I have been able to find recorded in writing, is the one made a little before Keno's arrival, while the city was still held by the Sciringians, with part of the Hunesgonii, who are counted under the name of the middle district, against Keno, in the year 1415, in the month of March. Its chief point is the defence of the country's liberty against Keno and all outsiders, with mutual aid contributed for it; and besides this, the preservation of whatever right each person held, and finally the entry into the treasury of the rents and leases of the family of Onsteni for as long as that exile lasts.

units.la: Alterum cum Hummercys, Langewoldys, Fredewoldys, afscriptis etiam Oftopagicis Transla-vicanis, anno sequente eiectis jam Sciringiys, ipsis Nonis Iunij iilum in proximum decennium, & hoc quoq; pro tuenda libertate, & jure patrio, conjuncta opera & opib. contra exteros principes: in quo porro cautum expresse, ut eppidani eam vrbis & finium suorum curam habeant, ne quid ex iis detrimenti sociis possit accidere: ut controversiis componendis arbitri a partibus designentur, qui nisi ante Trinitatis eas composuerint, eadem a conventu juridico omnium sociorum Groningae definiantur: ut conventus hujusmodi quotannis Groningae agatur stato die, mense Iunio: nec exules Coppenus Iargaeus, Iacobus Scelgius cum socijs receptentur: caetera de pace tenenda, de solvendis captivis, de poenis caedium & injuriarum aliarum loquuntur.
units.tr: The second, made with the Hummercii, Langewoldii, Fredewoldii, together with the Ostopagici and Translavicani, who had been driven out of Sciringia the year after, on the Nones of June, for the following ten years, is likewise for the defence of liberty and the ancestral right, by joint effort and resources against foreign princes. In it there is also expressly provided that the townsmen shall have care of the city and its borders, so that nothing may happen to the detriment of the allies; that arbitrators shall be appointed by the parties to settle disputes, and if they have not settled them before Trinity, they shall be decided by a court assembly of all the allies at Groningen; that such an assembly shall be held every year at Groningen on a set day in the month of June; and that the exiles Coppeno Iargaeus and Iacobus Scelgius with their associates shall not be received. The rest speaks of keeping the peace, of ransoming captives, and of the penalties for killings and other injuries.

units.la: Tertium non foedus, sed pactum cum Omcone Snelgero & Dammonensibus initum a civitate eodem anno, tantum de caedibus aliquid determinans, in cujus formula DAMMONENSES nominatos invenies, de gemeine buren van de Dammc In eodem vero hoc, vt & in tertio euidens indi-dicium extat, paulo ante cum vniuersis FIVEL-GONIIS & HVNESGONIIS in noua pacta & foedus consensisse eandem ciuitatem: quorum exempla periisse dolemus. Anno sequente M. CCCC. XVII, mense Iunio, cum glisceret rumor de consiliis Vltraiectini (cui sederat in animo, Groningam ad iusiurandum sibi dicendum adigere) & vicissim de Occone Broecmerio Kenonis filio aliquid suspicionis effet, cum FIVELINGIIS & HVNESGONIIS conuenit ciuitati, ne pars altera fine altera de cooptando domino consilia iniret: secus fa-cienti bis mille scutatorum veterum poena esset. Et cum biennio post ciuitas importunitate episcopi superata in fidem se eius vel inuita contulisset, agrarij ordines quoq; hi idem, & cum his HVM-MERCII, LONGOWOLDII, FREDOWOLDII, autore ciuitate episcopum etiam eundem pactis conuentis sibi obligarunt: quorum haec summa:
units.tr: The third, not a covenant but an agreement made by the city with Omco Snelgerus and the Dammonenses in the same year, determining only something about killings, in whose formula you will find the Dammonenses named, <bl>the common farmers of Damme</bl>. Indeed in this same agreement, as well as in the third, there survives clear evidence that a little before, the same city had consented to new pacts and a covenant with all the Fivelgonii and Hunesgonii; we regret that their texts have perished. In the following year, 1417, in the month of June, when the rumour grew about the plans of the Utrechter (who had settled in his mind to compel Groningen to swear the oath of allegiance to him), and in turn some suspicion arose about Occo Broecmerius, son of Keno, the city came to an agreement with the Fivelingii and Hunesgonii that neither party should enter into plans about choosing a lord without the other; for anyone acting otherwise there would be a penalty of two thousand old shields. And when two years later the city, overcome by the importunity of the bishop, had put itself under his protection, even against its will, the agrarian orders likewise, and with them the Hummercii, Longowoldii, Fredowoldii, at the instigation of the city, bound themselves to the same bishop by agreed pacts; the sum of these is as follows:

units.la: Episcopus ptomisit, iuri, libertati, ditionibus ordinum agrariorum, cu ufmodi tum erant, impedimento se nunquam futurum, modo ipsi vicisim in Vltrajectinos injuriu [?] non sint, & cum ciuitate Groningana in eadem amicitia, societate, & institutis prefentibus permaneant constantes, imo contra oppressores gratia & consilio ipsis adfuturum, item procuratorum, ne quid injuriae à suis, aut per diuisionem suam cuiquam eorum inferatur impunè: nec ullum se castellum vllamvé munitionem excitatu-rum aut recepturum in agro hoc, unde agra-riis ordinibus periculum creari queat. Hoc
units.tr: The bishop promised that he would never be an obstacle to the right, the liberty, and the jurisdictions of the agrarian orders as they then were, provided that they in turn do not unjustly injure the Utrechters, and that they remain steadfast in the same friendship, alliance, and present arrangements with the city of Groningen. Indeed, he would stand by them against oppressors, with favour and counsel. Likewise, concerning the agents, he promised that no injury would go unpunished if it were done to any of them by his people or through his division of the land. And he would not raise up, nor receive, any castle or fortification in this territory from which danger could arise for the agrarian orders. This was done on the day of the summer solstice.

units.la: F factum ipso æstivi solstitij die. Et cum suffi-cionis aliquid, ceu fieri in mutationibus solet, FI-VELINGIIS[?] esset iniectum, seorsim rursus hi cum civitate, & civitas cum ijs pacti fiere in fine hu-jus anni, minuendæ libertatis, ditionum, iuris sociorum autores se non futuros ullo tempore, imo minuere conantes alios repressuros pro viritum modo, salvis tamen foederibus, & pactis omnibus prioribus.
units.tr: Then, when some suspicion, such as usually arises in times of change, had been cast upon the Fivelingians, these men again made a separate agreement with the city, and the city with them, at the end of this year: that they would never at any time be authors of a diminution of liberty, jurisdictions, or the rights of the allies; and indeed, that they would try to diminish these and would check others according to their means, all prior covenants and agreements remaining nonetheless in force.

units.la: Interea toto hoc tepore ab eiectis Groninga Sci-ringiis gravi inimicitia, adeoq; bofili odio inter se arserant & adhuc ardebant Ciflavicani & Tras-lavicani (hi enim Sciringicii nomen profitebatur, & multos adversae factionis in exilia pellebat, quib. Groninga & apud locios eorum receptus erat) fru-straq; legati Sigismundi Cæsaris conati fuerant in concordia eos reducere. Qui legati cum Frisia ex-cessissent, tandem malorum ex intestina dissensione pertasae partes ipsa anno M. CCCC. XXI Gronin-ga convetu instituto inter se transsegere. De qua re prolixè scribo in historia. Altero anno post inter præpositum Lopperf. & plebem vicinam his com-posita est per arbitros, e quibus tres HOVET-MANNOS Groninganos in tabulis transfactionis nominatos invenio, qui eodem illo tempore CONSVLES oppidani fuere: quod noscenda antiquitatis causa est observandum. Anno M. CCCC. XXV Groningani Hummerzij, Langowoldy, Fredowoldy, cum Upsterānis trans Lavicam, item ydem, & omnes socij in agro vicino cum Octopagicis Tranflavicanis anno M. CCCC. XXVI de coercendis furib. pacta iniere. Deinde hæc bac ad Orientem Amafi inter Occonem & Foccónem dissensio ne enata, atq; armis cómo-tis, cum Occonis fortuna labasceret, Focco Gro-ninganis fuccéfens Occone fœdere iunctis, traiectto cum suis Amafo, & excitata illic factione sua, pralio Groninganos vicit; victorq; in patria rever-sus Occonem in pugnacepit: iterum, primo vere anni M. CCCC. XXVIII, Amafo trafmiffo, aspirante undiq; fortuna, totú pene agrú, qui inter Amafum & Lavicam est, à civitate avertit, & in novas leges ac nova fœdera cum adegit. Sed Medachio-rum, Humerziorum, Longowoldiorum, Fredowoldi-orum multi non assensere, & fœdus etiam cum Groninganis finito jam fœdere priore, pro libertate & legibus prisctis rursum pepigere, in quo appella-tio ad Hovetmannos urbanos à judicib. cæ-teris in agro litigantib. permissa, & vt conven-tus juridici quatuor quotanis agantur in vrbe; urq; non nisi voluntaria tributa sint, exigan-turve ab agrariis, statutum. Quo cognito, Focco illuc cum exercitu accurrens disiectis, qui se op-ponere ausi erant, rem turbavit, & in eas angustias civitatem coniecit, ut petitis inducis consulere sibi ipsa necesse habuerit. At dominuregre fo Foccone, & reb. difficilib. implicito, adeoq; in ordine redacto, omnia priori statui restituta: nominatim cum Fivelgoniis universis, & peculiariter cum Dammonensibus, itemq; cum maxima Hvnesgoniorum parte fœdera repetita & conditionib. novis ampliata. Simul Hamavr-Gensib. Emnonis Grethani & filiorum eius focys Endapotitis hominib. negociationu studio deditis. quibus commodum videbatur cis ultraq, Ama- sum mercari & quaestum facere, per eos mercatus aut stapula ibi, in cuius possessione Groningani ex voluntate sociorum erant, imprimis in Amasi & Dullarti ora, turbatum Groninganis fuit. Et haec, reliquis per agrum quietis, simul atis inter duas civitates aemulas materia tum fuit. Hamburgensibus vero ex nobilitate quidam, praecipue Haiio Ripperda Farmsumanus, Ailco Hovverda Muntensis, Eppo Gockinga Brocaeus, magis odio civitatis quam amore ipsorum, tacite studebant. Inter haec Guilhelmus VVICHERINGIVS consulari familia Groninga natus, tum temporis mercato- rum praefectus, dum jus civitatis tueri vult, in- ditione Ripperdaa concursu seditiosorum est occi- sus. Quod cum ultimo ire captis armis se ostenderent Groningani, HAIIO RIPPERDA, cui caedes acceptae ferebatur, timore perculsus, satius esse duxit, placare offensos, quam vim eorum ex- periri. Itaq; oblata satisfactione transegit cum iis, & promisit, in possessione juris TAPVLAE seu mercatus se civitatem non turbaturum, sed reiecturum eis hoc jus liberum; nec solum non impedimento in hac re, sed auxilio etiam, si usus poscat, futurum; deinde caedis VVicheringio, & aliorum damnorum illatorum causa se cum suis D. Arnoldicos esse soluturum: ad haec eosdem cum civitate hostes internos aut externos habituros, operam et laturum, arcem suam Farmsumanam [?] praesidio ejus pariter & confugio aperturum. Ita haec & signata
units.tr: Meanwhile, throughout this whole time, the Ciflavicans and the Traslavicans had blazed with bitter enmity and a hatred of cattle-herders, and they were still burning with it. (For these latter professed the name of the Sciringians, and drove many from the opposing faction into exile, and those exiles had been received in Groningen and among their allies.) The envoys of the Emperor Sigismund had tried in vain to bring them back to concord. When these envoys had left Friesland, at last, weary of the evils caused by internal dissension, the parties agreed among themselves in Groningen in the year 1421, with a convention established; I write about this matter at length in my history. Another year later, a dispute between the provost of Loppersum and the neighbouring commons was settled through arbiters, among whom I find three Hovetmanns of Groningen named in the records of the agreement, who at that same time were consuls of the town. This must be noted for the sake of knowing antiquity. In the year 1425 the Groningers, with the men of Hummerzij, Langewolde, and Fredewolde, together with the Upstrians across the Lauwers, likewise, and all the allies in the neighbouring land, with the Octopagians and the Trans-Lavicans, made agreements in 1426 concerning the restraint of thieves. Then this dissension arose here to the east of the Ems, between Occo and Focco, and, with arms set in motion, when Occo's fortune began to totter, Focco, angry at the Groningers who had joined themselves to Occo by treaty, crossed the Ems with his men, and, having stirred up a faction of his own there, defeated the Groningers in battle; and returning victorious to his homeland, he attacked Occo. Again, in early spring of the year 1428, having sent his forces across the Ems, and with fortune favouring him on every side, he turned nearly the whole land that lies between the Ems and the Lauwers away from the city, and compelled it to new laws and new treaties. But many of the Medemblikers, Hummerzijers, Langewoldians, and Fredewoldians did not assent, and, the earlier treaty with the Groningers now having ended, they again pledged, for liberty and their ancient laws, a covenant also with the Groningers, in which it was decreed that appeal to the town Hovetmanns be permitted by the other judges in the litigating lands, that court sessions be held four times a year in the town, and that no tributes be exacted from the agrarians except voluntary ones. When this became known, Focco, rushing there with an army, scattered those who had dared to oppose him, threw the matter into confusion, and cast the city into such straits that it was compelled to seek a truce to provide for itself. But the lord Focco, being entangled in difficult affairs, and reduced to order, all things were restored to their former state: namely, the covenants with all the Fivelgoers, and particularly with the Dammonians, and likewise with the greater part of the Hunsgoers, were renewed and extended with new conditions. At the same time, with the Hamburgers, the Emmon of Grethe and the friends of his sons, the Endapotians, men devoted to the pursuit of trade, who thought it advantageous to trade on both sides of the Ems and to make profit, the Groningers were disturbed by their trading or staple there, in whose possession the Groningers were by the will of the allies, chiefly on the shore of the Ems and the Dollart. And these things, while the rest of the land was quiet, were then the subject of contention between the two rival cities. But certain men from the nobility, especially Haio Ripperda of Farmsum, Ailco Houverda of Munten, and Eppo Gockinga of Brokum, secretly favoured the Hamburgers, more out of hatred for the city than love for them. In the meantime Guilhelmus Wichering, born in Groningen of a consular family, then prefect of the merchants, while he wished to defend the rights of the city, was killed in the territory of Ripperda by the attack of seditious men. When the Groningers showed that they were taking up arms for the sake of this final outrage, Haio Ripperda, to whom the killing was said to be attributed, struck with fear, thought it better to placate the offended than to test their force. Therefore, having offered satisfaction, he came to terms with them, and promised that he would not disturb the city in its possession of the right of the staple, or of the market, but would give up to them this right as free; and that he would not only not be an obstacle in this matter, but would also give help, if use required it; then, for the killing of Wichering, and for the other damages inflicted, he himself and his people would pay at D. Arnoldicos; in addition, he would have the same as enemies, internal or external, to the city, would work on its behalf, and would open his fortress at Farmsum to its garrison and refuge alike. Thus these things were both agreed and sealed.

units.la: anno M. CCCC, XXXIV, pridie Laurentij. Hinc post menses fere duos inducia inter Hamburgen- ses & Groningenos in proximum biennium facta, & per eas liber commeatus negociantibus utrimq; datus, decretum etiam, ut interea de pace perpetua compositis omnibus differentibus inter has civitates ageretur.
units.tr: In the year 1434, on the day before the feast of Laurence. About two months later a truce was made between the Hamburgers and the Groningers for the next two years, and free passage of goods for traders was granted on both sides; it was also decreed that in the meantime a discussion should take place toward a perpetual peace, with all disputes between these cities settled.

units.la: Anno sequente feorsim cum vicis quatuor Farm[?]fumano, Weiwerdico, Hevenschæo, Oterdumzo, mox cum duobus aliis in eadem vicinia Holuerdico & Merfumano in eandem sententiam, cum Wijnscota- nis, deniq; cum Finseranis & Egeftanis in pre- sectura veteri civitas pepigit: Et cum his quidem postremis sic convenit, ut si universa vetus præ- sectura cum civitate fœdus iniret, tum ut ipsi quoque eo comprehenderentur, & his pactis præsentibus non tenerentur amplius: sin mi- nus, hæc valerent in annos XII: cum primis vero & fecundis sic [?]fi contingeret civitatem cu Dammonensibus priore fœderis tempore fi- nito, aut etiam ante, in novum fœdus confen- tire, tum, ut hæc pacta irrita effent: alioquin in annos XII vim haberent. VINSCOTANI simpliciter in easdem leges consenserunt cum DAMMONENSIBVS, & reliquis FIVELGONIIS, ac HVNESGONIIS, in annus similiter XII:
units.tr: In the following year the city made a separate agreement with the four villages of Farmsum, Weiwerd, Hevenschaen, and Oterdum, and soon afterwards, with two others in the same neighbourhood, Holwerd and Marsum, on the same terms; then with the Winschotans, and finally with the Finsters and the Eegstans in the old prefecture. And with these last it agreed in such a way that if the whole old prefecture made a covenant with the city, then they too would be included in it, and would no longer be bound by these present pacts; but if not, these would hold for twelve years. With the first and second [villages], however, it was agreed that if the city, after the earlier term of the covenant with the Dammonians had ended, or even before, should come to consent to a new covenant, then these pacts would be void; otherwise they would have force for twelve years. The Winschotans simply consented to the same laws as the Dammonians and the other Fivelgoers and the Hunsgoers, likewise for twelve years:

units.la: sed expresse de provocatione ad tribunal oppidanum ex formula fœderis HVNESGONII & FIVELGONII, ac more prisco. Eodem die, quo cum Winscotanis facta conventio, (id fuit v Iduum Aprilis) cum Haiyone Ripperda & filio eius BOLONE, pactis quoq; prior iterata, denuo rite signata, & vinculo fidei novo firmata val- F 3 dim. dius. Sic enim obligarunt se Ripperdei, & ha- redes suos, si quid delinquerent contra foedus aut pacta haec, ut bona sua omnia, & omnes possessiones caderent in commissum, ce-derentq; civitati. Adiccere etiam placere sibi, & rata habere, qua cum vicinis vicis quatuor civitas pepigisse. Nec diu post Midwoldy, Oftwoldy, Fmferwoldy, Veenhusy, Scemedam, Egiftani, Medensfes, Muntendammenses, Suidbroky, Nortbroky, Wagenborgy, in praefectura vetere omnes etiam ipsi cum civitate pacti sunt in annos totidem. In pactis praecipua fuere: ut libertas patria, & ius cuiq; suum, ditiones, iurisdictiones, illesae conservarentur: in exilio sine causa iusta nemo pelleretur: iudiciis & legibus controversiae disceptarentur & finirentur: vis omnis abesset: exteri principes, alijq; libertatem pressuri, aut iniurii cuiquam futuri mutua ope finibus regionis arcerentur; ad hoc rem non ferenti opem gravis multa esset: multa aequaliter inter socios dividerentur: si qua pars agri huius socii, si quis vicus, si vir nobilis ignobilisve, in fraudem civitatis aut agri praesidium haberet, peregrinumve militem intra fines vocaret, ei iisve coniunctis omnium virib. resisteretur. Deinde de maleficiis & iniuriis coercendis prolixe, de obsidib. expeditionum tempore in urbe habendis. Tum porro haec: a quatuor pluresve in urbe quotannis haberen-tur: tur: violans euntem ad vrbem mercatus cau-fa,aut inde redeuntem triplæ pœnæ reus esset: tributum à sociis agrariis non exigeretur, nisi ex ipsorum consensu. Signata hac die viii, Maij, anno M. cccc. xxxv.
units.tr: but expressly concerning appeal to the town tribunal, according to the form of the covenant of the Hunsgoers and the Fivelgoers, and by ancient custom. On the same day on which the agreement with the Winschotans was made (which was the fifth of the Ides of April), the earlier pact was also repeated with Haio Ripperda and his son Bolo, renewed, duly sealed again, and strengthened by a new bond of faith. For the Ripperdas bound themselves and their heirs in this way: if they should offend against this covenant or these pacts, all their goods and all their possessions would fall to forfeit and pass to the city. They also added that they would hold valid and ratify whatever the city had agreed upon with the four neighbouring villages. Not long after, Midwolde, Oostwolde, Finsterwolde, Veenhuizen, Schemerhorn, the Eegstans, the Medemblikers, the Muntendammers, Zuidbroek, Noordbroek, and Wagenborg, all in the old prefecture, likewise made pacts with the city for as many years. The chief points of the pacts were these: that the liberty of the country, and the right of each to his own, their domains and jurisdictions, be preserved unharmed; that no one be expelled from exile without just cause; that controversies be disputed and settled by judgments and laws; that all violence be absent; that foreign princes, and others who would oppress liberty or be wrongful to anyone, be kept out of the borders of the region by mutual aid; that for one who did not bring aid when required there would be a heavy fine; that fines be divided equally among the allies; that if any part of this land, any ally, any village, or any nobleman or commoner should have a protection that was to the fraud of the city or the land, or should summon a foreign soldier within the borders, they would be resisted with the strength of all of them and of those joined to them. Then, at length, concerning the restraint of crimes and injuries, and concerning hostages to be kept in the town during times of expedition. Furthermore, these: that four or more markets be held each year in the town; that one who hindered a man going to the town for the sake of trade, or returning from it, should be liable to a threefold penalty; that tribute should not be exacted from the agrarian allies except by their own consent. Sealed on this day, the eighth of May, in the year 1435.

units.la: Eo tempore varia quoq; cum Ailcone Houverdeo, & Eppone Gockinga Brocaeo acta. De quibus res monet, ut pauca nunc dicam. Uterq; enim opibus validus in præfectura vetere fuit. Ex his Ailco Mennonis Houverdæ Ebone nati filius, Muntensis, temporibus Kenonis Broecmerij [?] sive iritatus à Sciringiis, seu sponte sua impulsus, auxilio Kenonis proxi-mos aliquot eius ora genere & opibus præcipuos, & uti reor, Sciringicarum partium suspectos, fortunis & patria eiecerat, domos plerorumq; everterat, ex materia earum ipse arcem sibi validam apud Muntensis ea parte, quæ Hol-ma dicitur, extruxerat, deniq; se Rectorem vicinorum pagorum inde vsq; ad Dullarti oram constituerat. Post cum Focco Leranus Vconis F. feceßione à domo Broecmeria factâ, bello, Groninganis & sociis, Broecmeriorum parti inhærentibus illato, victoriaq; reportata, Ailconem quoq; in ordinem redegisset roga-tus ab exulibus, atq; æqua cum pati coegisset, exules quidem restituti in integrum sunt: sed eodem, domi cum dominatum strueret, à suis vicissim in ordinem redactus, Ailco cum Hamburgensibus Focconianarum partium ho-stib. Emdam tum tenentibus societate iuncta, auxilio eorum exules rursum exturbarat oppres-feratve; deinde ut gratum novis socijs faceret, & suas res proveheret, societati civitatis Groninga-na, & ijs, quae societatem sequebantur, se coepit obijcere. Mox exemplum vicinum Ripperdaeo-rum metuens, & simul ab exulibus formidinem habens, ac iniuriarum in diversos, adeoq; in oppi-danos sibi conscium, praesidium sociorum in arcem-suam recepit. Eo fretus liberius jam societatem & pacta conventa cum Groninganis turbare, commercia impedire, negociantibus infestus esse: inter Hamburgenses quoq; & Groninganos si-multas & odia asperari. Interea & Eppo Gockinga in ea praefectura veteris parte, qua ager palustris & nemorosus est, quae in austrum vergit, apud Suidbrocaos sedem habens, Aiyoldi & Tammonis Gockingiorum haereditate locuples ac potens, ut est natura hominum, a magnis ad majora contendebat, & jus, quod multorum erat, in se solum sensim trahebat, seq; summum praetorem per totam illam oram haberi volebat: atque hanc ad rem amicitia Hamburgensium, & Ailconis Howerdaei, & affinitate GRE-THANORVM, qui tum in Frisia orientali supra reliquos in nobilitate eminebant, quorum erat gener & sororius, abutebatur. Hinc factiones[?] vicinorum contra ipsum, & inimicitiae mutuae, interdum & injuriae: & ipse Eppo turbidior Groningani, & societati eorum infestus, ac vicissim civitatis animi non satis in eum placati. Videbantur, ad arma res tendere, cum inter HamburHamburgenses & Groninganos inducię bienniș sunt facte. His inducijs durantibus pactionș illę, de quibus dixi, anno M. CCCC. XXXV. cum civitate inita.
units.tr: At that time various things were also done with Ailco Houverda and Eppo Gockinga of Brok. These matters prompt me to say a few things now. For both of them were powerful in the old district. Ailco, son of Mennon Houverda and Ebo, of Muntens, at the time of Keno Broecmer [?], either provoked by the Sciringi or driven on by his own will, with Keno's help had driven out of their lands and homeland several of his nearest neighbours, men outstanding in birth and wealth and, as I suppose, suspected of supporting the Sciringi party; he had overturned most of their houses and from their materials built himself a strong fortress among the Muntenses in the part called Holma, and finally had set himself up as ruler of the neighbouring districts as far as the shore of the Dollart. Afterwards, when Focco Leranus, son of Uko, had broken away from the house of Broecmer and waged war on the Groningers and their allies, who sided with the Broecmer faction, and had won the victory, he forced Ailco too into line when the exiles asked him to. He made Ailco endure equal terms, and the exiles were restored to their full rights. But when Ailco was plotting to rule at home, he was in turn brought into line by his own people. Ailco then joined with the Hamburgers, who at that time held Emden in alliance with the enemies of Focco's party, and with their help again drove out or crushed the exiles. Then, to win favour with his new allies and advance his own affairs, he began to set himself against the civic alliance of Groningen and those who followed that alliance. Soon, fearing the nearby Ripperda family's example and at the same time harbouring fear of the exiles, and conscious of his wrongs against various people, and so against the townsmen, he took a garrison of allies into his fortress. Relying on this, he now more freely disturbed the alliance and the agreements made with the Groningers, hindered trade, and made himself hostile to merchants; between the Hamburgers and the Groningers too, quarrels and hatreds were sharpened. Meanwhile Eppo Gockinga, who had his seat at Suidbrock in that part of the old district where the marshy and wooded land lies, facing south, rich and powerful by inheritance from Aiyold and Tammo Gockinga, as human nature is, pressed on from great things to greater, and gradually drew to himself the right which belonged to many, and wished to be regarded as chief magistrate over that whole shore. He made use for this purpose of the friendship of the Hamburgers, of Ailco Houverda, and of his marriage ties with the Gretha family, who at that time in East Friesland stood out above the rest in nobility, and of whom he was son-in-law and brother-in-law. Hence came factions among the neighbours against him, mutual enmities, and at times injuries; and Eppo himself became more turbulent against Groningen and hostile to their alliance, while the feelings of the city towards him were not sufficiently soothed. Matters seemed to be heading to arms, when a two-year truce was made between the Hamburgers and the Groningers. While this truce lasted, those agreements of which I have spoken were concluded with the city in the year 1435.

units.la: At inducijs vixdum finitis incrudescere priora, Ailco & Eppo inter cives aut socios Groninganos injuriį esse, & vi-ciffim à Groninganis pati, quæ nollent, Eppo præcipuè, qui parte opum est ejectus Hamburgensibus in Amasana occupatis. Demum per arbitros rursum inter civitatem utramque, atque item cum Howerdæis res compositæ. Hac compositione Groninga in possessione juris & patrum per agrum relicta: injuriarum oblivio inter civitatem & Hovverdæos fancita, controversiæq; compositæ. Exulibus, quos Houverdæi, quosq; Eppo expulerat, & fortunis everterant, reditus & restitutio decreta.
units.tr: But scarcely had the truce ended when the earlier troubles flared up again: Ailco and Eppo were doing wrong to citizens or allies of Groningen, and in turn were suffering from the Groningers what they did not wish, especially Eppo, who had been driven from part of his wealth when the Hamburgers occupied Amasana. At last matters were settled again by arbitrators between both the city and the Houverdas. By this settlement Groningen was left in possession of its rights and of its fathers' land throughout the district; an oblivion of injuries between the city and the Houverdas was ratified, and the disputes were settled. For the exiles whom the Houverdas and Eppo had expelled, and whose property they had overturned, return and restoration were decreed.

units.la: Inter Epponem porrò & civitatem sic convenit, ut Epponi res redderentur cum pace ad biennium: intra hoc biennium controversiæ inter eos per arbitros componerentur: Sed cum Ailco & Eppo ad ingenium redissent, & Hamburgensium navarchus Groninganos quoq; esset deprædatus, civitas iniuriam ultura arcem Muntensem Ailconis invasit, & cum præsidio Hamburgensi redegit in potestatem. Eodem impetu cursum Epponem quoq;, nuper reditus iterum eiecit, & pluribus aliis exuit: turrim munitam in Bellinguvoldis vi captam solo aequavit. Hoc casu consternatus Houverdæus cum à socijs nil auxilij expectaret (erant quippe armis ab exulibus tum forte lacessiti atq; occupati) cum Groninganis transegit in hanc sententiam: vt ipse haberet reliqua sua omnia, prædia, jura, jurisdictiones inter Amafum, & Lavicam fl. Groninganis relinqueret, possessionem arcis Muntensis cum agri jugeribus cc in pignus servandæ fidei: id valeret ad transactionem plenam & perpetuam, in quam bini utrinque arbitri deligerentur. Factum anno M. cccc. xxxviii, die Gereonis. Ludovicus Hornkenius præfectus arci a civitate datus. Nec diu post compositionem banc Ailco supervixit, & civitas anno proximo, arce minoris Muntæ ab ijs, quorum erat, empta, cum Hissa uxore Ailconis vidua, atque item liberis eius denuo pepigit in hunc modum. Civitas Hissae & liberis ejus omnes eo-rum res, quæ bono jure & sine controversia eorundem sunt, relinquit usq; quo liberi omnes, aut quidam ex iis ad justam ætatem pervenerint: tum ex formula compromissi, in qua civitati cum vivente Ailcone convenerat, omnis controversia vel per arbitratores, vel per judices definietur in perpetuum: interea civitas reti-net arcem Muntensem cum iugeribus agri centum è numero ducentorum nec optimis, nec deterrimis: & totam jurisdictionem arci co-hærentem, querelæ de injuriis aut detrimen-tis mutuis, quæ in bello accidere, omnes suspenduntur tantisper. Signatum anno M. cccc. xl. mense Novembri. Sic civi-tas in possessione hac, atque administratione ju-ris per omnem illam vicinam volentibus peten-tibusq; vicinis discordiarum & inæquabilis ju-rifdictionis pertæsis mansit usq; in annum M. cccc.
units.tr: Between Eppo and the city it was further agreed that Eppo should have his property restored with peace for two years: within these two years the disputes between them were to be settled by arbitrators. But when Ailco and Eppo had returned to their former ways, and the Hamburger admiral had also plundered the Groningers, the city, avenging the wrong, attacked Ailco's fortress at Muntens and, with a Hamburger garrison, reduced it to its power. With the same onslaught it also expelled Eppo, who had lately been restored, and stripped many others of their possessions; it captured by force the fortified tower at Bellingwolde and levelled it to the ground. Dismayed by this turn of events, Houverda, who could expect no help from his allies (they had at that time been attacked by the exiles and were occupied with arms by chance), came to terms with the Groningers on this basis: he himself should keep all his remaining property, estates, rights and jurisdictions between the Amasus and the river Lavica, and should surrender to the Groningers the possession of the fortress of Muntens together with two hundred acres of land as a pledge for keeping faith; this should hold for a full and perpetual settlement, for which two arbitrators on each side were to be chosen. Done in the year 1438, on the feast of Gereon. Ludovicus Hornkenius was appointed by the city as prefect of the fortress.
