Transla-vicanis, atq; à fœdere Groningano vi & aperto bello aversis, inq; fidem suam adactis, Groningam quoq; & agrum vicinum tentavit. Nam hos quo-q; ad imperium sibi commissum pertinere ferebat, habebatq; pro se interpretem controversiæ Maxi-milianum. Verum cum res per intercessiones & colloquia non procederet, ipse ob filij casum, quem Tranflavicani Franekeræ[?] obsederant, secundo in Frisiam veniens, liberato filio, & rebus Tranflavicanis pro tempore constitutis exercitum eis Lavicam adduxit, nulloq; negocio agrum in suam potestatem & fidem redegit. Sed in obsi-denda urbe dum haret, intercedente rursum
units.tr: At this time King Maximilian made an arrangement with Albert, Duke of Saxony, for subduing Frisia. Albert, as if going to be a helper for the Scarlingers, sent soldiers into Frisia; soon afterwards he sent another, having concealed his name and purpose, of Vetkopers, who were to serve for pay, so that they might wear down the region and render it weak. Then, when it seemed the right time, and almost all were weary, a charter was sent into Frisia, by which the government of Frisia was assigned by Maximilian and the orders of the Empire to Albert of Saxony under the title of Governor; and it was ordered that this should be perpetual, passing to heirs. It was added, however, that once the expenses of war had been repaid and a certain sum of money paid, the whole government and all right in Frisia should pass to Philip of Burgundy, son of Maximilian. Albert, through his men whom he had sent ahead, having overpowered all the Translavicans and turned them away from the Groningen covenant by force and open war, and brought them into his faith, also attempted Groningen and the neighbouring territory. For he also claimed that these lay within the authority committed to him, and he had Maximilian as an interpreter of the dispute on his side. But since matters did not advance through mediation and conferences, he himself, on account of his son's misfortune, whom the Translavicans had besieged at Franeker, coming a second time into Frisia, having freed his son and settled Translavican affairs for the time being, brought an army to Lauwers, and without any trouble brought the region under his power and faith. But while he was occupied in besieging the city, by the intervention again

units.la: e[?] = ornamental mark in the text, presumably a reference or a flourish.
units.tr: The e[?] above is a printer's ornament, a flourish rather than any words of the text, so there is nothing to translate here.

units.la: GEORGIO THORENIO equestris dignitatis viro nobili ad hoc à principibus Germaniæ misso, &c cum eo FRIDERICO BADENSI episcopo Vltraiectino, colloquium denuò coiit, anno M. D. mense Augusto: in quo colloquio res tandem composita & bellum diremptum. Conditionum praecipuae fuere, ut controversiae inter Albertum & civitatem, de potestate prætoria in agrum vicinum cum Hovetmannis, de imperio in præfecturam veterem, de jure stapulæ rerum χωρίων[?], de usu solius cerevisiæ Groningæ in tabernis ac diversoriis per agrum, de non coquenda cerevisia quæstus causa in agro, & quæ alia pactis & fœderibus nitebantur, aut more inolita erant, quæ omnia sibi dimitti poscebat Albertus, Cameræ imperij judicio definienda permitterentur: interea THORENIVS nomine reip. Germaniæ SEQVESTER reb. illic præesset, agrarios ordines ea fide, qua civitati obligati erant, solutos, in fidem suam adigeret, jus æqualiter ex more & legibus regionis aut ipse diceret, aut dici curaret, usq; dum Camera litem definiret, eo facto, ei omnia singulaeve rursum traderet, cui Camera addixisset: partes quoq; jurarent, judicio Camerae se obsequuturos: Tantisper verò Groningani manerent in posses- sione juris stapulæ, nundinarum, eius, quod ad cerevisiam pertinet, & similium aliorum, eo modo, quo fuerat antelitem hanc à Saxone illatam ab ultima usque hominum memoria, nec liceret butirum, caseos, equos, boves, vac» cas,cæteraq; id genus mercimonia alibi quam » Groninge in stapulæ loco more solito venun-dare, venū ve proponere, vel in regiones alias » præterita Groninga exportare aut abigere: Excepta modo effent, quæ hujus generis viris nobilibus in prædiis ipsorum provenirent, quibus jus effet pro libitu & commodo suo ea divendere: idemq; valeret de DAMMONENSI-BUS. Exempta quoque stapulæ legi mane-ret præfectura vetus, utereturque jure ac liber-tate pristina, emeret, venderet, cerevisiam co-queret pro libitu, uti folebat, quoad duraret » hæc sequestris ratio: Groninganietiam in exi-» genda pecunia credita & reditibus aliis per » agrum retinerent jus & morem solitum, » modò ut judex in eo tribunali in urbe esset » ipse Thorenius, aut legatus eius, aliusve » pro eo sequester ab ordinibus imperii datus.
units.tr: with Georgius Thorenius, a nobleman of equestrian rank, sent for this purpose by the princes of Germany, and with him Frederick of Baden, bishop of Utrecht, a conference was again held in August 1500, in which the matter was at last settled and the war ended. The chief terms were these: that the disputes between Albert and the city, concerning the praetorian power over the neighbouring territory with the Hovetmen, concerning authority over the old prefecture, concerning the staple right of goods, concerning the use of Groningen beer alone in taverns and inns throughout the countryside, concerning not brewing beer for profit in the countryside, and other matters which rested on agreements and covenants or had grown up by custom, all of which Albert demanded should be dropped for himself, should be left to be decided by the judgment of the Imperial Chamber; meanwhile Thorenius, acting in the name of the Germanic Commonwealth, was to preside there as sequestrator, and was to bind the rural orders, released from the faith they owed the city, to his own faith, and himself declare or cause to be declared the law equally according to the custom and laws of the region, until the Chamber should settle the dispute; and when this was done, he would hand back everything, individually or collectively, to whomever the Chamber should award it; the parties too were to swear that they would obey the judgment of the Chamber. Meanwhile the Groningers were to remain in possession of the staple right, of the markets, of what pertains to beer, and of other similar things, in the same way as they had been before this dispute was brought by the Saxon, from the furthest memory of men; and it was not to be lawful to sell or offer for sale butter, cheeses, horses, oxen, cows, and other goods of that kind anywhere other than at Groningen in the staple place, as is customary, or to export or drive them to other regions without passing through Groningen. The exception was made only for such goods of this kind as would grow on the estates of the noblemen themselves, who should have the right to sell them at their pleasure and convenience; and the same was to hold for the people of Dammen. The old prefecture was also to remain exempt from the staple law, and it was to use its ancient right and liberty, to buy, to sell, and to brew beer at its pleasure, as it was accustomed to do, for as long as this sequestration arrangement lasted; the Groningers too were to keep the usual right and custom of exacting money owed and other revenues throughout the countryside, provided that the judge in that court in the city was Thorenius himself, or his deputy, or another sequestrator given for this by the orders of the Empire. These and other matters having been approved and signed by both parties, and confirmed also with the seals of two intercessors, finally peace was established. Not long afterwards Albert, already carried away from the body, died at Emden. But Thorenius, having been called away from Frisia at an unseasonable time by Henry…

units.la: Atq; hæc probata signataq; ab utraq; parte, & sigillis quoq; duorum intercessorum ad fidem munita: deniq; pax constitutu. Nec multò post ALBERTUS jam tum corpore agro Emdam de-latus, atq; ibi vita functus est. THORENIUS vero intempestive Frisiâ evocatus ab HENRI-CO Alberti filio, malis adhuc haud bene posi-tis, quæ in rep. sociorum hærebant, (erant .n. nobilitatis agraria animi in civitatem, & huius vicissim in illam ex injuriis mutuis exacerbati) quibus ipsum se interponere, remedium, adhibere convenieb at, cum ditius etiam quam par esset, emansitaret, occasioni fuit, ut anno proximo in arma rursum sit itum, transactio, neglecta pene evanuerit. Et quo tempore repetitis sepe indu-cÿs suquys fussetata[?] diu res, & colloquys iterum tentata, tandem anno M. D. V in acerbissimum & maximum bellum erupit. Eo civitas ab omni parte obsessa, & in extremas tandem redacta, angustias, ob acerbitatem & ὕβριν[?] Saxonicam, urgente necessitate, duro telo, in fidem demum Edsardi Comitis Frisiae Orientalis bactenus[?] hostis[?] postis fui se contulit. Id enim satius putavit, quam ipse dedere, quorum verba & facta pluf-quam barbara & crudelia in obsidione proximis mensibus audierat, videratq;. Id factum anno M. D. VI, mense Aprili. Conditiones sane dure, quibus se dedidit, & non satis è iure pri-stino. In quibus fuere hæc: Vt Edsardus in urbem reciperetur cum armatis DCCC: ut magistratum civesq; iurejurando adigeret in fidem suam: ut locum in urbe, quem vellet, muniret, & præsidio insideret: omnia in eventum iudicij principum ac reliquorum ordinum Germaniæ. Deinde & hæc. Vt idem Edsardus ex ordine honestiorum civium deligerent pro arbitratu suo, qui pecuniæ creditæ iudicia, aliaq;[?] Hovermannis solita in urbe excerent in eos qui agrum habitant, idq; more & modo pristino, sed nomine ipsius: Vt fruamenta in agro nata non alibi quam Groninga-NINGÆ & DAMMONÆ venirent: decas-teris ἐτέροις χωρίοις[?] Edsardus adhibitis in confi-lium Groninganis certi quid statueret, quod esset ex commodo urbis & agri. Dè cere-visia nihil mutatum. Cautum, ut omne jus hoc ad heredes Edsardi & fratris eius V CONIS: transtransiret[?]. Signatum utrinq; postridie Georgij. Hoc facto omnium animi suspensi, maximè verò Saxonum, qui quo animo esset Edsardus, erant incerti. Et quia de eventu judicij scriptum in conditionibus intellexerant, ad cognitionem cau-sa rem deducere maturabant. Cognitioq; solennis instituta est Constantiæ: sed iis eventus ibi fuit, ut civitas haud dubie jure, Georgius Saxo gratia esse superior videretur. Definitum tamen illic nihil. Deinde colloquijs multis & variis per aliquot annos tentatum denuò negocium: sed nec his quicquam profectum. Nam Saxo decedere jure in agrum, & fœderibus renunciare civitatem jubebat: civitas ut id faceret, nulla ratione persuaderi volebat. Igitur anno M. D. XIII resumptis armis, EDSARDO cum civitate in Saxonis gratiam proscripto, concitata in hos magna Germaniæ parte, bello, summis viribus, summa contentione longo tempore continuato, Frisia orientali pessundata, tribus Edsardi arcib. occupatis, Edsardus imparem se solum tanta moli sentiens ad CAROLVM GELDRIÆ ducem Gallorum regis socium, Burgundis & Austriacis inimicum se contulit, ut auxilia ab eo pararet. Is fortunam sequens versuti princeps ingenij, promisit benignè, pecuniamq; etiam in eum finem accepit. Sed miles promissus non ante venit, quam DAMMONA quoq; vi esset à Saxonib. occupata, & GRONINGA in arctum redacta. Et tum Geldri legatus, qui auxilijs præerat, Guilhelmus Oyensis, in extrema civitatis necessitate cum eum differri diutius deditio non posse videretur, profissus etiam est, sic sibi mandatum à principe, « ne quid opis pressis ferret, neu rebus Edsardi civi- « tatis, ullo se modo misceret, ni prius hæc illius « fide soluta in Geldricum nomen jurasset: nec .n. [?] « æquum esse, principem tantam rem tam sumptuo- « sam, difficilem, periculosam ag gredi, tanti hostis « offensionem in se suscipere, omnemq; pene Germa- « niam irritare, & nullum opera sua pretium ferre. « His addidit de optima principis voluntate in civi- « tatem, imprimis de privilegiorum ac juris pri- « stini restitutione, deq; arcis demolitione, alia, qua « ducendis animis esse putabat. Itaq; inclinante « huc civitate, ex hominum natura melioris condi- « tionis avida, nec libenter manente in ea fortuna, « cujus ipsos pænitet, EDSARDUS quoq; quamquam « inopina oratione attonitus primum & indignans, « tamen quod sapientis erat, parendum necessitati « putavit. Nec mora, exautorata ab eo civitas « apud Oyensem in fidem GELDRIÆ ducis iura- uit, vergente jam anno M, D. XIIII. Con- ditionum contractus hujus summa fuit hæc. Geldrus causam civitatis contra Vltraiectinos non solum auxilia non ferentes laboranti, uti debebant, sed vim quoq; cum hoste inferen- tes, impendio suo, fine molestia & sumptu ip- sius, ageret & tueretur: civitas in nomen Gel- dricum juraret in perpetuum, imperiumq; in agrum universum Lavica & Amaso clausum, in quo & vetus præfectura, principi cederet: prætoriam potestatem à principe delegatam in res agri tenerent, & velut principem repræ- sentafentarent, unus è consiliariis principis à principe datus, & quatuor viri è numero honestiorum civium ad hoc idoneorum à senatu urbano electi, ijdemq; eodem jure essent, quo Hovetmanni illi veteres quondam fuerant antebellum Saxonicum, eadem omnia, quæ olim isti, haberent & facerent, servato more antiquo: jus stapulæ, quod vocant, omnium rerum venalium quæ in agro sunt, proveniutve, integrũ per omnia maneret civitati eo modo, quo ante hos motus & arma Saxonica fuere; In frumento quoque & cerevisia idem servaretur, quod olim solebat: ἀυτονομία[?] civitati & agro, atque usus patriarum legum maneret; quisque jus suum integrum & illibatum retineneret[?], quisque possessiones, res, prædia intra extraq; aggeres haberet: nec princeps quicquam novi instituerct: idem nullo unquam tempore vel ipse separaret à civitate agrum, vel separari per alium sineret, aut occasionem separationi daret: munitiones quoque omnes in agro demoliretur, nec novas alias extrueret, extruive paterertur: deniquetributo[?] annuo æquo ac tolerabili ex agro sibi hæredibusque suis pendendo cum civib. & agri incolis compararet, à quo nullæ possessiones aut res in agro sitæ immunes essent. Hæc concepta tum, & probata utrimq.: sed in solennem formam redacta, & signata post annos demum tres, cum ager totus ab hoste quoq; liberatus, & principi subiectus esset. Is fuit annus à Christo nato M. D. XVIII, & mensis Februarij dies XVIII. Deinde anno M. D. XXI inter prinprincipem & ordines agri in curia Gronin-gana per legatos Geldricos senatumq; vrbanum sic convenit, ut ipsi in fide principis essent, & haeredum eius in perpetuum: princeps & haeredes integra servarent ipsis privilegia, jura, instituta, leges, consuetudines, secundum foedera & pacta olim inter ipsos & civitatem inita. Sic in nomen Geldricum ab ordinibus juratum, praemissa conditione hac, non diutius valituram vim juramenti huius, quam Geldrus tueri regionem posset. Et mox haec pacta a principe sunt signata die Junij xx. Verum cum progressu temporis cum longius paulatim tendere, & a pactis recedere, & civitatis jura aratre deprehenderetur GELDRVS, à MARVVICO praetore primum incitatus, cui simultas cum senatu intercedebat, deinde irritatus, quod, belle pro Balthasaro Esenfi in Frisia Orientali contra Ennonem Comitem vicinum suscepto, in ejus impensas tributu sibi a civitate negaretur, & suapte natura potentia per fas & nefas augenda auidus, & turbulentus, occasione rapta, quam fors offerebat, per MEINHARDVM Hammenfem cla- rum militia virum, Daniae regis auspicia profitentem, occultis mandatis suis instructum, adducti copys tumultus in agro, & ad ipsas portas urbis cieret, suburbia vastaret & incenderet, DAMMONAM summa festinatione muniret, postremo in colloquio Esena componenda rei causa instituto per Henricu Grovium ERCLENII dominum legatum suum, & Hacfordum militum praefepræfectum palam jam poscéret, arcem munitam in urbe sibi extrui, DAMMONÆq; munitione perfici, civitas merito ab eo animis alienata, ad partes BVRGVNDICAS se vertit: Nec mora, re cum agrariis ordinibus deliberata, ex eorum consensu ad GEORGIVM SCENKIVM Teuto-burgium, qui Transflavicanis pro CAROLO V IMP. tum præerat, legatos misit, ac deditionem obtulit. Atq; ille edoctus celeriter de voluntate MARIÆ sororis Caroli imp. Belgij Gubernatricis, ad quam scripserat, sine mora cum iis, quas in promptu habebat, copiis Groningam profectus, cum de conditionibus imperandi parendiq; convenisset, civitatem ordinesq; agrarios simul in fidem Caroli imp. Brabantiæ ducis & Hollandiæ Selandiæq; comitis, & Frisiæ ac Transisalanæ[?] domini, velut unius reip. populum recepit die Iunij mensis VIII anno, quem dixi, M. D. XXXVI. Eo facto, cum exer-citu DAMMONAM præfectus eam obsedit, occupatoq; interea die VIII Iulij per deditionem castello Delffilano, quod Geldri quoq; tenebant, copiisq;, quæ auxilio obsessis a DANO ve-nebant, duorum circiter millium, concisis, tandem extremas in angustias redactam dere se coegit, durissimis conditionibus. Nam sic convenit, ut duces militiæ Meinardus & Hacfordus in vincula Teutoburgio traderen-tur: reliqui cohortium præfecti ac milites captivorum instar, inermes, virgam albam manu gerentes sine sarcinis exirent, suaq; omnia
units.tr: Having been approved and signed by both parties, and confirmed with the seals of two intercessors as well, the peace was finally settled. Not long afterwards Albert, already carried off in body to Emden, died there. THORENIUS, however, was called to Friesland at an inopportune time by HENRY, Albert's son, while the evils of the old quarrel still remained unsettled in the commonwealth of the allies (for the minds of the rural nobility and of the city had been inflamed by mutual injuries, each against the other), and it was his duty to interpose himself and apply a remedy to these. But because he lingered there for longer than was fitting, an occasion arose for taking up arms again the following year, and the agreement was almost forgotten and came to nothing. And at the time when, after truces were often renewed, the affair was dragged on for a long while and negotiations were attempted once more, at last in the year 1505 it broke out into a most bitter and great war. Then the city, besieged on every side and at last driven into the narrowest straits, under the pressure of necessity, with a hard blow from the bitterness and insolence of the Saxons, betook itself, as a last resort, into the protection of Edzard, Count of East Friesland, until then an enemy. For it thought this better than surrendering to those whose words and deeds, more than barbarous and cruel, it had heard of and seen during the siege in the preceding months. This was done in the year 1506, in the month of April. The conditions on which it surrendered were indeed harsh, and not sufficiently in accordance with its former law. Among them were these: that Edzard should be received into the city with 800 armed men; that he should bind the magistrates and citizens by oath to his allegiance; that he should fortify whatever place in the city he wished and garrison it; all of this subject to the outcome of the judgment of the princes and the other estates of Germany. Then also this: that the same Edzard should choose, at his own discretion, from the body of the more honourable citizens, men who would exercise in the city the jurisdiction over loans of money and other matters customary for the Hoverman, over those who inhabit the countryside, and that this should be done in the former manner and form, but in his name; that the grain grown in the countryside should be sold nowhere but at Groningen and Dammona, and not in other places; that Edzard, having consulted the Groningers, should decide on some definite matter that would be for the advantage of city and countryside. Nothing was changed concerning beer. It was provided that all this right should pass to the heirs of Edzard and of his brother Count... Signed by both sides on the day after St. George's. Once this was done, the minds of all were held in suspense, and most of all those of the Saxons, who were uncertain what disposition Edzard had. And because they had understood from the conditions that the outcome would be decided by a judgment, they hastened to bring the matter to a hearing. A formal hearing was set up at Constance, but its outcome there was such that the city seemed, without doubt in law, but George the Saxon seemed superior in favour. Nothing was defined there, however. Then the matter was tried again through many and various conferences over some years, but nothing was gained by these either. For the Saxon ordered that the city should, by right, withdraw from the countryside and renounce its alliances; the city refused to be persuaded in any way to do this. Therefore, in the year 1513, arms were taken up again, with Edzard proscribed in the Saxon's favour and the city; a great part of Germany being stirred against them in war, which was waged for a long time with the utmost forces and the greatest exertion, East Friesland was laid waste, three of Edzard's fortresses were occupied, and Edzard, feeling himself alone too weak for so great a burden, betook himself to CHARLES, Duke of Guelders, ally of the King of the French and enemy of the Burgundians and Austrians, to obtain auxiliary forces from him. He, following fortune, a prince of shrewd talent, promised kindly, and even received money for that purpose. But the promised soldiers did not come until DAMMONA also had been taken by force by the Saxons, and GRONINGEN was pressed into a narrow strait. Then the Guelderish envoy who was in charge of the auxiliaries, WILLIAM of Oye, when the surrender seemed unable to be delayed any longer in the city's extreme necessity, declared also that, as he had been ordered by the prince, "he should bring no help to the oppressed, nor should he in any way meddle in the affairs of Edzard or of the city, unless first, with these matters loosed by his faith, they swore allegiance in the name of Guelders; for it was not fair that the prince should undertake so great, so costly, so difficult and dangerous an affair, take upon himself the enmity of so great an enemy, and stir up almost all Germany, and gain nothing worthwhile by his efforts." To these he added concerning the excellent good will of the prince towards the city, especially concerning the restoration of privileges and of former right, and the demolition of the fortress, and other things which he thought would win over their minds. And so, while the city was inclining this way, being by human nature eager for a better condition and not willingly remaining in a fortune which they regretted, Edzard too, though at first astonished and indignant at this unexpected speech, nevertheless, as was the part of a wise man, thought he must yield to necessity. Without delay the city, released from him, swore allegiance to the Duke of Guelders before Oye, the year 1514 now nearing its end. The sum of the agreement of this contract was this: that Guelders should undertake and defend the cause of the city against the men of Utrecht, who not only were not bringing aid, as they ought, to the one in distress, but were even bringing violence together with the enemy, at his own expense, without trouble and cost to them; that the city should swear allegiance in the name of Guelders for ever, and that dominion over the whole countryside enclosed by the Lavica and the Amasus, in which was also the old prefecture, should pass to the prince; that the judicial power delegated by the prince should be held over the affairs of the countryside, and that they should represent, as it were, the prince, one of the prince's councillors being given by the prince, and four men chosen from the number of the more honourable citizens fit for this purpose by the city senate, and that these should have the same right which those former Hovetmen had been before the Saxon war, and should have and do all the same things which those men formerly had, the ancient custom being preserved; that the right of staple, as they call it, for all saleable goods which are in or come from the countryside, should remain whole to the city in every respect in the same way as it was before these disturbances and the Saxon arms; that the same should be kept for grain and beer as was formerly the custom; that the city and the countryside should keep their autonomy and the use of their native laws; that each should retain his right whole and unimpaired, each should hold his possessions, goods and estates within and without the dykes; and that the prince should institute nothing new; that he himself should at no time separate the countryside from the city, nor allow it to be separated by another, nor give occasion for separation; that he should also demolish all fortifications in the countryside, and should not build or allow to be built any new ones; and finally that he should, by an annual tribute, fair and tolerable, to be paid from the countryside to himself and his heirs, make an agreement with the citizens and the inhabitants of the countryside, from which no possessions or goods situated in the countryside should be exempt. These terms were then drawn up and approved by both sides, but they were reduced to a formal document and signed only three years later, when the whole countryside had also been freed from the enemy and made subject to the prince. That was the year 1518 after the birth of Christ, on the eighteenth day of February. Then in the year 1521, an agreement was reached between the prince and the estates of the countryside in the court of Groningen, through the Guelderish envoys and the city senate, to the effect that they themselves should be in the prince's allegiance, and that of his heirs for ever; the prince and his heirs should keep for them their privileges, rights, institutions, laws and customs intact, according to the treaties and pacts formerly made between them and the city. Thus the estates swore allegiance in the name of Guelders, with this condition premised: that the force of this oath would not last longer than the Duke of Guelders could defend the region. And soon afterwards these pacts were signed by the prince on the twentieth day of June. But as time went on, the prince was gradually found to be extending his reach further, and departing from the pacts, and infringing the rights of the city. GUELDERS, first stirred up by MARWICK the praetor, with whom he had a quarrel with the senate, and then irritated because, in the war waged in East Friesland against Ennon, Count and neighbour, on behalf of Balthasar of Esens, the tribute that he demanded from the city for his expenses was refused him, and being by his nature greedy and turbulent, eager to increase his power by right and wrong, seizing the opportunity which chance offered, through MEINHARD of Hamm, a man distinguished in arms, who professed the auspices of the King of Denmark and was furnished with his secret instructions, brought together a tumult of troops in the countryside, and at the very gates of the city, laid waste and burned the suburbs, fortified DAMMONA with the greatest haste, and finally, in a conference instituted for the settling of the affair at Esens through HENRY GROVIUS of Erclenz, his envoy, and HACFORD, the prefect of the soldiers, openly demanded that a fortress be built for him in the city and that the fortification of DAMMONA be completed. The city, rightly alienated from him in its feelings, turned itself to the BURGUNDIAN side. Without delay, after deliberating the matter with the rural estates, and by their consent, it sent envoys to GEORGE SCENCK of Teutoburg, who at that time commanded the Transflavicans on behalf of CHARLES V, the Emperor, and offered surrender. And he, quickly informed of the will of MARY, sister of Emperor Charles, Governess of the Netherlands, to whom he had written, set out for Groningen without delay with those troops which he had at hand; and when terms of command and obedience had been agreed, he received the city and the rural estates together, as one people of a single commonwealth, into the allegiance of Emperor Charles, Duke of Brabant, and Count of Holland and Zealand, and lord of Friesland and Transisalania, on the eighth day of the month of June in the year I have mentioned, 1536. This done, the prefect with an army besieged DAMMONA, and having meanwhile taken the castle of Delfzijl, which the Guelderish also held, on the eighth day of July by surrender, and having cut to pieces the forces of about two thousand which were coming from Denmark to aid the besieged, he was at last forced, reduced to the utmost straits, to surrender on the hardest conditions. For it was agreed that the commanders of the army, Meinhard and Hacford, should be handed over in chains to Teutoburg; the remaining prefects of the cohorts and the soldiers should go out unarmed, carrying a white rod in hand, like captives, without baggage, and should leave behind all their goods in the town, and should not fight against the Emperor within three months; the citizens of DAMMONA, conscious of their guilt, should leave on the same terms with the soldiers, while the others who wished to remain should excuse themselves...

units.la: {?} Groninga & socii in agro in fidem Caroli V. Caesaris ducis Brab. concedunt. omnia in oppido relinquerent, nec intra tres menses contra Cesarem militarent: Oppidani DAMMONENSES, male sibi conscij cum militibus conditione eadem egrederentur: ceteri manere volentes excusandi sui, & experiunda gratiæ facultatem haberent. Facta hæc die VI Septembr. Deinde cum Bruxella responsum, venisset, quo retulerat de omnibus Teutoburgius, ex regina mandato captivi Bruxellam missi, DAMMONÆ munitiones diruta: pro oppido ipso ac ædificiis, quæ & ipsa excidio à REGINA & TEVTO-BVRGIO destinata, deq; eo mandata jam data IoANNI HESSO, ab amicis per preces intercessum, decretumq; suspensum: dein gratia facta. In tanto tum discrimine DAMMONA fuit, propterea quod oportuna tumultuantibus & quieti publicæ infestis fortunaq; urbanæ inimicis sit. Parendi imperandiq; leges sub Burgundis hæ scriptæ signatæq;. Omnes & singuli totius provinciæ ordines, qui Amalo & Lavica continentur, retinerent jura & privilegia sua per manus à majoribus accepta, leges patrias, statuta, consuetudines: imperium præfecturæ veteris, & Seluverdicæ subvrbanæ effet ac maneret civitatis: munitiones per agrum omnes quæ jam essent, everterentur, nec aliæ in futurum extruerentur, nisi id defensionis requireret necessitas: domus principe digna sed inermis & immunita Cæsari ædificaretur in vrbe, sumptibus pro-vinciæ. vinciæ totius: reditus ex agro solveren-tur Cæsari & hæredibus ejus quotannis duo decies mille aureorum Carolinorum. Dammona capta, à Teutèburgio totâ Drentiâ Geldri eiecti, Wedda, Coverdiaq; capta, bellum ex universa illa vicinia, eodem adhuc anno profligatum. Deniq; Decembri mense pax inter Burgundicam domum & Geldrum composita. Conditiones dictæ inter alias, ut fœderi Gallico, Hollatico, aliisq; contra Cæsarem & subditos eius initis Geldrus renunciaret: valediceret juri omni in civitatem & agrum Groninga-num, Drentiam, Tuentiam, si quòd haberet, aut habere se putaret. Ea pax publicata Gro-ninga die XVII Decemb. lætissimis, animis ab omnibus accepta, cum omnes bellorum tæderet.
units.tr: Groningen and its allies in the open country submit to the protection of Charles V, Caesar, Duke of Brabant. They were to leave everything in the town and not bear arms against the Emperor for three months. The townsmen of Damme, conscious of their guilt, were to leave on the same terms as the soldiers; the rest, who wished to stay, were to have the chance to clear themselves and seek grace. This was done on 6 September. Then, when the reply from Brussels came, to which Teutoburgius had reported everything, the captives were sent to Brussels by the Queen's order. The fortifications of Damme were razed. As for the town itself and its buildings, which the Queen and Teutoburgius had also marked for destruction, with orders already given to John Hesso, the matter was halted by the intercession of friends through prayers, and the decree was suspended; then grace was granted. Damme was in such great danger at that time because it was a convenient base for rioters and an enemy to public peace and the town's prosperity. The laws of obedience and rule were written and sealed under the Burgundians: all and each of the orders of the whole province, who are contained within Amasum and Lavicum, were to keep their rights and privileges received by hand from their ancestors, the native laws, statutes and customs; the authority of the old prefecture and of the suburban Selwerd was to remain with the city; all the fortifications throughout the countryside that already existed were to be overthrown, and no others were to be built in future unless the necessity of defence required it; a residence fitting for a prince, but unarmed and unfortified, was to be built in the city at the expense of the whole province; the revenues from the countryside were to be paid to Caesar and his heirs every year, two hundred thousand Carolus gold coins. Damme taken; by Teutoburgius all Drenthe was driven out of Gelderland; Wedda and Coverden were taken; the war was finished in that whole neighbourhood in the same year. Finally, in the month of December, peace was made between the Burgundian house and Gelderland. Among other conditions agreed: that Gelderland should renounce the alliance with France, Holland and others made against Caesar and his subjects, and should give up all right over the city and country of Groningen, Drenthe, Tubantia, if it had any, or believed it had. This peace was proclaimed at Groningen on 17 December and received with the greatest joy by all, since everyone was weary of wars.

units.la: Ab hoc tempore vixit civitas concors cum agri ordinibus, manfitq; in usu ac possessione juris prioris de Hovetmannis & Hovetmannorum potestate, de stapula rerum venalium, de frumento, de cerevisia ex formula GELDRICA, ut de sententia BVRGVNDICÆ formula, & de mente paciscentium dubitari non posse videatur. Et est ex eadem formula Burgundica, durante eodem, quem dixi, usu, post annos XIII à civitate simul & agrariis ordinibus jusiurandum datum PHILIPPO Caroli filio, HISPANIÆ regi, idq; coniunctim rursus, ac PHILIPPVS jurejurando reciproco bis obligatus, nulla tum prodente se controversia, aut controversia sufficione. Nam Dammonenses quod moverunt, velut exempti le[?]gi communi, ac praecipui aliquid habentes, id cuiusmodi fuerit, quamve habuerint rationem, dicam suo loco. Demum post aliquot annos per Dammonenses incitati agrarij, paucosq; alios, quibus negociatio allubescebat, de stapulae jure, imprimis in rebus exoticis aliunde importatis queri caperunt, querelasq; ad aulam Burgundicam detulerunt. Aula eodem anno, qui erat M. D. LIX, Arembergio Comiti Gubernatori mandavit, ut inter partes amica trans-actionem tentaret. Ea frustrà per eum tentatâ (nam longius paulatim tendebant querentes, totumq; pene fori jus studebant convellere, & oppidani de possessione aut iure suo decedere nole-bant.) Arembergius idem die xvi Martij, anno M. D. LX[?] jussit utrosq; documenta ante exitum sex hebdomadum apud se producere, & ex his sententiam expectare provisionalem, uti vocant, usq; dum controversia plenius cognita tota definiretur: interea voluit Oldermannum juris stapulae praefectum more suo contra de-linquentes agere, sed poenarum executionem usq; ad sententiae provisionalis promulgatio-nem suspendere. Et cum pars neutra jussui satisfecisse videretur, ad documenta quod attinebat, idem denuò die xiiii Maij praecepit utrisq;, ut apud HOVETMANNOS cognitores causam agerent ordinario modo usq; ad momentum ferendae sententiae: Hovetmannos jussit acta ea omnia exhibere sibi: interea Oldermannus id observaret, quod ante erat mandatum. Quod ipsum cum iniquius putarent oppidani de Oldermanno (nam extractum iri in longum actionem trahantur, atque interea sine nervo futurum jus civitatis) rem ad Margarethamn Parmensem gubernatricem Belgii retulerunt. Illa cum senatu suo commode interpretata sententiam Arembergii benignè respondit, mandavitq; ut ab Oldermanno damnati cautionem praestarent in eventum litis de solvendo judicato; & simul quae species rerum venalium litigiosarum intelligerentur sententiâ Arembergii comprehensa. Id factum Bruxellae die XIIII Maii, anno M.D.LXI. Post quae pendente judicio rursus institutae actiones amicâ ad componendam controversiam demumq; hujus ergo cum mandatis in urbem missus Philippus Cobelius ex secreto senatu regio: cujus prudentiâ & industriâ effectum, ut in capita certa, de quibus erat controversia, formata ab ipso pars utraq; acquiesceret, & consentiret, quae vim juris haberent interea, dum judicio integro tota causa finiretur. Consensus is solenniter initus & signatus in curia Groningana die IIII & V Augusti, anno M.D.XLIIII. (Capitum praecipua fuere: In frumento ἐγχωρίῳ[?] & cervisia id servare-tur, quod est foedere anni M. CCCC. LXXXII definitum: pecora equini & bubuli generis venalia Groningae in foro sisterentur, ista biduo, haec uno die horis antemeridianis: quo facto licerent, soluto vectigali usirato[?], quolibet abigere: butyrum, caseum, lardum, sevum, adeps, terga bubula Groningae & non alibi venum proponerentur,venderentur ve: peregrino ni-hil horum,nec pecorum,nec cæterorum eme-re in agro liceret, in foro Groningano liceret cuivis,civi,agricolæ,peregrino, liberaq; emp-torum exportatio effet vectigali soluto. Mer-catus folennes in commodum negociationū plures in urbe instituerentur. Exempta fori iuri effent pecora pastionis causâ aliunde in agrum adducta: venalia navibus advecta si efculéta & corruptioni subitæ obnoxia sint,jus effet ubivis in agro distrahi: reliqua durabilia cuiuscúnq;generis,frumenta,legumina,saperdæ, aleces salitæ, ligna, lapides, calx, ferrum, carbones, similiáq; non venundatentur intra horas xx iiii,ut copia veniendi ad portus civib. effet; tum conjunctim cum civib. tantum emerent agricolæ,quantū ad usus suos domesticos haberet opus; & post alteras horas xxiv si quid mercium effet reliquū, id emere etiam institoribus agrariis non effet vetitum. Quin imò si quis agri incola etiam post primas ho-ras xxiiii in usum domesticum aliquid emptum ex his vellet, quæ jam à civibus sint empta, mercibus nondum loco motis, eiid negari eodem,quo prima emptio facta,pretio exhibito non liceret, Mercatores agrarii ve-ctigal aut portorium solverent in usum agri.
units.tr: From this time the city lived in harmony with the orders of the countryside, and the former right concerning the Hovetmen and the power of the Hovetmen, concerning the staple of goods for sale, concerning grain, and concerning beer, according to the Gelderland formula, remained in use and possession, so that no doubt can seem to exist about the intention of the Burgundian formula or of the contracting parties. And from the same Burgundian formula, during the same practice I have mentioned, after thirteen years an oath was given by the city and the rural orders together to Philip, son of Charles, King of Spain, and again jointly, and Philip was twice bound by a reciprocal oath, no controversy then coming forward or hindering. For the Damme townsmen, as exempt from the common law and having something special, what it was and what reasons they had, I will state in its proper place. At length, after some years, the countrymen, stirred up by the Damme people and a few others who liked trade, began to complain about the right of the staple, especially regarding foreign goods imported from elsewhere, and carried their complaints to the Burgundian court. The court in the same year, which was 1559, commanded Count Aremberg, the governor, to attempt a friendly settlement between the parties. This attempt by him failed (for the complainants gradually extended their claims and tried to overturn nearly the whole right of the market, and the townsmen were unwilling to give up their possession or their right). On 16 March of the year 1560, the same Aremberg ordered both sides to produce their documents before him within six weeks of his departure, and to await from these a provisional judgment, as they call it, until the controversy should be fully known and finally decided. Meanwhile he wished the Oldermann, prefect of the staple right, to proceed in his manner against the offenders, but to suspend the execution of the penalties until the provisional sentence was published. And since neither party seemed to have obeyed the order, as regards the documents, the same man again ordered both sides on 14 May that they should plead the case before the Hovetmen as investigators in the ordinary manner until the moment of pronouncing sentence; he ordered the Hovetmen to show him all those records; meanwhile the Oldermann was to observe what had been ordered before. The townsmen, thinking this more unjust toward the Oldermann (for the action would be dragged out to great length, and meanwhile the city's right would be without strength), reported the matter to Margaret of Parma, governor of Belgium. She, having interpreted the matter with her council, kindly replied with Aremberg's sentence, and ordered that those condemned by the Oldermann should give security for payment of the judgment in case of a lawsuit; and at the same time that the kinds of goods for sale that were under dispute should be understood as included in Aremberg's sentence. This was done at Brussels on 14 May 1561. After this, while the judgment was pending, actions were again begun for the sake of settling the dispute amicably; and for this purpose Philip Cobelius, of the king's secret council, was sent into the city with instructions. By his prudence and diligence it was brought about that both parties agreed to and consented to certain heads, formed by him, concerning which the controversy was, which were to have the force of law meanwhile, until the whole case was finally decided by full judgment. This agreement was solemnly entered into and sealed in the Groningen council chamber on 4 and 5 August 1564. (The chief heads were these: that for native grain and beer what was defined in the treaty of the year 1482 should be observed; cattle of the horse and ox kind for sale were to be brought to the market at Groningen, the former for two days, the latter for one day in the forenoon hours; after this was done, they might drive them away anywhere, the toll having been paid; butter, cheese, bacon, lard, tallow, and hides of oxen were to be offered and sold only at Groningen and nowhere else; no foreigner was allowed to buy any of these, nor cattle, nor other things in the countryside, but in the Groningen market anyone, citizen, countryman or foreigner, might buy, and the free export of the purchases was permitted once the toll was paid. Solemn markets for the advantage of trade were to be established in the city more often. Cattle brought into the countryside from elsewhere for grazing were exempt from market law; goods for sale brought by ship, if they were perishable and liable to sudden spoiling, might be sold anywhere in the countryside; other durable goods of every kind, grain, pulses, salted herring, salted anchovies, wood, stone, lime, iron, charcoal, and the like, were not to be sold within twenty-four hours, so that citizens would have the opportunity of buying at the harbours; then only jointly with the citizens were countrymen to buy as much as their domestic use required; and after a second period of twenty-four hours, if any goods remained, it was not forbidden for countryside merchants to buy them too. Indeed, if any inhabitant of the countryside wished, even after the first twenty-four hours, to buy something of these things for domestic use, which had already been bought by citizens, the goods not yet having been moved from their place, it should not be refused to him, the price being paid in the same way as the first purchase was made. Country merchants were to pay toll or customs for the use of the countryside.)

units.la: Quæ quis ex agri incolis aliunde importaret, onere stapulæ essèt libera, quemadmodum & omnia reliqua in his capitibus non nominata.
units.tr: Whatever anyone from the inhabitants of the countryside imported from elsewhere was to be free of the burden of the staple, just as all other things not named in these heads.

units.la: Postremò nemo ad jusiurandum ab Oldermanno adigeretur apud judices mercaturæ præfectos sine præcedente documento legib. sufficiente: atque in hoc ipse Oldermannus & judices jusiurandum darent reip. Verum cum ne his quidem conditionibus contenti possent esse agrarij, ALBANO duce rerum potiente in Belgio, rursus ad eum querelas detulere: Ille causâ cognitâ anno M. D. LXXI, die VII Augusti decretum iterum interposuit verbis variantibus à capitibus his, re pene idem. Eius summa haec, Groninganis integrum sit ius stapulæ & mercatuum in butyro, caseo, pecore equino bovinoque, frumento omnis generis: quorum nihil liceat exportare, nisi Groningæ venale habitu ab hora matutina ad meridiem. Nulli peregrino liceat quicquam sive ἐμπορίου[?] sive ἀστάκτου[?] in agro emere aut vendere: in urbe liceat: attamen liberum eidem sit ea, quæ ipse advexerit, in ipsis portibus, aut prope eos è navigiis venundare, cui volet. Vitandæ fraudis causâ, quæ Groningæ promercalia fuere, ea à præfecto ad id dato in indicem referantur, vasaq; butyri notâ insigniantur. In trutinâ urbanâ pondera sint uniformia: nec civis, nec agri incola negotiationibus deditus mensibus Maio, Iunio, Iulio, Augusto jumenta aliave quæstus faciendi causâ per agrum emere jus habeat, reliquo tempore reliqua mercimonia fœdere anni M. cccc. LXXXII non comprehensa ius habeat quovis loco, nec tamen liceat nundinationes instituere præterquam Groningæ. In usum domesticum cuivis in agro quidvis quocunque loco & tempore emere liberum sit. Contrà fecisse deprehensus primò aureos florenos xxv, secundò L Oldermanno pendat; tertiò & deinceps arbitrali mulćta puniatur : mulćte trientem civitas, alterum fiscus regius, tertium Older-mannus capiat. Hic juramento neminem adigat, nisi semiplena probatione cōftriḉtum: citra eam si quem in judicium trahat, in fusipse [?] damnetur. Putans se iniquâ sententiâ apud mercatorum aut Oldermanni tribunal gravátum, si ex agro fit, Hovetmannos, si civis, senatum appellet, nisi aliud à rege decretum fuerit: Hovetmanni & senatus compendiosè litem expediant. Civitas non miscat se vectigali vinario & cervisiario, cui accisae nomen, in agro: sed id agrarius impendendum vsibus agri relinquat. Publicanus aut quaestor rationes de eo reddat quotannis coram praetore regio, aut Hovetmanno, & ab agrariis ad id delectis. His additum aliquid de conventibus. Si quid in his dubij inciderit, eius explicatio aut definitio penes regem sit, ejusve in Belgio gubernatorem. Hoc decreto perem-ptae sint omnia priora ad hanc controversiam pertinentia. Sed isto quod repulsa [?] dicto decreto, quadriennio post, cum Gro-ninga coeffent agrarij, ut fe vinculis his semel exuerent, foederi ac societati omni, quam cum oppidanis habebant, renunciarunt ritu solenni. Fuit anno M. D. LXXVI, mense Januario. Quo facto, cum pergerent nihilominus oppidani, uti solent, & possessionem tuerentur, illi opposuere se; protestari acriter, judicij ministros repellere, mandata contemnere, [illegible, ~10 letters] conventus seorsim habere, ad regium senatum provocare: regius senatus praecipitantius quam par erat, decernere, & in fraudem civitatis id quod ad Albanoscitum, interpretari. Interea pace Gandavensi promulgata, capto Groninga a militibus suis Casparo Roblesio praefecto regio, Georgio Rennebergio in locum eius ab Ordinibus generalibus suffecto, crescente indies dissensione & odio inter partes, agrariis nova collegia, nova tribunalia instituentibus, re ad tumultus atq; arma spectante, tandem Rennebergius velut reip. studio ad avertenda pericula & constituendam provinciam, conventum ordinum eius indixit in urbe ipsis Cal. Novemb.-anno proximo M. D. LXXVII.
units.tr: Finally, no one was to be put on oath by the Oldermann before the judges, the prefects of trade, without a preceding document sufficient by the laws; and in this respect the Oldermann himself and the judges were to take an oath to the commonwealth. But since the countrymen could not be content even with these conditions, while Duke Alba held power in Belgium, they again brought their complaints to him. He, after hearing the case, in the year 1571, on 7 August, issued a decree again, in words differing from these heads, but nearly the same in substance. Its sum is this: the Groningers shall have full right of the staple and of trade in butter, cheese, horse and cattle, grain of every kind, none of which may be exported unless it has been offered for sale at Groningen from morning until noon. No foreigner may buy or sell anything in the countryside, whether of the emporium or of the unstaple kind; he may in the city. Yet it shall be lawful for him to sell freely to whomever he wishes, at the harbours themselves or near them from ships, whatever he himself has brought. To avoid fraud, what were the merchandise at Groningen shall be entered in a list by the prefect appointed for this, and vessels of butter shall be marked with a sign. In the city's weigh-house the weights shall be uniform. Neither a citizen nor a countryman devoted to trade shall have the right to buy beasts of burden or other things for the sake of gain in the countryside during the months of May, June, July and August; in the rest of the time he shall have the right to trade in other merchandise not included in the treaty of the year 1482, in any place, yet it shall not be lawful to hold markets except at Groningen. For domestic use anyone may buy anything anywhere and at any time in the countryside. Whoever is caught acting against this shall pay, for the first offence, 25 gold florins; for the second, 50 to the Oldermann; for the third and afterwards he shall be punished with a fine assessed by arbitration. Of the fine the city shall take a third, the royal treasury another, and the Oldermann the third. The Oldermann shall not put anyone on oath unless he is bound by a half proof; if anyone brings another before a court without it, he shall himself be condemned in the suit. If a man thinks himself wronged by an unjust sentence before the tribunal of the merchants or the Oldermann, he shall appeal, if he is from the countryside, to the Hovetmen, if a citizen, to the senate, unless the king has decided otherwise; the Hovetmen and the senate shall settle the suit summarily. The city shall not interfere with the wine and beer excise, which is called the accise, in the countryside; but the countryman shall leave it to be spent on the needs of the countryside. The collector or treasurer shall render the accounts of it every year before the royal praetor or the Hovetmen, and before those chosen for this by the countrymen. Something further was added about the assemblies. If any doubt should arise on these points, its explanation or definition shall rest with the king, or with his governor in Belgium. By this decree all earlier things pertaining to this controversy were destroyed. But when the said decree was rejected, four years afterwards, when the countrymen began with Groningen, so that they might once for all free themselves from these bonds, they renounced with the solemn rite the alliance and fellowship they had with the townsmen. This was in the year 1576, in the month of January. Upon this, since the townsmen nevertheless continued, as they usually do, and defended their possession, the others set themselves against them, protesting fiercely, repelling the officers of justice, despising orders, [illegible, ~10 letters] holding assemblies apart, appealing to the royal senate; the royal senate decreed more hastily than was right, and interpreted what pertained to Alba's decree in a way that defrauded the city. Meanwhile, the Pacification of Ghent having been proclaimed, and Groningen having been taken by his own soldiers under Caspar Robles, the royal prefect, and George Rennenberg having been appointed in his place by the General Estates, the disagreement and hatred between the parties growing daily, the countrymen setting up new assemblies and new tribunals, the matter tending toward tumults and arms, at length Rennenberg, under pretext of zeal for the commonwealth, to avert dangers and settle the province, called an assembly of its estates in the city on 1 November of the following year, 1577.

units.la: Illic cum statim in initio altercationes essent orta, contumaciusq; & ferocius agere ac loqui agrarii viderentur quam ferendum oppidani putabant, quotquot illorum aderant (nec enim venerant omnes) ab his in custodiam sunt dati. Hinc maior secuta animorum exacerbatio; cui medenda, ac reparanda concordia (periculosum .n. ignis videbatur, qui toti Belgio in isto rerum statu magno malo esse posset) ab Avraico principe & generalibus Ordinibus Groningam missus fuit summi ingenii, summaeque doctrinae, & auctoritatis vir Philippus Marnixius Aldegondius, & cum eo Sillius jureconsultus Ordinibus a secretis. Eorumq; studio tentata atq; agitata[?] multa, conditiones scriptae inducianum litis; postremo cum confici res non posset, hoc solum obtinuere, ut legati Antwerpiam ad MATHIAM AVSTRIACVM novum Belgij gubernatorem, prin-cipemq; AVRAICVM legatum eius, & genera-lium Ordinum Senatum a partibus mittentur. Illic intercedente & allaborante ipso Av-RIACO cum Comite SVARTZBVRGIO duobusq; e senatu aliis, quibus erat id a Mathia ac senatu demandatum, tandem in hac capita a legatis facta consensio est. Ab armis & vi utrim-que abstineretur, captivi à civitate dimitte-rentur, restituerenturq; in integrum, cum cae-teris vim passis; sententiæ à tempore [illegible, ~9 letters] hujus latæ haberentur pro nullis, injuriæ al-ternæ oblivione essent inducta. Groningani manerent in possessione juris pristini, præser-tim eius, quod ante annum M. D. LXXI. tenuerant, idque tamdiu, donec de controversia in judicio esset pronunciatum: cognitores in eam rem darentur à Mathia Gubernatore è senatu ordinum Belgicorum: apud hos utriq; rem agerent, & producerent ea, quæ pro causa suâ [?] facere arbitrarentur: interim & à cognitoribus transactio amica tentaretur inter partes, conficeretur que, si posset. Processus finiretur intra biennium: id si fieri non posset, terminus pro necessitatis ratione à Gubernatore proferretur. Si qua pars cum culpâ suâ in morâ esset, C marcas auri multam daret, & quidem toties, quoties hoc committeret, ac nihilominus pro more iudicij in causâ pergeretur. Cognitione finitâ, cuncta ad Gubernatorem referrentur: Gubernator adscitis in consilium sibi è senatu secreto, vel collegio maiore Mechlinensi viris prudentibus tot, quot poscere rem putaret, contra quos ex-cipere partes non possent,ex actis istis sententiam ferret, cui sine contradictione parendum utraque a parte esset. Interea utrinque a vi & injuriis mutuis verborum factorumque sibi temperarent sub poena amittendi juris sui, & M. insuper marcarum auri: ac si privatim aliquis contra delinqueret, poenam ferret pro delicti modo. Agrariis vero durante hac actione liberum esset, quoties & quocunque loco vellent ob res ad hanc causam pertinentes, quae ad oppidanos non pertinerent, inprimis ad conficiendam in lumptus litis pecuniam, conventus agere separatim, & tributum decernere, dummodo oppidanos & eorum res in hunc usum non gravarent: conventionem hanc partes utrimque in conventu ordinum suorum probarent, & sibi mutuo caverent, sub poenis jam dictis: quinimo juramentum darent praesidi provinciae suae, (is tum erat RENNEBERGIVS, qui eis utraque Lavicam Frisiae, item Transisalanis, Drentiæ[?] & Lingæ praeerat) fideliter se servaturos ac praestituros haec omnia, & si quid contra committerent hi aut illi, executorem poenae eundem hunc non recusaturos: postremo quo firmiora & certiora essent omnia, partes, conventione hac probata, procuratores ex sui medio ederent, scriptisque mandatis ad eam rem idoneis instruerent, ijq; porro Mathiae & ordinum senatui potestatem darent judicandi & condemnandi in capitibus his omnibus, ut omnia haec effectum sortiantur. Actum Antwerpiae die xxx Maij, anno M. D. LXXVIII. Subscripsere princeps ipse Guil. Guilhelmus, Guntherus Suartzburgius, N.Lyf-feldius, Iacobus Imannus, & duo agrariorum legati, duo item oppidanorum, quorum alter clarissimus atq; optimus & magnae doctrinae vir REGNERVS ALBERDA vrbis Consul. Sed reversi domum legati animos suorum magis & magis exulceratos, ac minime omnium ad hanc rem compositos repererunt. Nam Bartholdus ENTENIVS, quem jam ante quam legati domo discessissent, agrarij clam mandatis instruxerant, ut milites scriberet, & civitati bellum facerent, interea dum in Brabantia aut in itinere legati hi iidem sunt, arma per Drentiam moverat. Civitas vero celeritate usa, cum exissent frequens, priusquam copiae eius omnes coire possent, disjectis, quae occurrerant, praetoriaq; cohorte fusa, in arcem [?]overdiam male tum munitam ipsum confugere, & sese dedere coegerat, atq; in urbem captivum cum socijs traxerat. Quo tempore sane adeo fuit inopina re asperata plebs, ut vix a furore ejus captivum servare rectores potuerint. Itaq; difficillima tum fuit vulneris illius contrectatio. Et tamen hortatu generalium ordinum, & studio meliorum tentata rursum res, conventuq; institutis, sed profectu nullo; praesertim custoditorum plerisq;, durante hoc conatu, communicato inter se consilio, eodem simul tempore, eademq; pene hora e custodia elapsi. Quapropter bono pacis & concordiae Belgicae tu renascentis ex consilio ac voluntate principis GVILHELMI, senatusq; generalium ordinū MATHIAS edictu interposuit. In eo jussit, ut qui apud Groninganos in custodia reliqui erant, atq; ipse simul Bartholdus Entenius, statim dimitterentur: omnes a vi & factis sibi temperarent: controversias suas,& hanc captivitatis, fugæ, motorum armorum, aliarum injuriarum aut criminum causam iudicio æquo & legitimo, quale in conventione priore de-scriptum,permitterent: dein cætera omnia ea-dem conventione comprehensa haberent ra-ta,& sine vitio servarent. Entenius,& cæteri è custodiâ dimittendi obligarent se, iudicio se staturos,& iudicato satisfacturos. Oppidanis restitueretur possessio[?] iuris prioris sine defe-ctu & sine mora, in qua turbati ab agrariis e-rant,eaq;iisdem maneret ad latam usque sen-tentiam : Similiter agrarii ab oppidanis re-stituerentur in integrum in rebus unde con-troversiæ huius causa erant deiecti. Præses Rennebergius,& reliqui ejus vicinię præfecti inferiores viderent; curarentque diligenter, ne quid contra decretum hoc a quoquam committeretur, committentesque ne ferrent impune. Signatum Antwerpiæ die xxiiii Octob. anno eodem M. D. LXXVII. Nec diu post dimissi captivi. Sed occultis consiliis RENNEBERGII Hispanicas partes jam tum respectantis impedita omnia, atq; ita sensim dire-cta res, ut oppressis melioribus in civitate, & in-carcerem detrusis, conspirantibus cum eo, quibus odium religionis, studium rerum suarum, patriæ incuria inerat, civitas in partes Hispanicas sit delapsa. In eo rerum statu civitas actionibus partis adversa provocata controversiam, & conditioconditionem suam ad PARMENSEM, qui tunc pro rege Belgio praesidebat, retulit, eiusq; opem ravit. Parmensis ex libellis & adjunctis documentis causa cognita, & cum secreto Senatu regio communicata, ex eius sententia in hunc modum decrevit. Ob studium tuendae servandae religionis Romanae Catholicae religionis, & fidem ac obsequium constans erga regem Groningani habento ad tempus totum jus stapulae rerum promercalium tam peregrinarum qua in agro vicino nascentium. Oldermanno potestas esto contra hoc jus delinquentes ad tribunal societatis mercatorum huic quaestioni destinatum trahere, ac reos agere; condemnatiq; si velint Senatum civitatis tantum, nec quenquam alium appellanto:is in executione moderatione & aequitate utitor, ob afflictam fortunam agrariorum. Cerevisiae in tabernis cauponariis ac diversoriis usus non esto nisi Groningano: delicta contraria modo solito puniuntor. Opificia per agrum non exercentor in fraudem societatum oppidanarum, fervatorq; in hoc sententia anni M. D. XX. die Veneris post pentecostes lata ab arbitrio Ius administrator per legatum regium & quatuor Hovetmannos a Senatu oppidano delectos more solito: omnesque agri incolae potestati & judiciis edictisque eorum parento: Iudices & officiarii nuper contra morem foedera litum judiciorum causa instituti abrogati fun- to: tributa aut onera alia publica toti regioni aut provinciae communia non decernuntor, promulgantor, colliguntor, nisi ordinib, pec- legatum regium & hovetmannos convocatis, & re in eorum & oppidanorum conventu de-liberata & probata. In iisdem conventibus utriusque partis negotia omnia totius reipub. provincialis tractantor. Aerarium commune unum esto: Acta omnia, pacta, foedera, conventiones, decreta his contraria irrita, ac pro nullis sunto. Hoc decretum valeto, donec Rex ipse causa cognita sententiam ferat. In calce addit, de vectigali petito, si cum commendatione civitatis ob summam fidem & studium in regem & regias partes ad regem relaturum: sperare, si civitas in eadem fide & studio ac obsequio perstet, regem non negaturum, sed insuper novis & amplis privilegiis ad reparandam pristinam fortunam eandem civitatem ornaturum. Signatum Valenchenae die xv Aprilis anno M.D.LXXI. Et hoc decretum Philippus rex, cum ad eum hac de causa legati in Hispaniam missi essent Ioachimus Vbbena consul & Ioannes Goudanus urbis Syndicus, causamque totam Parmensis commendassent, prolixo diplomate, repetitis omnib. decreti huiusce verbis, sed abrogata Parmensis sanctione, laudata prolixe civitatis fide & constantia, & meritis egregiis, confirmavit Olyssippone in Lusitania, cum annus ageretur M.D.LXXXII, die ultimo Octobris: jussit esse perpetuum, ac pro privilegio à se dato haberi.
units.tr: There, as soon as the disputes began at the outset, and the townsmen thought the Agrarians were behaving and speaking more stubbornly and fiercely than could be tolerated, all of those Agrarians who were present (for not all of them had come) were put into custody by them. From this came a greater heightening of feelings. To remedy this and restore concord (for the fire seemed dangerous, since in the state of affairs then it could be a great evil for all of Belgium), the prince of Orange and the General Estates sent to Groningen Philip Marnix Aldegonde, a man of outstanding talent, learning and authority, and with him Sillius, a jurist and secretary to the Estates. Through their efforts many things were attempted and discussed; terms were written out for a truce in the dispute. Finally, since the matter could not be concluded, they obtained only this: that delegates should be sent from the parties to Antwerp, to Matthias of Austria, the new governor of Belgium, and to the prince of Orange, his lieutenant, and to the Senate of the General Estates. There, with Orange himself intervening and working hard, together with Count Schwarzburg and two other members of the Senate, to whom Matthias and the Senate had entrusted this task, agreement was at last reached by the delegates on these points: that both sides should abstain from arms and force; that the prisoners should be released by the city and restored to their former position, together with the others who had suffered violence; that sentences passed since the time [illegible] should be considered void, and mutual injuries be set aside by oblivion. The Groningers should remain in possession of their former right, especially that which they had held before the year 1571, and this for as long as the controversy was not decided in court; commissioners for this purpose were to be appointed by Matthias the governor from the Senate of the Belgian Estates; before them each side would plead its case and produce whatever it judged useful to its cause; meanwhile a friendly settlement between the parties was to be attempted by the commissioners and concluded, if it could be. The proceedings were to be finished within two years; if that could not be done, the term was to be extended by the governor according to the need of the case. If either party was at fault for the delay, it should pay a fine of one hundred marks of gold, and indeed as often as it committed this, and nevertheless the trial should proceed in the usual manner. When the examination was finished, everything was to be referred to the governor; the governor, taking into council wise men from the secret Senate or the greater college of Mechelen, as many as he thought the matter required, against whom the parties could not object, was to pronounce judgment on these proceedings, and each side was to obey it without contradiction. Meanwhile both sides were to refrain from force and mutual injuries by word and deed, under penalty of losing their right and, moreover, of 500 marks of gold; and if any private person offended against this, he should suffer punishment according to the nature of the offence. During this action, the Agrarians, however, were free, as often and wherever they wished, to hold separate assemblies concerning matters pertaining to this cause that did not concern the townsmen, chiefly to raise money for the costs of the lawsuit, and to decree a tax, provided they did not burden the townsmen and their property for this purpose; each party was to approve this agreement in its own assembly and give mutual guarantees to each other under the penalties already stated; moreover, they were to give an oath to the governor of their province (at that time this was Rennenberg, who presided over both Friesland, Lingen, Drenthe and the Transisalan region) that they would faithfully keep and fulfil all these things, and that they would not refuse this same man as executor of the penalty if either side committed anything against them; finally, so that everything might be firmer and more certain, the parties, once the agreement was approved, were to appoint procurators from among themselves and equip them with written mandates suitable for this purpose, and these in turn were to give power to the Senate of Matthias and the Estates to judge and condemn in all these matters, so that all these things might take effect. Done at Antwerp on the 30th day of May, in the year 1578. Signed by the prince himself, William; Gunther Schwarzburg, N. Lyffeld, James Imann, and two delegates of the Agrarians, two likewise of the townsmen, of whom one, the most distinguished and excellent man and of great learning, Regner Alberda, Consul of the city. But when the delegates returned home they found the minds of their people more and more inflamed, and least of all disposed to this settlement. For Bartholdus Entenius, whom the Agrarians had secretly instructed, even before the delegates had left home, to enlist soldiers and make war on the city, had in the meantime, while these same delegates were in Brabant or on the journey, raised arms through Drenthe. The city, however, acted swiftly: before his forces could all gather, it scattered those that had come together, routed the praetorian cohort that met it, and forced him to take refuge in the castle of Overdiep, which was then poorly fortified, and to surrender himself, and brought him into the city as a prisoner together with his associates. At that time the common people were so enraged by this unexpected event that the magistrates could scarcely protect the prisoner from their fury. Therefore the handling of that wound was then most difficult. And yet, at the urging of the General Estates and through the efforts of the better men, the matter was again attempted and assemblies were instituted, but with no success; especially since most of those in custody, while this attempt was going on, having communicated their plan among themselves, escaped from custody at the same time and at nearly the same hour. Therefore, for the good of the peace and concord of a Belgium now being reborn, by the counsel and will of Prince William and the Senate of the General Estates, Matthias issued an edict. In it he ordered that those who remained in custody among the Groningers, and at the same time Bartholdus Entenius himself, should be released at once; that all should refrain from force and deeds against one another; that they should submit their disputes, and this matter of the imprisonment, flight, armed uprisings, and other injuries or crimes, to a fair and lawful judgment, such as was laid out in the earlier agreement; and that they should then hold and faithfully observe all the other things comprehended in that same agreement as ratified. Entenius and the others to be released from custody were to bind themselves to abide by the judgment and to satisfy what was judged. The townsmen were to have restored to them, without delay or deficiency, the possession of their former right in which they had been disturbed by the Agrarians, and this was to remain with them until the sentence was pronounced; likewise the Agrarians were to be restored by the townsmen to their former condition in the matters from which they had been driven out because of this controversy. President Rennenberg and the other lesser prefects of the neighbourhood were to see to it and take diligent care that nothing against this decree was committed by anyone, and that those who committed it should not go unpunished. Signed at Antwerp on the 24th day of October in the same year 1577 [sic: 1578 in the original printing as M.D.LXXVII]. Not long after, the prisoners were released. But by the secret counsels of Rennenberg, who was already then looking toward the Spanish party, everything was obstructed, and the matter was so gradually directed that, with the better men in the city overpowered and thrust into prison, and with those who conspired with him, who had hatred of religion, zeal for their own affairs, and carelessness for their country, the city slipped into the Spanish party. In this state of affairs the city, provoked by the actions of the opposing party, referred its controversy and its condition to the Duke of Parma, who then governed on behalf of the king of Belgium, and sought his aid. Parma, after examining the pleadings and the attached documents, and after communicating the matter with the royal secret Senate, decided on it in the following manner, in accordance with their opinion. In consideration of the zeal for preserving the Roman Catholic religion, and the constant faith and obedience toward the king, the Groningers shall for the whole time have the entire right of staple for goods, both foreign and those grown in the neighbouring country. The alderman shall have power to bring those who offend against this right before the tribunal of the merchant guild appointed for this inquiry, and to prosecute them as defendants; and if the convicted so wish, they may appeal to the city Senate alone and to no one else; the Senate is to use moderation and equity in its execution, on account of the afflicted fortune of the Agrarians. The use of beer in taverns and inns shall not be allowed except Groningen beer; contrary offences shall be punished in the usual way. Trades shall not be practised in the countryside to the detriment of the townsmen's guilds, and the sentence pronounced in the year 1520, on the Friday after Pentecost, by the judgment of the arbiter, shall be kept, the administration of justice being carried out by the royal delegate and four headmen chosen by the city Senate in the customary manner; and all the inhabitants of the countryside shall obey their power, judgments and edicts. Judges and officials recently instituted against custom, the leagues for the purposes of lawsuits, shall be abolished. Taxes or other public burdens common to the whole region or province shall not be decreed, promulgated or collected, except by the royal delegate and the headmen summoned and the matter deliberated and approved in their assembly and in that of the townsmen. In these same assemblies all the business of the whole provincial commonwealth of both parties shall be handled. There shall be one common treasury. All acts, pacts, covenants, agreements and decrees contrary to these shall be void and of no effect. This decree shall stand until the King himself, the cause having been examined, pronounces judgment. At the end it is added that, concerning the beer tax sought, he will report it to the King with commendation of the city for its great fidelity and zeal toward the King and the royal party; they hope that if the city persists in the same fidelity, zeal and obedience, the King will not deny it, but will moreover adorn the same city with new and ample privileges for restoring its former fortune. Signed at Valenciennes on the 15th day of April in the year 1571. And this decree King Philip, when delegates were sent to him at Spain for this cause, Joachim Ubbena, consul, and John Goudanus, syndic of the city, and had entrusted the whole cause to Parma, confirmed by a lengthy diploma, repeating all the words of this decree, but with Parma's sanction abrogated, greatly praising the city's fidelity and constancy and its outstanding services, at Lisbon in Portugal, in the year 1582, on the last day of October; he ordered that it should be perpetual and be held as a privilege granted by him.

units.la: Simul eodem die loco, aliud diploma civitati dedit de tributo cerevisiario, sanxit, ut id, quod ex Albani decreto agrarii soli tractarant, & in rem verterant suam, civitati esset cum ordinib. agri commune, eique aerarium poneretur in urbe feris clausum duabus, pendereturque in res communes parti utrique, ex voluntate & consensu conjunēto : Ἀτὴ, hoc jure usa civitas est, quantum licuit, ad annum usq; xciiii, quo anno ad societatem foederis ordinū Belgicorum, reliētis partibus Hispanicis, restitu-tis & ad gubernacula locatis exulibus, magistratu priori exautorato, rediit. Tum repetitis veteribus querelis ab agrarys, judicium de controversia ordinibus generalibus integrè permissum.
units.tr: At the same time, on the same day and in the same place, he gave the city another charter concerning the beer tax. He ordained that what the land-holders had gained and turned to their own use under the decree of Alba should belong to the city together with the orders of the countryside as common property, and that a treasury should be set up in the town, closed with two keys, from which money would be paid out for common purposes to each party, by mutual will and agreement. [Greek word: Ἀτὴ]. The city used this right, as far as it was allowed, until the year 1594, when, with the exiles restored and placed in charge of the government, and the Spanish party left behind, it joined the alliance of the Belgic orders and the previous magistracy was deposed. Then, with the old complaints of the land-holders renewed, the dispute was handed over in full to the General Orders for judgment.

units.la: Ab his mox in initio tres intercessores aut arbitratores dati, viri clarissimi, & πολιτικῶτα-toi, Elbertus Leoninus Geldria Cancellarius, Sebastianus Lose summa in Hollandia curia senator, Ioannes Vvittenivs Consul Campensis intima mecū amicitia coniunētus, ones in senatu & consiliys ordinum generalium diu versati, qui si possent, unà cum illustri gubernatore D. Gvilhelmo Lvdovico Comite Nassavio controversiam inter partes componerent amicè : si non possent, statuerent pro tempore, quod quieti & regimini expedire videretur, ʼatisper donec plenirejudicio cognitā causa omnia definiretur. Il, adhibitā summā diligentiā & studio cum gubernatore, cum frustrā diu in compositione controversia universa laborāssent, tandem ea, quae ad formam & ordinem politiæ provincialis in hac conjunctione cum ordinibus fœderatis, & ad pecuniæ communis administrationem faciebant, acceptā in id plenā à partibus potestate, primum constituerunt. In his siverunt ante omnia, ut civitas & ager una sint provincia in perpe- tuum sub uno gubernatoretut conventus pro- vinciæ communes sint utrique parti, habean- turq; non alibi quam Groningę. In primis collegium novum instituerunt ad modum cæteris in provincijs fœderatis usitatum, in quod quatuor viros oppidani,totidem agrarij darent, coniunctionis atq; vnitatis vinculum & nervum : ejus collegii munus effet, curare & administrare pecuniam provinciæ ex tribu-to & vectigali provenientem in usus pacis & belli , bona item monastica in ærarium commune relata; adhæc dare operam, ut reli-gio vera propagetur & confervetur', exercitio erroneæ locus non detur, neque fraus bonis Ecclesiasticis & similib.ad pios usus à maiori-bus destinatis fiat, provinciæ ordines ad con-ventus, cum opus est, absente gubernatore convocare, in conventib. deliberanda propo-nere,ordinum suffragiis decreta exequi,deniq; partem curæ & potestatis in iis,quæ belli sunt, cum Gubernatore, tenere. Collegii caput sit gubernator, isq; in eo compareat quoties velit aut posit : collegæ vicissim præsideant per septimanas, & alternatim ex urbe aut agro. Collegio quæstor etiam additus communibus suffragiis legendus tractandæ pecuniæ,itidem scriba à secretis, ostiarius, ministriq; inferiores alij : Præterea sic studio atq; autoritate eorundem inter partes convenit, ut duo semper ex[illegible, ~4 letters] ex hac provincia assessores sint if collegio« generalium ordinum, qui cum caeteris deliberandi & statuendi potestatem de rebus« foederis habeant, alter ex oppidanis, ex agrariis alter: unus item in ordinum senatu,« & unus in senatu rerum maritimarum, idq; alternatim, ita ut si iste ex urbe fuerit,« hic sit ex agro, & contra: Provincia pro« modo virium certam partem sustineat onerum, quae tuendo foederi sunt necessaria: in negotiis provincialibus aut communibus vno utatur sigillo ex urbano & agrario confecto. Civitas in consessibus & actionibus« nibus ac rebus omnibus priores partes« teneat, agrarij secundas: in suffragijs« tamen pares sint: quae si discrepent, delectis pari numero utraq; a parte permittatur res; qui & ipsi si nequeat consentire inter se, gubernator suffragio suo dissensione dirimat. Et hac ex partium consensu. De mercatus iure,& controversis rebus aliis sic, uti iudices, pronunciarunt. Civitas in possessione« juris STAPVLÆ pariter in reb. in agro natis& peregrinis maneto: propolæ & propolia in agro non funto: de cerevisiæ usu res ma-« neto in eo statu, in quo solet ex foedere esse:« HOVEIMANNI[?] quoque ad iudicandas res« relinquuntur iidem, & eadem in potestate, qui & qua in potestate constituti sunt ab ordinum senatu statim in initio deditæ Groningæ. Cuncta hæc valento, quoad ab ordinibus generalibus in pleno possessorio, aut petitorio aliter fuerit definitum. Quæ contra hæc ab agrariis quoquo modo acta, coeptaque irrita sunto, nec fas esto, imposterum quicquam eosdem impediendis his tentare: contra commissa ex legib. puniuntur: quæstio de accisis, uti vocant, evanescito ex partiu cosensu. Omnia hæc, quæ hac sententia definita sunt, ut effectum suum sortiantur sine mora ac sine vitio, & sarta tecta serventur, gubernator, & hovetmanni operam danto.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, at the beginning, three arbitrators or referees were appointed: men of great distinction and political experience, Elbertus Leoninus, Chancellor of Gelderland; Sebastianus Lose, a senator of the supreme court of Holland; and Johannes Wittenius, consul of Kampen, who is bound to me by close friendship. These men, long experienced in the Senate and the councils of the General Orders, were to settle the dispute between the parties amicably, if they could, together with the illustrious governor, Lord Willem Lodewijk, Count of Nassau; if they could not, they were to decide for the time being whatever seemed expedient for peace and government, until the cause was fully heard and everything settled by final judgment.
