They, applying the utmost diligence and zeal with the governor, after labouring for a long time in vain to compose the whole controversy, at last, having received full power from the parties to do so, first settled those matters which concerned the form and order of the provincial government in this union with the confederated orders, and the administration of common money. In these matters they decided above all the following: that the city and the land should be one province forever under one governor; that the provincial assemblies should be common to both parties and be held nowhere but in Groningen. In the first place they set up a new council, on the model customary in the other confederated provinces, into which the townsmen and the land-holders should each give four men, as the bond and sinew of the union and unity. The duty of this council would be to take care of and administer the money of the province arising from the tax and excise, for the uses of peace and war, and likewise the monastic goods brought into the common treasury; furthermore, to take care that the true religion be spread and preserved, that no opportunity be given to false worship, and that no fraud be practised upon the church property and other endowments for pious uses assigned by our ancestors; to summon the provincial orders to the assemblies when necessary in the absence of the governor, to lay proposals for deliberation at the assemblies, to carry out decrees by vote of the orders, and finally to hold a share of the care and authority, with the governor, in matters of war. The governor shall be the head of the council, and he shall attend it as often as he wishes or is able; the colleagues shall in turn preside for weeks at a time, alternately from the city and from the countryside. To the council there shall also be added a treasurer, chosen by common vote to manage the money, likewise a secretary, a doorkeeper, and other lower officers. Moreover, by the zeal and authority of the same men it was agreed between the parties that always two assessors from this province should be in the council of the General Orders, with the other members having power to deliberate and decide on matters of the confederation: one from the townsmen, the other from the land-holders; likewise one in the Senate of the Orders and one in the Senate of maritime affairs, and this alternately, so that if the one is from the city, the other shall be from the countryside, and vice versa. The province shall bear a fixed share of the burdens necessary for defending the confederation, according to its strength; in provincial or common business it shall use one seal, made up of one from the city and one from the countryside. The city shall hold the first place in assemblies and in actions and in all matters, the land-holders the second; but in voting they shall be equal; and if they disagree, a number of chosen men equal from each side shall be allowed to settle the matter; and if these too cannot agree among themselves, the governor shall end the disagreement with his vote. And this was done by the consent of the parties. Concerning the right of the market and other disputed matters, they pronounced thus, as judges: the city shall remain in possession of the right of STAPLE, equally in matters both native and foreign in the land; there shall be no forestalling or engrossing in the countryside; the matter of the use of beer shall remain in the condition in which it usually stands by the covenant; the HOVETMEN [?] also are left to judge cases, the same persons, with the same power, and in the same manner as those who were appointed by the Senate of the Orders at the very beginning in Groningen. All these shall remain in force until the General Orders decide otherwise in a full hearing of possession or of title. Whatever has been done or begun by the land-holders contrary to these matters shall be void, and it shall not be lawful for them henceforth to try to hinder these things in any way; whatever is committed contrary to these terms is punished by law; the inquiry concerning the excise, as they call it, shall lapse by consent of the parties. The governor and the hovetmen shall take care that all these things, which are settled by this judgment, obtain their effect without delay and without fault, and are kept safe and sound.

units.la: Pronunciatum præsente gubernatore, & parte utrâq; die XVII[?] Feb. Juliani, anno M. D. XCV Groninga. Sed agrarij autore Verrucio jureconsulto offensi pronunciato non solū abrogationem huius, sed etiam reformationem aut reductionem totius causæ ordines generales flagitarunt.
units.tr: Pronounced in the presence of the governor and of both parties, on the 17th [?] of February, Julian calendar, in the year 1595, at Groningen. But the land-holders, offended by the judgment, on the advice of the jurist Verrucius, demanded from the General Orders not only the annulment of this, but also a reform or a re-hearing of the whole cause.

units.la: Ab ordinibus novi judices numero IX, peritissimi quique, dati, hisque cognoscendi definiendique summa potestas tributa. His tota re diligenter excussa & considerata tandem anno M. D. XCVII, die XI January Juliani in consessu generalium ordinum, patentibus conclavis valuis sententiam tulere.
units.tr: From the Orders, nine new judges, all very skilled, were appointed, and the highest power of hearing and deciding was given to them. After the whole matter had been carefully examined and considered, at last, in the year 1597, on the 11th of January, Julian calendar, in the assembly of the General Orders, with the doors of the chamber open, they gave their judgment.

units.la: Qua ut intelligi posset, qua partium postulata fuerint, aperiendum. Agrarij ordines secuti vestigia consiliorum priorum de solvendo fœdere, divortium postularunt, separationem integram, per quam sibi consulerent seorsim, suamque tenerent, remp. divisam a civitate, nec quicquam cum hac habērent commune, prætor viciniam & commertia libera. Speciatim vero Hovetmanniorum à senatu oppidano datorum jurisdictionem recusa-bant omnino, conventus habere suos, quando & ubi commodum sibi, seclusa civitate, in iis de rep. consultare & statuere, collegium provinciale suum tenere, judices summos ex se edere volebant: jus fori rerum venalium in oppido, & id quod de frumento & cerevisia dixi, ex fœderib. promanans, in universum rescissum cupiebant. Minora mitte.
units.tr: So that it may be understood what the parties demanded, it must be explained. The land-holders, following the path of the earlier counsels about dissolving the alliance, demanded a divorce, a complete separation, by which they might look to their own interests separately and keep their own state, divided from the city, and have nothing in common with it, except neighbourhood and free commerce. In particular, they absolutely refused the jurisdiction of the Hovetmen appointed by the town Senate; they wished to hold their own assemblies, whenever and wherever it suited them, and there, with the city shut out, to consult and decide about the state; to keep their own provincial council, and to appoint their own highest judges. They wished also that the right of the market-court for saleable goods in the town, and what I have said about grain and beer, arising from the covenants, should be utterly annulled. Leave out the smaller points.

units.la: Civitas contra coniunctionem solitam summa ratione institutam olim, longissimo tempore probatam, translationibus & decretis multis robora-tam, poscebat: Hovetmannorum electionem & potestatem ex more prisco, & quæ cum ea cohærent, pactum item vetus de cerevisia, legem de frumento ἐγχωρίῳ[?] deniq, STAPVLÆ jus integrum in omnibus rebus venalibus domi natis aut peregrinis & importatis, relinqui sibi, & firmari petebat. Judices pronunciarunt hoc modo.
units.tr: The city, on the contrary, demanded that the union customary, established long ago with the highest reason, approved over a very long time, and strengthened by many transfers and decrees, should stand; the election and power of the Hovetmen according to the ancient custom, and what coheres with it; likewise the old agreement about beer, the law about grain, [Greek word: ἐγχωρίῳ?] and finally the full right of the STAPLE in all saleable goods, whether home-grown, foreign or imported, should be left to it and confirmed. The judges pronounced in this way.

units.la: Sententia triumvirorum deputatorum anno M. D. XCV lata abrogata esto. Civitas & a-ger[?] una provincia, una ditio sunto, & coniun-ctim ab ordinibus suis reguntor. Omnia jura & reditus, qui quondam principis fuere, omnes item ex tributis recentib. omnis generis provenientes pecuniæ exercentor, & impedi-tor, quo debent, ex consensu communi partis utriusque: monasteria & bona monastica, & quæ ejus generis in urbe & agro, item in præ-sectura vetere & suburbana conjunctis senten-tiis conferuntor in usus pios: ad administrationem pecuniæ publicæ & censuum, ac ad ea, quæ ab ordinib. decernentur exequenda & efficienda deliguntor viri idonei pari numero utraq; a parte, ijsque mandata & muneris limites prescribuntor, cujusmodi e re esse provinciæ ordines putabunt: interea collegium ante biennium institutum, ea forma qua institutum est, maneto tantisper donec hæc erunt confecta: munera à principe conferri aut committi solita ab ordi-nibus coniunctim conferuntor & deman-dantor. Camera justitiæ, uti vocant, id est tribunal Hovetmannorum, & ejus præses (legatum dicunt) & officiarii cæteri istuc pertinentes, exceptis ipsis Hovetman-nis, quos sola civitas edet, constituuntor, committuntor, juramento obligantor conjunctim ab ordinibus provinciæ, ut nomine reip. aut potestatis superioris jus dicant ex legib. provincialibus, & consuetudine antiquitus receptâ, in causis ab anno M. D. XXI. ad annum M. D. LX in hoc tribunali cognosci solitis: provinciæ totius negotiâ neutra pars seorsim, nec quisquam omnino partis alterius extra conventus provinciales tractato. Agrariis liberum est negociari cum quibuslibet, quocunq; loco, quibuscunque in mercimoniis iis libitum erit: exceptis rebus quæ in agro proveniunt aut sunt, ut butyro, caseo, equis, bubus, frumento, quarum exportatio vetita esto, nisi [?]ante Groningæ promercales fuerint; Et tamé agratij[?] jus habento mercandi & vendendi muò in usus rei suæ familiaris, etiam ea, quæ Groningæ promercalia non fuere. Si de formaac[?] modo habendi forum convenire inter se partes non poterunt, compendio ea, quæ controversa ipsis sunt, exponunto, sententiam generalium ordinum de ijsdem expectanto. Agrarijs liberum esto cerevisiam in usum fa-ciendi, causa non esto, nec in tabernis aut diversoriis ullius cerevisiæ præterquam Gro-ninganę usus pertotum agrum concessus ha-betor. Groningani in possessione loci prioris in scribendo, signando, sedendo, suffragiis se-sendis manento, pariaq; suffragia in actionib. & deliberationibus provincialibus retinento. Suffragiis inter se pugnantibus omnes modi & rationes æquæ & vsitatæ adhibentor ad ea concilianda: si id non successerit, per guberna-torem, & delectos[?] ab utrâq; parte pari numero dissensio dirimitor, usque dum modus alius melior fuerit ad hanc rem repertus & introdu-ctus: conventus ordinum indicuntor suffragiis ordinum eorundum congregatorum, aut edicto gubernatoris, aut denunciatione eorū, qui eadere[?] mandata habebunt, idq; ijs locis, qui idonei maximè videbuntur. Acta, no-vationes, usurpationes, quæ adversantur his, ac impedimento sunt, abrogata & pro nullis sunto, nec quicquam imposterum simile ten-tator: De subsidio ab agrariis petito ad solu-tionem æris alieni veteris, & impensas neces-sarias, quoniam non satis adhuc res liquet, ijdem tenentor æs illud alienū & impedia necessaria apud ordines generales exponere, ut re cognita ab ijs statui & ferri sententia possit. Omnia hæc salvo jure fœderum & pactorum inter provincias socias in Belgio, & sine diminutione auctoritatis ordinum generalium & Gubernatoris, quæ ex transactione Groningana anni M. D. XCIIII, aut aliàs his debetur. Postremò postulata reliqua partium rejiciuntur, & sumptus compensantur. Pronunciatum die XI januar. anno M. D. XCVII. Subscripsit nomine ordinum generalium AERS. Verum ex sententia huius veris cum nova lis esset orta partibus, ea ad ordines generales iterum relata, ab ijs cognitio & judicandi potestas prioribus judicibus delegata fuit. Hi à biennio, anno scil. M. D. XCVII, die XXVII Febr. Iuliani partim interpretantes sententiam priorem, partim illiquida definientes hunc in modum pro-nunciarunt denuo Omnes merces aut res importatæ in agrum, etiam si in agro iam sint, non sint obnoxiæ STAPVLÆ juri, easque emere, vendere, commutare inter se agrarij liceat: exceptis equis, hinnulis equinis, bubus, vaccis, trimestre longiusve tempus in agro pastis, qui in agro natis accenseri & fori oppidani juri subjecti esse debent. In agro nata & stapulæ subjecta non alia censeri debent quam hæc: butyrum, caseus, equi, pulli, boves, vaccæ, triticum, secale, hordeum, avena, far: atqui hæc omnino, ni ante promercalia[?] Groninge fuerint, distrahere in agro licitum non fit. Sub ijs, quæ in vsum rei familiaris vendere & emere licet, etiam ea comprehendantur, quæ lanij, pistores, propolæ, aut institores in vsum rei suæ in agro coë-munt, ut minutim rursum vendant. Agra-rius peregrino vendens res suas fori juri fubie-ctas immunis à pœna fit, nisi constiterit, scisse, peregrinum esse, quo cum contraxit. HOVET-MANNI ab oppidanis electi, ab ordinib. totius provinciæ potestate judicandi accipiant; & iis, ac apud eos sacramento fe obligent ex for-ma folenni, in sententiâ affcripta. Ante hoc factamentum præstitum Hovetmanni pro Hovetmannis non habeantur, & acta eorum velut non acta censeantur. Præses, Hovet-manni, scribæ à secretis, accensi, in fide sunt utriufq; partis pari modo, nullo præcipuo civitatis jure præter Hovetmanorum electio-nem: & officij limites ab utraq; parte ijs præ-scribantur. Præses & Hovetmanni solam ju-rifdictionem tractent in causis solitis ab anno M. D. XXI adannum M. D. LX, potestatem reliquam magistratus, & politicü regimen agri non attingant: agrariis liceat separatim suos conventus habere in causis ad ipsos feorfim. fine civitate pertinentibus. Ordines hujus pro-vinciæ, ordines urbis Groninge, & Omlandiæ, agrarios sólos Omlandios inter Amafum & Lavicam appellare, rectum fit. Agrarij vecti-galia nulla, mercatus folennes, trutinas publi-cas instituant fine consensu ordinum provin-ciæ omnium: agrariorum postulatum de sub-divisione tributorum & onerum inter civita-tem & agrum adhuc non audiatur: interim quod in onerum modo,quem pro rato pro- [?] vincia hæc tenetur sustinere, ex tributis & censib. jam usitatis solui non potest, id conficiatur ex quintâ censu aut proventus omnium bonorum immobilium,agrorum pariter & ædificiorum,rusticorum urbanorum q;, ex formâ anni M. D. LXXVII; & hoc servetur, donec de modo alio partes convenerint,aut aliter ab ordinib. generalib. fuerit decretum. Cætera actionis huius nondum satis explicata ac probata explicentur & probentur plenius, ut ferri sententia possit; & teneantur oppidani rei respondere peremptorie. Interea quæ servanda sint in usu juris STAPVLÆ, recensent & præcipiunt ex formula Cobelia aut Albana, de tempore proponendi in publico mercés,de loco, de indice earum, ex quib. vectigal fori solutum, de modo vectigalis certo in singulas mercium species: interdicuntque oppidanis institutione novorum vectigalium & aggravatione veterum: addunt de trutinæ cura & inspectione contra fraudes. Denique de Oldermanno, & ijs, qui illo in subsellio de STAPVLÆ jure judicant, subijciunt; statuuntq;, ne Oldermannus carens semiplena probatione quenq; ad jusjurandum adigat, utq; accusatus in hoc casu velut innocens absolvatur, Oldermannus vero in sumptus, & poena pro excessus modo arbitrariam condemnetur: ut femi-
units.tr: The sentence of the three deputed commissioners, pronounced in the year 1595, shall be annulled. The city and the country shall be one province and one jurisdiction, and they shall be governed jointly by their orders. All rights and revenues which once belonged to the prince, likewise all the money arising from the recent taxes of every kind, shall be managed and disbursed, as they ought, by the common consent of both parties. The monasteries and monastic goods of this kind, in the city and countryside, as well as in the old and suburban prefecture, shall by joint judgment be applied to pious uses. For the administration of the public money and the levies, and for carrying out and effecting what the orders decree, suitable men shall be chosen in equal number from each side; their commissions and the limits of their office shall be prescribed as the orders of the province think fit. Meanwhile the college instituted two years ago shall remain in the form in which it was established, until these matters have been completed. Offices which the prince was accustomed to confer or commit shall be conferred and entrusted jointly by the orders. The Chamber of Justice, as they call it, that is, the tribunal of the Hovetmen, together with its president (whom they call the legate) and the other officials belonging there, excepting the Hovetmen themselves, whom the city alone shall furnish, shall be appointed, commissioned and bound by oath jointly by the orders of the province, to declare law in the name of the commonwealth or the higher power, according to the provincial laws and the custom received from antiquity, in the cases which from the year 1521 to the year 1560 were customarily heard in this tribunal. No party shall deal separately with the affairs of the whole province, nor shall anyone of the other side transact anything outside the provincial assemblies. The country folk are free to trade with whomever they like, in whatever place, and in whatever goods they please, except those products which grow or are raised in the countryside, such as butter, cheese, horses, oxen and grain, whose export is forbidden unless they have first been offered for sale at Groningen. Nevertheless the country people shall have the right to buy and sell for the use of their own households only, even those goods which were not offered for sale at Groningen. If the parties cannot agree among themselves on the manner of holding the market, they shall briefly set out the points in dispute and await the judgment of the general orders on them. The country people shall be free to brew beer for their own use, without restriction, and no beer other than that of Groningen shall be granted for use throughout the whole countryside in inns or taverns. The Groningers shall retain their prior place in writing, sealing, sitting and casting votes, and shall keep equal votes in the provincial actions and deliberations. When votes conflict, all fair and customary methods shall be used to reconcile them; if this does not succeed, the dispute shall be settled by the governor and by men chosen in equal number from each side, until another and better method is found and introduced for this matter. Assemblies of the orders shall be called by the votes of the same assembled orders, or by the edict of the governor, or by notice from those who shall hold the commission for it, and this shall be done in those places which seem most suitable. Acts, innovations and usurpations which oppose or hinder these arrangements are annulled and shall count as void, and no one shall attempt anything similar in future. Concerning the aid sought by the country people for paying off the old debt and the necessary expenses, since the matter is not yet sufficiently clear, the same people shall set out that debt and the necessary outlays before the general orders, so that once the matter is known a judgment may be pronounced and delivered by them. All this is to be without prejudice to the right of the alliances and treaties between the allied provinces in the Netherlands, and without diminution of the authority of the general orders and the governor, which is owed under the Groningen settlement of 1594 or otherwise. Finally, the remaining demands of the parties are rejected, and the costs are set off. Pronounced on the 11th day of January, in the year 1597. Signed in the name of the general orders, AERS. But when, after the sentence of this judgment, a new dispute had arisen between the parties, it was again referred to the general orders, and they delegated the cognizance and power of judging to the earlier judges. These, from two years earlier, that is in the year 1597, on the 27th day of February (Julian), partly interpreting the earlier sentence and partly defining what was unsettled, pronounced again in this manner: All goods or wares imported into the countryside, even if they are already in the countryside, are not subject to the right of the staple, and it shall be lawful for the country people to buy, sell and exchange them among themselves; excepted are horses, foals, oxen and cows which have been pastured in the countryside for a quarter of a year or longer, and these shall be counted as home-raised and must be subject to the right of the town market. The following home-raised goods subject to the staple are to be counted as such: butter, cheese, horses, colts, oxen, cows, wheat, rye, barley, oats and spelt; and these, unless they were first offered for sale at Groningen, may not be sold in the countryside. Among those things which it is permitted to buy and sell for the use of one's household, let those also be included which butchers, bakers, retailers or hawkers buy in the countryside for their own use, to sell again in small quantities. A country man selling his goods to a foreigner, which are subject to the market right, shall be immune from penalty, unless it is proved that he knew the foreigner with whom he dealt to be a foreigner.

units.la: plena probatio habeatur testimonium affirmativum testis jurati, modo is non fit in ministerio ipsius Oldermanni, qui rejiciut suspectus potest. Oldermannus & judices hi nihil potestatis, aut jurisdictionis sibi sufurpent in agrarios præter id, quod ad ipsorum cognitionem proprie pertinet: Idem Oldermannus ad hoc tribunal suum ne-minem citet ex agro nisi per mandatum Cameræ provincialis, id est, præsidis & Hoetmannorum: agrarij & peregrini à sententia hujus tribunalis Hovetmannos cum præside, cives senatum urbanum appellet, & recognitionem petant: Huic sententiæ in consessu ordinum generalium pronunciatæ, & nomine eorundem à summo scriba à secretis scripta, addidere judices idem aliam quod, eode die & loco. In eâ concedunt agrarijs ad exsolvendum æs alienum tributum agro toti imponere secundum jugera per octen-nium eo modo, quem ipsi sufficere arbitrantur, atque insuper ex bonis monasticis ex decreto ordinum generalium aureorum xvi millia capere: Vtramenæs hoc alienum prius liquidem fiat apud ipsos provinciæ ordines, nec excedat summam lxiiii millium aureorum, quam summam ipsi agrarij ante erant professi: utq; quotanis de hoc tributo apud generosum gubernatorem, & deleēctos ordinum provincialium rationes reddatur; ut agrariis ipsdem liceat vectigal cerevisiæ & vino in tabernis aut diversoriis publicis imponere, & singulis femestrib. locare tanti, quanti id proximè fecerant oppidani, pecuniamq; illam stipendiis impendere, ac salariis officiariorum suorum, & negotiis aliis necessariis: quod si tamen vectigal annum excesserit aureos quatermille, excedens pars ut cedat in ærarium commune, ejusq; quæstori numeretur.
units.tr: …plena probatio habeatur: the affirmative testimony of one sworn witness counts as full proof, provided he is not a servant of the Oldermann himself, for such a witness may be rejected as suspect. The Oldermann and these judges shall claim for themselves no power or jurisdiction over the country people beyond what properly belongs to their own cognizance. The same Oldermann shall summon no one from the country to this tribunal except by a mandate of the provincial chamber, that is, of the governor and the Hoetmanns. Country people and strangers may appeal from the sentence of this tribunal to the Hovetmanns with the governor, and citizens may appeal to the city senate, and seek a review. To this sentence, pronounced in the assembly of the general estates and written in their name by the chief secretary, the judges added another on the same day and in the same place. In it they grant the country people that, to pay off their debts, a tax may be laid on the whole land according to the acres, for eight years, in the manner they themselves think sufficient; and in addition, by decree of the general estates, they may take sixteen thousand gold pieces from monastic property. But first this debt is to be clearly established before the provincial estates themselves, and it shall not exceed the sum of sixty-four thousand gold pieces, which the country people themselves had earlier declared. And each year an account of this tax is to be rendered before the noble governor and the chosen members of the provincial estates; so that the country people may impose a duty on beer and wine in the taverns or public inns, and let it at each half-year for as much as the townsmen had most recently paid, and spend that money on the pay and salaries of their officials and other necessary business. But if the duty should exceed four thousand gold pieces a year, the excess is to pass into the common treasury and be counted out to its quaestor.

units.la: In hoc statu res hæsit[?], cum hæc recognoscerem. Sequitur de aliis ad civitatis dignitatem & jura pertinentibus.
units.tr: In this state the matter stuck, while I was reviewing these things. What follows concerns the other matters pertaining to the dignity and rights of the city.

units.la: ALIA PRÆCLARA CIVITATIS IVRA ET LEGES.
units.tr: OTHER OUTSTANDING RIGHTS AND LAWS OF THE CITY.

units.la: Habet vero præter hæc alia quoq; præclara jura civitas hæc nostra. Inter quæ illud censeri potest, quod in toto ANGLIAE regno commerciorum ac negociationum libertatem jam ccc, xlv ante annos cives habuerint cum conditionib. haud pœnitendis: ut testatur diploma Henrici iii regis anno regni eius XLI signatum, quod est in reip. archivis illæsum. Deinde illud etiam, quod ante complures hominum ætates amplissimo FOEDERI ANSEATICO civitas adscripta sit, locumq; in eo perhonestū inter civitates socias tenuerit[?] semper, & adhuc teneat.. Sed hoc nobilius & illustrius priorib. quod privilegio ornata sit a maioribus. acce-pto, & (asarum diplomate confirmato, & sine vitio ad hoc usq; tempus continuato, ne cuiquam omnino vel regi vel principi vel ordini liceat quenquam, qui civis aut incola civitatis sit, aut quoquo modo civitati subiectus, iudicii causa, e civitate evocare, aut ad ullum tribunal exte-rum citare. Nec eo inferius id, quod nulla sit a Senatus sententia aut decreto provocatio, nulla alterius iudicis tanquam superioris appella-tio, nec in civilibus nec in criminalibus causis: quo sane nihil amplius, nihil maius, nihil publi-cius dari civitati potest: quod denique tale est, ut in nulla civitate Germaniae extra Helvetiam, nulla Belgii, nulla Galliae, Angliae, Scotiae, Poloniae, Vngariae, Sueciae, Daniae simile queat inveniri. Nec solum senatus hoc iure pollet, sed & collegium Hovetmannorum, quam Cameram vulgo vocant, a cujus judicio decretove similiter appellatio non est, non plebeio, nō nobili.
units.tr: Moreover, this city of ours also has other outstanding rights. Among these may be counted that for more than three hundred and forty-five years before now the citizens have enjoyed freedom of trade and commerce throughout the whole kingdom of England, on terms that are not to be regretted. This is attested by a charter of King Henry III, sealed in the forty-first year of his reign, which is preserved unharmed in the public archives. Next, that many generations ago the city was enrolled in the most honourable ANSEATIC LEAGUE, and has always held, and still holds, a most respected place among the allied cities. But this is more noble and illustrious than the earlier privileges: the city has been adorned with a privilege received from its ancestors and confirmed by the charter of the Emperors, and continued without flaw to this day, that no king, prince or order at all may summon anyone who is a citizen or resident of the city, or who is in any way subject to the city, out of the city for the purpose of trial, or cite him before any foreign tribunal. Nor is this inferior in that there is no appeal from a sentence or decree of the Senate, and no appeal to another judge as to a superior, in either civil or criminal cases. Certainly nothing more, nothing greater, nothing more public can be granted to a city. Finally, it is of such a kind that no similar one can be found in any city of Germany outside Switzerland, or of the Netherlands, France, England, Scotland, Poland, Hungary, Sweden or Denmark. Not only the Senate enjoys this right, but also the college of Hovetmen, which is commonly called the Chamber, from whose judgment or decree there is likewise no appeal, whether for commoner or nobleman.

units.la: Nec aliud in conventu juridico ordinum agrario-rum valet, in quo maxima autoritas Hovetman-norum nunc est, & fuit per centum fere annos, olim vero ante Saxonica tempora stante integra reipub. libertate, universi senatus cum Hovet-mannis esse solet, qui conventus non alibi quoquam in urbe agitur. Nam ultra huius tribunal tendere nemini licet. Nec vero istud in posterio-ris privilegiorum huius civitatis posuero, quod le-gum & statutorum suorum ipsa domina est: ipsa seredi abrogandi; potestate liberrima habet, nec necessum habet ad voluntatem & consensum cujusquam respicere alterius: atq; ita scisci & antiquat, quemadmodum temporum ratio ac usus postulat. Eandemq; potestatem in suas leges & statuta agrarij tenent, si se cum civitate conjungant, & ex voluntate consilioq; ejus potestate utantur: sine ea autem hac in parte nihil possunt; quamquam ante Kenoniana ac Focconiana, & ijs priora tempora haud dubie potuerint. Deniq; hoc etiam civitati egregium, quod argentea aereaq; pecunia signanda ab annis non minus CCCC, aurea vero ab anno Christi M. CCCC. LXIIII jus habuerit, adeoq; nunc quoq; habeat.
units.tr: Nor does anything else hold good in the judicial assembly of the agrarian orders, in which the greatest authority now belongs to the Hovetmen, and has belonged for nearly a hundred years; formerly, before the Saxon times, while the freedom of the commonwealth stood intact, the whole Senate was usually present with the Hovetmen, and this assembly is not held anywhere else in the city. For no one is permitted to appeal beyond this tribunal. Nor have I placed this last among the privileges of this city: that it is itself mistress of its own laws and statutes; it itself has the freest power to repeal them, and it need not look to the will and consent of any other party, and so it enacts and abrogates them as the nature and custom of the times demands. The agrarian districts hold the same power over their own laws and statutes, if they join themselves to the city and use that power according to its will and counsel; without it, however, they can do nothing in this respect, although before the Kenonian and Focconian times, and in the earlier periods, they undoubtedly could. Finally, this is also an outstanding distinction of the city: that it has had the right to coin silver and bronze money for not less than four hundred years, and gold money from the year of Christ 1464, and so it still has that right today.

units.la: Porro in legibus reip. hujus ita scriptum, ut consules officio decedentes die VIII Cal. Martij novis arcam publicam cum sigillo civitatis & clavibus tradant, rationesq; expediant intra dies XIIII; & si quid aris publici residui habeant penes se, id exsolvant: ut consulum quilibet cum assessoribus suis in praetorio rationes reddat accepti & reliqui coram quaestore reipub. & Triumviris concilij jurati: ut causae maiores non cognoscantur nisi in senatu: ut senatus controversias expediat celeriter, & quidem intra XII septimanas a lite conclusa: idem ut in rebus difficilibus senatum veterem, aut si placeat, alios etiam e civium numero prudentiores vocet in curiam; vocati tamen suffragium non habeant, sed consilio tantum senatum iuvent, penes quem solum suffragij jus: Provocans a consulis & assessorum [?]ssessorum sententia in praetorio lata ad senatum totum, & causa cadens, ut multam reip. solvat marcam unam: ut eundem appellare senatum, qui pronunciavit, si quid per errorem pronuncia-tum videatur, liceat intra dies x: ne quis eorum, qui in senatu sunt, intercedat pro quoquam, qui reip. multam debet: si fecerit, x aureos Rhen. reip. pendere damnas sit. Consul senatorve in munere suo non fideliter versari compertus loco moveatur, nec unquam ad reip. aditum rursum habeat. Item, ydem multam, si quam debent, ante alios reip. solvant, nec fas sit reliquos cogere, priusquam ab his factum, quod oportet. Nec hi, nec Sculthesius, nec tabellarius reip. verba pro altero in senatu aut judicio faciant, nisi tutores pupilli sint, cujus de re agitur. Cum senatus habetur, nemo emansitet impune, aut fero veniat: acta dictaq; in senatu nemo eliminet: cognati partium in senatu ferendis sententiis non intersint. Si quis causam suam, quam senatus semel definivit, finito eorum munere, qui eam definierunt, ad successores eorundem retulerit iterum, marcas x reip. pendat. Olim si qui solvendo non erant, mos fuit, ut nomina eorum certo tempore, exeunte nimirum anni quadrante, quo quis consulum in senatu praesederat, si poscerent creditores, ex sublimi curia fenestra in capite fori, concurrente ad hanc rem frequenti civium turba recitarentur: eoq; facto illi non solum infames fierent, sed & legum patrocinio exuerentur, non contra contumeliam, non contra vim ac firferrum essent tuti. Nunc catera manent, pœ-stremum tantum est sublatum. Proclamatus hoc modo honore suo, & bono nomine cadit, officij publici nullius capax est, in judicio stare, respondere, testimonium dicere non potest. Hoc ad fidem fori & contractuum colendam servandamq; sanctius est institutum. Quondam uti in agro, sic in civitate testamenti factio nulla omnino fuit. At pactorum dotalium jus viguit, eaq; pacta servare necessum fuit, si rite legitimeq; essent confecta. Legitimum vero in his erat, ut etiam nunc est, præsentibus & consentientibus agnatis & cognatis proximis, quorumve maxime interesset, ea iniri & scribi, ac ad senatum signandi causa referri. Nec in his hodie quicquam mutatum. De testamento nunc aliud jus ante annos aliquot inductum. Nam quibus xx ætatis anni sunt, si liberis legitimis carent, his de bonis suis omnibus non hæreditarijs, sed acquisitis, ni obstent pacta dotalia, testari libere pro libitu licet: De hæreditarijs non nisi ex semisse licet. At quibus liberi legitimi sunt, totius substantia sua semissem relinquere ijsdem cogun-tur, nisi justam causam, senatuiq; probatam contra eos, aut eorum aliquem habeant. De altero semisse pro arbitrio suo disponere similiter servatis ijsdem possunt.
units.tr: Further, it is written in the laws of this commonwealth that the consuls, when they leave office on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, shall hand over to the new ones the public chest with the seal of the city and its keys, and shall settle their accounts within fourteen days; and if they hold any remainder of public money, they shall pay it out. Each of the consuls shall render his accounts, of receipts and balance, together with his assessors, in the praetorium before the quaestor of the commonwealth and the sworn Triumvirs of the council. Greater causes shall not be heard except in the Senate. The Senate shall settle disputes quickly, indeed within twelve weeks from the conclusion of the suit. Likewise, in difficult matters, it shall summon the old Senate into the curia, or, if it pleases, other more prudent men from among the citizens; those so summoned, however, shall not have a vote, but shall only assist the Senate with counsel, the right of voting resting with the Senate alone. Anyone appealing from a sentence of the consuls and assessors pronounced in the praetorium may appeal to the whole Senate, and if the cause is lost he shall pay one mark as a fine to the commonwealth. It is permitted to appeal to the same Senate that pronounced judgment, within ten days, if anything seems to have been pronounced in error. No one of those who are in the Senate shall intercede on behalf of anyone who owes a fine to the commonwealth; if he does so, he shall be liable to pay ten gold Rhenish florins to the commonwealth. A consul or senator found not to be faithful in his office shall be removed from his post, and never again have access to the commonwealth. Likewise, the same persons shall pay any fines they owe before the others, and it is not lawful to compel the rest until this has been done. Neither these, nor the Schultheiss, nor the commonwealth's secretary, shall speak words on behalf of another in the Senate or in court, unless they are guardians of a ward whose matter is under discussion. When the Senate is convened, no one shall leave early or arrive late without penalty; no one shall divulge the acts and words spoken in the Senate; relatives of the parties shall not take part in giving votes in the Senate. If anyone brings back to the successors of those who decided it his cause, which the Senate has once settled, after the term of office of those who decided it has ended, he shall pay ten marks to the commonwealth. Formerly, if anyone was insolvent, the custom was that their names, at a fixed time, namely when a quarter of the year had run out in which one of the consuls had presided in the Senate, were read out, if the creditors demanded it, from the high window of the curia at the head of the forum, a large crowd of citizens gathering for this purpose; and when this was done, those men not only became infamous but were also stripped of the protection of the laws, and were not safe against insult or violence or the sword. Now the other things remain, only the most severe penalty has been removed. A man proclaimed in this way loses his honour and good name; he is not capable of any public office, and cannot stand in court, respond, or give testimony. This was instituted more strictly to maintain and preserve the trust of the marketplace and of contracts. Formerly, as in the countryside, there was no testamentary capacity at all in the city. But the right of dowry agreements was in force, and these agreements had to be kept if they were properly and lawfully drawn up. Lawful in these matters was, as it still is, that they be entered into and written down in the presence of, and with the consent of, the nearest agnates and cognates, or those whom it most concerned, and be referred to the Senate for sealing. Nothing has been changed in these matters today. Concerning wills, a different law was introduced some years ago. For those who are twenty years of age, if they have no legitimate children, may freely make a will as they please concerning all their goods that are not inherited but acquired, unless dowry agreements stand in the way; of inherited goods, they may dispose only of half. But those who have legitimate children are compelled to leave half of their whole estate to those same children, unless they have a just cause against them or one of them, approved by the Senate. They may likewise dispose of the other half at their own discretion, observing the same conditions.

units.la: Sed in his omnibus opus, ut a sanis lectove non affixis, ac mente integris id fiat, referaturq; ad senatum, aut testantis manu scriptum senatui offeratur, & sigillo publico civitatis muniatur. Quod si liberorum aliqui exhaeredes scribuntur ; hi tamen ex fructibus partis suae alimenta debentur ; pars ipsa liberis ipsorum, si quos habent, aut haeredibus proximis accrescit.
units.tr: But in all these matters it must be done by those who are sound and not confined to bed, and whose minds are intact, and it must be referred to the Senate, or the testator's handwritten document must be presented to the Senate and secured with the public seal of the city. If any of the children are written down as disinherited, nevertheless maintenance is owed to them from the fruits of their portion; the portion itself accrues to their own children, if they have any, or to the nearest heirs.

units.la: In successionibus olim hoc valuere. In bona parentum liberi succedebant, & potissimum mares : ii vero ex consilio & iudicio propinquorum proximorum aequam dotem sororibus, quae erant, dabant, nec licebat ipsis quicquam rerum patrimonialium alienare, priusquam cum sororibus de dote convenissent.
units.tr: In matters of succession this formerly held good. Children succeeded to the goods of their parents, and especially the sons; these, on the advice and judgment of the nearest relatives, gave a fair dowry to the sisters who existed, and it was not lawful for them to alienate any part of the patrimonial property before they had come to an agreement with the sisters about the dowry.

units.la: Si per propinquos confici res inter fratres & sorores non posset, auctoritas senatus interveniebat. Quinimo nepotes ex filiis potiores filiabus erant in successione hac, si filia dotem jam accepisset : sin minus, filia cum fratris defuncti liberis aequaliter in capita hereditatem parentum dividebant ; cum plurium vero fratrum defunctorum liberis utriusque sexus succedebant in stirpes.
units.tr: If the matter between brothers and sisters could not be settled by the relatives, the authority of the Senate intervened. Indeed, in this kind of succession the grandsons through sons had precedence over the daughters, if the daughter had already received her dowry; otherwise the daughter and the children of a deceased brother divided the parents' inheritance equally per head; but where there were several deceased brothers, the children of both sexes succeeded per stirpes.

units.la: Liberorum unus si decessisset parentibus adhuc vivis, non parentes, sed fratres & sorores utrique parente cum defuncto coniuncti aut coniunctae hereditatem capiebant, maribus tamen hic quoque sexu altero potioribus : uterinis autem & consanguineis parentes praeferebantur : fratres vero uterini aut consanguinei, item sorores huiusce modi, si propiores haeredes alii non essent, fratris aut sororis defuncti defunctaeve bona aliquis portionibus inter se partiebantur. Conjuges, genitis & defunctis communib liberis, ac liberorum liberis, sibi mutuo succedebant, succedunt q; etiam nunc, ex asse: si liberos communes non genuissent, moriente eorum altero superstites ex semisse haeres eius erat, ut etiam hodie est: sin genuissent, itaq; moriente altero in vivis essent, superstites nihilominus semissem capiebat, reliquu liberis communib. relinquebat: idemq; valebat, si vita decedens liberos legitimos ex alio matrimonio procreatos haberet superstites. Nec aliter quoq; hoc tempore res habet.
units.tr: If one of the children died while the parents were still alive, the inheritance was taken not by the parents but by the brothers and sisters who were related to the deceased on both sides, though here too males were preferred to the other sex. Parents, however, were preferred to uterine and consanguineous siblings. Brothers, uterine or consanguineous, and likewise sisters of this kind, if there were no nearer heirs, divided among themselves in shares the goods of the deceased brother or sister. Spouses succeeded each other in full (ex asse) when they had children in common, both born and deceased, and the children of those children; and so they still do. If they had no children in common, the survivor of the two, when the other died, was heir to one half, as is still the case today. But if they had children, and one of them had died while the other was alive, the survivor nonetheless took one half and left the other half to the children in common. The same held if the one who died left surviving legitimate children by another marriage. Nor does the matter stand otherwise at the present time.

units.la: Defuncti defunctaq; nepotes & neptes ex filijs excludebant eiusdem fratres & sorores; item ex filiabus nepotes & neptes, si ex filijs non essent: filia vero praefere-bantur filiarum liberis. Impuberis defuncti hereditas, non existentibus parentibus, devolue-batur ad patruum & avunculum, & non ad amitam & materteram, nec ad avum & aviam, excepto casu, si amita unica cum unico avunculo, aut matertera una cum uno patruo superesset: tum enim hereditas tota in duas partes pares dividebatur. Nec aliud in puberis defuncti bonis valebat.
units.tr: The grandsons and granddaughters through sons excluded the brothers and sisters of the deceased; likewise the grandsons and granddaughters through daughters, if there were no sons' children; but a daughter was preferred to the children of a daughter. The inheritance of a deceased minor, when there were no parents, devolved upon the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle, and not upon the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt, nor upon the grandfather and grandmother; except in the case where a single paternal aunt survived together with a single maternal uncle, or a single maternal aunt together with a single paternal uncle: for then the whole inheritance was divided into two equal parts. Nothing else held good for the goods of a deceased adult.

units.la: Sed avunculum & patruum, item materteram & amitam altero tantum parente coniunctos cum parentibus defuncti avus & avia a successione eiusmodi excludebant. Uterini & consanguinei fratres, item sorores, si patrui, avunculi, amita, matertera non essent, succedebant sibi mutuo, exclusis patruis, avunculis, amitis, materteris magnis.
units.tr: But the grandfather and grandmother excluded from such succession the maternal and paternal uncles and aunts who were related to the deceased through only one parent, together with the parents. Uterine and consanguineous brothers, and likewise sisters, if there were no paternal uncles, maternal uncles, paternal aunts or maternal aunts, succeeded each other, the paternal uncles, maternal uncles, paternal aunts and maternal aunts (the great aunts and uncles) being excluded.

units.la: Privignus ex vitrico aut noverca genitus sorores habens uterinas vel con-san[?] sanguineas a morte matris aut patris sui tenebatur cum vitrico aut noverca eas alere & velocare, dotare.
units.tr: A stepson born of a stepfather or stepmother, having sisters, uterine or consanguineous, was bound from the death of his mother or father to support, provide for and dower them together with the stepfather or stepmother.

units.la: Quod si in matrimonio secundo filij quoq; geniti essent, hos quoq; oportebat cum fratre ex priore matrimonio orto, & cum patre, idem sororibus suis germanis praestare. Sed pleraq; horum correcta nunc jure novo. Id sic habet. Liberi parentum suorum haeredes sunto sine discrimine sexus in mobilibus pariter & immobilibus: verum filius duplum semper capito, soror simplum. Fratres & sorores praeferuntur parentibus in bonis defuncti fratris aut sororis, & servator quoq; hic eadem proportio. Si moriens liberos relinquat, superstites, & simul liberorum pramortuorum liberos, hi locum parentum in adeunda hereditate teneto, & succedunto cum illis in stirpes, non in capita. At si moriens relinquat in vivis avum, aviam, fratres, sorores ex altero tantummodo parente, germanorum fratrum, & germanarum sororum liberos, patruum quoq;, avunculum, amitam, materteram, omnes pariter ad successionem vocantur.
units.tr: But if children had also been born in a second marriage, it was likewise incumbent upon them to render the same to their full sisters, together with the brother from the earlier marriage and with the father. But most of these provisions are now corrected by the new law. It stands thus: "Let the children be heirs of their parents without distinction of sex, equally in movables and immovables; but the son shall always take double, the daughter a single share." Brothers and sisters are preferred to parents in the goods of a deceased brother or sister, and the same proportion holds here as well. If the deceased leaves surviving children, and also the children of children who have died earlier, these shall take the place of the parents in entering the inheritance, and shall succeed with those others per stirpes, not per capita. But if the deceased leaves surviving a grandfather, a grandmother, brothers and sisters from one parent only, and the children of full brothers and full sisters, the paternal uncle, the maternal uncle, the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt are all likewise called to the succession.

units.la: Marito potestas non, esto vendendi, permutandi, aut alieno gravandi quicquam rerum coniugis sua, quae immobiles sunt, sine expresso & liberrimo eius consensu.
units.tr: A husband has no power to sell, exchange, or burden with another's claim any of his wife's property that is immovable, without her express and wholly free consent; nor is there any such power over his own.

units.la: Uxori similiter non permittitur non solum mariti res sed suas quoq; vivente marito quoquomodo alienare, aut gravare sine ejusdem consensu libero puroq;[?]: alioqui mariti & uxoris bona omnia statim a nuptiis aut cum nuptiis communia fiunt utriq; jure pari.
units.tr: Likewise, a wife is not permitted, while her husband is living, to alienate or burden in any way not only the husband's property but also her own, without his free and unclouded consent; otherwise all the goods of husband and wife become common to both, by equal right, immediately from or with the marriage.

units.la: Lex quoq; olim fuit, & est eadem non ita nuper renovata, ut sacro lavacro non initiati ritè ex more Ecclesiæ capaces hæreditatum non sint. Clandestina nuptia etiam graviter vetita, quibus qui se implicant, quinq; marcas multam dant: at si propinqui querelas de his ad senatum deferant, exulare coguntur, quoad uterq; vivunt; altero vero mortuo alteri conceditur ius civitatis exilio amissum pecuniâ reparare. Homicidium capite, adulterium pecuniâ ex legibus plectitur, Omnibus reip. partem gerentib. interdictum stipendio extraneo; coguntur, q; munus inituri jurare, non se, non liberos suos, non coniugem, nec quenquam alium nomine suo stipendio huiusmodi autoratos esse: idemq; ante annos LXVI ad omnes omnino cives, & inquilinos, ipsosq; adeo sacerdotes extensum, poenaq; contra facienti irrogata bonorum omnium confiscatio. Servis possessiones tenere, aut habitare in urbe, extraq; urbem sub imperio senatus non licet: eorumq;, si illic moriantur, hæreditas ærario adscribitur. Hæreditatum ad exteros, qui ultra Lavicâ & Amasum, ultraq; Coverdiam Drentiæ habitant, devolutarum pars quarta ærario similiter accrescit. Reliqua prætereo, ne modum operis excedam, & quæ restant de reip. formâ in civitate expediam.
units.tr: There was also formerly, and still is, a law (not recently renewed) that those not duly initiated in the holy laver, according to the custom of the Church, are not capable of inheritances. Clandestine marriages are also strictly forbidden; those who enter into them pay a fine of five marks. But if relatives bring complaints about them before the Senate, the parties are compelled to go into exile for as long as both of them live; and when one of them has died, the other is allowed to recover the civil rights lost by exile by means of money. Homicide is punished by death, adultery by fine, according to the laws. All who take part in public affairs are forbidden to serve for foreign pay; and those about to enter office are compelled to swear that they have not, in their own name, nor their children, nor their wife, nor anyone else, been engaged for such pay. The same was extended, sixty-six years ago, to all citizens and residents without exception, and even to priests, and confiscation of all goods was imposed as the penalty on one who acted contrary. Servants may not hold property, or dwell in the city or outside the city under the authority of the Senate; and if they die there, their inheritance is assigned to the treasury. A quarter part of the inheritances that devolve upon foreigners who live beyond Lauwers and Amsum, and beyond the Coverden of Drenthe, likewise accrues to the treasury. I pass over the rest, lest I exceed the measure of my work, and will set out what remains concerning the form of the commonwealth in the city.

units.la: FORMA REIP. IN VRBE, ET MAGISTRATVVM ORDO.
units.tr: THE FORM OF THE COMMONWEALTH IN THE TOWN, AND THE ORDER OF THE MAGISTRATES.

units.la: Forma reip. in urbe ARISTOCRATICA est, modicè in democratiam declinans; quam exponere nunc animus est. Antiquitus, cum minor adhuc civitatis fortuna esset, Ra-tionales quatuor, Oldermanni VIII eam administrarunt. Nunc vero ab annis amplius trecentis CONSULES quatuor summum locum in ea tenent dignitatis. His additi olim XVI, nunc & proximis saculis XII SENATORES: qui omnes senatum conficiunt, totius reip. caput. Penes hunc senatum est jurisdictio urbana, potestasq; in rebus urbanis edicendi, decernendi vocandi, prehendendi, in custodiam dandi, coercendi, supplicia extrema irrogandi, gratia faciendi, pecuniam publicam tractandi, plerosq; magistratus alios, creandi, imprimis Hovetmannos illos, de quibus dixi saepe, praefectos item territoriorum extra urbem designandi, delectos edendi, qui in collegiis sedeant domi ac foris, quaestores, aedilem reip. aeditnos, publicanos eligendi, legationes mittendi: denique, huius officij est, toti reip. consulere, & in eam curas suas intendere. Senatorium munus bienne est, ita comparatum ut quotannis media senatus pars, (senatus vocé[?] consules quoq; comprehendo )cui duo ani in-mu-nere expleti sunt, collegio decedat; decedentium loco totidem alij numero octono succedant, col-legiumq; compleant. Quorum designatio quo-modo fiat, post exponam. In senatu consules dignitate, honore, autoritate antecedunt: suffragij vi ac jure senator consuli par, idemq; par referen-di potestate. Sed consulum nec inanis est, nec inefficax autoritas in dicendis sententijs: quorum jus est, per vices ternis mensibus eo ordine, quem-fors dat, senatui praesidere: quiq; eorum praesidet, is & sigilli publici custos est, apparitoribus aut accensus stipatur, vocationem prehensionemq; habet, plura pene solus ad senatum refert, quam-cateri in senatu omnes, senatum suffragia rogat, id quod maiori parti placet, pro sententia totius senatus pronunciat: deniq; si ingenio & industria pollet, si valet facundia, si animo non abiecto est, magnum momentum afferre reb. in omnem partem potest.
units.tr: The form of government in the town is aristocratic, leaning moderately towards democracy; I now intend to set it out. In earlier times, when the fortune of the state was still smaller, four Rationales and eight Oldermen administered it. But now, for more than three hundred years, four Consuls have held the highest place of dignity in it. To these were formerly added sixteen, and in recent centuries twelve Senators; all of these together make up the Senate, the head of the whole commonwealth. Civil jurisdiction rests with this Senate, and the power of issuing edicts in urban affairs, of decreeing, summoning, arresting, committing to custody, punishing, imposing capital penalties, granting pardons, managing public money, and appointing most of the other magistrates, especially those Hovetmannen of whom I have often spoken, likewise the prefects of the territories outside the town, and choosing and sending out delegates to sit in the colleges at home and abroad: quaestors, the aedile of the commonwealth, the aeditni, and the publicans, and sending embassies. Finally, it is the duty of this body to look after the whole commonwealth and direct its cares towards it. The senatorial office lasts two years, and is so arranged that each year half of the Senate (I include the consuls too in the term "senate") whose two years of service have been completed withdraws from the college; in place of those who withdraw, the same number of eight others succeed and fill the college. How these are designated I will explain later. In the Senate the consuls surpass the others in dignity, honour and authority; in the power of voting and in right a senator is equal to a consul, and equally has the power of proposing. But the authority of the consuls in giving opinions is neither empty nor ineffective: it is their right to preside over the Senate in turns, for three months each, in the order that chance gives; and he who presides is also the keeper of the public seal, is attended by the officers and by an accensus, has the power of summoning and arresting, and alone refers more business to the Senate than all the others in the Senate together; he calls for votes and announces to the whole Senate what the greater part favours as its opinion; and finally, if he excels in talent and industry, if he has eloquence, and if his spirit is not downcast, he is able to bring great weight to affairs in every direction.

units.la: Idem vero etiam cum tribus se-natoribus, quos vel fors vel comparatio cum colle-gis ei junxit, certo tempore in praetorio jus civib. dicit litigantibus inter se, aut iis, quibus contra cives actio est, idq; fere minores ob res, aut ad fidem solutionis pertinentes, nec nisi a meridie di-misso jam senatu.
units.tr: The same consul, however, together with three senators whom either chance or agreement with his colleagues has joined to him, at a fixed time in the praetorium declares law to citizens who are litigating with one another, or to those against whom a citizen has an action; and this mainly in minor matters, or those concerning the fulfilment of obligations, and not until the Senate has been dismissed, after noon.

units.la: In quo tribunali jurisdictio eiusmodi est, ut quam celerrime litigantes expe-diat, maxime antequam praesidis vices exeant, atq; ita fori debitorum q; fidem tueatur. Ab eo qui vult, ad senatum provocandi jus habet: a senatu provocatio ulterior non est.
units.tr: In this tribunal the jurisdiction is of such a kind that it dispatches the litigants as quickly as possible, especially before the presiding consul's term runs out, and so protects the forum of debtors and the good faith of contracts. From this tribunal anyone who wishes has the right of appeal to the Senate; from the Senate there is no further appeal.

units.la: Post senatum, ut Hovetmannos hic praeterea, de quibus est dictum jam saepius, & dicendum post rursum, collegium aliunde in civitate est virorum XXIIII ex honestissimo civium ordine, quod CONCILIVM IVRATVM vocant; propterea quod quotannis, non minus quam senatus, je solenni jurejurando obstringit reip.: & in collegio Triumviri velut collegii praesides ac rectores, qui ex eo quod nomine reliquorum verba faciunt in senatu, aut ubi res poscit, TALEMANNI sunt dicti.
units.tr: After the Senate, apart from the Hovetmannen (whom I have already mentioned several times and must mention again later), there is elsewhere in the town a college of twenty-four men drawn from the most honourable rank of citizens, which they call the SWORN COUNCIL (CONCILIVM IVRATVM); because each year, no less than the Senate, they bind themselves to the commonwealth by a solemn oath. And in this college the three Triumvirs, as it were presidents and rulers of the college, who speak in the Senate in the name of the rest, or wherever the matter requires, are called TALEMANNI.

units.la: Et horum quoq; qui in concilio hoc sunt, munus biennè est, XII quotannis decedentibus, & totidem in decedentium locum surrogatis. Munus quod sit, ex ipsa juramenti formula, qua se reip. obligant, est manifestum.
units.tr: The members of this council also hold office for two years: twelve retire each year, and the same number are substituted in place of those who retire. What their duty is is clear from the very form of the oath by which they bind themselves to the commonwealth.

units.la: Jurant autem apud consulem in senatu quotannis, vocatos in curiam, se venturos, reip. cum senatu consulturos, senatuíq; auxilio futuros, coitiones seorsim non facturos, neque factiones instituturos. Itaq; longius si tendant, & non jussi a Senatu si coeant, officij limites excede-re, & turbulentius agere putantur. Ubi autem recepit, ac in morem abiit, ut rerum graviorum, quae ad totam remp. pertinent, nihil agat senatus, aut de iis constituat, nisi ex assensu concilij hujus: Cuiusmodi sunt, bella suscipere, & finire, foedera inire, leges ferre & abrogare, munitiones novas, aut alia opera publica magni momenti instituere, in re monetaria aliquid mutare, alieno aere civitatem gravare. De quibus cum agitur, solet senatus eos, una cum iis, qui senatu proxime decesserunt, runt, quos senatum veterem vocant, in curiam accersere, & rebus diligenter deliberatis & excussis, ex eorum assensu aut dissensu de iis statuere. Hoc ad robur decretorum, & retinendam civitatis concordiam non parum profore maiorib. esse visum. Cujus rei gratia interdum etiam alios ex honestiorum civium ordine senatus convocat, ut huiusmodi deliberationibus intersint, & maxime ediles duos tribunitia potestatis, qui societatum, in quas opificum plebs est divisa, magistri & patroni sunt, easque in omnem movere partem possunt. Sed concilium hoc juratum ut consilii potestatem habet, ita imperii aut jurisdictionis partem nullam, ideoque nec accensum aut apparitorem habet. Verum aliud est ad munus concilii hujus pertinens non postremum, designare quotannis viros VIII, qui bienium in senatu sint, & reip. consilio & potestate praesint: quod jus sane amplum. Designatio autem fit hoc modo. Concilium ad VI Idus Febr. ex voluntate senatus coactum in curia coram senatu per sortem designabat olim ex suo numero viros IX, proxime autem saeculo tantummodo V, quos nunc gubernator adhuc ex pacto designat. Hi praesente senatu, consule verbis praeunte, jusiurandum dant, nil gratia, odio, invidia, cupidinis se daturos, solutisque reipub. rationem habituros: mox, digresso senatu, reliquisque e concilio, in conclavi inclusi non ante inde discedunt, quam in viros VIII liberis suffragiis lectos consenserint. Legunt autem non tam quod certa iubeat lex, quam quod more sic fit receptum, plerumq; duos, qui ex collegio Hovetmannorum, eodem forte tempore decedunt, deinde eos, qui in senatu prius fuerunt, nisi quid obstet, deniq; optimum quemq; ex honestissimo civium ordine, maximeq; ex concilio aut collegio suo, velut ex seminario Senatus. Eò facto, electos sine mora senatui in curia congregato edunt, domumq; discedunt: senatus editos per viatorem confestim in curiam vocat. Qui si electioni assentiantur, quod fere accidit, eodem momento ad praetorium deducti, ibi aperto sub cœlo circumfusi corona populi, qui excitus signo nolæ maioris, & moris huius gnarus istuc frequens concurrit, solenni juramento, præunte verbis præside consule e fenestra prætorij prospectante, stantes reip. se obligant una cum ceteris in senatu mansuris, in annum proximum: postridieq; cum iisdem collegis congregati, cumq; ys in suffragia occulta missi, consules è suo collegarumq; numero designant aut duos, si totidem loca vacant, id quod accidit ut plurimum, duob. fere quotannis è Cosulatu decedentib. aut tres, aut etiam nonnunquam quatuor, nonnunq; quoq; unum tantum. Designant autem ante alios plerumq; eos, si eorum copia sit, qui consulatu ante functi, judicesq; inter agrarios fuerunt. Sic demum die ab eo XIIII, qui Apostolo Petro sacer est, decedentibus veteribus totidem, munus suum capessunt. Quod si contingat, ut ex electis his unus plurisve delatum honorem recusent, eos reipub. multam Dare aureos x scutatos vicenos olim oportuit, nunc autem lata non multos ante annos lege aut capessere munus, aut civitate discedere oportet. Idq; cum accidit, (accidit autem raro) itemq; si qua alioqui senatorum consulumve loca seu morte, sive quacunq; ratione alia vacet, non iam Quin-quevirorum, aut jurati concilii est (quamq; olim id etiam, sed ante aliquot secula fuisse videatur) verum ipsum senatus, alios sufficere, & collegas cooptare. Octiduo deinde post quam hac senatus electio facta, coacto rursum concilio iurato, simili ratione quinq; ex ipsis alii, ut nunc mos habet (olim vero hac quoq; in re 1[?] x,) eodem in loco forte du-cuntur. Per hos xii designantur ex eo civium ordine, qui lautioris fortunæ sunt, aut dote aliquâ animi commendati, qui decedentibus è collegio totidem, biennium jam munere functis succedant, & cum iis, qui annum tantum in collegio fuerunt, reip. consulant. Tum totum collegium tres è sui medio capit, autoritate & usu rerum ceteris praestantio-res, qui collegium regant, sententiam q; eius, ubi opus est, velut oratores exponant: quos Talemanos ex eâ re appellatos dixi. Et olim quidem ante tu-multus hos civiles, ita in reb. his observatum, non lege quidem, sed more inveterato, ut in senatum nisi ex familiis nobilib. aut patriciis nemo fere le-geretur, nec temere ex iidem, nisi qui esset aut suis-set è concilio iurato tanquam senatus seminario, operamq; & fidem suam reip. minorib. in munerib. in procuratione ædium, ac aliarum rerum sacratu-rum, & similib. probassent: In concilium autem juratum similiter ex ipsdem familiis frequentes cooptarentur, quoad eius fieri posset, aut ex reliquo civium ordine honestissimo, ut quisque erat vel eruditione, vel alia aliqua prae ceteris dote conspicuus & commendatus; ex opificum autem aut institutorum collegiis aut nunquam, aut omnino rarissime quisquam caperetur. Indignum enim id concilio honoratissimo, & reip. periculosum propter abiectos huiusmodi hominum sensus praeter lucrum pene nihil spectantes, aut magni facientes putabatur. Hoc vero praetereundum hic silentio non est, non semel accidisse olim reb. sic poscentib. aut factionum vi, ut expositaratio in designandis quotanis consulib. duob. dimidiaq; senatus parte observata non sit; sed consules idem omnes vel biennium, vel ad annos complures, vel deniq; ad vitae exitum in munere ac honore permanserint: idemq; fit factum in reliquo senatu. Est praeterea aliud in civitate collegium, partem reip. curans, negociantium scil. disciplina, ac juri nautico tuendo, & dirimendis inde natis controversiis olim praefectum, cuius tribunal, Dat Gilburecht[?] lingua Teutonica ex re nominatum. Octo viris constat hodie; quorum etiam, ut senatorum, & eorum qui sunt in concilio iurato, munus est bienne, quaternis similiter quotannis collegio decedentib. ac totidem succedentib. Id hoc modo fit. Senatus ea pars, quae magistratu abit, quatuor viros eligit singulos e singulis civitatis regionibus, (haec quatuor omnino sunt) honestissimos & gravissimos quosque ex omni populo, nulla alia tum praestate publica praeditos. Hi quatuor electi totdem aliis, quibus expletum biennium est, suffecti, ceteris, qui annum tantum in munere fuere, adduntur. (Uncti hi statim ad VIII Calend. Martii ex sui medio Seniorem designant, quem OLDERMANNVM vocant, & duos fisci magistros, Bußherren dictos, fiscelli scilicet numerum curam habentes, omnes in his officiis annuos: praeter quos reliqui quinque societatis judices, Stadtrichters nuncupantur.
units.tr: They swear before the consul in the senate each year, when they have been called into the council chamber, that they will come, will deliberate on the affairs of the republic together with the senate, will be of help to the senate, will not hold meetings apart, and will not set up factions. Thus, if they go further, and assemble without being summoned by the Senate, they are thought to have overstepped the limits of their office and to be acting too turbulently. But when it has been accepted and has become customary that the senate does nothing about the more important matters that concern the whole republic, nor decides upon them, except with the assent of this council, then: such matters are these: to undertake and end wars, to enter into treaties, to pass and repeal laws, to build new fortifications or to institute other public works of great importance, to change something in the currency, to burden the city with debt. When these things are under discussion, the senate usually summons them, together with those who have most recently left the senate, whom they call the old senate, into the chamber, and, once the matters have been carefully deliberated and examined, decides upon them with their assent or dissent. This seemed to our ancestors to contribute not a little to the strength of decrees and to the preservation of the concord of the city. For this reason the senate sometimes also summons others from the order of the more honourable citizens, so that they may take part in such deliberations, and especially the two aediles of the tribunician power, who are the masters and patrons of the guilds into which the common people of the craftsmen are divided, and can move them in every direction. But this sworn council, just as it has the power of counsel, so it has no share at all of command or jurisdiction, and therefore it has neither an attendant nor a messenger. Yet there is another function of this council, not the least, which is to appoint each year eight men who are to sit in the senate for two years and preside over the counsel and power of the republic: a right indeed very ample. The appointment is made in this way. The council, convened in the chamber before the senate by the will of the senate on the sixth day before the Ides of February, once used to designate by lot nine men from its own number, but in the last century only five, whom now the governor designates by agreement. These, with the senate present, and the consul leading them with words, take an oath that they will give nothing to favour, hatred, envy or desire, and that they will render account of the public funds once it is over; then, when the senate has withdrawn and the rest of the council have left, they are shut in a room and do not leave from there until they have agreed on eight men chosen by free votes. They choose, however, not so much because a fixed law commands it, but because it has been received by custom: usually two who happen to leave the college of the Hovetmannen at the same time, then those who were previously in the senate, unless something stands in the way, and finally each of the most honourable men from the most honourable order of citizens, especially from the council or from their own college, as from a seminary of the senate. Once this is done, they bring the chosen men without delay to the senate gathered in the chamber, and go home; the senate, having been informed, at once summons the chosen men into the chamber by a messenger. If they assent to the election, which usually happens, they are at once led to the praetorium, and there, standing under the open sky, surrounded by a crowd of people, who, roused by the signal of the larger bell and knowing this custom, gather there in large numbers, they bind themselves to the republic by solemn oath, the consul leading the words from a window of the praetorium while watching, together with the others who will remain in the senate, for the following year. On the next day, gathered together with the same colleagues, and with them sent into secret voting, the consuls designate from their own number and that of their colleagues either two, if as many places are vacant, which happens most often, since usually about two leave the consulship each year, or three, or even sometimes four, or sometimes only one. They designate, however, before others, usually those, if there is a supply of them, who have held the consulship before and been judges among the agrarians. Thus at last, on the day after the fourteenth, which is sacred to the Apostle Peter, when the same number of the old ones have left, they take up their office. But if it happens that one or more of these chosen men refuse the honour offered, they once had to pay the republic a fine of ten gold scudi for each, but now, by a law passed not many years ago, they must either undertake the office or leave the city. And when this happens (it happens rarely), and likewise if any other seat of senator or consul is vacant, whether by death or any other cause, it belongs no longer to the Quinqueviri nor to the sworn council (though it seems that this was once also so, but some centuries ago) but to the senate itself, to substitute others and co-opt colleagues. Eight days after this election by the senate, the sworn council is convened again, and in a similar way five others from among them, as the custom now is (but formerly in this matter also there were ten), are by chance led to the same place. Through these twelve are designated from that order of citizens who are of more affluent fortune, or commended by some gift of mind, who, when as many have left the college, having already served two years, are to succeed, and to give counsel to the republic together with those who have been in the college only one year. Then the whole college takes three from its midst, those who are superior to the others in authority and experience, who are to govern the college and, where necessary, explain its opinion like spokesmen: whom I said were called Talemanni from that matter. And formerly, before these civil tumults, this was observed in these affairs, not indeed by law, but by inveterate custom, so that scarcely anyone was chosen into the senate except from noble or patrician families, nor was anyone from the same families chosen rashly, unless he had been, or had been, from the sworn council as from the seminary of the senate, and had approved his effort and his faith to the republic in the lesser offices, in the administration of buildings and of other sacred things, and similar. Into the sworn council, however, similarly, members were frequently co-opted from the same families, as far as that could be done, or from the rest of the most honourable order of citizens, as each was conspicuous and commended either for learning or some other gift above the rest; but from the guilds of craftsmen or of tradesmen, either never or extremely rarely was anyone taken. For that was thought unworthy of the most honoured council, and dangerous to the republic, on account of the abject feelings of such men, who look at almost nothing but gain or value it highly. But this must not be passed over here in silence: it has happened more than once in former times, when affairs so demanded or by the force of factions, that the established order of designating two consuls each year and half the senate was not observed; but the same consuls remained in office and honour either for two years, or for many years, or finally until the end of their life; and the same thing was done in the rest of the senate. Besides, there is another college in the city, caring for a part of the republic, namely, for the discipline of merchants and the protection of maritime law and the settling of controversies arising from it, once placed in charge of this, whose tribunal, from the German language, is named from the matter. It consists today of eight men; for these too, as for the senators and those in the sworn council, the office is for two years, with four likewise leaving the college each year and as many succeeding them. This is done in this way. That part of the senate which goes out of office chooses four men, one each from each region of the city (there are exactly these four), the most honourable and most serious men from the whole people, not then endowed with any other public charge. These four chosen men are added to others, equal in number, who have completed their two years, to the rest, who have been in the office only one year. These, having been anointed at once on the eighth day before the Calends of March, designate from their own midst a senior, whom they call OLDERMAN, and two masters of the treasury, called Bußherren, that is, having charge of the fiscal purse, all in these offices for a year: besides whom five others are called judges of the guild, Stadtrichters.

units.la: Senior, in collegio actor praecipuus, velut advocatus reip. in tuenda STAPVLÆ jure, de quo dixi supra, eiusque custos ac vindex, si quem contra id delinquere deprehendit, eum multam posci t, tergiversantem apud duumviros fiscales postulat, aut ad totum collegium rem defert: sententiam pronunciatam ipse exequitur, nisi reus ad superius tribunal aut senatus aut Hovetmannorum provocet.
units.tr: The Senior, the chief officer of the college, acts like the advocate of the commonwealth in defending the rights of the Staple, which I have discussed above, and is its guardian and champion. If he finds anyone breaking this rule, he demands the fine from the offender, and if the offender stalls, he brings the matter before the fiscal magistrates or refers the whole case to the college. He himself carries out the sentence once it has been pronounced, unless the accused appeals to a higher court, to the Senate, or to the Hovetmannen.

units.la: Duumviri fiscales fisci curam habent cum Oldermanno, atq; albi mercatorum: oportetq; eos, qui mercatum operam dare volunt, apud hos prius nomina sua profiteri; sine quo nemini id facere licet. Et sunt idem ὑπευθυνοι , id est, reddendis apud Consulem rationibus obnoxij quotannis cum eodem Oldermanno: quibus expeditis, successoribus fiscellum tradunt, pecuniae reliquum ara-rio reip. inferunt.
units.tr: The fiscal magistrates share the care of the treasury with the Oldermann and the white merchants. Those who wish to trade must first register their names with them; no one may do so without this. They are also the ὑπευθυνοι, that is, they are bound to give account to the Consul each year, together with the same Oldermann. Once this is done, they hand over the purse to their successors and pay the remaining money into the public treasury.

units.la: Sed est collegij huius cura antiquitus commissa praecipuè custodia totaj uris nautici, in codice reipub. diligenter descripti, jurisdictioq; universa ad res navales & maritimas pertinens.
units.tr: But the chief concern of this college, entrusted to it from ancient times, is the custody of the whole law of the sea, carefully set down in the city's code, and the entire jurisdiction relating to naval and maritime affairs.

units.la: Verum collegium hoc ipsum collegarum quoq; numero olim duplo fuit maius, (xiii enim prætor Oldermannum & duumviros fisci curatores fuere) & electionis ratio ab eâ, qui hîc exposita, diversa. Nunc cum numero potestas quoq; nonnihil arctata. Electio olim sic habuit. Senatus pars munere decedens è sui medio sortitò edebat quatuor: hi cum Oldermanno & duobus fiscelli magistris eodem die viros xvi eligebant optimos quosq; secundum urbis regiones, quorum nullus eo anno in senatu esset, aut senatu decessisset.
units.tr: This college was once twice as large in number of members, for there were thirteen praetors, the Oldermann and the two fiscal overseers. The method of election also differed from the one described here. Now that the number has been reduced, its power has also been somewhat curtailed. Formerly the election went as follows. The part of the Senate that was giving up its office drew lots and chose four of its own number. These four, together with the Oldermann and the two fiscal magistrates, on the same day elected sixteen of the best men, chosen by the city districts, none of whom was in the Senate that year or had left the Senate.

units.la: Electi xvi viri ex suo numero Oldermannum statim designabant, hac lege, ut per vices ex urbis regionibus aliis post alias designaretur in singulos annos; habebaturq; ea ratio propinquitatis, quae in senatu eligendo solet haberi. Cetera similia his, quæ jam dixi.
