Deinde prae-ter hos alij quoq; sunt Octoviri, regionum urbis magistri, bini ex singulis regionibus delecti, honore & autoritate non postremi; bis quotannis censum agunt omnium civium, & quid quisq; eorum gerat, quæ negocia tractet, quibus se suosq; tueatur, inquirunt, desides aut noxios reipub. cedere cogunt: ne quis aedificans publicè privatimve noceat, aut bono officiat, ne quid vitij canalibus ad deducendas aquas ac sordes per urbem accidat, quaeq; alia ad mundiciem urbis pertinent, providentq;: denique, si diligentes sunt, perutilem operam reip. præstant.
units.tr: The sixteen elected men at once designated an Oldermann from among themselves, under this rule: that he should be chosen in turn from the city districts, one after another, year by year; and the consideration of kinship that is usually observed in electing senators was also observed. The rest was similar to what I have already said. Besides these there are also the Octoviri, the magistrates of the city districts, two chosen from each district, men of no little honour and authority. Twice a year they take a census of all citizens, inquire into what each one does, what business he conducts, and by what means he supports himself and his family, and they compel the idle and harmful to leave the commonwealth. They provide against anyone building in a way that harms the public or private interest or prejudices the common good, and against any defect in the drains that carry water and filth through the city, and against whatever else pertains to the cleanliness of the city. In short, if they are diligent, they render a most useful service to the commonwealth.

units.la: Quinetiam scloppetariorum praefecti quatuor diu in civitate fuere, à senatu quoq; designati, perperpetui. Hi curam armorum habebant, juven-tutemq; maxime exercebant, in tractandis scloppetis, foro venalis annona, quae ad urbem defertur quotidie, praerant: à piscatoribus & ijs, qui cerevisiam coquunt, ne quid fraudis committeretur, ut justa esset ponderum & mensurarum ratio in officinis, carnum ut publicis locis amoveretur, procurabant. Quae omnia nunc ad centurio-nes oppidanos octo, qui iis successere, translata sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, four prefects of the musketeers were long in the city, likewise designated by the Senate, and perpetual. They had charge of the arms and chiefly trained the young men in handling muskets. They oversaw the market for provisions that are brought into the city daily, and they took care that fishmongers and brewers committed no fraud, that the system of weights and measures in the workshops was just, and that meat was removed from public places. All these duties have now been transferred to the eight town centurions, who succeeded them.

units.la: Deniq; ÆDILES duo in rep. sunt TRIB. POTEST. quam non lege datam, sed paulatim nitendo longius turbulentis actionibus quaesitam proximis saeculis usurparunt non magno sane reip. bono. Horum magnum esse nomen solet. Et quoniam cum plebe opificum & institorum connexi sunt, ac ab ea dependent, de plebis huius ordine & distinctione pauca hic dicam. Dividitur ipsa secundum artificiorum aut rerum, quas tractant, genera diversa in societates xviii[?]: exceptis, qui cerevisia coquenda officinas exercent, ac negocia maiora in emendo & vendendo gerunt. Dignioris quippe ordinis miscere se vilioribus nolunt, habenturq; post nobilitatem inter honestissimos totius civitatis. Hae[?] societates singulae ternos sibi praefectos suffragiis designatos creant quotannis mox à Paschatos: & in his primum quemq; SENIOREM vel Oldermannum, velut totius societatis praesidem, reliquos binos capita societatis dicunt: omnes universum numero LIIII. Et hi vicissim circiter idem tempus mox ab electione sui in coenobio Iacobaeo congregati, ÆDILES, quos dixi, edunt, non[?] aliunde quam ex his ipsis societatib. Quamquam fuit quondam tempus, quo duob. istis ter-tius quoq; è Senatu adiungebatur; qui dudum nunc collegio defluxit. Æt ÆDILES patronos se plebis professi, quam & suopte ingenio, & per præfectos in omnem facile impellere partem poterant, haud dissimiles veterib. in rep. Rom, tribunis, ab humili initio eo tandem progressi sunt, dum curam patrocinium q; egena & circumventa præsunt[?] plebecula, multitudine freti, ut in morem abierint[?], nulla recipere de maiore re decreta, quib. assensum hi ipsi ædiles non adhibuissent. Itaq; quoties huiusmodi aliquid actum, cum concilio iurato & cæteris isti quoq; in curiam sunt vocati. Qui si, cæteris accedentib. sententia senatus, vel soli dissensissent, levantes se ultimis subsellis[?] intercedebant: vetabantq; senatum & reliquos progredi, ac decernere aliquid, priusquam ad societatum plebeiarum præfectos, vel ad ipsas integras societates, si ita præfectis videretur, res esset relata.
units.tr: Finally, there are two Aediles in the commonwealth, the tribunes of the people, a power which was not granted by law but which, by gradually pressing forward through turbulent actions, they seized in the nearer centuries, not at all to the great good of the commonwealth. Their name is usually held in great esteem. And since they are connected with the common people of craftsmen and tradesmen and depend upon them, I shall say a few things here about the order and division of this commoner class. It is divided, according to the kinds of crafts or of the goods they handle, into eighteen [?] guilds, excepting those who run the brewing houses and carry on larger dealings in buying and selling. For men of higher rank are unwilling to mix with the lowlier sort, and they are counted, after the nobility, among the most honourable of the whole city. Each of these guilds creates, each year just after Easter, three prefects designated by vote for itself: the first of them is called the Senior or Oldermann, as the president of the whole guild, and the other two are called heads of the guild. In all they number fifty-four. And these in turn, about the same time after their election, gather in the Jacobean monastery and elect the aediles I have mentioned, not from anywhere else but from these very guilds. Although there was once a time when a third man from the Senate was added to these two, a practice which has long since lapsed from the college. The aediles, professing themselves patrons of the commons, whom they could easily drive in any direction by their own disposition and through the prefects, were not unlike the tribunes of the Roman commonwealth of old. From a humble beginning they at last advanced so far that, taking charge of the protection of a needy and easily imposed-upon little crowd, relying on their numbers, they came to the point of not allowing any decrees on a major matter to be accepted unless the aediles themselves had given their assent. And so, whenever anything of this kind was proposed, they too were summoned to the council chamber along with the sworn council and the others. If they, when the others agreed with the opinion of the Senate, or if they alone dissented, rising to the lowest benches, they interposed their veto, and forbade the Senate and the rest to proceed to decide anything until the matter had been referred to the prefects of the commoners' guilds, or, if the prefects thought fit, to the guilds themselves entire.

units.la: Sic convocatis primum præfectis, qui erant, ut dixi, numero omnes LIIII, in conclavi apud Iacobæos res in medium proponebatur. Ea si difficilior videretur, societates tota certis adesse locis iubebantur, & seorsim consulebantur a suis quaq; præfectis. Earum sententia, quam plerumq; præfecti dictabant[?], ad ædiles, ab ædilib. ad senatum & concilium iuratum relatâ, de negocio ac repub. statuebatur. Ita fiebat, ut optima quaq; consilia, ac reip. profutura plerumq; corrumperentur, impedirentur. Nam ædiles cum præfectis hisce ex opificum officinis, infimaq; plebe prorepentes, ac vilibus rebus innutriti resp. bene gerenda fere ignari sunt, improvidi, & supra ea, quae ante pedes sunt, nihil sapientes, gratiaq; insciti multitudinis dediti.
units.tr: So, when the prefects had first been summoned, who were, as I said, fifty-four in all, the matter was laid before them in the chamber at the Jacobean house. If it seemed too difficult, the guilds were ordered to be present in their entirety at fixed places, and each was consulted separately by its own prefects. Their opinion, which the prefects for the most part dictated, was carried to the aediles, from the aediles to the Senate and the sworn council, and a decision was made on the business and the commonwealth. Thus it happened that the best counsels, which would most often have profited the commonwealth, were corrupted and hindered. For the aediles together with the prefects, who have crept forth from the workshops of craftsmen and the lowest commons, and having been reared on mean things, are for the most part ignorant of how to conduct the commonwealth well, shortsighted, wise in nothing beyond what lies under their feet, and inexperienced in grace, devoted to the favour of the crowd.

units.la: Quo nomine, id quod plerumq; tum fiebat, si se plebi probassent, complures etiam annos suo in munere continuabantur.
units.tr: For this reason, when this was most often the case, if they had approved themselves to the common people, they were kept in their office for several years.

units.la: A[?]senatu tamen, ut cateri omnes, qui aliquid publici muneris aut potestatis habent, sic hi quoq; aediles, suum jus & olim accepere, & hodie etiam accipiunt, cum sacramentum apud eum dicunt quotanis: Suntq; ea, quae exorbitarunt in hac re, salubriter iam correcta, & ad metam revocata.
units.tr: Yet, like all the others who hold any public office or power, these aediles too have received their right from the Senate, both formerly and even today, when they take the oath before it each year. And those things in this matter that had gone beyond bounds have now been wholesomely corrected and brought back to the limit.

units.la: Porro de societatibus his pl. ita in legibus civitatis perscriptum est, non li-cere ipsis inconsulto, aut non probante senatu statuta sibi condere, aut foedera facere: praefectos vero earum teneri, vocante senatu, in curia sistere, instrumenta statutorum & privilegiorum suorum senatui exhibere, profiterique juratos, praeter ea nihil se statutorum aut scitorum in societatibus suis habere: praeterea, si quae societas civitati inutilis aut noxia videatur, in potestate senatus esse, eam abrogare: item, si quis in societate quid committat, quo se indignum societate fecisse videatur, deq; eo controversia existat, eius cognitionem senatui deberi cum tribus societatis praefectis: ad hac, societates cum praefectis suis teneri, summa ope, summis viribus ut tueantur dignitatem & jus senatus, eique auxilio & firmamento sint, ac poenas contumacium, cum res requirit, promo-veant. Habent tamen societatum praefecti in suâ quique societate potestatem cognoscendi controversias quasdam ad societatem pertinentes, easque definiendi, ac multas quoque capiendi ab his, qui contra societatis leges deliquisse deprehenduntur. Sed id totum sic habet, ut iurisdictionis species aut pars videri nequeat. Et si quis in eo laedi se iniuste a praefectis existimet, is pro more aedilis, tanquam summos magistros atque ἐπόπους, appellat, ab his porro, si placet, ad ipsum quoque senatum provocat.
units.tr: Moreover, concerning these guilds, the laws of the city have set down in writing that they may not make statutes for themselves or enter into agreements without the consultation of, or the approval of, the Senate; and their prefects are bound, when the Senate summons them, to appear in the council chamber, to show the Senate the documents of their statutes and privileges, and to declare under oath that they have no statutes or decrees in their guilds other than these. Furthermore, if any guild seems useless or harmful to the city, it is in the power of the Senate to abolish it; likewise, if anyone in a guild commits anything by which he seems to have made himself unworthy of the guild, and a dispute arises about it, the hearing of it belongs to the Senate together with three of the guild's prefects. Besides, the guilds with their prefects are bound to defend, with all their effort and all their strength, the dignity and right of the Senate, to be its aid and support, and, when the matter requires, to press the penalties upon the obstinate. Nevertheless, each guild's prefects have, within their own guild, the power to hear certain disputes relating to the guild, to settle them, and also to impose fines on those who are caught breaking the guild's rules. But all this is so arranged that it cannot be seen as a kind of jurisdiction or part of one. And if anyone thinks he has been unjustly wronged in this by the prefects, he appeals, in the customary manner, to the aediles, as to the highest magistrates and ἐπόπους, and from them, if he wishes, to the Senate itself.

units.la: Postremo societatum praefecti terni iurati, ut est in iisdem civitatis legibus, rationes accepti & expensi reddunt aedilibus; Aediles pecuniam impendunt aedificijs & structuris publicis, unde nomen ijs datum, ac vicissim accepti & impensi calculum ponunt apud eosdem hos praefectos, adeoque apud consules, si vel hi vel illi hoc requirant. Est vero etiam perhonesta in civitate procuratio aedituorum, qui sacras aedes, & quae istuc pertinent, tuentur, bonaque in eum usum a maioribus collata administrant: delecti fere ex patritia nobilitate, & bini aut terni in singulis parochijs: eaque procuratio si senatorijs hominibus commendata non est, viam saltem procuratoribus ad honorem atque ordinem eum sternit. Et cum his pari pene passu incedunt, provisores quos vocant, aut curatores ptochodocheiorum, quae quatuor esse in urbe dixi, maxime eius, quod est ad S. Spiritum, & alteri ad S. Gertrudem, propter magnitudinem, & possessiones ac reditus eorum pcramplos[?]. Ad quā administratione senatorij quoq; ordinis viri sepe vocantur, alijq; qui lautissimæ conditionis inter cives sunt. Nec prætereundi hic, qui ædib. præ-secti sunt, quas FRATRVM vulgo vocant, in quib. adolescentes literarum & pietatis studio dediti alij gratis, alij precio modico, pro cuiusq; fortuna ac loco aluntur & habentur honestè, ijsq; omnibus morum & studiorum inspector atq; exactor præest: quorum præfectorum ratio quoq; par cum prioribus. Et sunt hæ curationes omnes, quas recensui, non annuæ, nec determinati temporis, sed in arbitrio consulum, deq; his rationes apud eosdem reddantur consules, quoties & cum placet id ipsis. Quid de SCHOLARCHIS dicam? quibus Scholæ & totius rei Scholasticæ & literariæ cura, pecuniaq; in hunc usum destinata quæstura, denique omnium huc pertinentium copia à senatu demandata est: quorum alter consularis, alter senator, aut ordinis senatorij habitus fuit. Quid de reip. QVÆS ORE? qui pecuniæ, ac omnium redituum eius conquisitor & custos est, acceptiq; & expensi indices servat, atq; ex his rationes senatui debet. Quid de Trium-viris vectigalium, portoriorum, accisarum, uti vocant, magistris, ad forum & curiam loco idonea negocio huic & muneri suo vacantibus? Quid de iis, qui pecuniam sacerdotiis olim legatam, solvende ministris Ecclesiæ stipendio, & sartis tectis tenendis eorum domicilijs colligunt, & expendut[?]? Quid de orphanotrophej curatorib. & cleemosy- narijs pauperum domi sedentium alimonia præpo-sitis? qui omnes ex honestissimis civium ordinib. a senatu leguntur, in tempus incertum, ab eius arbitrio pendent. Adde ante hos nominan- dum honoris causa juris consultum, quem SYNDICVM dicunt, liberali resp. stipendio ornatum, summaque præditum dignitate; qui & a consilio est senatui, & eiusdem orator, adeoque universæ civitatis advocatus: quem locum amplissimus & consultissimus, clarissimusque vir, amicus mihi singularis, PANCRATIVS CASTRICOMIVS I. V. D. nunc, dum hæc cuduntur, tenet. Adde & summum SCRIBAM, qui eidem senatui est a secretis, & epistolis, scribendisque, & custodiendis decretis, & publicis chartis: cuius munus perhonestum & quæstuosum. Et ad hos armamen- tarii publici, id est, tormentorum æneorum, pulveris nitrosi, & omnis instrumenti ac apparatus huc pertinentis, fabrum quoque & fabricarum publicarum, itemque vigilum præfectos, manipulorumque magistros. Et hi quidem omnes, quos recensui, rem urbanam curant, e quib. alii vere reip. alii senatus ministri sunt. Præter hos vero collegium in urbe est juris dicundi causa antiquitus institutum, & sæpius iam ante nobis in hoc libro memoratum, perampla præditum potestate ac honore, quod HOVETMANNORVM CAMERAM vulgo indigetant. Id autem quamquam non in cives, sed in eos, qui vicinum agrum fœdere quondam civitati junctum inhabitant, jurisdictionem directam habet, tamen non abs re hoc loco potissimum recensee. Nec .n. solum in urbe semper, nec usquam alibi sedem tenet, & jus dicit, sed etiam prater cives opibus & dignitate praecipuos, & in his haud temere alios quam consulatu functos, collegas non admittit: nec ulli praeter senatum edendorum collegarum potestatem habent, nec aliunde quam ab eodem senatu expectare & accipere stipendia antiquitus ante dimissam integram libertatem collegae solent. Quo de collegio quamquam multa sparsim hoc libro dicta sint, tamen ut res manifestior fiat, paulo altius hic quoque quaedam repetenda. Et primum, quae prima collegii huius, aut Hovetmannorum origo, quod principium, dicere non possum. Nec enim id literis proditum usquam, quod sciam. Primos vero in monumentis reipub. mihi lectos Hovetmannos Kenoniansis temporibus, post annum millesimum quadringentesimum a natali Domini Servatoris nostri, superius ostendi, eosque tum tributis & tractanda pecunia per agrum praefuisse memoravi. De his porro, vestigiis monumentorum veterum insistens, & omnia expendens diligenter, sic reperi, cum concors cum ordinibus agri vicini civitas ageret, ac foedera in certos annos percussa identidem prorogaret, prope ut una utrorumque respub. videretur, ex consensu sociorum eos profluxisse, rectius atque aequalius expediendi iuris, & tenenda concordia, confervandaq; quietis publica causa : electos esse ex spectatissimis & inte-gerrimis quibusq; in civitate, interdum etiam ex iys, qui e nobilitate agraria in urbem commigrarant, & jus civitatis acquisiverant: quinos & quinos in collegio fuisse per annos am-plius LX, eosq; incerta ratione, prout operam suam probassent, aut grati reipub. essent, aut casus daret, vel permutatos successoribus, vel per annos complures, quod erat frequens, con-tinuatos : praetoriam potestatem tenuisse in omnes per agrum habitantes, eaq; usos to-tius provincia, id est, agri & civitatis no-mine, edictisq; nomen senatus cum nomine suo subscripsisse, & civitatis sigillo edicta & literas signasse : jus dixisse iis, qui fraudem sibi fieri apud reliquos per agrum judices, ali-ove modo suum se consequi non posse quere-bantur, exceptis successionum casibus, quarum cognitio pervetusto more conventui juridicali, de quo ante dixi, relinquebatur : Et tamen de his quoq; casibus appellatos fuisse, decre-tumq; suum, vsq; in conventus tempus in-terpusisse[?] : deinde huic etiam conventui aut solos, aut cum senatu civitatis interfuisse, immo praesedisse, aut saltem non ultimas in ea partes tenuisse : a sententiis decre-tisq; eorum, nisi ex partium consensu, pro-vocationem non fuisse : imprimis vero ope-ram dedisse, & auxilio fuisse iis, qui crediti debitiue aliquem eorum, qui in agrê habebant, sedes, cuiuscunq; is ordinis esset, possu-labant: nec declinare cuiquam cognitionem, nec lata sententia tergiversari licuisse: ita celerrime ius fuisse expeditum, & suum cuiq; tributum: multosq; adeo contractus tum paulatim eam conditionem habere coepisse, ut non alios apud iudices, quam hos, si quid controversia forte incideret, aut in solvendo mora existeret, causa ageretur: id institutum cum alias ob res, tum ob fidem contractuum & commerciorum tuendam salutare communi reip. visum, probatumq; in morem ivisse, atq; ita vim legis tenuisse.
units.tr: Finally, the prefects of the guilds, three sworn men, as the same laws of the city provide, render their accounts of receipts and expenditures to the aediles. The aediles spend money on public buildings and structures, from which they take their name, and in turn they lay their reckoning of receipts and expenditures before these same prefects, and so before the consuls, if either these or those require it. There is also, in the city, a most honourable office of the sextons, who look after the sacred buildings and what pertains to them, and administer the goods contributed to that purpose by their ancestors. They are chosen generally from the patrician nobility, two or three in each parish; and although this office is not entrusted to men of the senatorial order, it at least opens the way for its holders to honour and rank of that kind. Almost on the same footing go the men called providers, or curators of the almshouses, of which I said there are four in the city: the chief of these is the one at the Holy Spirit, and another at St Gertrude, on account of their size and their very large possessions and revenues. Men of senatorial rank are often called to this administration, as well as others who are among the citizens of the most distinguished standing. Nor should I pass over here those who are set over the houses which the people commonly call "of the brothers," in which young men devoted to the study of letters and piety are maintained and kept respectably, some free of charge and others for a modest fee, according to each one's means and station; and over all of them presides an inspector and overseer of morals and studies. The accounts of these prefects are likewise on the same footing as the former ones. All these offices I have listed are not annual, nor for a fixed term, but at the discretion of the consuls, and accounts of them are rendered to these same consuls as often and whenever they see fit. What shall I say of the scholarchs, to whom the care of the schools and of everything scholastic and literary, together with the money set aside for this use, the quaestorship, and finally the whole supply of all matters pertaining to these, has been committed by the Senate? One of them has been regarded as a consular, the other as a senator or of senatorial rank. What of the city treasurer, the collector and keeper of all the money and revenues of the state, who keeps the records of receipts and expenditures and owes accounts from these to the Senate? What of the three magistrates for taxes, customs and excises, as they are called, who are assigned to the forum and the council chamber, places suited to this business and their office? What of those who collect and disburse the money once bequeathed to the priesthood for paying the stipends of the ministers of the Church and for keeping the buildings in good repair and maintaining their dwellings? What of the curators of the orphanage and the almoners placed over the feeding of the poor who live at home? All of these are chosen by the Senate from the most honourable orders of citizens, for an uncertain term, and depend on its discretion. Add before these, to be named out of respect, the jurist whom they call the syndic, honoured with a salaried office and endowed with the highest dignity; he is both an adviser to the Senate and its spokesman, and so the advocate of the whole city. This post is now held, while these things are being printed, by the most distinguished and learned and renowned man, my singular friend, Pancratius Castricomius, doctor of both laws. Add also the chief clerk, who serves the same Senate as secretary, handling its letters and correspondence, and keeping its decrees and public papers; his office is very honourable and profitable. And to these add the keepers of the public arsenal, that is, of the bronze artillery, the saltpetre powder, and all the equipment and apparatus pertaining to it, also the smiths and public workshops, likewise the prefects of the night watch and the commanders of the companies. Now all these I have listed take care of the city's affairs, and some of them are truly officers of the commonwealth, others servants of the Senate. Besides these, however, there is in the city a college, established long ago for the purpose of administering justice, and mentioned several times already earlier in this book, endowed with very great power and honour, which they commonly call the Chamber of the Hovetmen. Although it has direct jurisdiction not over the citizens but over those who live in the neighbouring countryside, which was once joined to the city by treaty, still it is not inappropriate to list it here, and especially here. For it not only always keeps its seat in the city and nowhere else and pronounces judgment there, but it also does not admit as colleagues anyone other than those among the citizens who are outstanding in wealth and dignity, and among these, rarely anyone but men who have held the consulship. Nor do they have the power of appointing colleagues except the Senate, and in ancient times, before the complete liberty was lost, they were accustomed to expect and receive their salaries from that same Senate and from no other source. Although many things about this college have been said here and there in this book, nevertheless, so that the matter may be clearer, some things must be gone over here again, a little more deeply. And first, I cannot say what was the first origin of this college or of the Hovetmen, or what their beginning was. For, as far as I know, this is handed down in no record anywhere. But I have shown earlier that the earliest Hovetmen I have read of in the records of the commonwealth belong to the times of Kenonia, after the year one thousand four hundred from the birth of our Lord and Saviour, and I have recorded that at that time they presided over taxes and the handling of money throughout the countryside. Following the traces of the old records about these men, and weighing all things carefully, I have found this: when the city, living in harmony with the orders of the neighbouring countryside, and repeatedly renewing treaties struck for fixed years, came to seem almost as one commonwealth for both, the college arose by common consent of the allies, for the sake of administering justice more correctly and evenly, keeping concord, and preserving public peace. Its members were chosen from the most respected and upright men in the city, sometimes also from those who had migrated into the city from the rural nobility and had acquired the rights of citizenship. There were five and five in the college for more than sixty years, and they held office for an uncertain period, according as they had proved their service or were pleasing to the commonwealth, or as chance gave; they were either replaced by successors, or, which was common, continued for several years. They held praetorian power over all who lived in the countryside, and used it in the name of the whole province, that is, of the countryside and the city, and under the decrees they subscribed the name of the Senate with their own, and they sealed the edicts and letters with the seal of the city. They gave judgment to those who complained that a fraud was being done to them before the other judges of the countryside, or that they could not otherwise obtain their due, except in cases of succession, which by very ancient custom were left to the judicial assembly I mentioned before. Yet even in these cases appeals were made to them, and they interposed their own decree, even up to the time of the assembly. Then either they alone, or together with the civic Senate, were present at this assembly, indeed presided over it, or at least did not hold the last place in it. There was no appeal from their sentences and decrees unless by consent of the parties. Above all they took pains and gave help to those who were owed money or owed it to any of those who had their seats in the countryside, of whatever order he might be: no one could decline their jurisdiction, nor evade a judgment once pronounced. Thus justice was dispatched very quickly, and each was given his due. And so many contracts then gradually came to be of such a kind that suits were brought before no judges other than these, if any dispute arose or there was delay in payment. This institution, found wholesome for the common welfare of the commonwealth both for other reasons and for protecting the good faith of contracts and dealings, came to be approved as custom, and so held the force of law.

units.la: ¶Ad hac animadverti, eosdem, qui Hovetmanni erant, simul eodemq; tempore consules quoq; aut senatores reip. urbana fuisse, rationes eidem reip. eiusve senatui reddidisse, edicendi mandandiq; ius ac potestatem non solum apud Cislavicanos, sed etiam trans Lavicam habuisse: quod argumento irrefragabili est, nō ab agrarijs ordinib. vicinis eos electos fuisse, nec ab ijs pepedisse, delegatave ab ipsa potestate tenuisse, sed a sola civitate: nec enim ideo hos a Translavicanis munus accepisse, aut in eorum fide fuisse, legimus aut credimus, quod apud eos edicendi judicandiq; potestatem ex foedere tenuere; nec vero congruum est, eorum se potestati & judicio Translavicanos subjicere voluisse, quos Cislavicanis ordinibus agrarijs obligatos esse, & ab illis leges accipere noßent, quippe qui non cum his ipsis, sed cum civitate foedus percuterent.
units.tr: Furthermore, I have noticed that those who were Hovetmanni were at the same time also consuls or senators of the city government, and rendered accounts to that same government or its senate. They held the right and power of issuing edicts and giving orders not only among the Cisla­vicans, but also beyond the Lavica. This is an irrefutable proof that they were not chosen by the rural orders nearby, nor did they receive their office from them or hold their power delegated by them, but from the city alone. For we do not read or believe that the Translavicans received these men as their magistrates or placed themselves under their trust because they held the power of issuing edicts and judging among them by treaty. Nor is it fitting that the Translavicans would have wished to submit themselves to the power and judgment of men whom they knew to be bound to the rural orders on the Cisla­vican side and to take their laws from them, since they made their treaty not with these men but with the city.

units.la: Inveni etiam hoc collegium colligendis in agro tribu[?] ributis, si quando tributis opus, præfuisse, eamq; pecuniam tractasse, aggerum, viarum, aquæductuum curam habuisse, judices agrarios ad faciendum officium compulisse, exorbitantesq; eosdem compressisse, ad conventus ordines convocasse, denique velut ad clavum reip. sedentes, quietis & εὐταξίας custodes in tota provincia fuisse. Et hæc ad Saxonum usq; tempora. Ii partim sua sponte, partim stimulantib. nonnullis, qui ferre imperium non poterant, hac potestate spoliare civitatem conati sunt. EDSARDVS jus hoc in arbitrium redegit: quippe sui arbitrij electionem Hovetmannorum ex civium numero fecit, & jurisdictionem angustioribus terminis clausit. GELDRVS electionem senatui reddidit, & jurisdictionem restituit solitam, sed quatuor Hovetmannis a senatu lectis ex suis addidit quintum, qui præses collegii esset, ac legatus ipsius, atq; hi omnes ipsius quo nomine, atq; ipsius mandato jus dicerent. Nec quicquam CAROLVS CÆSAR, aut filius eius PHILIPPVS mutarunt, eoq; modo res ad hæc postrema tempora pervenit. Tum lis de toto fœdere, totaq; hac cum civitate conjunctione mota. Eam refusitatam nuper ORDINES GENERALES eo, quo exposui, modo definierunt.
units.tr: I have also found that this college was in charge of collecting the taxes in the countryside, whenever there was need of taxes, and handled that money; it had the care of dykes, roads and aqueducts; it compelled the rural judges to perform their duty and restrained those who overstepped; it summoned the orders to assemblies; and finally, sitting as it were at the helm of the commonwealth, it was the guardian of quiet and good order throughout the whole province. And this continued down to the time of the Saxons. Some of these men, partly of their own accord and partly urged on by others who could not bear to be ruled, tried to strip the city of this power. Edsardus reduced this right to his own discretion: indeed, he made the choice of his own discretion of the Hovetmanni from the number of the citizens, and he confined their jurisdiction within narrower limits. Geldrus returned the election to the senate and restored the jurisdiction to its customary state, but he added a fifth man of his own to the four Hovetmanni chosen by the senate, to be president of the college and his own deputy; and all of these were to give judgment in his name and by his mandate. Nor did Charles the Emperor, or his son Philip, change anything, and in this way the matter came down to these latest times. Then a dispute arose concerning the whole treaty and the whole union with this city. The General Orders recently settled this controversy, which had been stirred up again, in the manner I have described.

units.la: Sed aliud quoq; imperium in agro civitas habet haud spernendum. Id duas ampliatur præfecturas maiores, eam quam VETEREM nomi-nant, & SVBVRBANAM: quarum illa vicos egregios XVII, hac XII tantum, nec prioribus pares habet: & in his cænobia quoq; v. Utriq; a senatu præfectus datur, mutaturq; pro arbitrio. Præfectus prioris fere consularis, ac genere nobili natus, alterum etiam haud temere alius, quam senatorium. Atq; ille quidem cum judice, ex indigenis plerisq; et addito, jus dicit, cateraq; imperij peragit senatus nomine, sed nō aliter, qua secundū leges & morem patrium, à quo recedere non licet.
units.tr: But the city also has another jurisdiction in the countryside, not to be despised. It is extended over two greater prefectures, that which they call the Old and the Suburban; of these the former has seventeen notable villages, the latter only twelve, and it does not equal the former; and in these there are also five monasteries. A prefect is appointed to each of them by the senate, and is changed at its discretion. The prefect of the former is generally a former consul, born of a noble family; the other is not lightly chosen from any but the senatorial order. Indeed, the former, together with a judge chosen mostly from the natives, and with an assessor added, gives judgment and carries out the rest of his office in the name of the senate, but not otherwise than according to the laws and ancestral custom, from which it is not lawful to depart.

units.la: Ex hoc more præfectura in territoria distinguitur quinq;, quorum quodlibet tribunal suum habet, in quo præfectus vicissim certis temporib. jus dicit de criminibus, rebus soli, ædificijs, ac similibus momenti maioris: nec licet præfecto, cum de his agitur, quemquam extra territorium suum evocare: in cateris, ut crediti debitiq;, negocijs maximè licet. Nec fas est, nisi in territorio suo, in quo quis vel sedem habet, vel in maleficio prehensus est, maleficum supplicio afficere, aut custodia mandare. Et usus recepit, ut præfecto iis dicenti assideant aliquot, qui in plebe territorij eminent, honoris causa: utq; Wedmannus (judicij minister) in unoquoq; territorio sit, isq; & minora quædam, quæ judicum solent esse, pro judice agat, & custodia præsit, prehendendiq; pote-statem habeat. Territoria hæc sunt: Muntense, Midwoldicum, Finserwoldicum, Brocaum, Wynscotanum. Alter in præfectura suburbana jus dicit hoc modo. Habet Octo-viros[?] præfectura, optimos quosq; & maxime idoneos è plebe: quorum quatuor singulis biennijs mu-nere decedunt, & totidem alij ab ijs, qui in munere manent, collegæ adsciscuntur: semel adscitis[?] quadriennium in munere continuant, munusq; jurati gerunt: jurant secundum morem & leges patrias incorrupte se, judicaturos.
units.tr: From this custom the Old prefecture is divided into five districts, each of which has its own tribunal, where the prefect in turn, at fixed times, gives judgment on crimes, real estate, buildings and similar matters of greater weight; and when such matters are under consideration, the prefect may not summon anyone from outside his district; in other business, such as debts and credits, he is allowed most freely to do so. Nor is it lawful, except within his own district, where a person either has his home or has been caught in a crime, to punish a malefactor with punishment or to commit him to custody. And custom has established that several men eminent among the common people of the district sit beside the prefect while he judges, for the sake of honour; and that a Wedmann (an officer of justice) is in each district, who acts as judge in certain lesser matters, which are usually for judges, presides over custody, and has the power of arrest. These districts are: Muntense, Midwoldicum, Finserwoldicum, Brocaum, Wynscotanum. The other, in the Suburban prefecture, gives judgment in this manner. The prefecture has eight men, the best and most suitable of all from the common people: of these, four leave office every two years, and as many others are added as colleagues by those who remain in office; once added, they continue in office for four years and perform their duty under oath: they swear that they will judge incorruptly according to the custom and ancestral laws.

units.la: Ad hac forte è numero suo Octoviri ducunt duos, qui minorib. causis expediundis omnib. dieb.Ven. & Saturni Groninga (hæc tribunalis huius sedes est) præfecto assideant in trimestre[?], & cum eo jus dicant, idq; vicissim, donec circumactus sit totus annus.
units.tr: Moreover, from among their number, two of the eight men are chosen, who on Wednesdays and Saturdays at Groningen (this is the seat of this tribunal) sit with the prefect to dispatch the lesser cases, for a quarter of a year, and give judgment with him, alternating in turn until the whole year has run its course.

units.la: Reliqui cum assessoribus his, & cum præfecto ter stato tempore singulis annis, aut quoties res poscit, graviores controversias soli ac similes cognoscunt & judicant, simulq; si qua de re minore ad hunc eorum confessum provocatum sit à præfecti duum-virumq; sententia, eam quoq; definiunt.
units.tr: The rest, with these assessors and with the prefect, at three fixed times each year, or as often as the matter requires, examine and judge the more serious disputes concerning land and the like; and at the same time, if any matter of lesser importance is referred to this their assembly from the judgment of the prefect and the two men, they also settle it.

units.la: Ab eo vero, quod ab his præside præfecto definitum est, quemadmodum & à prioris præfecti sententiis ac decretis in præfectura vetere, ad SE-NATVM urbanum provocatio est, si quis eâ uti velit. In senatus sententiâ litium finis est.
units.tr: Appeal lies from what has been settled by this president, the prefect, just as from the judgments and decrees of the former prefect in the Old prefecture, to the city SENATE, if anyone wishes to use it. The judgment of the senate is the end of lawsuits.

units.la: Præter has SENATVS idem ditiones quoq; minores per reliquum agrum habet, in quas judices mittit. Sed ab his non ad senatum, sed ad conventum judicialem totius agri, de quo supra dixi, aut ad Hovetmannes patet appellatio.
units.tr: Besides these, the SENATE also has lesser jurisdictions throughout the rest of the countryside, to which it sends judges. But from these, appeal lies not to the senate but to the judicial assembly of the whole countryside, of which I spoke above, or to the Hovetmanni.

units.la: Finirem hic de rebus civilibus nisi sui monerent me munera, quae cum foedere Belgico nata fuere, & civitati agroq; sunt communia. De quibus quamquam & prius dicta quaedam mihi sunt, tamen & obiter modò id factum, & brevius quam res videtur poscere. Sunt ea duplicia: quorum foris alia, alia domi geruntur. Quae foris, sessiones sunt in collegiis amplissimis, quae communia sunt omnibus in foedere comprehensis: eaq; sunt tria. Primum est id, quod GENERALIVM ORDINVM nomen habet, honore potestateq; summum, totius foederis ac reipub. communis caput, à quo cetera pendent, & leges accipiunt, longè lateq; inclytum, haud dissimile concilio Achaico veteri, aut Ætolico in Græcia, aut Panionio in Asia, sed perpetuum. Sedes ei Haga in Hollandia, in quod mittuntur ex omnib. provincijs socijs viri summi. Alterum dignitate & potestate proximum huic, bellica potissimum curans. SENATVS ORDINVM nuncupatur, quod quoties res ardua ac magna incidit, quae consilio decretoq; habet opus, in partem curae & consilij vocatur, & nunc seorsim deliberat de ea, sententiamq; suam ad collegium superius refert, nunc cum eodem in deliberando conjungitur. Eodem quippe loco, eadem in arce sedem habet, quo expeditior sit coniunctio.
units.tr: I would end here on civil affairs, were it not that the duties which arose with the Belgic union and are common to the city and the countryside remind me of themselves. Some things about these have already been said by me, yet I have touched on them only in passing, and more briefly than the subject seems to require. They are of two kinds: some are carried on abroad, others at home. Those abroad are the sessions in the most august colleges, which are common to all who are included in the union; and these are three. The first is that which bears the name of the GENERAL ORDERS, the highest in honour and power, the head common to the whole union and commonwealth, on which the rest depend and from which they receive their laws; renowned far and wide, not unlike the old Achaean league in Greece, or the Aetolian, or the Panionian in Asia, but permanent. Its seat is at The Hague in Holland, to which the highest men are sent from all the allied provinces. The second, next to this in dignity and power, which takes care chiefly of war, is called the SENATE OF THE ORDERS, because whenever a difficult and important matter arises that needs counsel and decision, it is called into a share of the care and counsel; and it now deliberates on that matter separately and refers its opinion to the higher college, and now joins with that same college in deliberation. For it has its seat in the same place and the same citadel, so that the joining may be more convenient.

units.la: Tertium & ipsum illustre & magnarum virium est, MARITIMIS REBUS, quae maxime in Belgio sunt, PRÆFECTUM, distinctum in collegia minora velut membra totius, quorum unum in Selandia Middelburgi, alterum Roterodami, tertium Amsterodami, quartum Hornæ vel Enchusæ in Hollandia, quintum in Frisia Doccumi sedem tenet.
units.tr: The third, itself also illustrious and of great strength, is the PREFECT FOR MARITIME AFFAIRS, which is especially in Belgium, divided into smaller colleges as if they were members of the whole: one of these holds its seat in Zeeland at Middelburg, a second at Rotterdam, a third at Amsterdam, a fourth at Hoorn or Enkhuizen in Holland, and a fifth in Friesland at Dokkum.

units.la: In collegium ordinum generalium civitas è suis, agerá, item è suis mittunt assessorem spectatissimum ac prudentissimum quemq; in toto utroq; corpore; eisq; vel prorogant honorem, quoties & quamdiu volunt, vel successores dant: plerumq; vero in complures annos in munere relinquunt. Et sunt hi duo munere & honore pares, nec alter altero plus potest. Sic tamen observatur, cum praesentes pariter sunt in collegio, ubi praesidendi vices ad hanc provinciam venere, (per hebdomades enim vicissim provinciae id ius habent) ut urbanus verè eum locum teneat, verbaq; faciat, agrarius nunquam, nisi urbano absente.
units.tr: To the college of the General Orders the city sends one of its own, and the countryside likewise one of its own, and each of the two bodies sends the most distinguished and most prudent assessor it can find; and they either extend their term of office, as often and as long as they wish, or appoint successors; but for the most part they leave them in office for several years. These two are equal in office and dignity, and neither has more power than the other. Yet it is observed that, when both are equally present in the college, and the turn to preside has come to this province (for by weeks the provinces take this right in turn), the urban man truly holds that place and speaks, and the rural man never does, except when the urban man is absent.

units.la: Uteráq; non solum deliberat cum caeteris de tota repub. sociorum, & decernit, sed à suis accipit, quae res poscit, eaq; ad collegium refert.
units.tr: Each of the two also deliberates, together with the others, on the whole business of the allied commonwealth and decides matters; and from his own constituents he receives whatever the matter requires, and he brings it back to the college.

units.la: Quae si ad totam provinciam pertinet, eoniunctim hoc faciunt, eaq; à collegio accipiunt provinciali: sin solius civitatis sunt, à senatu certior fit urbanus, & solus collegio generali exponit. Idemq; saepe aut solus, aut cum collega vel praesens, vel per literas ex ordinum generalium voluntate ad suos, quae sunt opus, refert.
units.tr: If these matters concern the whole province, they do this jointly and receive them from the provincial college; but if they concern only one city, the city-magistrate is informed by the senate and alone sets them before the general college. The same man, often alone, or with his colleague present or by letter, with the will of the general orders, reports to his own people whatever needs doing.

units.la: Uteráq; à collegio provinciali per literas publicas in possessionem mune-ris mittitur. De eo, qui in senatu ordinum fessu-rus est, (uni quippe hic tantummodo e provincia nostra locus) sic nunc inter oppidanos & agra-rios est comparatum, ut illi in biennium, quem velint suorum designent, idemq; in alterum bien-nium faciant agrarij. Sed in collegium rerum ma-ritimarum, quod Doccumi nunc est, utraq; pars e suis unum legat. Et tres hi, nimirum qui in senatu ordinum futurus est, & qui in collegio Doccumano, literis collegij provinciae huius instruuntur, at sedendi, remq; publicam gerendi potestatem a summo generalium ordinum collegio accipiunt, ac in munus suum immittuntur: eiq; jurejurando se obstringunt: omnes spectatae dignitatis virtutisq; inter suos, & e civitate non nisi consulares aut senatorij.
units.tr: Each of them is sent into office by the provincial college through public letters of appointment. For the one who is to sit in the senate of the orders (since there is only one place here for our province), the arrangement now made between the townsmen and the countrymen is this: the townsmen designate for two years whomever they wish from their own number, and the countrymen do the same for the next two years. But for the college of maritime affairs, which is now at Doccum, each side chooses one of its own. And these three, namely the man who is to sit in the senate of the orders and the two of the Doccum college, are furnished with letters from the college of this province, but they receive the power to sit and to conduct public affairs from the supreme general college of the orders, and are installed in their office; and they bind themselves by oath. All of them must be men of recognized dignity and virtue among their own people, and from the city only consuls or senators are chosen.

units.la: Atq; omnia haec non honorata solum, sed lauta quoq; munera sunt, & opima. De cateris, quae collegio Doccumano cohaerent, ut scriba & fisci praefecti, quae provincia huic cum Translavi-canis sunt communia, & quae his similia alia, dicere non libet, ne prolixior fiam. Et hac quidem foris: reliqua domi. Horumprimum & praecipuum provinciale collegium, ut initio institutum fuit, collegas octo habet, pari numero hinc inde lectos: de quorum munere amplissimo ante nobis dictū. Oppidanos senatus edit, & fere ex his, qui in consulatu aut senatu fuere, eosq; pro arbitrio suo aut mutat anno exacto, aut in munere manere patitur. Nec alius agrariorum mos, qui reliquos designant. (collega, ut ante ostendi, per vices, atq; in orbem praesident, alternatim q; oppidanus & agrarius: vices septimanâ finiuntur. Quaestor autem collegij, cui amplissima pecunia tractanda committitur, item scriba à secretis, coniunctim ab oppidanis & agrarijs eliguntur in conventu communi, ab isdemq; pendent; munusq; habent perpetuum, si cum fide in eo versantur. Reliqua inferioris notae ministeria ostiariorum, scribarum, amanuensium, tabellariorum in potestate collegij sunt. Dein Quatuorviri sunt, ab isdem utrisq; pari numero electi, quos rationum magi-stros appellant, & his scriba adiunctus, chartarum custos. Horum officium est, indices censuum ac reditus omnium provinciae in promptu habere, & hos nervos reip. ad unguem nosse: largitiones, quae ex publico fiunt ab Octoviris, aliasq; item pecuniae assignationes censura subjicere, easq; vel calculo suo facere ratas, vel si iniquas aut decretis ordinum non congruas putent, suspendere, ac de suspensis Octoviros monere, & si sit opus, ad conventum ordinum referre: rationes quoq;, quoties libet, quaestores poscere: denique curare, ne tardatis solutionibus fraus aerario fiat, neve pecuniaria res provinciae quoquo modo detrimentum patiatur. Utilissimum institutum, si acrib. hominibus atq; integris, & boni publici studiosis, contraq; gratiam & offensam infractis fuerit commissum. Utrumq; hoc collegium, in urbe sedem tenet, urbemq; frequentia auget.
units.tr: All these offices are not merely honorable but also lavish and rich. As for the others that belong to the Doccum college, such as the secretary and the prefects of the treasury, which this province shares with the Translavian districts, and other similar offices, I do not wish to speak of them, lest I become too long. These are the matters abroad; the rest are at home. Of these, the first and chief is the provincial college, as it was originally established. It has eight colleagues, chosen in equal numbers from either side, concerning whose very great office I have spoken before. The senate appoints the townsmen, and nearly always from among those who have been consuls or senators; and it either changes them when the year is up or allows them to remain in office, as it pleases. The countrymen's custom is no different in designating the rest. (The colleagues, as I showed before, preside in turn and in a circle, alternately a townsman and a countryman; their turns last a week.) The quaestor of the college, to whom very large sums of money are entrusted, and likewise the secretary for confidential matters, are chosen jointly by the townsmen and the countrymen in a common assembly, and they answer to both; they hold the office for life, provided they conduct themselves faithfully in it. The remaining offices of lesser rank, of doorkeepers, clerks, secretaries and letter-carriers, are under the authority of the college. Next there are the Four Men, chosen in equal numbers by both sides, whom they call the masters of accounts, and attached to them is a secretary, keeper of the papers. Their duty is to keep at hand the registers of the assessments and revenues of the whole province and to know these sinews of the commonwealth to a nicety; to scrutinize the largesses which are made from the public treasury by the Eightmen, and other assignments of money, and either to confirm them by their own calculation or, if they judge them unjust or not in agreement with the decrees of the orders, to suspend them, and to warn the Eightmen about the suspended items and, if need be, to refer them to the assembly of the orders; also to demand the accounts from the quaestors whenever they like; and finally to see to it that no fraud is done to the treasury through delayed payments, and that the financial affairs of the province suffer no loss in any way. It is a most useful institution, if it is entrusted to men who are sharp, upright, and zealous for the public good, and unbroken by favour or enmity. Both of these colleges have their seat in the city, and they enlarge the city by their numbers.

units.la: Demum praeter eum, quem jam dixi, quaestores duos habet provincia rebus monasticis praefectos: quorum alterum civitas, alterum agrarij ordines designant. Hi monasticas res universas, quas amplissimas quondam fuisse in hac regione ostendi, arbitrio ordinum partiti inter sese, seorsim curantes partem suam, a conductoribus locaria annua, census, canones & quicquid huius generis exigunt, capiuntq; ex his onera primum, quae reb. incumbunt, expediunt, quae cui in alimenta aut aliam ob rem a collegio ordinibusve assignata pecunia est, numerant, omniumq; horum rationes apud rationum magistros, & quos ordines provincia his solent adjungere, reddunt.
units.tr: Finally, besides the one I have already mentioned, the province has two quaestors in charge of monastic affairs: one of them is designated by the city, the other by the orders of the countryside. These two divide among themselves, at the discretion of the orders, all the monastic property, which I have shown to have been very extensive in this region formerly; each looks after his own share separately, and from the lessees of the lands he receives the annual rents, the dues, the canons and whatever else of this kind they exact; first they pay out of these the burdens that fall upon the commonwealth, and they count out whatever money has been assigned by the college or the orders for maintenance or for some other purpose; and they render the accounts of all these things to the masters of accounts and to the orders which the province is accustomed to attach to them.
A post by no means costly.

units.la: Postremo publicanorum ordo in repub. provinciali est, in urbe & agro de-gens, invisus hominum vulgo, sed in hoc statu & fortuna reip. plane necessarius.
units.tr: Lastly, the order of the tax-farmers exists in the provincial commonwealth, dwelling in the city and in the countryside, hated by the common people, but in this condition and fortune of the commonwealth plainly necessary.

units.la: Hi vectigalia, portoria, tributa, & si quid aliud census huiusmodi est, conducunt in semestre, locante collegio provinciali, certamq; reip. summam promittunt, praedesq; dant: ipsi suo periculo colligunt, atq; interdum acerbius quam gratum provincialibus, exigunt, ut indemnes se praestent: quos fraudis compertos habent, ex legibus gravissime multant: interdumq; fit, ut si nimis magno conduxerint, cedere foro & facultatibus, aut cum repub. transfigere cogantur.
units.tr: These men hire the tolls, the customs duties, the taxes, and whatever other revenue is of this kind, on a six-month lease, the provincial college letting them out, and they promise a certain sum to the commonwealth and give sureties. At their own risk they collect, and sometimes, to keep themselves harmless, they exact more harshly than is welcome to the provincials; those whom they find guilty of fraud they punish most severely under the laws; and sometimes it happens that, if they have hired at too high a price, they are forced to give up their goods and their property, or to go bankrupt along with the commonwealth.

units.la: Ministris utuntur compluribus, & in omnes res omniaq; loca intentos oculos habent, ne quid per fraudem sibi decedat. Denique totum hoc genus a Romano more illo vetere non multum discedere videtur.
units.tr: They employ several servants and keep watchful eyes on all matters and all places, lest anything be lost to them through fraud. In short, this whole class seems not greatly to differ from that old Roman custom.

units.la: In omnia autem haec, quae provincia totius sunt, conconventu provincialis potestatem possidet, omni-busq; leges dat, mutat in ijs & statuit pro arbi-trio, si consentiat, modo ne quid contra leges fœderis communis, & conditiones quæ in deditione urbis & conjunctione cum reliquis fœderatis perscriptæ sunt. Conventus huius sedes antiquissimo more Groninga est: convocaturq;, quoties res postulat. Constat duob. membris, uti tota provincia, quam civitas agriq; ordines constituunt. Civitatis lo-cum in conventu senatus tenet. Agri ordines quondam antistib. cœnobiorum, nobilitate agra-ria, & plebe rustica censebantur, antistitesq; & præcipua nobilitas nominatim vocabantur: plebs reliqua vicatim plerumq;, suos cum potestate & mandatis ad conventus mittebat. Nunc an-tistites disjuncti sunt, resq; ad solam nobilitatem, & delectos plebis cum mandatis suorum instru-stos redijt. Conventui ædificium in urbe per-amplum & spaciosum destinatum est, in usum schola quondam exstructu, distinctum conclavib. diversis. In eorum maximo conveniunt omnes. Et si præsens gubernator est, in capite conclavis loco summo considet ad mensam, juxtaq;, eum, qui in collegio sunt provinciali. Deinde ad dextram gubernatoris, atq; in latere conclavis dextro con-sules & reliquus senatus sedem tenent: alterum latus ordines agri occupant. Proponit in con-sessu gubernator quæ agenda, aut collegii præses. Eo facto interdum manet collegium loco suo, in-terdum si causa requirit, discedit. Re deliberata senatus priore loco sententiam dicit per Syndicum suum,si adest,aut per consulem. Sequuntur agra-rij. Quibus si inter se convenire nequit, secedentes deliberant, & suffragijs inter se certant; nonnunquam etiam tripartito dividunt sese, vt supra ostendi, cum de agro agerem seorsim: atq; ita, si duæ partes in unam sententiam eant, tertia quoq; trahunt. Tum, quod sentiunt, per Syndicum quoq; suum, quem habent, senatui exponunt. Post disputationes vbi consensere senatus agrarijq;, decretum conficitur, atq; in publicum librum refertur. Decretum totam obligat provinciam.
units.tr: In all these matters, which belong to the whole province, the provincial assembly holds the power; it gives laws to all, changes and establishes them at its discretion, provided it agrees, but only so long as nothing is done against the laws of the common covenant and the conditions which were written down in the surrender of the city and in its union with the other allies. The seat of this assembly is, in the most ancient custom, Groningen; and it is convened whenever the matter requires. It consists of two parts, as the whole province does, which the city and the countryside orders make up. The city holds its place in the assembly through the senate. The orders of the countryside were formerly reckoned among the abbots of the monasteries, the rural nobility, and the common folk of the countryside, and the abbots and the chief nobility were summoned by name; the rest of the common people, village by village for the most part, sent their own representatives with authority and instructions to the assemblies. Now the abbots have been separated out, and the matter has returned to the nobility alone, along with chosen representatives of the commons equipped with the instructions of their people. For the assembly a very large and spacious building in the city has been appointed, once built for use as a school, divided into various rooms. In the largest of these all meet together. And if the governor is present, he sits at the head of the room in the highest place at the table, and beside him those who are in the provincial college. Then on the governor's right, and on the right side of the room, the consuls and the rest of the senate hold their seats; the countrymen's orders occupy the other side. The governor, or the president of the college, proposes what is to be done in the assembly. This being done, the college sometimes remains in its place, and sometimes, if the cause requires, withdraws. When the matter has been deliberated, the senate gives its opinion first, through its syndic, if he is present, or through a consul. The countrymen follow. If they cannot agree among themselves, they withdraw and deliberate apart, and contend among themselves by votes; sometimes they even divide themselves into three parts, as I showed above when I was treating of the countryside separately; and so, if two parts go over to one opinion, the third also is drawn along. Then what they think they set forth to the senate through their own syndic, whom they have. After the discussions, when the senate and the countrymen have agreed, a decree is drawn up and entered into the public book. The decree binds the whole province.
ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL MATTERS IN THE CITY.

units.la: Sic civilia: restat, vt ecclesiastica perstrin-gam. Solent in urbe esse, vt in principio ostendi, parochiæ tres cum totidem fanis. In his sacerdotes sacris operantes numero XXI: in quibus pastores tres singulì singulis in fanis ac parochijs. Tandem anno M. CCCC. LXXX unus ex his editus velut ἐφορος totius rei ecclesiasticæ in urbe & urbis vicinia, quem PERSONAM more suo vocabant: isq; erat velut minor quidam episcopus, aut episcopi vicem gerens, magna potestate & multis privilegijs ornatus à Romano Pontifice. Hunc cæteri pastores, & duo seniores urbis consules eligebant, & in munus suum immittebant, in magnoq; honore habebat. tota civitas. Deinde anno M. D. LXVIII, cum mutationib. Belgicis via divinitus struetur, novisq; episcopatus passim in his regionibus instituerentur, episcopusq; huic civitati datus Joannes Gnifius [?] ex ordine cucullatorum Ultrajectinus, Persona nomen munisq; peremptum, canonici constituendo collegio lecti, his alendis tuendaq; episcopi dignitati census omnes coenobij Werumani à rege ac pontifice versi, & Adeardy [?] quoq; annua aliquot millia huc conferre coacti: coenobium Fratrum domicilium episcopi factum, & Martiniana aedes cathedrali honore donata.
units.tr: So much for civil affairs; it remains that I touch briefly on ecclesiastical ones. As I showed at the beginning, the city has three parishes, each with its own church. In these the priests who perform the sacred offices number twenty-one, among whom there are three ministers, one for each church and parish. Finally, in the year 1480 one of these was set up as a kind of overseer of the whole ecclesiastical business in the city and its surrounding district; they called him the Persona, after their custom. He was, as it were, a lesser bishop, or one who acted in the place of a bishop, adorned with great power and many privileges by the Roman Pontiff. The remaining ministers and the two senior consuls of the city chose him and installed him in his office, and the whole city held him in high honour. Then, in the year 1568, when the changes in the Netherlands were being brought about by divine providence and new bishoprics were being established throughout these regions, John Cnifius [?] of the Utrecht order of the cowled friars was given to this city as bishop. The name and office of Persona were abolished; a chapter was constituted and chosen to be its college. To maintain these men and to support the dignity of the bishop, all the revenues of the monastery of Weerum were turned over by the king and the pope, and some annual sums of several thousand from Adeardy [?] were also compelled to be brought here. The convent of the Brothers was made the bishop's residence, and the church of Martin was honoured with the status of a cathedral.

units.la: Sed rarò fuit unus idemq; primus & ultimus episcopus Groninga. Cnifius fuit: quo vita functo, cum annus fuerit M. D. LXXII, res in priorem statum relapsa est. Nunc abrogata Romanensi superstitione & ἱεραρχία [?], is quoq; statu corruit. Sacerdotum loco introducti sunt ecclesiae ministri, suffragijs ejusdem ecclesiae lecti, volente & probante senatu, qui purum Dei verbum docent, & sacramenta ex forma divinitus tradita administrant duobus in-templis, ipsi numero sex: quorum nullus potestate eminet supra cateros, omnes agunt aequaliter inter se, quamvis alij alios, prout dotibus instructi ornatiq; sunt, autoritate & gratia praestant. His seniores additi numero fere XVI, qui cum ipsis presbyterium conficiunt, cui commissa custodia disciplinae & eutaxiae ecclesiasticae.
units.tr: But there was rarely one and the same bishop, the first and last, at Groningen. Cnifius was the one; when he died, in the year 1572, the situation fell back into its former state. Now, with the Roman superstition and hierarchy [?] abolished, that too has collapsed. In place of the priests, ministers of the church have been introduced, chosen by the votes of that same church, with the approval and consent of the senate. They teach the pure Word of God and administer the sacraments according to the form handed down by God, in two churches, numbering six in all. None of them stands above the others in power; all act equally among themselves, although some excel others in authority and influence, according as they are endowed and furnished with gifts. To these are added about sixteen elders, who together with the ministers form the presbytery, to which is entrusted the oversight of church discipline and good order.

units.la: Cum hoc singulis septimanis semel, aut quoties res requirequirit, & de rebus ecclesiasticis dcliberat[?] atq; agit; civile nihil attingit. Seniores, qui in hoc collegium cooptantur (quod ab ipso fit collegio) non genere aut opibus aut potentia spectantur, sed pietate & integritate vitae, & necessaria prudentia, fama denique inculpata. Et hi additi doctoribus sunt velut senatus ecclesiasticus. Frater hos & diaconi sunt in ecclesia numero plerumque XVI, qui peculiare collegium constituunt, & conventus suos habent: interdum etiam, ubi res poscit, imprimis tertio quoq; mense disciplinae causa cum presbyterio coniunguntur, & unum velut collegium cum eo faciunt. Hi similiter ex integerrimis ecclesiae civibus electi pecuniam pauperum tractant, eleemosynas colligunt, & distribuunt, ac de omnibus rationes reddunt publice, ad quas cuilibet, cui animus, licet accedere. Ac sunt hi diversi ab iis, de quibus in exponendis rebus civilibus dixi. Eliguntur a presbyterio, ut isti a senatu. Nec est hoc munus perpetuum, sed triennio aut quadriennio exspirat substitutis novis: fere, ex his, qui bene hoc munere functi sunt, presbyteri cooptantur. Est & in visendis, solandis, erudiendis, exhortandis aegrotis, ac in mortis periculo constitutis praefectus, quem visitatorem nuncupant, ex iis plerumque delectus, qui in munere docendae Ecclesiae in urbe vel in agro versati sunt. Is presbyteri pars est. De schola literaria hic dicere nihil attinet, quam liberalib. stipendiis constitutis in usum docentium senatus hic instituit aut instauravit post urbem foederi Belgico rursum conjunctam. Nam ordo ejus typis publicatus extat. Hoc solum hic repeto, docere in ea praeceptores VII, qui stipendia à reip. capiunt aureos Carolinos non minus bis mille sexcentos triginta, & domicilia libera, διδάκτρα[?] aut à discipulis non capiunt. Sedes schola in coenobio Franciscano, ut dixi ante, situ in urbe medio.
units.tr: This body meets once a week, or as often as the matter requires, and deliberates and deals with ecclesiastical affairs; it touches nothing civil. The elders who are co-opted into this college (which is done by the college itself) are chosen not for birth, wealth or power, but for piety, integrity of life, necessary prudence, and, finally, an unblemished reputation. These, together with the teachers, form, as it were, the ecclesiastical senate. Next to these are the deacons of the church, usually about sixteen in number, who form a separate college and hold their own meetings. Sometimes, too, where the matter demands it, especially every third month, they are joined with the presbytery for the sake of discipline and form one college with it. These likewise, chosen from the most upright citizens of the church, manage the money of the poor, collect and distribute alms, and render public accounts of everything, which anyone who wishes may inspect. These are distinct from those of whom I spoke in describing civil affairs. They are chosen by the presbytery, as those are by the senate. Nor is this office perpetual; it expires after three or four years, with new men substituted. Generally, from among those who have discharged this office well, presbyters are co-opted. There is also a prefect for visiting, comforting, instructing and exhorting the sick, and those in danger of death, whom they call the visitor; he is usually chosen from those who have been engaged in teaching the Church in the city or in the countryside. He is part of the presbytery. There is no need to speak here about the literary school, which the senate established or restored in this place, for the use of teachers, with liberal stipends set up for that purpose, after the city was joined again to the Belgic union. For its order has been published in print and is extant. I repeat only this here: seven teachers teach in it, who receive stipends from the commonwealth of not less than two thousand six hundred and thirty gold Carolus coins, and free lodging, and take no fees [διδάκτρα?] from the pupils. The school's seat is in the Franciscan monastery, which, as I said before, is situated in the middle of the city.

units.la: Porrò Ecclesiæ ministri dieb. dominicis ter docent in templo utroq;, atq; insuper, reliqua hebdomadae bis in S. Martiniano[?], semel in Mariano aut Annico: baptismum ipsdem in templis finitis concionibus praesente ecclesia administrant: (cœnam domini summa cum reverentia quolibet trimestri distribuunt communicantib. idq; vicissim in templis jam dictis, nec quenquam ad mensam hanc sacram admittunt, nisi ante de mysterio bene edoctum, & capitum doctrina Christiana praecipuorum mediocriter gnarum, & in vita probu piumq;[?] caeteros ab ea arcent. Reliqua quoq; ministerij sui rite expediunt. In primis quolibet mense semel coetum vel conventum agunt in urbe cum ministris ecclesiarum vicinarum, quae in praefectura sunt suburbana, disciplina & exhortationis mutua causa. Quotanis autem semel delecti eorum, reliquiq; presbyteri synodo intersunt ministrorum universae huius provinciae inter Amasum & Lavicam, in quam delecti singulorum classium coeunt, nunc in urbe, saepius in agro, locis celebrioribus. Caeteroqui, ad conventus menstruos & ordinarios quod attinet, nihil habent urbani cum ministris agrarijs commune. Hic tandem desino, prolixior factus, q; initio futurum existimaram.
units.tr: Furthermore, the ministers of the Church preach three times on the Lord's days in each of the two churches, and in addition twice in the rest of the week in St. Martin's, and once in St. Mary's or Annicus. They administer baptism in the same churches, at the close of the sermons, in the presence of the congregation. They distribute the Lord's Supper with the greatest reverence to the communicants every quarter, alternately in the churches just named; and they admit no one to this holy table unless he has first been well instructed in the mystery, has a moderate knowledge of the chief heads of Christian doctrine, and lives an upright and pious life; the others they keep away from it. They also duly carry out the rest of their ministry. Above all, once a month they hold a meeting or assembly in the city with the ministers of the neighbouring churches that lie in the suburban prefecture, for the sake of mutual discipline and exhortation. Once a year, moreover, their chosen representatives, together with the remaining presbyters, attend the synod of ministers of this whole province between Amasus and Lavicus, to which the chosen men of the individual classes gather, now in the city, more often in the countryside, at the more frequented places. Otherwise, as far as the monthly and regular meetings are concerned, the urban ministers have nothing in common with the country ministers. Here at last I stop, having become more lengthy than I had thought at the beginning would be the case.
F I N I S.

units.la: ENtibi,lector,consulum,eorumq;, qui pro consulibus in civitate Groningana fuere ab anno Christi M. CC. LX usq; ad præsens tempus, seriem positam ab oculos, per annos singulos digestam, velut consulares fastos. Hæc,ut scias,ex literis à senatu olim signatis partim publicis,partim privatis fideliter ac magno studio cōsecta & concinnata est. Mos .n. antiquitus in hac civitate fuit,ut in calce literarum, quas signabat senatus, plerumq; consulum nomina, qui remp. gerebant, ad certiorem temporis designationem adjcerentur : idemq; mos etiam nunc manet.
units.tr: Reader, I have set before your eyes the list of consuls, and of those who were consuls in the city of Groningen from the year of Christ 1260 until the present time, arranged year by year, like consular fasti. So that you may know, this has been faithfully and with great diligence compiled and arranged from letters once sealed by the Senate, some public, some private. For it was an ancient custom in this city that at the foot of the letters the Senate sealed, the names of the consuls who governed the state were usually added, to indicate the time more exactly; and this custom remains even now.

units.la: Quod vero in serie hac ab anno M. CCC. LVIII, usque in annum M. CCC. LXXI hiatum vides, nolo nescire te, inde id esse,quod eo maxime tempore inolevisse mo-rem deprehenderim scribendi signandiq; literas hujusmodi non expressis consulum nomi-nibus. Nam silentibus literis in re tam pro-cul à memoria nostra remota à nobis quoq; affirmari nihil potuit. Cæteros hiatus mino-res,qui hunc antecedunt, penuriæ literarum, ijsce annis signatarum, aut secordiæ scribarū, qui communem morem interdum neglexerint (nam literas istorum annorum nonnullas sine nominib.consulum vidimus)debemus. Vide-bus vero in hoc catalogo,lector, qui ab anno Christi M. ccc consules aut civium magistri dicti sunt,id quod suo loco in hoc libello quoq; notavi, eos ante id tempus rationales fere, ac fenasenatores Oldermannos esse vocitatos : nec minus hoc, aliquando non quatuor sed sex in civitate consules fuisse, idq; complures annos duraffe:item ter quaterve morem illum,quem in libelto exposui, mutandi consules negle- ctum esse, & ejus loco per multos annos aut ad vitę finem in munere eosdem consules du- raffe. Mihi autem, quod ex indice videri ne- quit, ex collatione literarum signatarum ob- servatum est,quando mutandi mos valuit,de- cedentium consulum munus cum die xxiI[?] Februarij jam ante cccxl[?] annos expiraffe,& succedentium die postero incepisse. Addidi huic seriei in margine uno velut verbo suis locis notatas memorabiles res atque eventus, velut indicem historiæ hujus reip. & quædam alia ad rem apta. Deniq; subieci catalogo huic Hovetmannorum catalogum, quotquot repertire potui,qui ab anno M. cccc. x ad annum M. cccc. xc111[?],& rursum ab anno M. D. xxv. ad hunc annum præfentem in hoc juris dicundi munere fuere.
units.tr: As for the gap you see in this series from the year 1358 to the year 1371, I do not wish you to be unaware that it comes from this: I have found that at that time especially the custom had grown up of sealing letters of this kind without the names of the consuls being written out. For when the letters were silent, nothing could be affirmed by us either, on a matter so far removed from our memory. The smaller gaps that precede this one we must attribute to a shortage of letters sealed in those years, or to the carelessness of the scribes, who sometimes neglected the common custom (for we have seen some letters of those years without the names of the consuls). You will see in this catalogue, reader, from what year after 1300 men were called consuls or masters of the citizens, which I have also noted in its place in this little book; before that time they were for the most part called reckoners, or Oldermen, that is, senators. Nor less, sometimes there were not four but six consuls in the city, and this lasted for several years; likewise three or four times that custom, which I explained in the little book, of changing the consuls was neglected, and the same consuls remained in office for many years or until the end of their lives. But it has been observed by me, from a comparison of the sealed letters (which cannot be seen from the list), when the custom of changing was in force: the office of the outgoing consuls had ended on the 22nd [?] day of February, now more than 340 [?] years ago, and that of the succeeding consuls had begun on the following day. I have added to this series, in the margin, with a single word in their places, the memorable things and events, as an index of the history of this commonwealth, and certain other matters pertinent to it. Finally, I have appended to this catalogue a list of the Hovetmen, as many as I could find, who held this office of judging from the year 1410 to the year 1493 [?], and again from the year 1525 to the present year.

units.la: Hæc accipe, lector, studio tui typis permissa, ftudiumq; ipsum benigne interpretare. Vale.
units.tr: Accept these things, reader, which have been committed to print for your sake, and interpret the effort itself kindly. Farewell.

units.tr: Treaty with the Leeuwarders. The covenant of Oostergo, extended further through Westergo. Seneca, given over on harsh conditions.

units.tr: The covenant of Oostergo confirmed by Emperor Maximilian at Kempen.
Garmet Allema. Roleff Ulger. Herman Lewe. Thezo Iarges.

units.la: Foedus novum civitatis cum VVeftergois, Oftergoo simile. Albertus Saxo militem sub praefectis diversis in Frisia mittit, ut ea atterat.
units.tr: A new covenant of the state with Westergo, similar to Oostergo. Albert of Saxony sends soldiers under various commanders into Friesland, to wear it down.
Garmet Allema. Coppin Iarges. Herman Lewe. Iohan Schaffers.

units.la: Foxus auspiciis Alberti Frisiam invadit, & in agrum Groning. venit. Albertus Saxo a Caesare gubernator Frisiae designatur.
units.tr: Foxus, under the auspices of Albert, invades Friesland and comes into the territory of Groningen. Albert of Saxony is appointed governor of Friesland by the Emperor.

units.la: Albertus Saxo in Frisia venit & homagium recipit. Cū Groninganis colloquia instituit. Groningani Dammonā praesidio Edsardi munitam per Vlricum Dorn. tentant.
units.tr: Albert of Saxony comes to Friesland and receives homage. He opens negotiations with the Groningers. The Groningers attempt Dammona, fortified with a garrison of Edzard, through Ulrich Dorn.

units.la: Albertus è Misnia reversus cum exercitu, filio obsidione Franck liberato, Groningam obsidet. Bellum pactione dirimitur studio Georgii Thorenii & Frid. episcopi Vltr. Albertus discedens Emdae moritur.
units.tr: Albert, returning from Meissen with an army, after the siege of Franeker was lifted by his son, besieges Groningen. The war is ended by agreement through the zeal of Georg Thoren and Bishop Frederick of Utrecht. Albert, departing, dies at Emden.

units.la: Edsardus Dammonam à Groninganis obsessa & oppugnatam cum clade eorundem obsidione liberat.
units.tr: Edzard, with the Groningers besieging Dammona and attacking it, frees it by defeating them, and lifts the siege.

units.la: Res ad inducias rursum studio Vltraiectini inter civitatem & Saxones ac Edsardi perductae.
units.tr: Matters are again brought to a truce through the zeal of the men of Utrecht, between the city and the Saxons and Edzard.

units.la: Induciis prorogatis saepius, variis colloquiis tentata compositio.
units.tr: With the truces extended several times, a settlement was attempted through various conferences.

units.la: Compositio tentata per Philippum Austriacum Burgundiae ducem.
units.tr: A settlement attempted through Philip of Austria, duke of Burgundy.

units.la: Groninga armis Saxonici: d.ce EDSARDO obsessa,& in angustias reda:ta[?].
units.tr: Groningen, armed by the Saxons, besieged by Edzard, and reduced to straits.
